Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims three years after deadly Hamas raid

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 20:27:03 GMT

Memorial events have taken place in Israel on the third anniversary of the devastating Hamas-led attack there that sparked the war in Gaza.

Families paid tribute to their loved ones at some of the sites where about 1,200 people were killed in the assault and 251 were taken hostage.

"The nation unites on this day in the longing for our dear ones," said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faced calls from protesters for an independent state inquiry into security failures that day.

In response to the attack, Israel launched a military offensive in Gaza which has killed more than 74,200 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.

Violence has continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed almost a year ago and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire.

On Wednesday morning, bereaved families and survivors gathered at a memorial for the 378 people who were killed at the Nova dance festival in southern Israel on 7 October 2023.

The festival site was near Kibbutz Re'im and not far from the border with Gaza, from where Hamas-led gunmen launched their dawn attack.

Witnesses have described how festival-goers were shot, sexually abused and tortured by gunmen during the raid.

Forty-four people were kidnapped, of whom 25 were brought back from Gaza alive.

Ahuva Yavin Mayze, whose 21-year-old daughter Adi was shot and killed at Nova, told the BBC what happened at the site was "dystopic, unimaginable".

"Today is a difficult day, not only for me but for a large part of the nation," said Shlomo Sharf, a former Israeli footballer, in comments reported by Channel 12.

He paid tribute to his granddaughter, May Naim, 24, who was also killed at the festival.

Former hostage Yarden Bibas, whose wife and two young sons were kidnapped from their home in Kibbutz Nir Oz and later killed in captivity in Gaza, was quoted by the Times of Israel as saying: "Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here."

Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.

Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened.

"This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."

A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.

Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".

In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October.

"We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.

At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.

In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack.

The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.

Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.

They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.

Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.

The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.

Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement.

"They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."

Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture".

"We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you."

"The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.

Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."

She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well.

"That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.

This is the first anniversary of the 7 October attack with no hostages remaining in Gaza, but a US-brokered ceasefire deal from last year has failed to deliver peace or bring security.

There has been no end to Gaza's deadliest ever war, as Israel continues to carry out near-daily attacks.

More than 1,460 people have been killed there since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health ministry. The Israeli military says at least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in the strip over the same period.

Most of Gaza is in ruins, with nearly all the 2.1 million population still displaced amid dire humanitarian conditions.

An estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up and 1.2 million people living in tents or shelters, according to the UN.

Families who have been displaced several times during the war increasingly ask where they could go next, and whether they might even be forced to leave Gaza altogether.

Mohammed Emad al-Din, a 38-year-old father of two who works as a barber in Gaza City, said he had been displaced five times. His home was destroyed and his barber shop was partially damaged.

He told the BBC that the fear of being forced out of Gaza now follows him even into his dreams.

"I don't believe Israel caused all this destruction for nothing," he said.

"They have turned Gaza into a place that is almost impossible to live in, and I fear that we will eventually end up outside the place where we were born."

Another displaced Palestinian, Atta Saeed Hassan Shweikh, told the BBC that his son, daughter, sister and her children had all been killed during the war.

Speaking from Gaza City, he said Palestinians were "living in graves while still alive" and have endured "severe suffering".

At least three Palestinians were killed in Israeli strikes in the northern town of Beit Lahia and the southern city of Khan Younis on Wednesday, medics said.

The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas operatives in northern Gaza overnight, one of whom it accused of planting explosives near the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the territory still occupied by Israeli forces.

Hamas - which is proscribed as a terrorist organisation by Israel, the UK and others - released a statement praising the 7 October attack as a "historic milestone" in its "ongoing struggle project".

The statement, attributed to the group and disseminated in Palestinian media, called the attack "a natural response" to "bitter suffering" imposed by Israel.

Ex-Spurs player Vega set to run for Fifa president

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 19:24:19 GMT

Ramon Vega made 23 appearances for Switzerland between 1993 and 2001

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.

The 55-year-old is the first person to confirm they want to challenge Gianni Infantino, who has defied calls to step down in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, which has sparked a major backlash across football.

A former Switzerland centre-back, Vega also played for Celtic and Watford and has worked in finance since retiring from football in 2004.

"I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," he said.

Meanwhile, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation - has written to Infantino, distancing himself from an external review of Fifa's governance system.

In his letter - seen by BBC Sport - Sheikh Salman proposes that Fifa's council sets up a working group to examine potential reforms, "rather than being outsourced to an external party".

Last month, Infantino said he was "fully committed to leading Fifa" despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to quit.

Vega considered running for Fifa's top job in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter.

Four years later he said he would stand against Infantino, but failed to garner enough support to be included in the ballot, having required the backing of five of Fifa's 211 member federations.

Candidates must also be proposed by a member association and played an active role in the game for two of the past five years, as well as passing an eligibility check by a review committee.

"I am standing because my life has prepared me to serve the game," Vega said in a statement announcing his candidacy.

"Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution.

"It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life.

"It belongs to every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and the billions of supporters whose passion makes football the world's game.

"Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family.

"The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged Fifa's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family. We must stop this conflict from escalating.

"Ego-driven battles within football administration must never be allowed to damage those who matter most: the players, coaches, referees and supporters around the world. They are not responsible for these conflicts. They deserve better."

Vega concluded: "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. Fifa needs a new direction and fundamental reform.

"We must reunite the football family, restore trust, bring stability and modernise Fifa's governance. This requires decisive change - not cosmetic adjustments."

Infantino should have no place in future of football - Pinto

It comes with Sheikh Salman appearing to soften his stance towards Infantino just two months after the AFC president signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception" over his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.

At the time, the three confederations said any review of Fifa's governance must be "conducted by a fully independent third party".

Now, however, Salman says he believes the process should be "driven by the football institutions themselves, rather than being outsourced to an external party".

He added: "I believe there is value in taking this opportunity to consider constructively whether Fifa's existing governance arrangements can be strengthened.

"The issue is not necessarily whether this requires a wholesale redesign of Fifa's governance system."

Fifa's council meets in Zurich next week for the first time since the FFE plan emerged in July.

Fraudster jailed over multi-million pound PPE scam

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 19:13:25 GMT

A fraudster has been jailed for helping to scam medical companies out of millions of pounds through bogus personal protective equipment (PPE) deals during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Craig Morris, 43, and Jogesh Bhandari, 60, bought luxury cars, holidays and a new home after pretending they could supply millions of boxes of nitrile gloves in the US and Germany.

They were convicted of two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation as well as concealing and transferring criminal property at Leicester Crown Court in July.

On Wednesday, Morris received three years and nine months in prison. Jogesh, of Mitchell Drive, Loughborough, Leicestershire, will be sentenced later.

Jogesh told his counsel he was taking a "very extreme painkiller" after having a pacemaker fitted last week and was not able to travel to Northampton, where the sentencing hearing took place.

His wife, former pharmacist Meenakashi Bhandari, 58, also of Mitchell Drive, did attend the sentencing hearing.

She was found guilty of concealing and transferring criminal property. She was given a two-year prison sentence, suspended for two years, 250 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of rehabilitation activity.

Judge William Harbage KC said there was "no medical evidence" to properly explain Jogesh's absence and said a bench warrant would be issued. He is expected to be sentenced on 16 October.

Prosecutor Michael Bisgrove told the court Jogesh was the "driving force and the instigator" of the offending, while Morris, of Forest Drive in Lytham St Annes, Lancashire, was "very much working for him".

He said: "The offences took place during the Covid-19 pandemic at a time when there was a desperate shortage of personal protective equipment (PPE).

"In that shortage, the offenders, particularly Mr Bhandari and Mr Morris, saw the opportunity to make money by fraud."

The court heard that Jogesh and Morris made fraudulent deals under a company called Banton.

"They pretended to be big players in the PPE market. They pretended to have PPE for sale and to be able to buy vast amounts of it," Bisgrove added.

The court heard they defrauded US company Med18 and German firm MedTech by sending contracts for equipment they did not have.

Bisgrove said: "In the course of the fraud, they took millions of pounds which they used for their own benefit to buy cars, luxury goods and property."

The court heard the Bhandaris also used the money to pay off family debt, while Morris bought a house, the court heard.

The value of money Jogesh obtained and kept in the course of the fraud was £1.75 million, and Meenakshi laundered money to the value of £960,000, the court heard.

Morris had been receiving regular £5,000 payments from Jogesh before the two men fell out at the end of 2021, the National Crime Agency (NCA) previously said.

The agency said Jogesh worked with Frank Labruzzo, an attorney in the Louisiana Attorney General's Office, who provided a fraudulent escrow service - a bank account which holds funds until pre-arranged conditions are met.

The court heard that Labruzzo and another person involved have been convicted and sentenced in the US.

Sentencing Morris and Meenakshi, Judge Harbage said the pandemic was a time when "all of us had to make sacrifices and pull together for the good of society as a whole".

He added: "There were a few people though who sought to exploit that to make money for themselves, motivated by greed.

"I'm satisfied Jogesh Bhandari and Craig Morris fall into that category."

Western civilisation at risk of 'atrophy, servitude and decline', Rubio says

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 18:47:40 GMT

Standing before the Acropolis in Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio swept through the history of ancient Greece to the rise of American industry in a speech on Wednesday that portrayed western civilisation at risk of decline.

Rubio said the world was at an "inflection point". Nations, particularly in Europe, should return to ancient Greek values and "rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together".

"We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago," he said.

While he spoke of cooperation, Rubio also said "nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests".

Rubio, often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, touched on what he considered dangers in the world, such as "radical mullahs" in Iran and suicide bombers.

But most of his speech focused on a broader threat, describing the current period as a crossroads.

"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century."

Rubio called for a return to the "classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim - reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation".

That appeared to include renewed national pride, which he said the ancient Greeks had embraced, but the west had abandoned as "we felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world".

"The word 'nationalism' became a dirty word," he said. "So we tore down our monuments. We condemned our own history, and in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.

"In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay."

Rubio's boss, President Donald Trump, has sought to carry out an "America first" agenda during both his terms in office, and taken a more confrontational stance toward traditional allies and in longstanding trade relationships.

Just six months ago, Trump again threatened to pull the US from the Nato alliance, which he has frequently criticised while pushing members to make larger contributions to defence.

Rubio's visit to the ruins of the Acropolis in Greece was part of his three-country tour of Nato allies that includes stops in Iceland and Portugal.

A man accused of attacking 13 people, including a British three-year-old and three other children, with a knife at a playground in the French Alps will go on trial charged with attempted murder, prosecutors have said.

In addition to the four children, who were aged between 22 months and three years, two adults were wounded in the attack.

The three-year-old British child was visiting the area with her parents. She suffered a single stab wound, French prosecutors said, but was later confirmed to be in a stable condition.

Hanoun will face trial at Haute-Savoie Assize Court in Annecy within the next year, the French public prosecutor's office said on Wednesday.

The prosecutor's statement said: "The defendant will have to answer charges of attempted murder in respect of 13 victims, violence with a weapon without total work incapacity in respect of two victims, and armed resistance."

It added that the defendant's mental state had been assessed by a panel of experts, who found he had not been "suffering from a psychological or neuropsychological disorder" at the time of the attack.

This means there could be "no grounds justifying the decision not to indict Mr Abdalmasih Hanoun".

The statement also said that the decision to order a trial to proceed could be subject to appeal.

Shortly after the attack on 8 June 2023, officials confirmed that the four young victims were in stable condition, including the British toddler.

One of the children was a Dutch national and the other two were confirmed to be French nationals from the eastern region of Haute-Savoie.

Two adults were also hurt in the attack, but were later said to be out of danger.

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 18:30:21 GMT

Declan Rice joined Arsenal from West Ham in 2023

Declan Rice is close to agreeing a new long-term Arsenal contract, sources have told BBC Sport.

The England midfielder has become a crucial player for the Gunners since his arrival from West Ham for £105m in July 2023.

His current deal expires at the end of next season but BBC Sport revealed in March that talks over a new contract were underway with the process now at an advanced stage.

The 27-year-old has made more than 150 starts for Arsenal, and is also a key player for England, with manager Thomas Tuchel saying this week he is one of the best midfielders in Europe.

Rice would receive a significant pay increase to his reported £240,000-per-week salary, putting him on a par with the club's best earner Bukayo Saka, who is believed to earn about £350,000 a week.

The news comes after Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta's new four-year deal with the Premier League champions was announced on Wednesday.

Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 19 in block of flats

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 18:12:58 GMT

A Russian missile has killed 19 people including five children in an apartment block in northern Ukraine, destroying 30 flats as families slept.

Three of the children were one-year-olds in the attack on Pryluky, east of Kyiv, early on Wednesday, and one of the boys died with his mother and grandmother, officials said.

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky said it was one of Russia's "most vile strikes", and suggested the Russian military had carried it out as a "birthday gift" to Vladimir Putin, who turned 74 on Wednesday.

Moscow made no mention of the attack on Pryluky but said its "massive strike" had targeted military industries in Kyiv and elsewhere.

Across the country, the death toll on Wednesday climbed to 25, as Russian strikes claimed two lives in the capital, two in Kremenchuk, and two more in Oleksandriya. More than 430 apartments and private homes were damaged and dozens of people were injured in the attack on the central city of Kremenchuk, the regional leader said.

Rescue teams in Pryluky spent hours searching for victims in the rubble of a five-storey block of flats.

Late in the afternoon rescuers said the body of a fifth child had been found at the scene. More than 50 residents were wounded in the attack that also damaged other residential buildings as well as a youth centre.

Chernihiv regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said the town was hit by five cruise missiles, one of which slammed into the apartment building.

Zelensky named the one-year-old victims as Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, and said a boy of eight called Maxsym had also been killed.

Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a boy called Sasha had died with his mother, Kateryna and her mother Viktoriia, and only the boy's elder sister Olha had survived.

Local reports said they had lived on the fifth floor and that Viktoriia had been looking after her grandson while her daughter worked in a factory.

"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively," Zelensky said, adding that 70 missiles were fired in total.

Zelensky added that Ukraine had itself struck targets in attacks on Russia's Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions in the past 24 hours, adding there was "also a response in the Black Sea", without providing further details.

In Kyiv, many residents spent the night in underground stations to escape the Russian barrage. Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said last week the capital was being torn apart by Russian attacks.

Ukraine's national police posted pictures online showing what it says is an unexploded Russian Iskander missile in the middle of a Kyiv district. BBC Verify has confirmed the images are genuine and the apparent missile fragments came down in an area of open land surrounded by high-rise apartment buildings.

Another verified video shows damage to cars and what appears to be rubble and a fallen tree in an area surrounded by apartment blocks in Kremenchuk.

Ukraine's air force said it had succeeded in shooting down five ballistic missiles and 39 cruise missiles and more than 100 drones, including 46 of Russia's jet-powered drones which have caused so much damage in recent weeks.

However, that would mean that as many as 26 cruise or ballistic missiles penetrated its defences, and Zelensky renewed a call for allies to provide air defence support packages to Ukraine.

According to Zelensky, one of the "key targets" of the attack was Ukraine's energy infrastructure, which Moscow earlier said it would intensify strikes on following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities.

In a separate post on Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had struck four targets in retaliatory attacks in the past 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground as well as a target in the Black Sea.

On Tuesday evening, footage emerged showing a huge plume of smoke engulfing an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, along the Black Sea in southern Russia.

The Russian transport ministry later said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio oil tanker. Authorities claim the crew was rescued.

Separately, Bulgaria has halted a search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov from the Maritime Administration Executive Agency said, as reported by Bulgaria's BTA news agency. No details of the crew are known, but Nikolov said it was assumed there were Syrians on board.

Tracking data shows the ship was anchored at the southern end of the Bosphorus strait until Monday when it entered the Black Sea heading north. Its last reported position on ship-tracking site MarineTraffic was at 23:43 GMT on Monday in what is known as the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea.

Bulgarian specialist news outlet Maritime. bg reported the Alfa Watan was attacked by a drone and sank 70nm (130km) east of Byala.

As well as the civilian cargo ship, a second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, its Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. The 18 crew members on the second vessel were rescued.

Bulgaria has not said who it believes was behind the attacks, and Moscow has not commented on the incident.

Russia has intensified strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. In an evening address on Tuesday, Zelensky claimed Russia was responsible for the attacks.

Notorious gangland enforcer Paul Ferris dies aged 62

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:57:55 GMT

A Glasgow gangland enforcer who wrote books about his underworld experiences has died at the age of 62.

Paul Ferris is believed to have died on Tuesday night at the city's Queen Elizabeth University Hospital after a short illness.

He was cleared of the murder of crime boss Arthur Thompson's son, Arthur Thompson Jnr, in 1992, before being jailed for seven years in 1998 for gun-running.

His first book, The Ferris Conspiracy, was published in 2001.

It was later made into a 2013 film, The Wee Man, featuring Line of Duty star Martin Compston as Ferris.

Photographer Brian Anderson, who first met Ferris for a newspaper assignment in 2002, broke the news of his death on his Naked City Facebook page.

Describing Ferris as a best-selling author and a "former notorious criminal", he wrote: "News of his death will come as a shock to many who knew him throughout the different chapters of his life."

Anderson later told BBC Scotland News: "We got on really well. I found him polite, funny and kind.

"It was a shock to everyone that I remained friends with Paul for 25 years."

Thompson, who had links to the Krays in London, was an old school Glasgow criminal known as The Godfather.

By the early 80s, Ferris had become part of his gang as an enforcer, someone who threatened and, when necessary, meted out violence. He rapidly built a fearsome reputation that extended beyond the city.

But their relationship took a remarkable twist in August 1991 when Arthur "Fat Boy" Thompson Jnr, was shot dead outside the family's Provanmill home.

It was named The Ponderosa after the ranch in the hit US Western television series, Bonanza.

Ferris was arrested as the prime suspect in Thompson Jnr's murder but two others were also incriminated.

His friends Joe "Bananas" Hanlon and Bobby Glover did not live to stand trial.

On the day of Thompson Jnr's funeral both men were found shot dead in a car on the cortege route.

The murders remain unsolved.

The following year Ferris's trial became, at the time, the longest and most expensive criminal case in Scottish legal history.

More than 300 witnesses gave evidence during the 54-day proceedings, which were estimated to have cost £4m.

The prosecution case relied heavily on the evidence of Dennis Woodman, who claimed Ferris had confessed to the killing while both men were being held in Barlinnie Prison.

Defence lawyers challenged the credibility of the evidence and argued the case against Ferris was deeply flawed.

After more than 24 hours of deliberations, the jury acquitted Ferris of murder and all other charges in 1992.

No-one has ever been convicted of Thompson Jnr's killing.

In 2020 Donald Findlay KC - who defended Ferris in court - told Hey Legal that the case had been the most memorable of his career.

He said: "The trial of Paul Ferris for the murder of Arthur Thompson Jr had virtually all the great characters of Glasgow in that trial one way or another.

"Young Arthur was dead, his father was a witness, Ferris was regarded by the police as the heir apparent to Arthur Thompson Sr.

"We had supergrasses, it just had everything that was going for it.

"I forget how many charges that there were but of course Ferris walked on each and every one of them."

Following his release from prison in 2002 after being jailed on gun-running charges, Ferris turned to writing.

His debut book was made into a movie which starred Martin Compston - who had found fame as a teenager in Ken Loach's Sweet Sixteen - as Ferris.

John Hannah played his arch rival, Tam "The Licensee" McGraw.

The crime boss, who died in 2007 aged 55, had been linked to crimes ranging from drug smuggling to murder for more than three decades.

The movie was shot in London due to problems securing permission from Glasgow City Council and the police to film in Ferris's home city.

Ferris went on to publish two further books, Vendetta and Villains, with crime writer Reg McKay, who died in 2012.

Graeme Pearson, former director general of the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency, first encountered the convicted gun-runner when he was a teenager.

Pearson told BBC Scotland News that Ferris went on to develop a fearsome reputation.

He said: "Certainly, in his active days, he wouldn't be a man that you would choose to go to dinner with."

The ex-Labour MSP added: "At one stage in his life he was a very dangerous character.

"He was someone who seemed to take pleasure in his reputation for violence.

"Having said that, I think that in later life he certainly seemed to outlive that reputation and would appear to have put that whole gangster profile behind him."

BBC's Nicky Campbell tells court teacher who attacked him 'completely lost it'

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:54:11 GMT

Broadcaster Nicky Campbell has told a court a maths teacher "completely lost it" and violently attacked him in the courtyard of Edinburgh Academy when he was a pupil there in the 1970s.

The 65-year-old said he was around 15 when he was initially "yanked from behind" by Colin Turner beside a school noticeboard when he was running late for class.

Campbell said he was then "rag dolled" by the teacher and described being shaken, slapped and dragged across the playground.

He was giving evidence during an examination of facts hearing held at Edinburgh Sheriff Court.

Turner and David Bourne, another former teacher, are accused of attacking pupils at the prestigious fee-paying school but have been deemed medically unfit to stand trial.

A sheriff will instead hear evidence in the case and determine whether there are grounds for a conviction.

Campbell was a pupil at Edinburgh Academy between 1966 and 1978, from when he was aged five until he was 17.

The BBC Radio 5 Live presenter told the court he was a "skinny teenage pupil" when he was attacked by Turner - who he said was a "physically imposing" man.

Prior to the incident, he said that he and another pupil were looking at a timetable on a noticeboard after the lunchtime break, trying to find out where they should be.

He said there were a few stragglers in the playground but most pupils had gone to class.

Campbell told the court he was "yanked from behind", adding: "I didn't know what was going on, didn't know who it was until I turned around and he [Turner] started hitting me.

"He shook me around and started slapping me. He utterly lost it. It was an absolute frenzy."

Campbell said immediately after the incident it was as if "the red mist lifted" and he and Turner went into a nearby common room and sat down at a table.

He told the court he was still sobbing.

The presenter said he told the teacher "I could call the police on you for that" and that the teacher appeared "chastened."

Campbell said he went home with a torn shirt. He told the court his mother saw he was "distraught" and called the school.

Following this, he said there was "correspondence" and that he remembered his mother later saying that Turner had been "dealt with".

Later in his evidence, Campbell told the court that he saw his Edinburgh Academy pupil file for the first time three or four weeks ago.

Asked if there was any record of this incident in it, he replied: "No, it was ridiculously scant."

Campbell will continue giving evidence on Thursday.

Is it too early to look at Premier League table?

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:28:33 GMT

Arsenal are chasing back-to-back Premier League titles

Just five games in, it might seem a bit early to pay much attention to the Premier League table - but it's probably more settled than you think.

While it would be no surprise if Manchester City and Arsenal finish as the top two - outside of any points deductions or sanctions directed City's way - will Brentford really qualify for Europe, Hull stay up and Tottenham be involved in yet another relegation battle? Recent history certainly suggests it is likely.

It has to be mentioned there is a huge asterisk hanging over the Premier League table at the moment after Manchester City were found guilty of the majority of the Premier League charges levelled at them.

The Premier League leaders have appealed but, if the guilty verdict remains, potential sanctions could have a significant impact on the table. Until then, we can only deal with the table as it is now.

If we look at the Premier League after five games last season and where teams ultimately ended up, the final table was already starting to take shape as 13 of the 20 sides finished within four places of where they sat even at this early stage (65%).

Eventual champions Arsenal were second, Sunderland were already seventh ahead of finishing there eight months later, and two of the three sides that were relegated were already in the bottom three.

There were some notable exceptions. Aston Villa and Tottenham effectively swapped places at either end of the table, with Villa rising from the bottom three to finish in the top four and Spurs dropping to 17th.

It is a similar story across the last 10 seasons of the Premier League. More than two-thirds of teams finished within four places of where they were after five games (138 out of 200), with 27 of those sitting in exactly the same position 33 games later.

Another 50 teams finished between five and nine places from where they were at this stage, meaning that just 12 teams in the past decade moved up or down the table by double digits after this point, with three of those coming last season.

However, one part of the table that does not settle quickly is the top spot. The side leading the Premier League after five games has gone on to win the title in just one of the past six seasons - Manchester City doing so in 2023-24 - and just three times in the past 11 seasons.

Even the fact that Manchester City have five wins out of five so far does not mean much. They also won their first five games under Manuel Pellegrini in 2015-16 and in Pep Guardiola's first season in 2016-17 but did not go on to win the title on either occasion (although they did in 2023-24).

Chelsea in 2018-19, Arsenal in 2022-23 and Liverpool last season were also top with a 100% record at this stage but had little to show for it at the end of the season.

However, the eventual champions have been in the top two at this point in each of the last four campaigns, suggesting - potential punishments aside - it will be Manchester City or Arsenal that lifts the trophy. The last team to be outside the top two after five games and win the title were Manchester City in 2021-22, who were fifth with just 10 points.

The top end of the table overall has sometimes settled surprisingly quickly in recent years. The top eight after five games in 2024-25 finished as the top eight at the end of that season (although not in the same order), while the top six in 2019-20 and top seven in 2016-17 were also in place at this early stage.

While being top after five games has not meant much in recent seasons, being bottom certainly has.

After finishing just one place above the drop in the last two campaigns, Tottenham could well be in trouble once again as the side bottom of the Premier League after five games has been relegated in six of the past seven seasons.

Being bottom this early did not used to be such a bad omen. Between 2013-14 and 2018-19, only one of the six sides that were propping up the table after five games ended up going down - Newcastle in 2015-16 - while Crystal Palace finished as high as 11th in 2017-18.

In fact, the good news for Tottenham fans is that the last time they were in this situation, they finished eighth. The club were bottom with just two points after five games in 2008-09 but, after replacing manager Juande Ramos with Harry Redknapp three games later, still finished in the top half.

Looking at the relegation battle more broadly, at least one of the teams in the bottom three at this stage has been relegated in the last eight seasons - so one of Tottenham, Fulham and Coventry will very likely be heading to the Championship in May.

The pool of contestants for this season's relegation battle may already be decided too as the three sides that ultimately went down in the past three seasons were all in the bottom six after five games, which would add Bournemouth, Aston Villa and Crystal Palace to the mix.

The last sides to be outside the bottom six at this point but relegated were Leeds and Southampton in 2022-23, who were both in the top half (7th and 9th). With their teams currently sat in 8th and 11th place, Hull and Ipswich fans will hope that is still the case at the end of this campaign.

While the season may well have barely begun, the Premier League table is already starting to take shape.

Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:18:30 GMT

Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.

Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.

Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.

The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.

Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.

It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.

In its most recent annual results, Boots generated £7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024.

Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".

She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help.

The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed.

Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".

The company was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham, offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849.

It has since expanded over the decades into selling various products, but health products have remained a key part of its business.

As well as vaccines, it offers eye and hearing tests, providing much needed health care support in everyday moments as well as at times of national crisis like the coronavirus pandemic.

It launched its loyalty scheme in 1997, the Advantage Card, which became hugely popular and a move repeated by various retailers since.

Galen Weston, the chairman of Wittington, will become chairman of Boots.

He signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services.

"We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said.

The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027.

The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn.

The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark.

The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost £19bn.

Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company.

Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

Tories united behind Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:31:06 GMT

It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.

Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham.

It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago.

The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence.

Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland.

Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that.

The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax – which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax.

Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income.

But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it.

Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people.

The Institute For Fiscal Studies said the "biggest beneficiaries" would be "a very well off group, mainly living in London and the south east of England".

It also said it would "encourage wealthy people to buy (or stay in) more expensive homes in their later years".

The proportion of estates subject to inheritance tax is rising rapidly, the IFS said, but forecasts are uncertain because it depends on, among other things, what happens to house prices.

The Conservatives estimate their inheritance policy change would cost around £6bn a year.

They claim to have identified £71bn pounds worth of cuts that can be made to government spending, including £36bn a year from benefits and welfare.

The largest savings are projected to come from reforming sickness and disability benefits, where the party believes it can save £13.7bn a year, with £9.5bn a year from ending access to benefits for non-EU nationals, £4.5bn from changes to housing benefit, and £3.1bn from reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit.

But Work and Pensions Minister Torsten Bell said "history is very clear that promising this scale of tax cuts ends one way: trashing your public finances".

Policy announcements aside, what stood out in this speech for me was a broader point. The veteran Conservative elections strategist Sir Lynton Crosby once suggested the party ought to "scrape the barnacles off the boat" as he put it, in reference to unpopular policies that could cause the Tories a headache during an election campaign.

This speech felt like Badenoch revelling in pointing at the clean hull of the Conservative ship, what she sees as those barnacles removed, not least the high-profile defections of Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

There was a striking glee and anger in her reflections about Reform UK. She sought to portray them as sleazy and pointedly decided to lean into an argument of recent months about Englishness.

Braverman has argued that, given her Asian heritage, "I'm not English".

"I'm proud to be British. My family and ancestors have a link to Britain which spans centuries. But in no way are we English," she wrote on social media last month, adding: "Englishness is an ethnicity."

Badenoch expressed her personal fury at this, saying that as the mother of mixed-race children "I don't want to explain to my son, when we're watching our brilliant England team play football, that some people don't think our black players are English".

The recurring message, today and over the last few days, is Badenoch cannot stand Reform and won't work with them before or after the next general election.

But what she said amounted to an attack on Reform's character and the judgement of their prominent figures, rather than a significant focus on the policies we hear talked about most often by Nigel Farage.

Badenoch did talk about immigration, but not at length. She largely left the issue – and the Conservative policy to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights, as Reform also advocates - to her shadow home secretary Chris Philp who spoke before her.

Instead, Badenoch grounded this speech in the big picture tussle to be trusted between Labour and the Conservatives – and in particular who was better placed to deliver a growing economy.

In tone, language and public enthusiasm for the argument, Badenoch and Andy Burnham are quite the contrast with their immediate predecessors Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer.

Badenoch and Burnham both look like they are enjoying themselves on the stage, and are both enthusiastic purveyors of the core of what are their very different worldviews.

Badenoch acknowledged this with what she called the "battle for the soul of this nation" in the opening minute or so of her address. It is a trailer for the debate to come this autumn and beyond.

The Conservatives feel chipper and are united. But while both of these things are better than the alternative for any party leader, they are not the same as being popular.

And, as Kemi Badenoch acknowledged, they are not there on that score yet, by a long chalk, with opinion polls suggesting they are more unpopular than when they were annihilated at the last general election.

The numbers, for them, are dire. Just not as bad, relatively speaking, as they were.

But they hope things are looking up for them: Reform has had a bruising few months, and Labour, they believe, are leaning to the Left, trying to lure Green and Liberal Democrat supporters towards them.

Can the Conservatives also lure recent Lib Dem supporters in the south of England with talk of help with childcare costs whatever your income, not hiking the council tax of very expensive homes and this inheritance tax plan?

This, Tories hope, there are now gaps in the political market they can exploit.

They crave catching and overtaking Reform in the polls, in the hope that after that there is a tipping point allowing them to credibly claim they are the most viable alternative to a Labour or Labour-led future government. Let's see.

What's in the Conservatives' inheritance tax plan and who benefits?

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:23:32 GMT

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has announced she will overhaul inheritance tax if her party wins the next general election.

She told the Conservatives' annual conference that "nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home" and couples will be able to leave an additional £1m tax free.

Tax experts say the party's £6bn per year estimate of the cost of the plan is reasonable, but warn the policy would primarily benefit wealthier households and could discourage older people from moving to smaller homes.

BBC Verify has looked into the details of the policy.

Under the current system, inheritance tax of 40% is paid when someone's estate - the total value of their money and property - exceeds £325,000. Anything under this amount is not taxed.

And, when a person dies, they can currently transfer this tax-free allowance to a surviving spouse or civil partner which increases the combined threshold for a couple to £650,000.

On top of this individuals can get an additional transferable allowance for a family home of £175,000 each when it is left to children or other direct descendants.

So at present most married couples can potentially leave £1m without paying inheritance tax.

The Conservative plan would increase the £325,000 threshold - the point at which you start paying the tax - to £500,000 and fully exempt a family home from inheritance tax.

At the moment an estate with a £2m house could be liable for £400,000 in inheritance tax. That would reduce to zero under the Conservatives.

Official figures show that in 2024-25 around 30,400 deaths in the UK left estates which were liable for inheritance tax.

This was around 5% of all UK deaths in that year.

But the number of estates paying inheritance tax is set to rise, due to the increasing value of inherited wealth being passed on and the threshold having been frozen.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has estimated that by 2032-33 around 12% of people will have inheritance tax due either on their own death or that of their spouse or civil partner.

Citing analysis by the consultancy Oxford Economics, the Conservatives say the number of estates paying the tax will rise to 52,100 in 2029-30.

The Conservatives estimate their reforms would reduce the number of affected estates in 2030 to 22,000.

Official data shows higher value estates pay the majority of the inheritance tax collected.

The IFS has estimated that if inheritance tax were to be entirely scrapped, which Badenoch has identified as a longer term aspiration, the wealthiest 1% of estates - those worth £2.1m or more - would get half of the benefit of the tax reduction.

And one long-standing criticism of inheritance tax is that the wealthy use legal ways to avoid paying it like putting their assets into family trusts to reduce the amount of inheritance tax ultimately due from their estates when they die.

In 2023-24, estates with a valuation of £10m only paid an average effective inheritance tax rate of 18%, according to estimates from HM Revenue and Customs.

Responding to Wednesday's conference announcement, the IFS said: "The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes – and their descendants.

"This is a very well-off group, mainly living in London and the South-East of England."

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the official forecaster, estimates inheritance tax will raise £9.5bn in 2026-27 - equivalent to around 0.3% of GDP.

The OBR projects this will rise to £14.5bn in 2030-31 or 0.4% of GDP.

The Conservatives estimate their plan would cost £6bn a year in 2029-30, based on Oxford Economics' analysis.

The party says it has identified £71bn in annual savings including £36bn a year from welfare cuts.

Prof Andy Summers, director of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation, told BBC Verify this was "just about about the worst possible way to deliver an inheritance tax cut".

"Exempting the family home however much it's worth will just encourage older people to concentrate their savings in their home, prevent downsizing, and so further gum up the housing market," he said.

The Conservatives argue in their press release accompanying the policy announcement that inheritance taxes are "bad for growth".

But analysis by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development suggests inheritance taxes in general are less damaging to economic growth than taxes on income from work.

Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett

Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss as Spygate ban suspended

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:11:15 GMT

This video can not be played

Eckert speaking to BBC Sport in September, days before the hearing took place

Tonda Eckert is free to continue as Southampton manager after being given a suspended ban for his role in the Spygate scandal.

A Football Association (FA) independent regulatory commission handed the German a six-week ban from all football, but suspended it until the end of next season.

Eckert has also been given a £28,000 fine and reprimand but avoided a lengthy ban that could have cost him his job.

The FA had proposed a three-month ban, but the commission gave credit to Eckert for what they called "considerable mitigation in this matter, most particularly around the genuine contrition".

The FA is yet to confirm whether it will appeal.

In a statement, Southampton welcomed the decision.

"We hope this now brings a conclusion to a regrettable period of our history, and measures have been put in place to ensure that such errors in judgement never happen again at our club," the club said.

"We want to take this opportunity to thank the supporters for their unconditional backing throughout this process."

Saints owner Dragan Solak said the club had "already suffered enough".

"We appreciate the panel's recognition of that," he said.

"We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role.

"I firmly believe that Tonda is one of Europe's most exciting young coaches, and with this distraction removed, I am confident he can lead the team to a successful season."

Solak said the FA process had been a "positive experience", but criticised the English Football League (EFL), saying "the way they have treated us is not something we will forget".

Saints were expelled from the Championship play-offs in May after admitting spying on training sessions involving Oxford United, Ipswich Town, and Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final.

They were also handed a four-point deduction for this season.

An English Football League (EFL) independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

The 33-year-old apologised in June - claiming he was unaware the practice was banned and that it had no impact on his team's performances - but the FA charged him with misconduct, and a hearing took place at the end of last month.

Eckert has been sanctioned for three breaches of FA Rule E3.1. The six-week ban from all football activity would be triggered if he was found to be involved in any other spying between now and the end of next season.

Eckert was appointed permanent Southampton manager in December 2025 after taking interim charge when they were 21st in the Championship. They finished the season in fourth place.

Saints, who face local rivals Portsmouth this weekend, are 13th in the Championship this season with four wins from their eight matches so far.

The FA did not charge Leeds United's former manager Marcelo Bielsa after the club were found guilty of spying on Derby in 2019, instead issuing a formal warning.

The EFL fined Leeds £200,000 - which Bielsa said he paid - and introduced a rule prohibiting any club from observing a rival's training session within 72 hours of a match between them.

The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year after opponents New Zealand were spied on.

Spygate: Eckert free to continue as Southampton manager

Eckert arranged spying on Oxford to establish whether they were playing a back four or a back five under a new manager.

In the Ipswich case, the panel accepted that Eckert did not initiate the move to obtain CCTV footage of their training session.

For the Middlesbrough semi-final, the panel accepted Eckert's evidence that he sent someone to the training ground to establish whether Boro midfielder Hayden Hackney was fit to play.

The panel concluded there was "a contrived and determined plan from the top down to gain a competitive advantage in competitions of real significance by deliberate attendance at opposition training grounds for the purpose of obtaining tactical and selection information".

The panel was "entirely satisfied" that Eckert was not aware the actions were in breach of the EFL rules or 'morally wrong'.

The commission had "no hesitation in rejecting any suggestion of a systemic or organised course of conduct".

"Spying on an opponent is a very serious offence", the panel said, while noting "that this does not prohibit observation of training outside of these hours".

The panel found Eckert to be "a particularly impressive witness", who has "reflected very deeply and seriously on what has happened" and "his level of contrition was as deep and meaningful as could reasonably be expected".

The panel was asked to consider that a ban of three months may cost Eckert his job - and concluded that this would "unquestionably be the equivalent of a further sanction being imposed" on the club. "We consider that this is a clear and compelling reason to suspend that part of the sanction which comprises the ban from all football and football related activity," the report said.

This video can not be played

Eckert avoids lengthy ban over Spygate scandal

It was the morning of Thursday, 7 May.

Middlesbrough were at their Rockliffe Park training base preparing for the game against Southampton 48 hours later.

The spy - Southampton intern William Salt - is said to have parked at the golf club, then walked a couple of hundred yards down a road that leads to a raised area of ground.

Sources told the BBC that Salt stood pointing his mobile at the training session, while wearing in-ear headphones.

Middlesbrough staff believe he may have been live-streaming the session via a video call.

A member of Middlesbrough's staff approached, say BBC sources, but the person would not identify himself. He then quickly deleted some content on his phone before running into the golf club.

He jogged into the toilets, changed his clothes and hurriedly left the site.

Middlesbrough's photographer took photos and matched him to a photo on the Southampton website. One of those pictures was subsequently made public.

Boro were furious and quickly reported the incident to the EFL, which charged Southampton with breaking two regulations.

During the investigation, details emerged about the club watching training sessions involving Oxford and Ipswich, in addition to filming Middlesbrough as they prepared for the first leg of their play-off semi-final.

Southampton did not win any of the three games - they lost 2-1 at Oxford, drew 2-2 at home to Ipswich and 0-0 at Boro.

Salt has since been appointed to a permanent role at Saints in the club's academy.

Southampton told the BBC "he's been through a tough time".

"When your photo is put out to the public, that is something tough to deal with," chief executive Phil Parsons told the BBC last month.

"A lot of people probably underestimated how that could have impacted a young lad so we've got a job to make sure that he's looked after in his early career. But he's a talented boy as well. I get good feedback and he's got a good role at the club."

The picture of intern William Salt went viral after the case came to light

Family tribute to 'kind and loving' GP found dead at home

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:10:36 GMT

The family of a GP who was found dead at her home say they have been "devastated" by her death.

Police discovered the body of Hannah Cain, known to her patients as Dr Hannah Terry, at her home in Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday morning.

"She was kind, generous and loving; a beloved mother, daughter, sister, auntie, daughter-in-law and friend," the 45-year-old's family said in a statement.

Her husband, Mark Cain, 45, of Fern Hill in Dersingham, appeared before magistrates in Norwich earlier, accused of her murder.

He did not enter a plea during the hearing and will return before a judge on Thursday.

"We are devastated by the loss of our beautiful Hannah," the family said.

They added: "We are incredibly proud of the woman she was and of the great care she took of all her patients who knew her as Dr Terry.

"We would ask people to respect our privacy at this difficult time."

Hannah Cain was listed as a member of the practice team at Grimston Medical Centre, which reopened on Wednesday after two days of closure.

She also served in a pool of doctors who were regularly on call for members of the Royal Family, The Sun newspaper reported.

Dersingham is on the edge of the royal Sandringham estate in west Norfolk, while Grimston is to the south.

Speaking at Norwich Magistrates' Court earlier, prosecutor Jacqui Hanlon said paramedics were called to Hannah Cain's home, on Fern Hill, at 02:25 BST on Sunday.

The GP was "found in an upstairs bedroom not breathing, not conscious", she said.

Hanlon said a post-mortem examination noted a "blunt force injury" to the right side of Hannah Cain's head, as well as an injury "that could be suggestive of compression of the neck".

District judge Matthew Bone remanded Mark Cain in custody to appear at King's Lynn Crown Court on Thursday.

After reopening on Wednesday, Grimston Medical Centre said it would not be commenting "on the circumstances surrounding the tragic death" of Hannah Cain.

Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:00:18 GMT

As the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.

It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.

The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure.

"I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.

The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.

Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.

And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies.

"Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.

Aside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.

For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.

Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza.

"There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored? We need to find out what happened – not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that."

"The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."

Over the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours – which he denies.

Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.

Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.

Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.

Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".

Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation.

"God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network.

"What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.

Yaakov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.

In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.

He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters.

"So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."

But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening.

"You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."

For years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.

A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie".

"On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."

Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.

He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.

Netanyahu has so far rejected any personal responsibility for the attacks.

Col Richard Hecht was the IDF's international spokesman on 7 October. He told me the refusal of political leaders - including Netanyahu - to accept responsibility was part of the reason he resigned six months later.

"It's a disgrace," he told me. "When you look at accountability, within the IDF I don't think there's a problem. And that's the pain. That's one of the main causes of bad blood between the political echelon and the military."

At a memorial ceremony in Jerusalem on Monday, the father of one of those killed on 7 October stood up to challenge the prime minister.

"You didn't protect my son, you didn't protect all those who were murdered," he said, before security guards led him away. "Shame! Disgrace!"

Three years on from the attacks, calls for accountability are growing. Campaigners have asked Israel's highest court to force the government into establishing a state commission of inquiry.

Yizhar Shai, a former minister and opposition politician whose youngest son Yaron, a soldier, was killed on 7 October, is part of that campaign.

"We are going into these elections almost blindfolded as it relates to October 7th," he told me during a protest in Tel Aviv last week. "Our prime minister has never given a detailed, thorough explanation under oath, where he would be asked all the tough questions and have to explain everything."

Netanyahu has consistently refused a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.

Before calling an election, his government proposed an alternative "national commission of inquiry", whose members would be appointed by political parties.

But despite passing a raft of other legislation before parliament ended its session in July, Israel's government said it ran out of time to pass a bill setting out its plans for the inquiry.

We approached several members of his Likud party for an interview, without success. We also requested that the party respond to their critics, and are waiting for their response.

Netanyahu's denial of responsibility has now become an election issue, as he prepares to run for re-election later this month.

A video game called Sleepy Bibi, released by the team of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, asks players to help the prime minister avoid responsibility by dodging warnings of an attack and "making it to bed safely".

Netanyahu has styled himself for decades as Israel's "Mr Security", and despite presiding over the worst security failure in Israel's history, is running on the same security platform again.

For the past three years, he focused on waging new wars against Israel's enemies - Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

Polls suggest a close race, and that the 7 October attacks are central to many voters' decisions.

Yaakov Katz says the legacy of 7 October is a coin with two sides.

"There are the failures, the mistakes that led to the Hamas invasion," he told me. "But there's the other side, which is Netanyahu's argument; that [he] has re-engineered the Middle East and made Israel a safer place today. And that is an argument Israelis take with them to the polls."

The shadow of the attacks hangs over this election, dividing Israel once again along political lines.

For supporters, it confirms that Benjamin Netanyahu is still needed to keep Israel safe.

Critics say his political survival puts Israel at risk.

Eleven arrested as pro-Palestinian marches held in London

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:00:17 GMT

Eleven people were arrested as several pro-Palestinian demonstrations were held in London on Wednesday, the Metropolitan Police has said.

Among them were five people arrested on suspicion of inciting racial hatred at a protest outside the office of the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London.

The force said the other arrests were made at student-led pro-Palestinian protests elsewhere in the capital, which went ahead despite calls for them to be postponed so they did not fall on 7 October. One of those arrested was part of a counter-protest.

Wednesday marked three years since the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, in which around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken as hostages by the militant group.

Israel responded to the attack by launching a military offensive in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

Footage from the demonstration outside the Board of Deputies' Camden office showed a few dozen protesters, several of whom were wearing face coverings.

In a statement following the arrests, the Board of Deputies, the UK's largest Jewish community group, said it "would not be threatened or intimidated" and thanked police for their "swift" response.

Slogans "calling for intifada" were chanted during the protest, according to the Met. The five arrested remain in custody.

The term intifada came into popular use during the Palestinian uprising against Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1987.

Jewish groups have described the term as a call for violence against Jewish people. Pro-Palestinian groups have said it is a call for peaceful resistance to Israel's occupation.

The Board of Deputies held a vigil in Whitehall, central London, later on Wednesday to remember the victims of the 7 October attack.

A pro-Palestinian march attended by around 100 people took place between Lincoln's Inn Fields to Russell Square.

The Met had previously called for the student protest to take place on a different day, saying demonstrations on 7 October would cause distress on a day of mourning for Jewish students and staff.

Counter-demonstrators carrying Israeli flags also gathered in Russell Square. There were some minor scuffles between the two groups.

Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march, which included an order not to wear face coverings, the Met said.

One of those who was arrested for breaching those restrictions was part of a counter-protest.

Another person on the pro-Palestinian march was arrested on suspicion of common assault.

The Met said the largest of Wednesday's demonstrations had ended ahead of a police-enforced dispersal time.

Pro-Palestinian protesters were heard chanting "Zionists not welcome here" and "free Palestine from the river to the sea".

Some use the chant as a call for Palestinian control of all land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, including Israel.

Critics say the slogan is a call for the destruction of the state of Israel.

That interpretation is disputed by pro-Palestinian activists, who say that most people chanting it are calling for an end to Israel's occupation of the West Bank and blockade of Gaza, not the destruction of Israel itself.
