World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 15:00:35 GMT

Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.

Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade.

According to the study, there were 63% fewer occupied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.

The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.

Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.

Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory.

In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain.

BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".

A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds.

This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.

The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change.

Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.

"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards.

"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.

The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.

Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.

Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.

"It's like a penguin Mordor."

Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening.

Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo).

Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame.

There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.

Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet.

Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans.

Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica".

"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added.

"It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."

As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.

The research is published in the journal Current Biology.

Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 14:33:11 GMT

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged to scrap inheritance tax (IHT) on family homes while also allowing couples to leave £1m tax-free, in her keynote speech at the party's conference in Birmingham.

Badenoch added her ambition would be for a Conservative government to abolish IHT "as soon as we can afford it", but said she could not currently propose this due to spending commitments on defence, prisons and the economy.

Badenoch also used her speech to try to make clear how the Tories differed to Labour and Reform UK.

She pitched them as the "no-nonsense party" compared to the Reform UK "circus" and accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to "live in the past".

Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".

She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.

"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."

With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".

Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".

Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."

One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.

She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."

Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.

"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."

She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".

In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".

In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT.

As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country".

She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home.

"On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional £1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half."

The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around £6bn a year and believe they have identified £71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts.

Under the current rules, estates worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold.

Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.

In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around £7bn for the government.

Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it".

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed.

"Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%".

The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a £500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000.

"The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country."

Elsewhere in her speech, Badenoch referred to other policies the party has announced in recent days.

These include a £10bn anti-missile defence system, 50,000 new prison places and halving the rate of employer national insurance on earnings for people aged between 21 to 24.

They also pledged to scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Another policy to be scrapped would be the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), dubbed the "mansion tax".

This is due to take effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey responded to the speech by saying Badenoch had been "lecturing the country on fiscal responsibility while making tens of billions in unfunded promises".

Green MP Carla Denyer added: "Kemi Badenoch once again defined the Conservative Party as pro-billionaires, pro-inequality and pro-damaging the environment."

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 14:28:55 GMT

This video can not be played

How sandpapergate was exposed

According to the man who helped catch them, it was blind luck.

Sandpapergate, the scandal that engulfed Australia eight years ago, was blatant cheating played out in real time on live television to a global audience.

As the Aussies prepare for their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering controversy in Cape Town, the director of the TV coverage that day admits serendipity took down Steve Smith and co.

"The way the Australians were caught was an absolute fluke," Alvin Naicker, in charge of SuperSport's live broadcast from Newlands, tells BBC Sport.

Not just one fluke, but a series of them.

That the "leadership group" of the Australian team hatched their plan during the lunch break on that Saturday afternoon in March 2018; that an alert camera operator lingered on Cameron Bancroft when others would have turned their attention elsewhere; that the big-screen controller showed in the ground what was also being broadcast to millions around the world.

In understanding how Bancroft was rumbled, a little knowledge of how live cricket is shown on TV is helpful.

"Coverage of rugby and football is very coordinated. It's camera one and two, then when the ball is dead you tell the story with close-up shots," explains Naicker, a highly respected and popular figure in the TV industry with more than 30 years' experience.

"Because cricket has so much dead time, there is a lot more storytelling. There are between 80 and 100 people coming together and putting the story together in a matter of seconds, coordinated by the director."

Captain Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Bancroft later explained they cooked up the ball-tampering plot during lunch on the third day of the third Test.

Reverse-swing had been a key factor in the first two Tests of a bad-tempered series: Warner clashed with Quinton de Kock in the first Test in Durban, then Smith was involved in an altercation with Kagiso Rabada in the second.

Australia were exposed before the afternoon session was done, thanks to Naicker and his team. At the time, SuperSport were not on the lookout for cheating, despite the shenanigans of the first two Tests.

"No one mentioned anything to me," says Naicker. "The first Test in Durban spiralled out of control in terms of behaviour, then in Port Elizabeth for the second Test, there were still some fireworks going on. We still didn't understand."

Reports written live by ESPNCricinfo suggest the ball began reversing in the first hour after lunch, 35 overs into the South Africa second innings. In the 43rd over, Bancroft was caught in the act.

"The ball went to the wicketkeeper, then to Bancroft and he was shining the ball," says Naicker. "First it was on his pants, then the next ball, the cameraman happened to stay on Bancroft because he was not shining the ball on his pants, but he was rubbing the ball on his palm.

"When he threw the ball on, he put his hand in his pocket. The cameraman - and these are big, big lens cameras - he zoomed into his pocket. The slow-mo operator looked at it, spooled it back and forth, then zoomed in and could see the yellow spot."

Cameron Bancroft is seen hiding a yellow piece of sandpaper down his trousers

The umpires inspect the ball as Cameron Bancroft looks on

1 of 2

Test cricket's biggest scandals - your results revealed

TMS Top 10: Cricket scandals

Bancroft's work on the ball was not shown live, but as a replay later in the over. Inside Newlands, the operator of the big screen – working independently from Naicker – showed the same footage.

"They take a feed from broadcast but they also have to insert their own graphics and commercialisation," says Naicker.

"Between deliveries they tend to stay with live play, then at the end of the over they go to their commercials or whatever in the stadium. It was quite fortunate that when we showed it, it was in between deliveries, not at the end of the over."

Bancroft would later admit he "panicked" when he saw himself on the big screen. Comically, he hid the sandpaper inside his trousers. SuperSport caught that, too.

"When Bancroft looked up at the screen and saw it, he removed it and put it in his jocks," says Naicker. "The cameraman recorded it. It still wasn't live, we played a replay."

Bancroft, with Smith by his side, was challenged by on-field umpires Richard Illingworth and Nigel Llong.

The opener turned out his pockets, revealing only a black bag for his sunglasses. The ball was not changed and Australia were not given a run penalty. Play continued, yet SuperSport were on to what had happened.

"Australia coach Darren Lehmann was on the walkie-talkie to 12th man Peter Handscomb, who went on to the field, then the umpires get involved," says Naicker.

"An entire team of cameramen played their part. There was one following the ball, one on Handscomb, one on Lehmann, one on Warner. They all told a story that I happened to put together with this great team of replay operators."

As for Naicker, there was no hesitation in airing what his team had captured, even with the realisation of the magnitude of what was unfolding.

"A lot of people who watch cricket on SuperSport will know we are quite brave in terms of being quite creative and editorially sound," he says.

"It was a natural instinct. It wasn't something I previewed with 10 other people to say 'What do you think, should we show it?' I just went for it."

The footage was pored over by Naicker's team of commentators, while his phone was "WhatsApping off the hook" with messages from around the world, asking him to show it again and again. Replays drew the attention of the third umpire, Englishman Ian Gould.

"He's got comms with me while I'm directing," says Naicker. "There was a moment when he asked me 'I think that's enough now, do you mind not showing it?'

"My response to him was 'I'm quite comfortable in what I'm doing in my job and I think you should do yours'."

When the day's play finally ended, Naicker and his team went to a bar and heard Bancroft and Smith confess in their news conference. Both men and Warner were sent home from the tour and handed lengthy bans. When he returned to Australia, Smith broke down in a tearful address to the press in Sydney.

"It became disheartening for us," says Naicker. "It started becoming emotional to see how they were feeling.

"The most difficult thing for me was to see Steve Smith shedding tears. That was not nice and never the intention. You have to have some emotion for those guys."

Steve Smith cries when speaking to the media on his return to Australia

David Warner was also emotional when he spoke to journalists

Australia coach Darren Lehmann struggles to hold back the tears after announcing his resignation

1 of 3

There was still a fourth and final Test to complete. Feelings were raw, and SuperSport's access to interviews from Australia was heavily restricted.

Naicker and his team faced allegations of bias, that they were somehow part of an orchestrated plot to take down the Australians. Now, with the Aussies back in town, Naicker maintains he would have pounced on the same "fluke" had it been South Africa caught cheating.

He also highlights the power of television. Bancroft and Australia were exposed mere moments after their act of cheating. TV viewers knew before the on-field match officials.

Naicker points to a conversation he had with Stuart Broad, who also faced tampering accusations for treading on the ball on a tour of South Africa in 2010 and is now building a post-playing career as a pundit.

"When you played the Broad footage in ultra-motion, it looked worse than it was," says Naicker. "He said he never realised how much control and power the TV crew has until he worked in the commentary box.

"I said that's what you have to remind your team-mates. You can't hide any more in international cricket. There are too many cameras and technology around."

Ex-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 13:52:13 GMT

Five former Barclays traders sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis have had their convictions overturned following a long-running legal battle.

Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham were convicted following trials for manipulating the interest rates used for loans between banks.

But their convictions were quashed on Wednesday by the Court of Appeal. The ruling came after two other former City traders had their convictions overturned last year, which paved the way for others to appeal.

The traders were cast by prosecutors as a symbol of banker greed amid public backlash and anger during the 2008 financial crisis.

Merchant, Mathew, Pabon and Bermingham have all served various jail terms. Moryoussef was sentenced in his absence in 2018, never returned to the UK to serve time after France refused to extradite him.

The prosecutions were over the manipulation of two key interest rate mechanisms: Libor and Euribor, which at the time were used to set borrowing costs on a range of loans such as mortgages and car finance deals.

Mathew said the "strain" of what he had gone through had been a burden on him for the last 10 years.

"Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it's about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened," the 45-year-old said.

"I now have two children and this means a great deal to have the record corrected for their sake as well."

Merchant, 55, added that he looked forward to moving on with his life, but said part of that would be "ensuring that those responsible for what happened are held fully accountable".

Lord Justice Edis said full reasons behind the overturned convictions would be given later on Wednesday.

The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.

There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.

The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.

Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.

Each of the former Barclays traders in Wednesday's successful appeal had originally been convicted of a single count of conspiracy to defraud as result of alleged attempts to influence financial benchmark rates.

Two other bankers have already had their names cleared.

Tom Hayes, a former trader at Swiss bank UBS, was the first banker jailed. He won a 10-year legal battle last year to have his conviction overturned at the Supreme Court in July 2025.

His victory alongside that of fellow trader Carlo Palombo, who was jailed in 2019, paved the way for others to challenge their convictions.

Hayes and Palombo argued they were wrongly prosecuted for what were normal commercial practices in order to appease public anger towards the banks over the financial crisis.

Pabon, 48, who had his name cleared on Wednesday, hailed Hayes for his refusal to "let it go". He had "pushed this through" for the rest of them, he said.

The Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original case against the traders, has not opposed the appeals.

Barclays bank has been contacted for comment.

The latest ruling means just two traders still have convictions over interest rate rigging - former Deutsche Bank trader Christian Bittar and former Barclays trader Peter Johnson.

Bittar was jailed in 2018 after pleading guilty and served two years in prison. He will challenge his conviction on 9 October.

Johnson was the original whistleblower calling attention to the Libor scandal but pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance of winning at trial. He also hopes to appeal.

Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 11:51:52 GMT

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.

The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.

For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.

But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.

In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.

You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.

And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.

When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.

So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.

The development of the Thalidomide drug is an example of this. In the 1950s it was prescribed to pregnant women suffering with morning sickness. But it is a chiral molecule - the right-handed version is an effective treatment, but the left-hand is toxic.

The original drug given was a mixture of the two, and it was later discovered that the body will convert between the two. The result was thousands of children, born to women who took the drug, developed severe disabilities.

Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."

By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule.

Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously.

"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible.

Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule.

In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed.

"Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat".

At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field.

Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society".

"Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added.

Prof Angus Davison, from the University of Nottingham, studies the biology of chirality and said that the Nobel-winning chemistry could help reveal how and why life favours "one-handedness".

"In ways that we don't yet quite understand, the chirality of the basic building blocks of life ends up making bodies that are themselves also chiral," he told BBC News.

This was the foundation, he explained, of our hearts being on left hand side of our bodies and snail shells that coil to the right.

Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said the research awarded this year's prize has become part of "our basic understanding of how chemistry functions".

He said showing how a mirror image is created is "probably the most fundamental question in life - because somehow that happened four billion years ago when life was created. And now we have, for the first time, mimicked that in the lab".

Stephen King's Carrie returns to explore the horrors of social media

BBC News Wed, 07 Oct 2026 08:39:36 GMT

Adaptations, remakes and reboots are all the rage right now, and there’s often one question that crops up - why?

See also "what's the point?" and "do we need another one?" whenever a story is resurrected from the past.

Carrie, Prime Video's new TV series based on Stephen King's debut novel, has been no exception.

It's not the first time the tale of high school bullies and supernatural powers has been adapted for the screen.

Director Brian de Palma's 1976 movie version is a horror classic, with some of its most famous scenes and imagery widely considered iconic within the genre.

But the cast and creator of the latest version, which drags Carrie's story forward 50 years into a world of social media, have been telling BBC Newsbeat why they believe it's still relevant in 2026.

Fans of the novel have been quick to complain the new version of Carrie is not "book accurate", pointing out that she was originally an abrasive, even unlikeable character.

In the TV adaptation, Carrie has been raised behind closed doors by her paranoid father and deeply religious mother, and only enters school after a tragedy reveals her existence to authorities.

Audiences see a different version of the character in the show - one who's naive, but open and eager to learn new things.

"There's a lot of opinions, and I purposely avoided the original movie and and the book before filming because I hadn't seen it or read it," Summer H Howell, who plays Carrie, tells Newsbeat.

"And I wanted to create this new, light version of Carrie that was excited to get out of her house and just curious about the world and people."

However, the 22-year-old actress says the journey her character goes on is not so different, and argues it's still relevant today.

"It's the story of an outsider, and bullying has not gone away in 50 years," she says.

"If anything, it's just gotten worse with social media."

Social media plays a huge part in the adaptation by horror director Mike Flanagan, who's best known for series such as The Haunting of Hill House.

In his version of Carrie, some of the most famous scenes, including the dramatic prom moment, are adapted to a world where everything is filmed and shared online.

Alison Thornton, who plays chief bully Chris Hargensen, says social media "is kind of a villain in the show".

"You can post something, or someone will take a video of something, and the fact that it can be permanently online is actually quite terrifying," she says.

Thornton says the adaptation aims to show how online posts can have "repercussions in real life".

Showrunner Flanagan tells Newsbeat it would have been "impossible to ignore the impact social media has had in changing the way we see each other".

Fifty years ago, he says, bullying would have been relatively "private", and confined to "the classroom, in the halls, in the school".

But that's all changed, says Flanagan.

"It's happening with the audience of the entire digital world and enshrined forever, permanently on these platforms.

"It's a whole different ball game that way," he says.

Carrie is the latest project from Prime Video targeted at Gen Z viewers based on a popular novel.

The Summer I Turned Pretty, Your Fault: London, and Off Campus have been huge hits for the streamer, and it's leaned into trends such as BookTok to generate interest in the shows.

Josie Totah, who plays Chris's sidekick Tina, agrees remakes and adaptations are popular, but says she would only get involved with one if the "intention" felt right.

"No one wants to just remake something for the sake of remaking it," she says.

"'Why now?' - unless that can be answered thoroughly, I don't think that I would want to do it."

There are worries from fans that revisiting existing works leaves less space for original stories.

Totah says projects such as this year's indie horror hit Obsession also deserve to be championed.

"Those are equally as important as the ones that we've already told in the past, if not maybe a little bit more," she says.

So far, Flanagan's version of Carrie has had a mostly positive response from critics, with an 85% positive rating on review website Rotten Tomatoes.

Most praised the performances and social commentary, although some reviewers felt it wasn't as scary as earlier versions and accused it of sanding down some of the original characters' harder edges.

The verdict from fans remains to be seen.

Flanagan hasn't just expanded on the original story, but has also made some fairly major changes, possibly laying the ground for further series to be made.

"I try to think about how fans will feel because I'm a Stephen King fan first," he says.

"So I have very strong opinions about changes that are made in adaptation."

Flanagan has brought other Stephen King novels to the screen before, but those have tended to be much more faithful to the source material.

Some of his best-known projects, reinventions of The Haunting of Hill House by author Shirley Jackson and The Fall of the House of Usher by Edgar Allan Poe, have been based on works by long-deceased authors.

"I've just never done this with an author who's still alive or one with whom I already have a very intensely productive working relationship," he says.

"I hope people are going to look at these changes and say: 'Oh, this is actually why it makes good sense to tell this story again today'."

Carrie will launch on Prime Video on 7 October

194-year-old tortoise has exceptional DNA repair systems that fight off ageing

New Scientist October 07, 2026

The world’s oldest known land animal – Jonathan the giant tortoise – has had his genome probed for the first time. This has revealed that parts of his genome to do with mitochondrial function are as efficient as those of a 5-year-old member of his species. Efficient mitochondria may give his DNA repair systems more energy to fight off the effects of ageing, enabling him to live to an estimated age of 194.

What’s more, some of his genetic changes seem similar to those of supercentenarians. “This study adds to the body of evidence that the mechanisms of ageing may be conserved across species,” says Stephen Clark at the Kallel Foundation, a non-profit organisation focused on interventions to extend human healthspan, in Nashville, Tennessee.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea), and Napoleon Bonaparte are the two most famous residents of St Helena island in the South Atlantic. Napoleon arrived at the remote British territory after he was exiled in 1815, while Jonathan is thought to have been shipped there, possibly from Aldabra Atoll, in 1882. Jonathan arrived as a fully grown adult that was thought to already have half a century under his belt, putting him at around 194 years old today.

Advertisement

The researchers calculated that Aldabra tortoises have an average lifespan of around 80 years, but they can live much longer. To understand the mechanisms behind Jonathan’s extraordinary longevity, Clark and his colleagues have studied his genome.

“I firmly believe we can learn about the global mechanisms of ageing by looking at the exceptions,” says Manel Esteller at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute in Barcelona, Spain, who led a study into a 117-year-old woman, once officially the world’s oldest person.

Free newsletter

Esteller and his team found that the woman had exceptionally efficient mitochondrial function, which led Clark and his colleagues to suspect Jonathan similarly had “very efficient and very young” mitochondria, says Clark.

They had to study his genome via saliva samples and cheek swabs. This was because St Helena authorities refused their requests to draw Jonathan’s blood, given his fame and the risk of infection.

This was a major limitation, because it meant the researchers were unable to isolate large pieces of DNA, which are more stable in blood. Instead, they had to assemble fragments from Jonathan’s saliva, where DNA is more prone to bacterial contamination, and fill in the gaps using DNA from another Aldabra tortoise.

Once they had made the best possible composite of his genome, they compared it to the DNA of four other Aldabra tortoises. “We found 287 genes that had changes in them that were unique to him,” says Clark.

A clinical trial to reverse age-related vision conditions using stem cell treatment could finally deliver on the promise of a major discovery in ageing and regeneration made 20 years ago, says columnist Graham Lawton

Of these genes, 41 are though to be functionally significant, meaning they actively contribute to an organism’s biology, survival and regulation. A dozen of them were also found in ageing databases of the genes of other long-lived animal species.

Parts of Jonathan’s genome to do with mitochondrial function were as young as a 5-year-old Aldabra, says Clark. “This, in turn, has helped him manage the effects of ageing by giving the DNA repair systems more energy from the mitochondria to fight off the effects of ageing.”

Kousuke Hashimoto at the University of Osaka, Japan, says the work is “fascinating”, but notes that Jonathan’s genome was compared against that of only a few other tortoises, which may have unique genetic changes themselves.

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. adw8887

Neanderthal Europe was as much a wooden age as a stone age

New Scientist October 07, 2026

Wooden tools, weapons, building materials and domestic items discovered in a Spanish cave challenge the assumption that Neanderthals’ technological life was based primarily on stone.

The finds have given an unprecedented glimpse into everyday Neanderthal life and are a rare opportunity to recover part of their missing world, says Josep Vallverdú at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution in Spain.

“Neanderthal technology was not only made of stone; it was also made of wood,” he says.

Advertisement

Before the Stone Age: Were the first tools made from plants not rocks?

“The archaeological record gives us a very biased picture of prehistoric technology. We see the stone because it survives, while a huge part of their material culture has simply disappeared.”

Vallverdú and his colleagues have now completed the first systematic review of nearly 600 wooden objects, all between 40,000 and 62,000 years old.

The finds have been collected by generations of archaeologists since the 1980s, excavated at a rock shelter site called Abric Romaní near Barcelona. They include timber imprints in travertine – a rock rich in calcium carbonate that precipitates out of water in certain environments. The rock preserves the patterns of the wood grain even though the timber long ago rotted away. Charred artefacts and actual preserved timber have also been found at the site.

See Alice Roberts at New Scientist Live 2026

The researchers’ first job was to determine exactly which pieces were used or made by Neanderthals. Only 13 qualified. Most of the remainder consist of trunks, branches, twigs, roots and firewood accumulations.

Maria Gema Chacón, also at the Catalan Institute, says the researchers have been surprised at how “complex Neanderthal woodworking could be, and how well they understood the properties of wood”, with the two spears being especially striking to her.

“Producing long, straight shafts and shaping them deliberately into pointed weapons required planning, skill and careful selection of the raw material,” says Chacón.

The technological behaviours preserved at Abric Romaní are comparable to those documented for Homo sapiens, she says.

Stick shaped by ancient humans is the oldest known wooden tool

Other finds included a mysterious wooden tripod, as well as timber trays reminiscent, in terms of likely utility, of the coolamons traditionally used by Indigenous Australians to carry food and water. Some of the wooden objects appear to be structural poles.

But perhaps the item that has most surprised the team is a “club-like” object that has no precedent from any other palaeolithic site.

Palmira Saladié, also at the Catalan Institute, says the club-like object is “not simply a stick with a thicker end”.

“There is a distinct narrow handle and an enlarged, asymmetrical head, giving the object a much more complex and deliberate form,” she says. “This particular configuration is what we have not been able to find a convincing parallel for in the prehistoric record.”

Vallverdú says the site shows that wood was a normal and important part of Neanderthals’ everyday life.

Why early humans radically changed their toolkits 200,000 years ago

“We have evidence of woodworking across many archaeological levels and over thousands of years, and the objects are associated with very different activities: hunting, domestic tasks, containers and the organisation of living spaces,” he says.

Chris Stringer at the Natural History Museum in London says the archaeological record of wooden artefacts has been “severely constrained” by the generally poor preservation of organic materials.

The finds reveal a much wider technological repertoire of woodworking skills, he says.

An analysis of ancient human artefacts finds that the container, a simple but critical tool, may have originated 500,000 years ago. Columnist Michael Marshall explores how slings, ostrich eggs and wooden trays helped our ancestors survive

“This is of course evidence from only one site, in one area, and one time span,” says Stringer, “so it’s just the tip of the iceberg in terms of a whole and mostly hidden technology that ran in parallel with the much better-known stone tools of the Palaeolithic.”

“Wood, plant fibres, hides, bone and other organic materials must have been central to daily life, but they normally disappear,” says Mariana Nabais, also at the Catalan Institute. “So when a site like Abric Romaní preserves wooden imprints and charred wooden objects, it is almost like suddenly seeing the missing half of the toolkit.”

Naoki Morimoto at Kyoto University in Japan describes the wooden objects as “remarkable”.

“Preserved organic materials are truly rare, and they reveal a ‘hidden’ aspect of Neanderthals that we have been missing,” says Morimoto.

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aeh2287

Don’t know where to start with AI? Kevin Roose’s new book has answers

New Scientist October 07, 2026

The AGI ChroniclesKevin RooseSimon & Schuster (UK) Farrar, Straus and Giroux (US)

I think about AI almost every day. Part of this is a hazard of being a science journalist, while part is simply that I think large language models (LLMs), the technical juice behind products like ChatGPT, are fascinating in both their flaws and successes. Even if you aren’t as AI-preoccupied as I am, you probably find it a tricky topic to escape, not least because we seem to get daily hysterical warnings about a coming AI apocalypse. But what is incredible is that the current AI era only really kicked off with the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

Sure, researchers had been tinkering with LLMs long before they became products, and many other forms of AI had previously taken the world by storm, such as IBM’s Watson in 2011 or DeepMind’s AlphaGo in 2016. What made 2022 different is that it was the year that anyone with an internet connection could easily start talking to a computer and get something reasonably comprehensible back.

Advertisement

Since then, the progress of AI has felt like a rollercoaster the world can’t get off. It is easy to forget how we got here after just a few years, which is why The AGI Chronicles by Kevin Roose is a very welcome read, documenting the past decade from the founding of OpenAI to the present day. It is a story that involves names you are probably familiar with – Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis – and many more that you aren’t, but who have played an equally important role in getting to where we are today.

Roose’s argument is that the race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI) is the 21st-century equivalent of the Manhattan Project to build a nuclear weapon during the second world war. One key difference between then and now is that much of the work today is being done by private companies, not government scientists, potentially making it much harder to document. Thankfully, Roose says he interviewed more than 150 insiders at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, and it shows – the access here is excellent.

One important thing to know is that Roose is self-declared “AGI-pilled”, Silicon Valley lingo meaning he believes that AI will achieve general, human-level intelligence in the near future. This AGI-is-coming lens warps his view of recent history and aligns him with internal AI company narratives more than I would like. In fact, his epilogue reveals that he thinks AGI is essentially already here, as long as you downgrade your expectations of what AGI means, which feels slightly pointless to me.

Despite this, The AGI Chronicles is an excellent historical read. It details how OpenAI was created by Altman, Musk and others out of fears that DeepMind would get to AGI first, how fallings-out led to Musk leaving and, separately, how Anthropic was created as an apparently more safety-first AI company.

Roose’s argument is that the race to build AGI is the 21st-century equivalent of the Manhattan Project

His dive into the history of the AI safety movement and its various factions also helps explain why AI executives can warn about AI destroying humanity at the same time as asking for billions of dollars to build it. There is some overlap with Supremacy by Parmy Olson, but her history goes deeper and her analysis is more sceptical, while Roose’s access is better, so it is worth reading both books.

Roose’s book is also an excellent technical read, explaining the mechanics behind LLMs, some of the crucial discoveries of the past decade and how the companies overcame various technical hurdles along the way. These two strands, historical and technical, give you a full primer on modern AI while never falling into textbook mode.

Roose has done an impressive job of covering an incredibly fast-moving field. Supremacy suffered in its final section, which was essentially just a rapid summary of everything Olson could squeeze in before her press deadline, but Roose has pushed right up to the limit and covered the “agentic” developments of early 2026, when AI tools were increasingly writing computer code and becoming more powerful. The only events he misses are the emergence of AI as a maths powerhouse earlier this year, and the Hugging Face hacking incident revealed in July. Both of these will be an important part of future AI histories, but the present moves too fast for publishing house speed.

Have we found the world’s nichest science-themed tourist attraction?

New Scientist October 07, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Feedback is on a quest to find the most niche science-themed tourist attractions in the world – by being told about them, rather than by actually visiting anything, as that would require a budget.

Reader Earle McNeil advises us to explore Zagreb, Croatia. This city “must have the most museums per square kilometre of any town on the planet”, he says. “This then has to include the oddest.” Earle evinces two examples: the Museum of Broken Relationships and the Museum of Hangovers. We initially didn’t believe this, but we looked them up and they are indeed real.

Advertisement

The Museum of Broken Relationships was founded by two former lovers: film producer Olinka Vištica and sculptor Dražen Grubišić. After breaking up, they joked that they should set up a museum for all the personal items left over from their relationship, and a few years later, they did exactly that. Two decades on, the museum is described by visitzagreb. hr as “the most popular museum in Zagreb”, and there is now a second permanent site in Chiang Mai, Thailand.

Feedback isn’t sure this really counts as science-themed, except in the absolute broadest sense of the word “psychology”, in which case Heated Rivalry is also scientific and New Scientist should assign someone to review season two.

However, the Museum of Hangovers surely does count, filled as it is with chemistry and neurophysiology. Visitors can try crossing a tilted floor while wearing goggles that let you experience what it’s like to walk while drunk, or take the wheel of a drunk-driving simulator to see just how badly alcohol affects your ability to drive (spoiler: a lot).

While researching these two institutions, Feedback fell down a glorious Wikipedia rabbit hole. We first learned about the Museum of Failure, a touring exhibition most recently found in Paris, that collects failed and unpopular products like the Apple Newton, Betamax video cassettes and the Tesla Cybertruck.

From there, we wandered afield from our science-themed mandate, but we do have to tell you that there is a Museum of Bad Art and that it has, or at least had, a competitor: the Museum of Particularly Bad Art.

In our 19 September instalment, we reported that there are now thousands of scientific papers that reference song titles or lyrics by the Beatles in their headings. This prompted readers to wonder which other artists are being heavily referenced by researchers.

Simon Shuel wonders if anyone has done a similar analysis for the work of musician Frank Zappa. Feedback prowled the internet for a while, to little avail. All we could find were some species named after him. For instance, the spider Pachygnatha zappa was so named because it has markings that resemble Zappa’s moustache.

Meanwhile, reader Jonathan Arch was recently alerted to a paper that uses a rather tortured Shakespeare reference in its title: “Through beta2 or not through beta2—That’s the question”. He first asked if Feedback might perform a systematic search for lines from Shakespeare in scientific papers. Readers are welcome to hope for this eventuality, but oft expectation fails.

Happily, Jonathan then flagged a 2005 paper from BMJ by Neville Goodman, “From Shakespeare to Star Trek and beyond: A Medline search for literary and other allusions in biomedical titles”. Between 1951 and mid-2005, Goodman found more than 1400 Shakespeare allusions in the titles of medical papers. There was a strong clustering effect in the allusions: “a third of them to ‘What’s in a name’ and another third to Hamlet—mostly to ‘To be or not to be’. ” However, Goodman did find some gems, like “Much ado about the null hypothesis” and “All that is excreted does not glister: Or why do we keep on collecting urine to measure creatinine clearance?”.

Goodman was disappointed to find that no obstetrical papers were titled “Once more unto the breech”. Feedback is happy to report that this gap has since been filled by a 2015 paper: “Once More Unto the Breech: Planned vaginal delivery compared with planned Cesarean delivery”.

We await with interest reader examples of papers referring to the works of R. E. M., Dolly Parton, Dan Brown and other artists of various calibres.

The roots of nominative determinism run deep. Reader Peter Mayer was reading a story in The New York Times entitled “Plumbing the Shipwrecks of an Infamous Pirate Cove“, about marine archaeology in the Bahamas. This mentioned “the godfather of Nassau’s pirates”, active in the early 1700s, one Benjamin Hornigold. Stop sniggering at the back there: the surname is apparently derived from an English place name.

Meanwhile, author Charlie Jane Anders took a break from writing her new Star Trek comic to tell us about a recent episode of American Campus Podcast. This was built around “an interview with a British professor of pharmacology who studies the history of drugs going back to their earliest botanical roots. His name: Rod Flower”.

Feedback was shocked to learn that Flower was flagged in New Scientist‘s pick of the best popular science books in July. Once again, if only we read our own magazine with proper care, we would probably find writing this column a lot easier.

What forces act on fluid moving through a pipe to make it spiral?

New Scientist October 07, 2026

What forces are acting on a particle of fluid that makes it start spiralling or moving helically down a pipe instead of flowing smoothly?

Ron DippoldSan Diego, California, US

The main players are the inertia of the fluid, the friction and adhesion between the pipe and liquid, and any turbulence due to variations in the material or temperature of the pipe wall.

Advertisement

Liquid and gas are both fluids and their flow is governed by the Navier-Stokes equations, which are non-linear. Microscopic defects cause much larger vortices, similar to how a fast-moving truck can be sent flying in another direction after hitting a pebble.

The simplest factor to understand is the inertia of all the fluid travelling down the pipe from gravity or pumping. In a perfectly temperature-controlled, frictionless pipe, it would be smooth and straight-flowing everywhere, even with kinks in the pipe. This is called laminar flow.

But nothing is frictionless, and chemical and electrical forces attract the liquid to the pipe wall. So, fluid at the edges is slowed by contact with the pipe – this cylinder of fluid that is slowed is called the boundary layer. If the pipe is perfectly straight and long, this actually helps calm things, but as soon as there’s a curve, it creates a spiral.

Liquid tends to hug the inside curve because of that boundary layer – this is called the Coanda effect. You can see this for yourself with a sink and spoon. Run a small, steady stream of water from your faucet, then slowly move the back of the spoon into the stream. In the absence of friction and the Coanda effect, you would expect to see the water just fall straight down, but instead, you will see it hug the surface of the spoon and come off the tip of the spoon at an angle. Back in our pipe, that means the fluid isn’t going straight down the pipe, which means it starts spiralling. Any curve, valve or pump will give you this spiralling.

And no pipe is completely smooth. Even “smooth” glass has microscopic defects. When the liquid hits a tiny defect, or even if there’s a slight temperature variation – since hot fluid is less dense and rises – a small amount is deflected. This creates a small eddy, or swirl. If the liquid is moving slowly enough, the boundary layer acts as a damper and these just die out. Once the fluid reaches a critical speed, however, the damping can’t keep up, and this is where the non-linearity comes in. Since the fluid closer to the centre of the pipe is moving faster than the fluid at the edges, it stretches these swirls down the pipe. And, like a skater pulling in their arms, a stretched, narrower swirl spins faster and harder, pulling energy from the fluid to grow longer and narrower. These swirls don’t cancel each other out; they just feed on each other and twist into crazy shapes. You get what’s called turbulent flow, for obvious reasons. You may see spiralling, but also unpredictable thrashing and surging around. Any trapped gas bubbles make things much worse as they tumble around wildly.

So, how do you stop this? Slowing down the liquid helps, but you usually don’t want much less flow. If it’s below the critical turbulence speed, you can run it through a long, straight pipe and it will settle down thanks to the drag from the boundary layer. In the best case, this length is about 15 times the diameter of the pipe after a single curve, but can be much longer – it depends on the viscosity of your liquid, the roughness of the pipe and how convoluted your pipes are.

Like a skater pulling in their arms, a stretched, narrower swirl spins faster, pulling energy from the fluid to grow

If we really need laminar flow immediately, we use flow conditioners. These divide the big pipe into many smaller pipes for a bit or just add flat plates with carefully designed holes cut in them. These kill any large swirls, which have most of the energy, because the swirls are much larger than the holes. And in smaller pipes, 15 times the diameter of the pipe is a much shorter distance.

The downside is that you are slowing the fluid by cutting down the pipe volume – so, if you need to get the final flow rate higher, you have to pump harder, which means, yes, more turbulence upstream.

So just invent frictionless pipes to solve all this, and please remember me when your royalty cheques arrive.

Why gatekeeping is needed in the age of AI

New Scientist October 07, 2026

Gatekeeping is a dirty word. For decades, the internet has steadily eroded the power of gatekeepers and democratised access to information. Attempts to resist that are seen as censorship or elitism, neither of which anyone wants to be accused of.

But our new AI era may flip the script. Social media gives anyone a voice, breaking the old model of one-to-many broadcasting from institutions, but no one is forced to listen to this cacophony. Large language models that extrude text at speed are now changing this, with institutions under a many-to-one assault by information they must attend to.

This shows up in many forms – indeed, including in literal forms, as people use AI in their bureaucratic interactions with courts, schools, local officials and more. These systems can’t deal with the volume of information and are clogging up. The implicit gatekeepers that kept such submissions under control – time, ability, access – have fallen to AI.

Advertisement

The same thing is happening in science. Mathematicians are calling for more mathematicians in the face of an AI onslaught. Meanwhile, the preprint server arXiv has seen submissions double in the past two years. Although preprints aren’t formally peer-reviewed, arXiv’s small team ensures minimum standards, and it is overwhelmed. In response, it recently announced it would limit submissions to two per month – still remarkably high, with few scientists producing 24 papers a year of any quality.

A kind of gatekeeping is the only way institutions can survive the AI era

This kind of gatekeeping is the only way institutions can survive the AI era, unless we want to fully hand over the reins to AI and let it handle inputs as well as outputs. But there are good reasons not to. As we report, tools for verifying mathematical conclusions are at risk from attack by AI, so keeping a human in the loop remains the only way for us to have a handle on the truth. That goes even more so for areas that are harder to verify than mathematics, which is essentially everything. So let’s cheer on the gatekeepers – they are going to have a lot of work to do.

Te Aitanga a Māhaki withdraws from Te Karaka stopbank hearing

New Zealand Herald October 07, 2026

The preferred stopbank alignment design in Te Karaka, approved by Gisborne District councillors last year. Graphic / Gisborne District Council

An iwi has accused Gisborne District Council of not acting with integrity in its dealings with it during a significant flood-resilience plan.

Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki has pulled out of a hearing about a stopbank upgrade in Te Karaka, and has withdrawn its submission on the resource consent sought by the council.

The council has been progressing its Tairāwhiti Flood Resilience Plan to reduce risk to life and property through options identified in reports and discussions with iwi, hapū and local communities, to be completed by 2028.

It has been holding meetings with multiple communities this week to provide updates on flood resilience plans and funding in North Gisborne City, Ūawa (Tolaga Bay), Tokomaru Bay, Mākarika, Tikitiki and Te Ārai.

As part of the wider programme, the stopbank upgrade in Te Karaka had been endorsed by Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki, and a consent application for the project was filed in April 2026.

The flood defences of Te Karaka, northwest of Gisborne, were overwhelmed during Cyclone Gabrielle and hundreds of people were evacuated.

However, in an email last week, the iwi withdrew from a hearing about the upgrade and its submission on the consent sought by the council.

The letter accused the council of not acting with integrity in its dealings with Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki.

Chief executive of Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki Trust and lead negotiator for Te Tiriti, Willie Te Aho, wrote on behalf of the iwi, the trust, Turanga Leasing Company and Toitū Tairāwhiti Builtsmart.

Council staff, councillors, East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick and media received the letter in which Te Aho wrote the withdrawal followed attempts to “clarify the partnership” with council community lifelines director Tim Barry online and via email.

“We were regrettably unable to maintain an understanding of partnership with Tim Barry acting on behalf of the Gisborne District Council to the extent that Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki believes it is unsafe to proceed on this matter with the Gisborne District Council.”

Te Aho wrote that the iwi supported the process so “concerns that have been expressed by members of the Te Karaka community in public meetings and in writing through submissions and evidence could be properly responded to in an open and transparent manner and then independently assessed”.

Following these discussions with Barry, the iwi withdrew from all engagement with the council.

“While we respect that the Gisborne District Council has a statutory role and determines matters under those statutory roles, we do not now believe that the Gisborne District Council actually acts with integrity with regard to Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki.”

Local Democracy Reporting has contacted Te Aho to get clarification on comments in the letter and any updates.

Barry said the council remained committed to delivering the project and protecting the community.

“Since Cyclone Gabrielle, council has worked closely with Te Aitanga-a- Māhaki and the wider community through the flood resilience investigations and development of the stopbank proposal.”

The partnership significantly contributed to the project’s progression, including consenting work underway, he said.

“We acknowledge Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki’s decision to withdraw its support. While this is disappointing at such a critical stage, particularly given the collective work undertaken to date, we appreciate that the iwi is not opposing the project and continues to recognise its importance to the community.”

The council would seek further clarification about the situation while remaining focused on the project.

“Our focus remains on maintaining momentum on this critical flood protection project while working to continue engaging constructively and in good faith with Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki,” Barry said.

Barry said this week the council was committed to developing a proposal and was working with “existing and new information to do so”.

The council could not provide further comment on the “new information” as discussions were ongoing.

The Royal New Zealand Air Force (RNZAF) said the aircraft were in the country for training, with flights scheduled through to Sunday – and some including altitudes as low as 150m-300m.

Today’s flight plans were expected to be similar to yesterday’s, when an RNZAF C-130J Hercules joined the two US aircraft for flights across the North Island, a New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) spokesperson said.

The group departed RNZAF Base Auckland and travelled down the east coast to Base Ohakea in Manawatū, carrying out airdrops at Raumai – with further airdrops planned at the same location today, the spokesperson said.

From Ohakea, yesterday’s flights were due to return to Auckland via the west coast.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

Tomorrow and Saturday, one C-17 is expected to fly at high altitude down the west coast of the South Island, through Milford Sound and Lake Te Anau and over Queenstown.

It would then head north over the Southern Alps and turn west at Nelson before returning to Auckland, the spokesperson said.

Both C-17s are scheduled to fly from Auckland to Base Ohakea on Sunday.

The RNZAF said the programme was weather-dependent and could change at short notice, and low-level flying would take place between 9am and 3pm.

On Sunday the C-17s would return to Hawaii carrying two RNZAF NH90 helicopters, which will take part in a US Army exercise, the NZDF spokesperson said.

Grandparents raising grandchildren: Woman in her 70s starts again with three boys

New Zealand Herald October 07, 2026

Mary is raising her three grandsons in her 70s after becoming their fulltime carer seven years ago. Photo / Nikoline Arns, Unsplash

At an age when she expected to have more freedom, Mary found herself starting over with three young boys.

Now in her 70s, Mary, whose name has been changed to protect the children’s privacy, is raising her three grandsons. The youngest is primary school-aged and the eldest is in his early teens.

The Bay of Plenty grandmother is one of about 20,000 non-parental caregivers raising children in New Zealand, which includes a large proportion of grandparents who have stepped up for round two of child-rearing.

Mary’s daughter and grandsons moved in with her years ago after her daughter’s relationship broke down.

Mary was still working at the time and increasingly found herself looking after the children when their mother couldn’t.

“One day I came back and the kitchen sink had overflowed and she was asleep.

“So I had enough and said she had to move on, like leave the kids.”

She became the boys’ fulltime carer when the youngest was still a baby.

“[It’s] sad for their parents, I think, because they’ve missed out, especially the little one … It’s all he’s ever known.”

Mary had already raised four children. And now she is doing it again, this time alone after being widowed.

“At my age, starting all over again, looking after, bringing up kids … I do the best I can.”

She has had years to learn what makes each boy tick, but Mary said raising them had been harder than she expected.

She said she had forgotten how much cooking was involved and the boys’ preferences made it harder to recreate the simple family meals she remembered from raising her own children.

Mary also said keeping up with their energy was a challenge.

“I wasn’t prepared to be sitting at a beach all day and they miss out on that.”

Mary has since left her job and has settled into life as a “stay-at-home nan” and said she is naturally a homebody.

The boys see their father on weekends and school holidays give her time to herself.

“They’re away on holiday now … It’s my respite.”

She said those breaks were important for her to catch up with friends and maintain her own life.

Mary found support through Grandparents Raising Grandchildren and said knowing she was not alone made a difference.

“There are a lot of other grandparents raising grandkids for the same reason.”

Mary said she still struggled at times with having to start child-rearing again at an age she expected would come with more freedom.

Her focus now is on giving the boys stability and seeing them through school.

“I just want them to stay at school because they’re quite bright kids.”

Grandparents Raising Grandchildren general manager Braden Clark said his data showed that 85% of children came into their grandparents’ care because of care and protection concerns.

Those included family violence, parental substance abuse, mental health issues and other child protection concerns.

The organisation supported grandparents and other whānau carers through one-on-one advocacy, training and education, and peer support groups across the country.

Clark said grandparents faced emotional and social challenges as they adjusted to a life they had not expected.

“They might be working and all of a sudden they’re caring for a 2-year-old.

“They’ve got to juggle work and doing that, plus they’re older, so it’s harder to do that sort of thing. It takes up more energy.”

Children coming into their care may have experienced trauma, which could lead to behavioural and emotional challenges, he said.

Relationships with the children’s parents could also be complicated, while some grandparents found themselves isolated from friends who were at a different stage of life.

“They can lose friendships as a result and not have that social support in that same way.”

But alongside the challenges were rewards, Clark said.

“Pretty much all of the grandparents we talk to would say they would do it again in a heartbeat.

“They get such a special relationship with their grandchildren.”

He said grandparents often felt a deep sense of pride as they watched the children overcome challenges and reach milestones.

Clark said the public often did not realise how many families were in this position.

About 20,000 children in New Zealand lived with someone other than their parents, and Clark said grandparents made up a large proportion of those carers.

“It’s actually really common. And lots of the grandparents feel alone, they feel isolated, they feel like they’re the only ones doing it.”

He said that feeling of isolation often changed once they connected with other grandparents in the same position.

“One of the most common things we hear is, ‘Oh my gosh, there are other people doing this as well’.”

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post.

Rotorua QE Health building: National to explore new surgery, dialysis centre if re-elected

New Zealand Herald October 07, 2026

The National Party will explore using the former QE Health building as a new elective surgery and dialysis centre in Rotorua if re-elected. National’s Health spokesperson Simeon Brown (left) and Rotorua MP Todd McClay pictured outside the building.

The National Party will explore using the former QE Health building as a new elective surgery and dialysis centre in Rotorua if re-elected.

QE Health, which provided health and wellness services, went into liquidation in November, ending its more than 80-year history in Rotorua.

It closed in December after failing to secure a buyer for the business.

The company reported in the first liquidator’s report it had been unable to generate enough income to cover its costs.

QE Health started in 1942 as a temporary hospital to rehabilitate World War II soldiers. It opened to the wider public in 1948.

It moved to a new $19 million purpose-built health and wellness facility on Hinemaru St in 2023, which taxpayers contributed $8m towards through a Government loan.

The first liquidator’s report, released in November, showed QE Health owed at least $13m across 132 creditors, including $8.04m to the Crown and $2.5m to the Rotorua Trust.

The second liquidator’s report, released in June, said the Crown and Rotorua Trust received about 1c on the dollar from its loans.

In a joint statement today, Rotorua MP Todd McClay and National’s health spokesman Simeon Brown said they met with landowner Pukeroa Oruawhata Trust to discuss the “suitability” of the former QE Health building as a new elective surgery and dialysis centre in Rotorua.

Trust chief executive Mark Gibb took the two MPs around the facility and spoke about its healthcare history.

Brown said he was impressed with the building and saw its potential for the Rotorua population.

“If re-elected, National will progress a business case to explore delivering surgery and dialysis from this existing facility, so more people in Rotorua can get the care they need closer to home,” Brown said.

Reducing waitlists and wait times was a priority, which was why it reintroduced targets for the health system in 2024.

He said the proportion of patients waiting less than four months for elective treatment had improved in the Lakes district, which includes Rotorua and Taupō.

Health NZ data showed it had lifted from 66% to 81.1% in a year. The target for 2030 is 95%.

McClay said the QE Health building was purpose-built for healthcare and only opened in 2023, “so it makes sense to look at whether it could be put to good use for our community”.

He cited its history of caring for World War II soldiers and people with arthritis and rheumatism.

McClay said more elective surgery theatres and an enhanced dialysis service would mean Rotorua people would not have to travel to Tauranga or Hamilton when demand was high.

“That matters to a lot, especially for those who need regular treatment like dialysis.”

The Bay of Plenty Times previously reported on a Tauranga woman who had been travelling to Waikato Hospital three days a week for haemodialysis because she could not get treatment at Tauranga Hospital.

The former interim chief executive of QE Health previously told the Rotorua Daily Post the primary reason for closure was Health NZ’s “lack of meaningful increases” since 2018 to contract funding, making it “impossible” to cover operating costs.

Emails released under the Official Information Act showed “critical” funding increases were requested in September 2025 to keep the business afloat.

Health NZ told QE Health there was “no wriggle room” for funding increases that financial year.

Following its liquidation, a potential sale of the business collapsed after Health NZ refused to transfer its contracts, which represented 80% of the business’s income.

Health NZ has said it does not believe its contracting decisions caused QE Health’s closure, and that it understood the decision to place QE Health into liquidation was not based on whether service contracts would transfer.

Patient services formerly provided by QE Health were now being delivered by Health NZ teams and contractors.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

National is proposing to introduce random drug testing of beneficiaries and would cut the level of support for some on the Jobseeker benefit by as much as $81 per week, expected to save a National-led Government almost $600 million.

It follows the coalition Government’s decision to end Jobseeker payments to 18- and 19-year-olds whose parents earn more than $65,000 coming into force next month.

The party’s social development spokeswoman Louise Upston today argued that National’s new five-point plan focused the welfare system on directing beneficiaries towards employment and ensuring the system was “fair and affordable for taxpayers”, insisting it isn’t “about punishing someone because they haven’t found a job”.

The first of National’s five initiatives was to introduce random drug testing, proposing 10,000 tests in the first year and increasing in later years.

Under the policy, Upston said a first failed test would be recorded and a second fail would result in a clinical alcohol and drug assessment. Beneficiaries could be sanctioned as a result of failed tests, including possible cuts to their benefit.

National’s policy document estimated the cost of the drug-testing scheme to be about $1.5 million per year and expected it to be funded from the Ministry of Social Development’s baselines.

The party also wanted to reduce the Jobseeker benefit for those who had accessed it for two of the previous three years.

Proposed to come into force from April 2028, recipients without children would have their benefit cut by $48.05 per week based on current figures.

Couples without children would receive $552.18 a week, an effective reduction of $81.76 per week. Recipients with dependent children would face a smaller cut of $24.02 per week.

The party noted actual reductions would reflect Jobseeker rates in 2028, after annual increases to reflect inflation over the next two years.

The change was expected to save a future National-led Government $572m over the four-year forecast period, almost all of the total plan’s estimated savings of $583m.

The remaining three items of National’s plan included doubling the non-entitlement period for beneficiaries who repeatedly leave employment without a sufficient reason from 13 weeks to 26 weeks, extending the minimum residence period to qualify for main benefits from two years to five years and providing more “work-focused support” for 30,000 jobseekers who have been on the benefit for more than a year.

“This isn’t about punishing someone because they haven’t found a job,” Upston said in a statement.

“It’s about making sure people receiving Jobseeker Support meet reasonable expectations to be ready for work, which also helps ensure it is fair to hardworking taxpayers who fund the system.”

Next month, an estimated 4300 18- and 19-year-olds with parents earning more than $65,000 will no longer be able to access the Jobseeker benefit under changes from the coalition Government.

In July under questioning from Green MP Ricardo Menedez-March in the House, Upston acknowledged about 1800 of them had a psychological or psychiatric condition.

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.
