Police have confirmed this morning that missing Christchurch father, Braydon Hepworth, has died.

But they are unable to shed any further light on the investigation into his disappearance, and how he met his fate.

The 21-year-old was last seen in September and since then, police had his family have been searching for him.

His mother has also made increasingly desperate appeals for information about the missing man on social media.

Police today confirmed the worst fears of Hepworth’s family.

Detective Inspector Scott Anderson said a number of search warrants had been executed at properties in Linwood and Edgeware this morning.

“Our inquiries to date suggest Braydon is no longer alive,” he said.

“We know there are people in the community that know what has happened to Braydon and request that they come forward with information.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

“Braydon is a father and a son and police are determined to get answers for Braydon’s family. We are continuing to appeal to anyone who may have information in relation to Braydon’s disappearance.

“Any information, no matter how small, could be a piece of the puzzle we need to locate Mr Hepworth.”

Anderson said that “at this time” police were “unable to share details on the findings of the search warrants”.

The last confirmed sighting of Hepworth was at a Linwood service station on September 3.

Security footage showed him wearing a Monster Energy-branded beanie with a pair of headphones over the top.

Police first appealed for help to find Hepworth on September 23 after he was reported missing.

On Friday, they issued a fresh appeal for information and confirmed they were searching a property in Linwood in connection with his disappearance.

The house is located on the corner of Hereford and England Sts and police said it was believed to be Hepworth’s last known address.

It is understood the house runs as a backpackers of sorts and has several residents of varying lengths of stay.

During the search, police cordoned off the corner property, which has caravans at the back.

Officers stood guard outside while investigators worked

“Staff have made extensive inquiries to date, and Braydon has not been located. We are very concerned for Braydon,” police said in a statement.

“Police continue to appeal for anybody with information regarding Braydon’s whereabouts to please get in contact with us.

“Police and Braydon’s family have serious concerns for his wellbeing, as this is extremely out of character for him.”

Earlier this week police refused to comment on the status of the investigation, including who Hepworth last spoke to or contacted, when he last accessed his bank accounts or used his phone, if he has accessed medication he uses daily, whether they believe the young father has been a victim of foul play, and if so, whether any persons of interest had been identified.

On Tuesday Detective Senior Sergeant Karen Simmons issued a statement.

“A scene examination at the address believed to be Braydon’s last known address has now been completed,” she said.

“The operation to understand the circumstances surrounding his disappearance remains ongoing.

“Police continue to appeal for anybody with information regarding Braydon’s whereabouts to please get in contact with us.”

Hepworth’s mother, Char Huntley, has been appealing for information on Facebook since September 22.

“Please help me keep looking for my boy … Braydon Hepworth. He’s 21 and Type 1 diabetic. He needs insulin daily to stay alive,” she wrote four days later.

“This is devastating, not knowing where he is, if he is safe, if he needs help but can’t get it, if he is still in Christchurch or has gone further willingly or not.

“He has a 9-month-old daughter and two siblings as well. He’s loved and very missed by many, and we are all concerned for his health and wellbeing. He is not in any trouble; we just need him home.”

Huntley revealed that as of August 4, Hepworth had “a month’s worth” of insulin.

“So we are desperately needing to find him to help him,” she said.

She had called hospitals “all over the South Island” as well as bus, shuttle and ferry companies in case Hepworth was sick, injured or had travelled away from Christchurch.

“Have been in the city where he would frequent and been showing his photo in multiple shops. No luck,” she said.

“Messaged friends and our extended family that know him or he may go to. No luck.

“His phone is off and all social media are non-active and everything is only delivered but not received his end. This is unnaturally out of character for him to not be heard from for this long. I am very scared for his safety, and the not knowing is the worst.”

Huntley said she was in a situation “no parent should ever go through”.

“I won’t stop looking until I find him safe … I am heartbroken not knowing where he is,” she updated later in September.

“His health and safety is a serious concern. Someone must know something that will lead to his location. Please help me find him. I love him, and I need him home.”

In her most recent update last week, 27 days after the last confirmed sighting of Hepworth, she begged anyone with information to “please speak up”.

“Remain anonymous if you need, but let me get my son back safe,” she said.

“Our family is broken with the uncertainty of his whereabouts and well-being. We have searched many places, made multiple calls and have no solid leads yet. I’m needing any information leading to his discovery.”

The grandfather of Hepworth’s daughter also posted online urging people to come forward with any information that could help the family.

“Although Braydon is not my biological son, he was in a relationship with our daughter and they have a beautiful 9-month-old daughter together. From the very first day we met Braydon, he called us Mum and Dad, and we called him our son. Over time, we built a very strong bond with him, and he has become an important part of our family,” he wrote.

“I received a message from Braydon on 2 September telling me that he was planning to get his car licence and was also sorting out other appointments. He had been doing so well, which is why everything that has happened over the past few weeks is so concerning and completely out of character for him.

“The search will continue, and we are asking everyone to please keep sharing the missing-person posts and keep an eye out for Braydon.”

He thanked everyone who had supported Hepworth’s family during “an extremely difficult and stressful time” and helped to search for him and spread the word about his disappearance.

“It truly means more to us than we can put into words,” he said.

“Thank you from the bottom of our hearts for continuing to support Braydon, our family and especially his little daughter during this incredibly difficult time.

“We are desperately hoping and praying that we receive good news soon.”

Over the weekend, he posted a message directly to Hepworth, revealing he had spent “countless hours driving and walking around looking for him”.

“I’m just lost for words, Braydon – please let us know where you are. You’re not in trouble; we all just want you back home,” he wrote.

It is unclear if Hepworth was working at the time he went missing.

In June 2025, he posted on Facebook looking for fulltime work “urgently”.

Brazilian woman Erika Rodrigues Coelho, 47, has been missing from Queenstown since September 18.

The family of missing Queenstown woman Erika Rodrigues Coelho say they have been left “devastated” and with no answers after police paused the search for the 47-year-old almost three weeks after she disappeared.

Erika has not been seen or heard from since September 18.

Police said the investigation remained active despite the physical search being paused and that they are “keeping an open mind” as to what occurred.

Her older brother, Alexandre Coelho, told the Herald the hardest part for the family was having no indication of what might have happened to her.

“We don’t know what to think.”

He said even a small piece of evidence pointing to what might have happened would give the family some direction.

The family had considered sending someone to New Zealand, but Alexandre questioned what they could do once they arrived.

“We don’t know what to do.”

He said his mother, Aldivina Coelho, was “devastated” and becoming increasingly distressed with each development.

She was now struggling even to speak to him and other family members, he said.

His father was also struggling and Alexandre believed he had lost hope that Erika would be found alive.

Erika’s close friend Bruna Rech said she’s been in touch with Erika’s family in Brazil.

“They are very sad,” she said.

For Rech, the lack of any trace of her friend was the hardest part to understand.

“They haven’t found anything,” she said.

“Apparently, she was carrying a backpack and had also bought a bottle of vodka, but neither has been found.

“I noticed there was a river along the track and wondered whether she might have fallen in, but if that were the case, wouldn’t some of her belongings have been found?”

She said she was left anxious with a feeling of “anguish” over the uncertainty of what had happened to her friend.

She said Erika had spoken to Rech about personal difficulties before she disappeared and had been seeing a therapist.

Police announced on Tuesday they had paused the physical search after extensive efforts since Erika was reported missing on September 20.

Sergeant Terry Wood described it as a “difficult decision” and thanked the Land Search and Rescue volunteers, Coastguard volunteers, dog teams, members of the public and others who had contributed “countless hours”.

A formal review of the search is now underway.

“Enquiries are continuing in the background,” Wood said.

“Today, police met with a search reviewer, and he will continue to review the search to date.

“It is anticipated that he may find further tasks for us to complete prior to any formal suspension of the search.”

New information from the public could also trigger further searching, Wood said.

“At this stage we are keeping an open mind as to what has occurred.”

The man police previously appealed to after he was seen on the Mt Dewar summit track about 12.30pm on September 18 has still not been identified or come forward.

“He is not and was not considered a suspect but a witness to possibly sighting Erika,” Wood said.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Alexandre and Rech criticised the assistance they said they had received from the Brazilian Embassy in Wellington.

Alexandre said the embassy responded when the family contacted it but had not proactively provided them with updates.

“They are not helping us with anything.”

He said most information reaching the family had come through Rech, Erika’s partner, police information published online and media reports.

Rech said police have been “amazing” but described the Embassy support as “useless”.

“They haven’t called us even once. They respond to our emails, but that’s about it.”

Police said it had taken possession of Erika’s belongings for safekeeping at Queenstown Police Station, and, if she was not found, arrangements would need to be made to return them to her family in Brazil.

Rech said she approached the embassy seeking practical advice about how the belongings could be transported.

According to Rech, she was simply told Queenstown was a large town and there would be companies able to provide the service, without being given contacts or further assistance.

The Embassy of Brazil said it had been in direct contact with Erika’s family members and friends, as well as New Zealand Police.

“The Embassy has been providing the family with all information received from the relevant New Zealand authorities,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

The embassy confirmed the family had raised concerns about returning Erika’s belonging to Brazil.

“Unfortunately, under the applicable legislation governing consular assistance, the embassy is not authorised to cover the costs of transporting personal belongings to Brazil,” the spokesperson said.

“The embassy will, however, provide all further assistance within its remit to help the family address the practical arrangements involved.”

Police continue to ask anyone with information about Erika’s whereabouts to contact them via 105, quoting reference 260921/8173.

New Zealand’s primary industries slow to take up new AI tech

New Zealand Herald October 07, 2026

AWS research found that AI adoption across agriculture, forestry, and fishing is just under 40%. Photo / NZME

By Gianina Schwanecke of RNZ

New Zealand’s primary industries are believed to be one set to benefit from artificial intelligence (AI) advances, but new research from Amazon Web Services (AWS) suggests the industry is also one of the least prepared to take it up.

AWS research found AI adoption across agriculture, forestry and fishing sits just under 40%, compared with 50% nationally, and the majority of adopters are at the “most basic stage”.

It found physical AI – including robotics, autonomous systems, and computer vision – offers the most opportunity for the industry in relation to crop management, livestock monitoring and processing.

Yet only 30% of agricultural businesses have heard of it, and just 7% of those are using or piloting it.

Only 9% consider themselves ready to adopt next-generation AI tools.

A shortage of AI and digital skills, as well as other business priorities taking precedence and limited access to next-generation AI tools or infrastructure, were considered the greatest barriers.

AWS country manager for New Zealand Manuel Bohnet said the biggest barrier comes down to skills.

“Only 10% have really moved to an advanced usage, and this is where you also really get most of the value out of it – use of agentic capabilities, or robotics or physical AI.

“We really see that there also needs to be more confidence built, and we truly believe that confidence is a consequence of skills and having a better understanding.”

It’s why AWS is running a free agritech school to upskill those in the primary industries.

Lone Star Farm’s stock manager, Carey Pawson-Edwards, said its five South Island sheep and beef farms used over 30 apps or programmes, which had helped improve productivity.

He said there had been a big shift in how farmers trust data as the results had been proven, with more keen to get on board now.

In addition to productivity gains, he said there were environmental and animal welfare benefits.

“Practically on farm we’re underway with Halter virtual fencing,” he said.

“Halter collars versus non-Halter collars with cows and calves at foot, we’re increasing the ME [metabolisable energy] of our pasture by roughly 1 to 2 after 30 days, and we’re 10kg heavier in our weaning weight.

“Across the whole company, all of our sheep have got electronic tags within their ears.

“Not only are we seeing production gains from that where we can see how animals are performing and do things about it, but we’re also able to supply a lamb programme called Lumina Lamb, and that’s enabling us to extract a premium out of the market for those lambs and EID [electronic identification] traceability is one of the requirements of that.”

Pawson-Edwards said for farmers it was about seeing a return on investment.

Going forward, he wanted to see more integration across the various apps to grow their benefits.

People in Auckland and Coromandel will not be allowed to gather certain species of seafood in intertidal areas this summer.

The move is part of major fishing rule changes that will also introduce a daily catch limit of 10 for all shellfish outside the zone, without their own limits, says Oceans and Fisheries Minister Shane Jones.

“Fossicking in a rockpool is a Kiwi tradition. It’s a pastime that’s been enjoyed by generations of New Zealanders.

“However, it’s being exploited by a selfish few who are taking far too much kaimoana. This behaviour is endangering these fragile ecosystems and putting at risk our beloved coastal areas.”

A substantial area of the intertidal zone will be closed to recreational fishing for species including cat’s eyes, mussels, and limpets from November 1.

The closure covers beaches, rocky shores and rockpools on Auckland’s east and west coasts, Waiheke Island, and Coromandel, from the mean high-water mark to a point offshore where the water is 2m deep.

“This will protect a broad range of species that are vulnerable to overharvesting and other pressures, while keeping access to highly valued species that can sustainably be caught in the intertidal zone, such as rock lobster and squid,” Jones said.

The closure prohibits the take of marine invertebrates except for cockles, crabs, kina, octopus, oysters, pāua, pipi, rock lobsters, scallops, sea cucumbers, prawns/shrimps, squid, and tuatua.

The daily catch limit on shellfish outside of the zone will reduce the risk of overharvesting shifting to offshore or subtidal areas, the minister said.

The daily limit for green-lipped mussels outside of the zone will be reduced from 25 to 10 per person.

Continual monitoring and review will determine the changes’ impact and whether further measures are needed.

The new rules will stay in place until revoked by the Oceans and Fisheries Minister, Jones said.

The moves respond to community concerns about the sustainability of marine life in tidal areas, he said.

“The overwhelming majority of submitters during public consultation wanted far-ranging and meaningful restrictions. While I am reluctant to close our coastlines, it is a necessary step.”

“Kiwis should be able to enjoy our coastline and gather kaimoana but we have a responsibility to make sure fisheries resources are protected for all to enjoy.”

Jones labelled the new rules as “broad prohibition, with some sensible and evidence-based exceptions”.

The Government is also working to set up an infringement regime for the closure so Fishery Officers can hand out instant fines, Under-Secretary Jenny Marcroft said.

“It is clear that a robust but proportionate penalty response is required.”

Discretion will be exercised by officers, she added.

“For example, tamariki exploring the rockpools with a bucket and spade will not face punishment for their curiosity. But where it is obvious our rockpools are being cleared out of all marine life through greed and selfishness, authorities will act.”

Anna Torv was always told ‘don’t go out in that skirt’. Her superb new show challenges that idea

Sydney Morning Herald October 08, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Anna Torv knows how the cop stuff works: the purposeful walk down a hallway, the crime-scene crouch and the coaxing of information from a victim or a suspect. She’s done it enough times across her storied career that she was almost reluctant to do it again. “I’m like, oh God, here we go again’,” says Torv.

But with Dustfall, her new ABC crime drama about the drugging and rape of a young woman, it was less about what she could do on screen and more about what the show could say about sexual assault and consent.

“It takes it seriously,” says Torv, who is, as always, wonderfully forthright to talk to. “I specifically was really interested in the 360 idea of it. That it is not just the victim that’s impacted; it’s the ramifications of it, across generations and friendship groups.

“I have a son – and I love men – and I find the whole concept of consent really, really interesting: how people view it, how you have those conversations and also the generational difference and separation between what we now find unacceptable and what was acceptable. I just felt there was a way we could tell that or show that, open a conversation and a discussion without, you know, banging people over the head.”

Torv plays Detective Tig Pollard, who is called in when a naked and disorientated Edie (Zoe Phillips) is found in a cane field early one morning with no recollection of what happened after she left the pub the night before.

What follows is a nuanced drama – the best I have seen this year – that doesn’t flinch from the aftermath of sexual assault, but also layers in all the ways, big and small, consent can be corroded. For Tig, that includes battles with her overbearing mother (Juliet Stevenson) and a former boyfriend (Peter Fenton) keen to re-enter her life. It’s not easy, and that’s the point.

“I’m right in the middle of that older generation and the newer generation, and we were taught – I was taught specifically by my mother – ‘do not go out in that skirt’,” says Torv. “That is how you keep yourself safe. Do not go and leave your friends. That was it. And then you have a new generation that’s like, but we should be able to go out and not live in fear. We should.

“As a detective, Tig is going, ‘My job is to protect these women, and they should be able to do that.’ And yet, if I had a daughter, I would want to say, ‘Don’t f---ing go out.’ That’s the murky world we live in in the show, but also live [in real life].”

The series, which was shot in the Gold Coast hinterland, is adapted from Vikki Petraitis’s 2022 award-winning novel The Unbelieved by Dianne Taylor and directed by Emma Freeman. And while the story is fictional, it is depressingly easy to find echoes of Dustfall’s story in real life.

You only have to look at the news recently to see the alleged rape of a teenage girl by three boys from an elite private school in Sydney last month and the growing furore over the delayed response to gang-rape allegations at Cornell University in the US, where a woman said she was sexually assaulted after being plied with alcohol and drugs in 2024.

“I didn’t want to objectify the female experience,” says Freeman, who directed all six episodes. “It was about actually having a front-row seat in what it’s like at different stages of your life to deal with sexual assault. It’s a conversation that we need to have. It’s a conversation here. It’s a conversation worldwide.

“When you’ve got one in five women who are victim-survivors of sexual assault in Australia, we need to talk about it. And that’s reported figures. So I just really hope it provokes a conversation.”

Torv agrees. “Vikki’s book was brilliant, but I knew that there was going to be room to move and also Trojan horse, I guess, a little bit more stuff in,” she says. “You take people into a genre that feels very familiar and where people feel comfortable, and then you can then just slowly start to push the parameters a little bit.”

That push can be seen most clearly during a confronting scene in episode one, where Edie is examined in hospital after her assault. The nurse takes her time documenting the teenager’s injuries – every cut, bruise and bite. She talks Edie through the vaginal swab, and offers her the morning-after pill.

In real life, it’s standard procedure. But many crime dramas prefer the easier shot of the victim being led away, covered with a blanket. Dustfall, however, refuses to look away.

“I didn’t feel there was a need to dramatise [that] because what is going on is dramatic enough,” says Freeman. “And I think, also looking at [other] projects, you don’t often get the victim-survivors’ point of view of what it’s like after you have experienced sexual assault. I haven’t seen that scene before, so I really wanted to be in the point of view of Edie and really understand what it feels like to go through that process.”

Filming that scene required providing support for those not only in front of the camera, but behind it as well. The sexual assault and domestic violence service Full Stop Australia gave counselling and advice, while intimacy co-ordinator Kate Wormald supported cast and crew on set.

“Many people on that particular day found that incredibly confronting and couldn’t stay in the room,” says Freeman. “It was a very upsetting scene to shoot and really moving.”

Even Freeman, who is now directing Baby Reindeer star Jessica Gunning’s new Netflix series Feral, began to feel the emotional line between fact and fiction starting to blur.

“It was a really hard show to make, and I would come home many nights in tears,” says Freeman. “But I just accepted that that was also OK – that it was something I was looking at and was moving me.

“[It was also difficult to] sit through it every day in the edit as well, because it’s only me and two editors. You shoot it, and you go through this extraordinary experience – which was a really positive one – but then you’re alone in the edit for months, looking through all this material. Thankfully, I’m pretty robust and have good mental health, and I had Anna on the side, going, ‘Keep going!’”

For her part, Torv had the support of a former detective who had worked on sexual assault cases. “The thing that she constantly hammered on the head was that your job is to give the victim consent,” says Torv. “The victim must give consent. You must ask her for everything: ‘Can I do this?’, ‘May I touch you?’

“You have to give her control and power back because that’s the thing that she has lost. And you have to be as soft and as gentle [as you can]. If she doesn’t want to do something, she doesn’t have to do it.”

Torv and Freeman have known each other for more than 20 years, having first worked together on The Secret Life of Us in 2004. It was Freeman’s first directing gig and Torv’s first on-screen role (“I came in when the show was dead,” says Torv, laughing. “I killed the show”). They also both grew up on the Gold Coast (and have since returned to live there) and even, briefly, went to the same high school.

“The only thing I remember from that experience – and I wasn’t in it – was the grade 12 or 11 drama competition show [Sister Act],” says Torv. “I just have never forgotten it. It was just so great. Years later, I realised, ‘oh, Emma directed it!’”

Since then, they have worked together on two award-winning dramas – Secret City on Foxtel and The Newsreader on the ABC – and have fine-tuned their relationship, knowing when to push each other and (sometimes) pull back.

When asked – during separate phone calls – to describe their relationship, they both reply “brutally honest”.

“We have the same taste,” says Torv. “It’s funny because we don’t have the same taste in life, but on a set, we know [what we’re doing]. I’ll try anything she asks me to do. But that’s been honed over 25 years.

“Whatever the show is, the joy of it has to be in the making. That’s kind of where my job ends. If you don’t enjoy that process, then I’m like, ‘well, why are you f---ing doing it?’ And Emma’s the same. I think both of us feel more at home on a set than anywhere else. I love it.”

Freeman, of course, agrees. “We’re not servicing each other’s egos. We’re servicing the story and the performance and the filmmaking. It’s the closest I’ve ever come to a serious collaborator.

“We’re constantly talking … We often change the script. We have conversations at night. It’s a very intense collaboration – but I feel like it shows in the work.”

Dustfall premieres at 8.20pm on Sunday, October 11, on ABC and ABC iview.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

This Aussie actor was ‘raised on Chicago’. Now she’s starring alongside Catherine Zeta-Jones

Sydney Morning Herald October 08, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Growing up in Mount Eliza on Victoria’s Mornington Peninsula, Hattie Hook began her performing career via dance and musical theatre. Though she got into film in her teenage years, she never thought she would be starring alongside a Tony award-winner like Catherine Zeta-Jones.

“I’ve never said this to her, so I hope she doesn’t read this, but I was raised on Chicago,” Hook says, ahead of the release of the pair’s new show Kill Jackie. “Oh my God. I’ve loved her work forever. I mean, are you kidding me? It’s Catherine Zeta-Jones – like, dude.”

In all their scenes together, Hook says her main priority was trying to be “cool as a cucumber”.

“She really was so warm and encouraging, and I felt really supported on set with her. As the lead actor, you’re such a tone-setter and I really admired the way she carried herself on set. I learned so much from her. Her camera technique is like nothing I’ve ever seen. Her command of camera, her awareness of camera, the way she uses her eyes...

“And she’s hilarious. She has that incredible Welsh sense of humour which I’m so happy she gets to use in the show.”

An eight-part crime action thriller, Kill Jackie is fuelled by offbeat characters, rat-a-tat repartee and a high-stakes cat-and-mouse dynamic. It’s also part of a wave of recent action series – from Killing Eve to Ride or Die to The Assassin – that are led by women.

Based on the 2018 novel The Price You Pay by best-selling author Nick Harkaway, writing as Aidan Truhen, Kill Jackie is a skirmish of rage, revenge, dark humour and unexpected twists with the action led by Zeta-Jones as former international drug smuggler Jackie Price. (Notably, in the book the main character is a man named Jack Price).

Contributor

Price stopped selling cocaine years ago, transferring her dealing skills to a successful career trading high-end fine art to the ultra-wealthy. But her past is catching up with her. Cue unexpected explosions, uninvited gun-wielding hitmen in her luxury flat and the discovery she is the target for a hit led by a mysterious international terrorist organisation known as the Seven Demons.

Hook, known best for the Stan*-BBC TV series Ten Pound Poms, ABC crime drama Savage River and feature film Of An Age, stars as Charlie, Jackie’s assistant. Loyal and trusting of each other, the pair face increasingly perilous stakes as Jackie’s luxurious, settled and anonymous life of two decades is threatened at every turn.

“Charlie is that classic Gen Z tech-savvy assistant,” Hook says. “She’s no-nonsense and straight to the point,” she says. “[Charlie is also a] kid who has no one and has come from nothing. And Jackie has given her a life. Charlie is very attached to her and so everything with Charlie is about Jackie: making sure she’s okay, and she’s happy and that nothing is going to threaten her.

“It’s a really interesting relationship in that way. It’s nothing I’ve really played before: this older sister-younger sister, friends-but-not friends dynamic.”

Directed by Damon Thomas (Killing Eve, Crooked House) and co-created by Conor Keane, Tom Butterworth (Gangs of London) and Peter Lawson (John Wick), Kill Jackie is also rife with eclectic acting talent. From Sidse Babett Knudsen (Borgen) to Ron Perlman (Hellboy), Julian Barratt (The Mighty Boosh, Flowers), Julian Rhind-Tutt (Britannia, Green Wing) and Daniel Ings (The Gentlemen, The Crown), the series’ range of characters is vast and varied.

“Every character is so original,” Hook says. “It’s such a mixed bag of puzzle pieces and characters that I’ve never seen before ... Seeing them all interact is so delicious.”

She says Ings, who plays Jackie’s lawyer and crush, was particularly memorable.

“He’s the most exciting scene partner I’ve ever had because, in this piece, he’s very freewheeling,” she says. “He’s an absolute stick of dynamite, and he would be completely different take-to-take, always improvising. I’ve never felt so unprofessional on a set. I was just constantly cracking up. He is so, so good.”

Though Hook has been acting since her teenage years, she says she still has “such a complex” that she didn’t do any formal training. “I feel like all my mistakes have been immortalised on camera which is kind of mortifying. I definitely am someone who’s learning as I go.”

She says being part of Ten Pound Poms, in which she played Pattie, a 16-year-old who migrates to Australia and faces life as a single mother in the 1950s, was a particularly important step in her acting education.

“That was my university, my study,” she says. “You delve into so many high-stakes emotions [in that show] so it was a great training ground. And particularly working with Faye Marsay [Game of Thrones, Lady Chatterley’s Lover]. Shout out! I learnt so much from her.”

Hook, who moved to London permanently this year, has several other projects on the way too.

“I’m starting on something in November which I’m in prep for right now,” she says. “It’s another screen thing and I think literally the only thing I can say is that I’m really genuinely excited about it.

“There’s so much opportunity in the arts, and there’s just so much going on over here. But also, I just love London as a city.”

She’s still always thinking of audiences back home, though. “I really hope the Aussies like [Kill Jackie],” she says, ahead of the show’s release. “I think the Aussies will really appreciate the sense of humour.

“It feels so original to me and I just really hope people enjoy it.”

Kill Jackie is streaming on Stan now.

*Stan is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead.

WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 20:46:07 GMT

‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says

The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.

Darya Shipilova died two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms. She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.

The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.

At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.

On Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”

Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”. “We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.”

The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked.

In an interview with local media, Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said.

She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job. Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hardworking and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”

The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low.

On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised.

According to the Baikal Medical Journal, health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday.

“The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours. She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’”

Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair campaign sign

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 20:21:59 GMT

Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story in order to fight for victims of sexual assault

This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual assault.

A congressional candidate in Arizona says she was attacked and raped in August while trying to repair one of her damaged campaign signs.

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a trucker and small-business owner, shared her account with the Phoenix New Times, a local publication. The assault took place on 14 August, according to the campaign.

The Democratic candidate, running in a district that includes parts of Phoenix, told the newspaper that she was walking across a parking lot just after 2am to fix a campaign sign when an attacker smashed her over the head, causing her to black out.

Greene-Placentia told the newspaper that she awoke to find a man on top of her and discovered he was raping her. She recalled another man coming over and pushing her leg, at which point she said she swung her foot at him. The man said, “Not even worth it”, and the two attackers left, leaving her face down in the parking lot, she recalled.

The candidate said her memory of the incident and its aftermath was hazy, telling the newspaper she did not remember picking herself off the pavement or returning home.

“It’s just these little tiny flashes of things that I do remember,” Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times. “As much as I don’t want to remember, I’ve tried very, very hard to remember more stuff. But that’s where I’m at.”

She said she may have had a concussion as a result of the attack and that her body was covered in bruises. She said she initially wanted to forget what had happened and felt “embarrassed”, at first choosing not to report the assault. But she told the paper that on the campaign trail, she often spoke about fighting for Arizonans, “and I didn’t feel like I could keep saying that if I weren’t also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault”.

Greene-Placentia told her campaign staff and husband about the assault days after it happened and reported it to the Maricopa county sheriff’s office two weeks later, according to the Phoenix New Times. The newspaper interviewed Greene-Placentia’s relatives, friends, campaign staff and landlord about the aftermath of the assault.

“Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokesperson told the Guardian on Wednesday after the Phoenix New Times story was published. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.”

The spokesperson added: “She hopes the focus remains on supporting survivors and making sure people who have experienced sexual violence know they are seen, heard and supported.”

“I need to let women know that it’s OK to talk about it,” Greene-Placentia told the newspaper.

Stephanie Simacek, a state representative and friend of Greene-Placentia, said the congressional candidate told her of the assault in early September, telling the Phoenix New Times, “I felt sick to my stomach, and it was extremely disturbing. It was a big wake-up call for me. I think oftentimes, as candidates and electeds, we think that it’s not going to happen to us.”

A Maricopa county sheriff’s spokesperson declined to comment, saying the investigation was ongoing.

Greene-Placentia is running against an incumbent Republican member of Congress, Abraham Hamadeh.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

Eckert’s Spygate ban may be lenient, but no sane manager will try the same trick again

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 20:00:04 GMT

Verdict has been a long time coming and the Southampton head coach has recaptured hearts and minds at St Mary’s

“Hi Tonda, are you a cheat?” That simple, succinct, question cut to the heart of a matter that has vexed the Football Association all summer. It was posed by the Northern Echo’s Dominic Shaw after Southampton overcame Middlesbrough in the second leg of May’s Championship playoff semi‑final and proved the cue for Tonda Eckert to walk out of his press conference at St Mary’s.

Although Southampton’s manager subsequently admitted to authorising spying on opponents, England’s football authorities struggled to decide what punishment best fitted an act some regard as heinous but which others fail to take seriously. Now, in autumn, we finally have an FA verdict, with Eckert given a six-week ban suspended until the end of the 2027-28 season, a £28,000 fine and a reprimand.

Despite the apparent leniency of the sanction, one thing is clear: Eckert’s summer in purgatory surely dictates no sane England-based coach would contemplate engaging in espionage now.

Eckert may wish he could turn back time to early May and rewrite history. On the eve of the playoff semi-final first leg on Teesside, William Salt, then an intern Southampton first-team analyst, was caught lurking awkwardly beside a tree while filming a Middlesbrough training session on his iPhone. Spygate was born and an independent disciplinary commission convened by the Football League (EFL) expelled Southampton from the playoff final against Hull after their win against Boro across two legs. The governing body also decreed the Saints would begin the current Championship season on minus four points.

By then Southampton had also admitted to spying on Oxford and Ipswich training. There is a certain irony that Eckert’s team won none of the three games – albeit Middlesbrough were ultimately beaten on aggregate – involving covert surveillance. Yet the EFL independent disciplinary commission panel made plain its discomfort regarding the “particularly deplorable” pressure placed on a young worker hired on a temporary contract. Salt has since been given a staff job as an analyst in Southampton’s academy and is reportedly progressing well.

With the EFL empowered to sanction clubs but not individuals in such cases, it was down to the FA to punish Eckert. The 33-year-old German issued a public apology in June but was not charged with misconduct by the FA until late July. A further hiatus ensued before a hearing at Wembley on 24 September.

This extraordinary delay afforded Eckert ample time to regret dispatching Salt to Middlesbrough’s training ground adjacent to the luxury Rockliffe Hall Hotel and golf course just south of Darlington. Salt’s primary mission was to discover whether Hayden Hackney, Middlesbrough’s star midfielder and the Championship player of the season, was fit after injury. Unfortunately, clandestine manoeuvres were evidently not his strong suit. Salt soon found himself being chased into hotel toilets, and realised that using his bank card to buy a coffee at Rockliffe had not been the smartest move. That payment facilitated a search for his name on Southampton’s website. It was swiftly identified, enabling Steve Gibson, Middlesbrough’s owner, to make a formal complaint to the EFL regarding a breach of its anti-spying regulations.

It is understood that, until this point, Southampton’s manager remained unaware of the Bev Priestman precedent. The former head coach of Canada Women was banned from all football activity for a year by Fifa after being found guilty of initiating spying. During the 2024 Paris Olympics her staff secretly filmed a New Zealand training session using a drone and the former England women’s assistant manager paid a high price.

It is unclear whether Eckert has since been in touch with the 40-year-old, now in charge of Wellington Phoenix. Priestman met such extreme hostility in previously welcoming Canada that she relocated her family to New Zealand. During ‘Spygate’, Eckert’s wife was heavily pregnant and based in Berlin, preparing for the birth of their first child. Back in Hampshire, her husband received death threats via LinkedIn. Southampton supplied the manager with protection while police advised him that driving his own car was unsafe and that he should restrict his movements.

Plenty of people were extremely angry, with St Mary’s regulars polarised between those who believed the manager had shamed their club and should be sacked, and others who reflected that what is euphemistically called “training observation” of opponents is commonplace and largely unpunished across tracts of Europe. The second camp remembered that, seven years ago, Leeds were fined £200,000 after the club’s then manager, Marcelo Bielsa, sent an analyst to monitor a Derby training session. Frank Lampard, then in charge of Derby, complained after spotting him perched up a tree.

After that incident the EFL tightened its regulations regarding espionage appreciably. Nonetheless, Eckert’s advocates claim that, given he started last season as Southampton’s under-21s coach and became the manager after Will Still’s sacking in November, he had missed the EFL’s annual managerial summer rules refresher course.

Eckert, who began his career as a Germany national team analyst before moving into coaching at Cologne, RB Salzburg, RB Leipzig, Bayern Munich, Barnsley and Genoa, was only half-joking when he recently told reporters that the EFL handbook was his staple bedside summer reading. He also made contact with Gareth Southgate and visited the former England and Middlesbrough, manager, with the pair discussing English football culture and its zero tolerance for spycraft at length.

“I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,” said Eckert last month. “I’ve asked the FA for forgiveness.” He has had unwavering support from Southampton’s board who made it clear they had no desire to sack him in the face of considerable dressing room hostility on the part offrom players who felt betrayed by ‘Spygate’.

With first-team hearts and minds since seemingly recaptured by the coach who led them so close to promotion last season, Southampton have won four and drawn two of their opening eight Championship games. Next up on Sunday is the visit of Portsmouth. South-coast derbies are invariably tense but Eckert’s reprieve may ensure he cuts an unusually relaxed figure in the technical area.

Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 19:45:47 GMT

Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land

Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen, approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.

The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador to Yemen, Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.

Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west.

Houthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded.

The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that the Houthis have stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”.

There has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims about Yemeni government advances issued at the beginning of the week.

Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people.

The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel.

Southern Giants forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. The group is now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Judge orders officials to preserve all evidence tied to Christa Pike’s botched execution

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 19:22:25 GMT

Judge tells Tennessee officials all items in execution room must be saved as Pike remains restrained in hospital bed

A judge ordered Tennessee officials on Wednesday to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution attempt on convicted murderer Christa Pike, as it emerged that the state has refused pleas from medical staff to allow her to be unshackled from her hospital bed.

At a hearing in Nashville on Wednesday, judge I’Ashea Myles said: “Anything that was in the actual room” during the attempted execution a week ago must be preserved by the state, including all drugs, intravenous lines and tubing used in the death chamber.

The order came as Pike’s lawyers said she has pneumonia, a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms, after she regained consciousness on Tuesday.

“The first thing she said was: ‘Where am I and who are you?’,” one of Pike’s lawyers said on Wednesday afternoon.

Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber last Wednesday after two supposedly lethal doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital. She had been on a ventilator, with an unknown prognosis, before she woke and spoke on Tuesday.

“There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people. She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family … I think she is angry and confused about everything right now,” one of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, said.

The updates came after a contentious court hearing where Pike’s legal team accused Tennessee officials of “secreting away” evidence. Attorney Luke Ihnen said items from the attempted execution could be key to future legal challenges by Pike, should the state attempt to kill her again.

“The state has made no promises that Ms Pike will not be subject to a future execution, and the evidence that we are seeking to preserve now is relevant for any future challenge that she makes, because as we pled in January, the same thing is likely to happen,” Ihnen said.

Pike survived a lengthy procedure and the large doses of the sedative as Tennessee officials had attempted to put her to death, in a case that shocked many in the US and created headlines around the world.

At a press conference after Wednesday’s hearing, Spivey said it was unclear “what if any function” Pike would regain in her arms. “Her hands look like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” Spivey said.

Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm.

“Based on our understanding, medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request [by the Tennessee correction department],” he told Myles earlier. He added: “We would also amend our request and ask for that relief.”

Witnesses to the attempted execution of Pike described how they heard her breathing raggedly after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her and was declared to be in critical condition.

Sign up to Breaking News US

after newsletter promotion

After the botched execution attempt, Spivey called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.

Her lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.

There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or a lot of the drug missed her vein and went into tissue, that one of her veins, which were problematic and this fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, or that the drug was faulty, or a combination.

Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995.

According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her.

Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years.

Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 19:16:24 GMT

Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms

Two men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less.

A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward.

Ward, who was freed in 2017 after serving 10 years more than his one-year minimum and was later recalled to prison, was also in court, sitting in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced.

Relatives of Ings and Bennett hugged in the public gallery at Wolverhampton crown court on Wednesday as Mr Justice Choudhury told them the IPPs had been “cancelled”.

Choudhury said Bennett would instead be sentenced to four years and 264 days, Ward to two years, and Ings to 42 months with a 30-month extended licence.

All three men’s original sentences were quashed and replaced after they argued that judges had wrongly found them to be dangerous or had not considered alternative sentences.

Choudhury, sitting with the magistrate Norma Grant, told the appellants: “You have already spent considerably longer than those [replacement] sentences in custody. The effect is that you, Mr Bennett, and you, Mr Ings, will be entitled to release without further supervision, and you, Mr Ward, will no longer be subject to supervision.”

The ruling came after the CCRC referred the cases of the three men back to the crown court to review minimum terms imposed on them by judges in Wolverhampton, Reading and Leicester respectively in 2006 and 2007.

Bennett and Ings, now both 38, were 17 when they committed offences that led to them being classed as dangerous offenders and given indeterminate sentences with respective minimum terms of 24 months and 21 months in 2007 and 2006.

Bennett was originally sentenced at Wolverhampton crown court in May 2007 after being found guilty of reckless arson for setting fire to items in the loft space of an empty council property, and admitting criminal damage and burglary.

Ings was sentenced to detention for public protection after appearing at East Berkshire youth court in March 2006 and admitting offences including a robbery in an underpass and an assault on a teenager in a fast food outlet.

Ward, now 41, was 21 when he was given a one-year minimum sentence in 2006 at Leicester crown court for arson and criminal damage. He admitted arson – after setting fire to items in his prison cell while serving time for assault – and was released in 2017, but was later recalled to prison and remained in custody until August this year.

Muin Boase, representing Bennett, successfully argued that the judge who sentenced him in 2007 did not give proper weight to his youth, lack of maturity and capacity to change after a difficult childhood.

In its ruling, the appeal court said there had been no proper basis for the original finding of dangerousness.

Detention for public protection and imprisonment for public protection (DPP and IPP) sentences were abolished in 2012, having been made available to tackle offenders considered a significant risk to the public in 2005.

The law was changed to stop courts handing out IPP sentences after warnings that they were being applied too widely, but the abolition was not retrospective, meaning many prisoners serving such sentences are still behind bars.

The government has faced calls to take action on IPP jail terms, with the former justice secretary Ken Clarke saying last month that ministers should not to be too cautious.

His comments came a week after the current justice secretary, Alex Norris, told MPs that the government planned to bring forward legislation to end IPP sentences “once and for all” by the end of this parliament.

More than 2,000 prisoners remain held indefinitely under IPP sentences, with 99% past their original tariff and 80% having served 10 years or more.

DeChambeau’s preference has always been an elongated version of LIV but that competitive model remains open to much question.

LIV Golf, along with BC Partners Credit, has been outwardly bullish about its future. “Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf’s emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season,” said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement. An immediate winner from this mess is likely to be the DP World Tour. Golfers are expected to gravitate towards that circuit for 2027 as a means to potentially play their way back on to the PGA Tour. LIV has already cut ties with all but a skeleton staff.

Contact review – Jonny Donahoe delivers a heated reunion at a bonfire of family photos

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 19:00:02 GMT

Òran Mór, GlasgowBlythe Duff and Mark Barrett are excellent as two people helplessly bound to each other in this bitter two-hander

The arrival of a first baby changes everything. It is not just the upheaval of fitting the child into your life: the shift is also psychological. Children become parents. Parents become grandparents. Responsibility and accountability move down a generation.

That is why, in Jonny Donahoe’s knotty, bitter two-hander, a man known only as Son (Mark Barrett) has called on Mother (Blythe Duff) after an eight-month gap. She is spikily indifferent to his appearance, here in her back garden where she is burning family photographs on a bonfire. Despite the frosty reception, he must persist.

Son’s wife Alice (pronounced Malice, according to Mother) is expecting a Christmas baby. With that in mind, he is eager to end the resentment harboured by the older woman since he was six. He wants their relationship to be civil. She is having none of it.

The damage is not in their surface chitchat. If you did not know better you could miss it. Duff captures the sparkle of Donahoe’s hard-bitten wit and can be waspishly funny. Barrett counters with low-status calm, avoiding confrontation. It could all be quite innocent.

But Mother’s lack of sentiment goes deep. Incapable of empathy, she has been brutalised by her past. “Not everything you feel has to be expressed,” she scolds her son, sounding ever more the sociopath. The shadow of Son’s abusive father looms over them, but their own personalities also play a part in a trauma that has left them stressed, depressed and trapped in a destructive cycle.

With its short, fractured sentences, the play is a tad slow, but in Ben Standish’s lunchtime production for A Play, a Pie and a Pint (with the Traverse and OneRen), Duff and Barrett are excellent in their depiction of two people helplessly bound to each other, inflicting pain even when they try to do the opposite.

At Òran Mór, Glasgow, until 10 October. Then touring until 23 October

The Guardian view on Conservative conference: struggling to break out of the comfort zone

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 18:02:22 GMT

Kemi Badenoch’s personal brand is not strong enough to revive a party that so thoroughly lost the trust of the British people

For a party that keeps losing elections, the Conservatives have enjoyed a remarkably upbeat conference in Birmingham this week. A party with a strong regicidal impulse is united behind Kemi Badenoch. Opinion polls show the leader’s personal ratings, while not spectacular, outperforming the wider Tory brand. Mrs Badenoch exuded confidence in her keynote speech on Wednesday, setting out what she believes is a path back to power.

The strategic focus is the economy. The Conservative leader expects Andy Burnham’s honeymoon to come to an end when his chancellor delivers a painful budget later this month. A spending review will then compound the pain, forcing grim trade-offs on a prime minister who has a reputation for deferring hard choices.

Mrs Badenoch presents herself as made of sterner stuff. By that she means she is prepared to say that an overgrown state does too much for too many people. What the Tory leader imagines to be fiscal courage is really ideological complacency pitched at her party’s comfort zone. The Conservative conference generated multiple commitments to cut taxes, mostly for upper-middle- and high-income families, alongside pledges to boost spending on defence and prison places, while also reducing the national debt. This is affordable, according to Mrs Badenoch, thanks to £70bn of “savings” the Conservatives claim to have identified in cuts to the civil service, regulators and working-age benefits.

It is a phoney equation that doesn’t account for the increase in costs to government once the social consequences of austerity become apparent. But the proposed reallocation of resources from mythical undeserving benefit-claiming idlers to enterprising but overtaxed middle-class families is a trusted campaign device.

Mrs Badenoch presents this agenda as “something for everyone”. In reality, she is trying to reach two particular audiences. The Tories need to attract voters in their former “blue wall” heartlands, now held by Liberal Democrats, and people who backed Boris Johnson in 2019 and then switched to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. These groups have very different attitudes, crudely represented by the polarised political identities that coalesced into leave and remain blocs – one nationalistic, the other more liberal – on the question of Brexit.

Mrs Badenoch spent two years courting the former camp with hardline positions on immigration and hostility to net zero climate policy. She has belatedly noticed the existence of people who are appalled by Mr Farage’s agenda. A significant passage in her speech on Wednesday rebuked Reform UK politicians who use a narrow ethnic definition of Englishness.

But mostly the Conservative leader talked about tax cuts, because she believes they appeal across the spectrum. That is often a reliable assumption, although the same plan didn’t help the Tories in 2024. Reckless pre-election giveaways succeeded only in poisoning the fiscal well for Keir Starmer.

The problem for the Conservatives then was that people didn’t trust them to govern responsibly or competently. This hasn’t changed. Mrs Badenoch thinks victory is available by attaching her personal brand to a classic Tory formula, unrevised for decades. Judging by the mood in Birmingham, her MPs and members agree. This is what happens when a party speaks to itself. A much harder test awaits when they have to speak to a country that remembers Conservative government well enough to be disinclined to listen.

Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 18:00:02 GMT

DNA analysis of oldest living land animal reveal patterns on genes that appear to protect functioning of mitochondria

The ancient quest to extend human lifespan has received a boost after scientists analysed the genetic code of the world’s oldest living land animal, a giant tortoise called Jonathan.

The tortoise, which lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the governor of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, is believed to be 194 years old, making him a contemporary of Queen Victoria and Charles Darwin.

Analysis of the animal’s DNA revealed a host of genetic variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing that scientists have discovered. Together, they help organisms to survive by repairing damaged DNA, regulating their metabolism and fending off cancer.

But more intriguing to the researchers were chemical patterns on Jonathan’s genes that appear to protect the healthy functioning of his mitochondria, the tiny battery-like structures that power biological cells. Ailing mitochondria have been strongly linked to ageing and age-related diseases.

“We’re still trying to work out how ageing occurs and Jonathan gives us a real window on to what happens over a long period of time,” said Stephen Clark, a senior researcher on the project at the non-profit Kallel Foundation. “His mitochondria must be especially stable and that’s an insight into longevity in general. It’s important that the mitochondria are kept as pristine as possible.”

The insight came when the international team, led by Benjamin Vaisvil, looked at chemical tags that attach to DNA, creating patterns that change over time. The tags, known as methyl groups, typically silence the genes they latch on to.

Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how they compared the methylation patterns on Jonathan’s genes with those from other giant tortoises. The patterns on many of his genes were similar to those of other old tortoises, but the patterns on genes linked to mitochondrial function matched those from much younger animals.

It is unclear whether, or how much, the chemical patterning contributes to Jonathan’s impressive lifespan. Clark said the team now needed to validate the finding. “How do we test this idea?” he said. “Is there a way that makes the mitochondria young, or can we replace the mitochondria and see if it extends longevity? That’s one of the next steps.”

The former senior veterinary officer of Saint Helena, Joe Hollis, took over Jonathan’s care in 2009. He was not faring well at the time. Cataracts had left him blind, he had lost his sense of smell and his beak was soft and crumbly, making it hard to forage. Hollis began hand-feeding him and six months to a year later, the tortoise had regained weight and sported a hard, serrated beak.

In April, Jonathan was caught up in a viral crypto death scam when a message from a fake X account posing as Hollis claimed the tortoise had died. The news spread around the world before the Guardian made contact with Nigel Phillips, the governor of Saint Helena, who interrupted his bedtime routine to check on Jonathan. He found him asleep under a tree but “very much alive”.

Jonathan certainly appears to be enjoying life. A few months ago, he was found mating with Emma, who shares his paddock. Shortly afterwards, the wife of the governor, who is also called Emma, checked on Jonathan and found him upside down. “Emma [the tortoise] has a very semicircular shell,” said Hollis. “So if you slip sideways fast enough the momentum will flip you right over. It’s phenomenal though. He’s 194. You’re going to have an accident, aren’t you, at 194?”

The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:59:43 GMT

Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the economic struggles of voters have boosted Democrats. But with less than a month to go, there is no complacency

For once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates.

Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That would require flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck.

Even putting aside the ongoing questions about polling accuracy, there are very good reasons for caution. The first and most glaring is that the Democrats remain unpopular. Voters are being turned off the Republicans rather than drawn towards their rivals; pundits talk of a red undertow rather than a blue wave.

Second, the picture is extremely patchy. Democrats’ striking progress in key races where few had favoured them is tied to standout candidates and especially unpopular opponents – notably in Texas, where the Christian pastor and economic populist James Talarico is leading Ken Paxton, viewed unfavourably by a third of his own party’s supporters. Yet Democrats are struggling in some places where they initially had good reason for optimism, such as Maine. Third, the huge Republican spending advantage is now materialising – with $700m of advertising booked since the start of September.

Mr Trump, who has fared better than his party in elections, is hitting the campaign trail. He may make sure his base turns out. But candidates – including those who benefited from his endorsement – are increasingly distancing themselves from the president because he alienates others. He is visibly more energised by his construction projects than how his voters can pay their bills. His war on Iran looks not only reckless and ineffectual, but is pushing up prices. Strikingly, voters are now more likely to identify Republicans than Democrats as “elitist”. Latino voters who swung to him are changing their minds, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement excesses contributing.

Outrageously, Mr Trump has used taxpayer-funded adverts to laud his presidency. It goes without saying that he cannot be expected to respect the midterm results. The supreme court rejected his efforts to restrict mail-in voting – used by almost a third of the electorate – but he continues to smear it.

Just as he disrupts the electoral process, in office he rejects the norms and restraints that his predecessors recognised, and relies more and more on executive orders – seeking to avoid checks on issues ranging from war to vaccines. But should Democrats manage to take both House and Senate, they would regain both legislative control and investigative powers. In these elections, most votes will be driven by economic stress rather than democratic peril. But their outcome will be critical to the defence of American democracy – or its continued erosion.

Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich.

The Tory leader also said couples would be able to leave an additional tax-free sum of £1m to their families, as the party attempts to shore up its traditional base in southern England.

The move would mean the number of families paying inheritance tax – currently less than 5% do so – would fall by more than a half, Badenoch said, with the £6bn cost to be paid for by cuts the party says it has identified, including to the welfare bill.

“My ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it,” she told the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. “I believe the people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort. So this is my guarantee: no stamp duty when you buy your home, no mansion tax when you live in your home, and no inheritance tax on your home when you pass it to your children or grandchildren.”

The Tories’ policy plans announced this week – also including support with childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and repealing the mansion tax – have been firmly focused on affluent middle-class voters, many of whom deserted the party at the last election.

They have been welcomed by Conservative MPs and activists, who are relieved that Badenoch appears to be trying to shore up the party’s core support despite her natural proclivity to lean into culture wars on the right.

However, the inheritance tax plans are likely to raise fears about overheating the housing market, giving elderly homeowners an incentive to stay in large family homes rather than downsize. The move also prompted accusations the party was favouring the rich over struggling families.

In a statement, Tax Justice UK said: “Kemi Badenoch has just announced a massive inheritance tax giveaway to some of the wealthiest people in Britain. This is a reckless policy that will deprive public services of cash when they most need them.”

Stuart Adam, a senior economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes. These will mostly be people living in London and the south-east.”

Reform UK suggested Badenoch’s inheritance tax plans would affect only 2% of houses, the majority in London. Its finance spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said: “The Tory party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country.”

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair and minister for equalities, said: “The Tories haven’t changed. Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories’ choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead.”

Despite the Tories appearing more united this week than they have done for years, Badenoch did acknowledge in her speech that the party, still polling lower than at the time of its catastrophic 2024 election defeat, faced a long path to recovery.

She issued an appeal to Reform voters to back her. “We let them down and we want them to come back home. They deserve better than Reform politicians,” she said. “We have changed our party. There is still a lot of work to do. People are looking through the shop window. They like what they see, but let’s be honest, not enough of them are buying it. We need to fix that.”

Senior Tories have been urging Badenoch to focus more on the economy, which they hope will help them to win back middle-class swing voters in their traditional heartlands, and to pivot away from culture wars and migration.

Badenoch added that economic growth would be the “central organising principle” of the next Conservative government, cutting red tape in areas such as planning, building a third runway at Heathrow and implementing a new energy policy, while also creating jobs.

But she added: “Let me tell you, I’m not someone who gets written off, and neither is the Conservative party. There is a reason our party is still here after 200 years. British Jewish organisations gathered in central London on Wednesday for a vigil honouring victims of the 7 October attacks in Israel, after a day of tributes from politicians and community leaders.
