The Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Three years ago, Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel, murdering 1,200 men, women and children, injuring thousands and taking 251 people captive. May their memories for ever remain a blessing.”

The Jewish Leadership Council said 7 October 2023 had been “the deadliest day for our people since the Holocaust”.

The attacks were followed by Israel’s war in Gaza. The Palestinian death toll in the past three years exceeded 74,000 last month, according to Gaza’s health ministry.

Andy Burnham assured British Jews “we stand with you” against antisemitism, in a statement marking the anniversary.

However, the Israeli embassy said in a statement: “It is a source of deep sadness that in the years since 7 October the position of the British government towards Israel has changed so substantially from the solidarity expressed in those first days,” claiming “the atmosphere for Jewish people continues to worsen” in the UK.

Last month the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine.

The Community Security Trust (CST), which monitors antisemitism, said its research showed there were 1,926 antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK from January to June 2026, up by a fifth on the first half of last year. It was the second highest total reported to the CST in the first six months of any year, exceeded only by the 2,019 incidents recorded in the first half of 2024.

Celebrations of Jewish life have been continuing in public spaces. From 27 September to 2 October, the Jewish festival of Sukkot was celebrated in the heart of Manchester, with the Sukkah in the City event in Albert Square.

In his statement, the prime minister described the rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK since 2023 as “disturbing” and pledged that his government was “committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred”.

Burnham referenced an attack just over a year ago, on the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, by Jihad al-Shamie, 35, at Heaton Park Hebrew congregation synagogue in Manchester, which left two worshippers dead.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from stab wounds and his fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors from Al-Shamie. Police shot al-Shamie dead during the attack.

Burnham said: “Three years on from the 7 October attacks on Israel, we remember those who were senselessly killed by Hamas terrorists. The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day.

“In the years since, we have seen a disturbing rise in antisemitic behaviour in the UK. I want Britain’s Jewish community to hear this from me directly: we stand with you. “That’s why we are funding protection for synagogues, schools and community buildings, and why we will come down hard on antisemitism wherever it is found – in classrooms, on campuses and in neighbourhoods.”

He continued: “At home, we are committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred. Abroad, we continue to work towards a two-state solution, with Israelis and Palestinians living side-by-side in peace and security.

Brendan Venter began his long-awaited public appearance with head bowed, uttering one‑word answers and with a general demeanour suggesting he would rather be anywhere else. By the end he had compared Prem Rugby to an “autocracy”, mentioned Ukraine and Gaza, and detailed an inspirational talk he recently gave at a school. Of course there was wine to talk, too.

An audience with Saracens’ technical director and head of culture is rarely boring and the latest was worth the wait.

To recap, it was announced in February that Venter would replace Mark McCall as director of rugby, returning to the position he left 15 years ago. He has been conspicuous by his absence at press engagements this season, however, and was fined by Prem Rugby.

His job title was changed to head of rugby culture and wine consultant, which felt like a two‑fingered salute to the powers-that-be, and then changed again. The missed media appearances continued until he held court on Wednesday on a rainy afternoon at Saracens’ training base in St Albans.

After some monosyllabic responses Venter finally opened up. “I have the desire as a human being not to want to talk, because it’s not supposed to be about me, it’s about a team, and I expressed that desire before I came.

“And I’m not the director of rugby of this club. This club does not have a director of rugby. This club has an unbelievably competent head coach in Joe [Shaw]. And I ask really kindly, and eventually I bend over backwards to explain my situation and I’m expected again to come and do an interview.

“Joe’s input is way more valuable than my input. And if we get obsessed and we get into an argument and we fine a club, that for me does not make sense. It sounds like something we do in an autocratic land, in a country, not in a democracy where people have got the right to say: ‘This is not what I want to do.’”

Venter has history here, and found himself in disciplinary hot water for speaking his mind when previously in charge. Hence biscuit-gate and a bizarre interview when he offered the immortal line: “three cheers for Sireli Bobo”. That he has little time for post-match platitudes, means he has been determined to keep a low profile on his return to north London.

“It stole my joy the previous time,” he added. “I wanted to have a low profile. That was my desire. I want to coach or help coach the rugby team. I do not want to be doing interviews. And it’s not because of you or anybody else.

“It’s not because I’m mean or I think I’m better than other people. I think the input people can get is brilliant from the people that work with me. To be put over as an arrogant person that thinks he’s better than interviews, it’s not at all that. My motivation is completely different. It’s how do I just get on with my job and help coaching this rugby team. That is my desire.

“I am going to be authentic. And then I am going to have to go to Dublin and sit in some hearing and get a €10,000 fine. So I just want to prevent that. At my age, we actually look at life and go – I call them joy givers and joy stealers. There are things that give me joy and I do more of them. There are things that steal my joy and I cut them out of my life. And that was one of the things that took my joy.”

Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:14:17 GMT

Owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spills

South West Water owner taps investors after sewage spills

Water is “a service where the shareholders never lose and the public never win,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told the Labour party conference last week, reflecting the popular feeling towards the industry in England.

And, of course, his big-picture point is familiar: the £80bn, or thereabouts, that has been paid in dividends over the past 35 years represented over-the-top rewards for investors in many cases. It is easy to agree the public was taken for a ride.

But the idea that shareholders never lose is not correct – and has been out of date for a while. For starters, the current owners of Thames Water have been wiped out. Their shares are worthless whatever the outcome of the interminable talks over whether to put the company into administration or opt for a recapitalisation by the creditors (who will get a sharp haircut on their debt in all circumstances).

Meanwhile, the owners of Southern Water have been obliged to shove in cash on dilutive terms. Now comes something similar at Pennon Group. The owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its shareholders for £550m via a rights issue to fund, in effect, the cost of clearing up past failures.

The new-ish Pennon chief executive, Keith Haslett, outlined an extra £1bn of capital investment on top of the existing £2.6bn in the current five-year period. Of the new £1bn, only £400m represents spending on new infrastructure that can be charged to bills (an extra £10 a year for South West customers if Ofwat gives a thumbs up). The other £600m hits shareholders directly and is the catch-up cost of fixing things that should not have gone wrong in the first place.

Reading between the lines, Haslett seems shocked by what he found. The rights issue document talked about sustained improvement requiring “a fundamental change in how we plan, deliver and maintain our assets” and how previous efforts have been “held back by the way accountability sits within the organisation and gaps in the capability”.

Mr Fixit is not saying it’s an overnight job. All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism.

The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low.

For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine.

One could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation. It’s a point of view but, since Burnham has pretty much ruled it out for water as a blanket policy (we wait to see what happens at Thames), the argument feels academic at this point.

If Burnham, despite it all, is going to live with a privatised system, he could do everybody a favour at this point by hurrying up and deciding what he means by his “public control” overlay. Keir Starmer’s water bill, based on Sir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sector and including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper.

Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.

Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:02:22 GMT

Jorge Messi wanted his country to fall in love with his son. That ambition was fulfilled during a brilliant international career that ended this week

“What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”.

Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidents we all saw around the Argentina team, she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote.

Much was made of Messi’s silence at the time. Then again, much has been made of his visible discomfort with words throughout his epic career. Journalist John Carlin once said that having interviewed Messi twice, he would decline a third opportunity, such was the challenge of getting the little giant to say anything of consequence. In 2010, Juan Sebastián Verón said he had never seen Messi as nervous as when he had to address his teammates for the first time as Argentina captain. In terms of public speaking, perhaps Messi’s most famous outburst was at the 2022 World Cup when he told a Dutch player to “go away”.

Despite this reticence, Messi has always meant something, even when he doesn’t speak. Messi and Argentina were treated as darlings when they won the World Cup in 2022. By the time the 2026 final ended in defeat to Spain, they had become villains.

“That’s why it’s important to understand that when Messi, in the middle of a game that was lost, looks at the sky, and then after that he turns the game around and smashed it, there is something very mysterious there. Right? That we can’t explain. That we just feel,” Lacombe said after Argentina’s semi-final victory over England this summer. “I started supporting England but by the end of the match I was weeping, surrendered to the commitment, the passion, the love that I saw the Argentina team pour on to the pitch. It’s only in that moment of intense passion that we reach the sacred.”

Not everyone surrendered to the sacred in the same way. The final against Spain lacked sublime power and opened the floodgates of vitriol from all corners of the globe. Argentinian fans were offended, hurt, defensive and aware they may have just seen Messi’s last appearance in an Argentina shirt. When he confirmed he would end his international career – his final appearance for Argentina came against Benin on Tuesday – a wave of grief and gratitude swept the nation.

Messi grew up in Barcelona’s youth system, and he was eligible to play for both Spain and Argentina. His debut for Argentina – in a youth match against Paraguay – set up a rush to ensure he pledged his allegiance to the country of his birth, before Spain could tempt him. He was already one of the Barcelona’s academy most promising stars, but he was little known in Argentina. His father, Jorge, wanted nothing more than for his son to represent Argentina, and sent videos to then-manager Marcelo Bielsa hoping to expedite the process. For years, Jorge endured an uphill struggle to consolidate the ties between Lionel and Argentina. Messi’s prowess, seemingly unstoppable in a well-oiled Barcelona system, did not come through at national level. For a long time, Jorge would ask his compatriots the same question. How can we get Argentina to love my son?

Now, as we start to write Messi’s football obituary, some of the most grievous incidents against him are resurfacing. There was the time when a panel of pundits stood in a minute’s silence in protest against Messi’s performances for his country. He was criticised for not singing the national anthem. We learned that before Argentina matches he suffered bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea. Diego Maradona mocked him, saying he was no leader (although he would later make Messi Argentina’s captain). And when the campaign to win over the nation stepped up and he gave interviews, his discourse was shockingly basic and he gave little away.

But Messi never gave up. He missed penalties, wept, and stood to take them again. “What characterized Messi in the national team is that he lost. He lost a lot. He’s constituted in defeat” Argentinian journalist Alejandro Wall says.

But the vitriol more often came from the press than the people. When he quit the national team in 2016, a spontaneous show of love and desire swept the nation, and he reversed his decision. From then on, the Argentinian Football Association’s main priority mirrored that of Jorge Messi: finding a coach who could adapt the entire system to Lionel. It wasn’t easy.

Perhaps it was only after Maradona’s death in 2020 that the new Messi started to emerge. He walked taller, more confident and comfortable in his role as leader. In 2021, Argentina won the Copa América, and snippets of Messi’s pep talks to his teammates filtered out. He made simple statements in his unmistakable Rosario accent, aspiring the ‘s’ and not pronouncing most final consonants. His – and Argentina’s – achievements since then speak for themselves.

Tuesday’s farewell at the Monumental Stadium – much like that first youth game against Paraguay – had a rushed, improvised air. The Argentinian FA struggled to secure opponents, not wanting to share box office with another footballing power. Benin were mocked by some as unworthy, and even Lionel Scaloni made reference to a desire to face bigger opponents than Bolivia and Burkina Faso, the other teams Argentina played this window. Burkina Faso ended up sending an Under-23 side who arrived a few hours before the match, and the stadium was not filled to capacity. Ticket prices were extortionate, and diehard fans refused to fall for what they called “a scam”.

But against Benin they turned up in numbers. Earlier, Messi had picked up an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires, in a small and shabby ceremony in a back office of the Argentinian FA. Delicately produced homages to No 10 were aired. Social media posts full of hyperbolic emotion appeared. “Like Scheherazade, he mocked destiny match by match, to gift the Argentina people another day of his magic. The thousand and one nights of Lionel Messi with the light blue and white come to their end,” read one post. “Whoah, hold it! It’s 9am. I can’t start weeping yet” came a swift reply.

To paraphrase Wayne Rooney, the entertainment around the match was crap. There was a drawn out homage by Soledad Pastorutti, who sang the same number she had once performed with Maradona. A veteran of the Falklands/Malvinas War sang the national anthem, and then clad himself in the same flag that fell on the pitch in Atlanta. The terraces chanted against AFA president Chiqui Tapia in a beautiful chorus, which went some way to atoning for the drone show at the end, with adverts for an insurance company glittering in the sky.

But football is about redemption, and the night was redeemed. Benin actually put up a fight, bookended by the team’s captain gifting Messi a statue of a Dahomey Agojie, the group of women who fought against French occupation. Messi set up three of his team’s three goals and took a penalty. He didn’t miss.

The cameras zoomed in on weeping faces but the sounds from the concrete terraces were decisively celebratory, relentless, trembling. It was football through and through. And Messi loved it. You could tell. He picked up the microphone and launched into a speech so articulate and confident that it merits a dissertation studying its every word. He addressed conspiracy theories surrounding the World Cup final: “Nothing odd happened. The match against England wore us out at an emotional level”. He warned of hard times to come but said team unity is the way through.

“We had the dream of fulfilling our dream,” he said, adding: “I don’t know, I’m talking more than ever. I don’t want to leave here. I love you”. And Argentina loves him back.

As Lacombe said, when Messi looks at the sky, then turns a situation around and smashes it, there is mystery. There is something sacred.

Beware rightwing economic myths such as ‘maxing out the nation’s credit card’

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:01:00 GMT

Readers respond to an article in which Larry Elliott argues that Andy Burnham must challenge neoliberal nostrums

Larry Elliott’s column on the rightwing economic myths constraining Andy Burnham’s government should be required reading before John Healey’s budget (Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes, 1 October).

I spent 20 years trading bonds, and agree that the household budget analogy bears no relation to how the UK state finances itself. Parliament votes on the spending, the Treasury instructs the Bank of England, and the Bank credits accounts in the private sector. Taxes withdraw money afterwards.

The same accounting exposes the “black hole”: every pound of government borrowing ends up as a financial asset held by households, firms and pension funds. That money hasn’t disappeared into any hole, black or otherwise.

The triple lock is debated as a question of whether Britain can afford its pensions, yet a government that issues sterling cannot run out of sterling to pay them. John Maynard Keynes and Clement Attlee understood this, and so did an unlikely ally. Asked in 2005 whether US pay-as-you-go pensions were secure, Alan Greenspan, then chair of the Federal Reserve, told Congress that there was “nothing to prevent the federal government from creating as much money as it wants and paying it to somebody”.

The same is true of sterling. The real question, he added, was whether the economy creates the real assets those pensions are used to buy. Deciding how to provide the care workers, homes and medicines is a political and moral question of the kind democracies exist to settle.

Elliott warns that Burnham risks becoming the prime minister who asked the right questions without finding the answers. Ending Treasury-Induced Decline, a report that I co-wrote, sets out the institutional reforms he needs. He could start by dropping the wrong question: “How will we pay for it?”Vince GomezThe 99% Organisation

Larry Elliott is right: Burnham’s government needs to challenge neoliberal ideas, “the nostrums of the past four decades”, like the one about the government being like a household, if it is to repair the damage done to our social services by the Tories. There are others which Elliott didn’t mention.

The Laffer curve cannot be accepted by a government when chronically underfunded public services are crumbling, and the richest 1% in the UK own 36.5% of all financial assets, with a value of £1.8tn. We must reject arguments against equalising capital gains and income tax and imposing wealth taxes – and of course increasing income tax when fiscal rules allow – which use this old and long-disproved Tory economic myth.

The same applies to the silly notion of trickle-down economics when tackling the excessive profits of banks and companies cashing in on the effects of war. That leads to the Bank of England’s inevitable blaming of wage increases for inflation, ignoring the relatively recent research in the US showing that that most price inflation comes from “companies seeking to maintain profit margins”. Bernie EvansLiverpool

Grateful thanks to Larry Elliott for demolishing the conditioned belief that we must not “max out the nation’s credit card”. Producing and spending is fundamentally important to the ultimate revival of the UK economy and the restoration of industrialisation. My late husband always insisted that we could afford what we needed to and I didn’t believe him. I do now. Val BynnerLondon

Plan to cut disability support will harm young people

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:00:33 GMT

Anna Bird and Rick Burgess respond to the government’s proposal to axe the health element from universal credit that disabled people under 25 receive

Reports that the government is considering removing the universal credit health element for disabled people under 25 will be alarming for families (Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes, 1 October). For many, it raises serious concerns about how they will keep disabled young people supported and able to participate in everyday life.

At Contact, we hear from families worried about universal credit and its impact on disabled family members. Some receiving the health element are studying, working part-time or volunteering; others have disabilities so significant that paid employment is impossible.

We recently joined more than 40 charities urging ministers not to take financial support away from disabled young people. We share the government’s ambition for young people to work and thrive, but we do not believe removing financial security will create those opportunities. Ministers have said that those with the most severe disabilities will be protected. But worried families still don’t know what criteria would apply or how hard it would be to prove eligibility.

Crucially, receiving the health element of universal credit does not mean a young person is not in education, employment or training (Neet). Before making such a fundamental change, ministers must publish the evidence. How many young people receiving the health element are actually Neet? And among those who are, how many cannot participate because of their disability or health condition?

Disabled young people need opportunity and security. One cannot safely be traded for the other. Anna BirdCEO, Contact

This proposal to cut support for disabled young people rather than provide equal access to welfare sends a message to them that they matter less to society. Far from improving their independence or opportunities for work, such cuts would harm their health and push more people into poverty. It is careless to assume that employment support could fill the gap.

Disability does not discriminate based on age; nor should the welfare system. A wheelchair, specialist equipment, transport or social care still costs the same whether you are 20 or 60. Young disabled people deserve a social security system that respects their human rights and dignity equally. Rick BurgessChair, Amnesty International UK’s Disabled People’s Human Rights Network

‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 17:00:00 GMT

TaxWatch contradicts claims about David Reuben’s departure and questions stories of super-rich exodus

Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground

When the Sunday Times broke the news that David Reuben, one of the richest men in the UK, had apparently fled to the tax haven of Monaco, there was much pearl clutching. Reuben had moved from his Holland Park house in London to live full-time in the principality.

Labour’s tax regime was blamed and there were said to be fears there would be a cascading effect across the economy, with wealth draining from the UK. It was reported that he had probably left because of potential taxes on wealth in the upcoming budget.

However, research by TaxWatch has found that Reuben, 88, has been a tax resident in Monaco since at least 2014.

A spokesperson for the Newcastle United shareholder, who with his brother Simon, 85, shares a combined estimated wealth of almost £28bn, confirmed this was the case.

Simon Reuben has lived in Monaco for 40 years since moving on health grounds while having cancer.

The principality is a popular place for those who do not wish to pay UK taxes as it does not impose income tax, capital gains tax or inheritance tax.

In July 2019, when David became a director of the Reuben foundation, the paperwork filed at the UK company registry stated he was “usually resident” in Monaco.

In 2024 he provided a signed declaration to a Los Angeles court stating: “I reside in Monaco. I have resided there for approximately 10 years.”

It was reported that the Reuben brothers were “non-doms”, which allowed them to pay UK tax only on income generated in the UK. The then chancellor Rachel Reeves axed this system in April last year, prompting a reported exodus of foreign super-rich individuals.

Asked whether Reuben would have been caught by changes to these rules if he had not decided to move out of his UK residence, a spokesperson said: “That’s an entirely hypothetical question to which it would be impossible to give an answer.”

Mike Lewis, the director of TaxWatch, told the Guardian: “When we started looking into this, we were surprised that publicly available documents completely contradicted a major news story. Sadly, these kinds of stories dominate the UK’s public and political conversation about our tax system.

“The autumn budget may see some of the biggest changes in years to how gains from wealth are taxed. Perhaps it’s time that our politicians, and our media, debate these changes based on public facts and verifiable numbers – not anecdotes and anonymous reports from billionaires and their spokespeople.”

The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who campaigns for a wealth tax, said: “If you want to live in this country, being British, having access to the culture of London, people want that, and there are lots of billionaires and millionaires who do stay because of that.

“It’s instructive that there is a grouping of commentators who put on the scare tactics to say the wealthy are leaving this country. We can see that many of these billionaires don’t reside here anyway, many of them do stay here, and those who want to go, we can’t stop them anyway. This has always been the case.”

Some of the super-rich are leaving. Analysis of Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index has found that super-rich UK residents worth a combined £121bn have either left or loosened ties with the UK since the Labour government came to power in 2024. This represents more than half of all billionaire wealth.

Among those who have left are the steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, the Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and the shipping magnate John Fredriksen.

Inheritance tax changes in Reeves’s budget were also blamed for pushing the wealthy out, and it is thought capital gains tax may be increased this autumn.

The Reuben brothers were born in Mumbai, moved to London in their teens, and went to a state school in Islington, leaving education aged 17 with no A-levels. They started businesses in metal trading and carpet importing. Since then, they have built a property empire.

They own prestigious locations including Mayfair’s chandelier-festooned Burlington Arcade, Admiralty Arch, which is being developed into a five-star hotel, and Millbank Tower in Westminster.

All three will be sentenced at the conclusion of the trial, which is scheduled to open on 19 October. The case was due to begin in early September, but has faced several delays for legal and practical reasons.

At a hearing on Tuesday, the jury of three men and nine women were told by Judge Maurice Greene that the husband had provided a witness statement detailing “what it is he says happened”, which had been disclosed to defence lawyers and meant the trial would be delayed while they went through it.

The jury, including two female reserve jurors bringing their total number to 14, were sent away and told to return to the same court on 19 October.

Eleven men are due to stand trial, denying a range of offences including rape and attempted rape, with the abuse alleged to have taken place between 2018 and November 2025.

They are Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport; Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester; Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport; Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport; Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode; Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich in Cheshire; Richard Townsend, 37, from Heywood in Greater Manchester; Karl Lindsay, 55, from Taunton in Somerset; Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable in Kent; and David Graves, 59, from Ilkeston in Derbyshire.

The trial is expected to last about nine weeks and due to conclude in mid-December.

Labour could oversee worst parliament on record for living standards, study warns

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:30:55 GMT

Energy and housing costs threaten biggest decline in modern times unless bold action taken, says thinktank

Soaring energy and housing costs mean Labour is on course to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times, a stark analysis warns.

Three weeks ahead of John Healey’s budget, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation said Britain faces a “dire” outlook unless the government takes “bold policy action”.

The JRF predicts that, after housing costs, average household incomes will be between £440 and £770 lower in real terms in 2029-30 than when Labour came to power two years ago.

Even the lower end of that range would mark the biggest decline in living standards since modern records began in 1961, the thinktank said, and come on top of a tight squeeze in the last parliament.

Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has been tasked by Andy Burnham to lead the Cabinet Office cross-government taskforces, with two focusing on turning around living standards. One is looking at short-term cost of living measures to help on housing and energy, and the other at big structural interventions such as public control that might alleviate those pressures long term.

Their work will eventually form part of the 10-year plan expected later this autumn, which Burnham began discussions about with cabinet ministers at a Chequers away day this week.

Haigh has repeatedly told officials that there will have to be “trade offs” in order to prioritise alleviating the cost of living and public control.

At the budget, Burnham has promised to offer a “breathing space” to voters and Healey is expected to offer £1bn in additional support to energy consumers; but there are concerns inside government about whether that goes far enough.

Healey is minded to rebuff a call from the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether. The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.

The chancellor is understood to be considering raising this by £100, with the rise funded by taxpayers.

The foundation’s living standards analysis used the Bank of England’s two projections for energy prices – a “central” and an “adverse” scenario.

The thinktank has pointed out that since the Bank set these out in July, real-world events have tracked close to the adverse scenario, with oil prices surging back above $100 a barrel after hostilities resumed in the Middle East.

By driving up the cost of energy, the renewed conflict has also increased expectations that the Bank will raise the base interest rate to tackle resurgent inflation. Markets are now betting on four quarter point increases to 4.75% by the end of next year.

Borrowing costs for homebuyers have already jumped in response to the resulting turmoil in bond markets – with the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hitting 6% this week for the first time in three years.

Chris Belfield, the chief economist at the JRF, said: “Without bold policy action on living standards, families are set to be poorer than they were a decade ago. This is terrible both for families who are just treading water to get by and the more than 7 million families who are already routinely going without essentials like food and basic toiletries.”

Some forecasts have suggested the typical household dual-fuel bill could leap by 16% to the equivalent of £2,000 a year in the first quarter of next year. Given the scale of the looming squeeze, the foundation has argued for a more ambitious package of measures on energy than Healey appears minded to offer.

It would like to see a baseline level of energy offered to all households at a cheaper price, with those in greater need entitled to more of these cut-price units of gas and electricity.

Other recommendations include making benefits more generous by relinking local housing allowance to average rents; and increasing universal credit, as the Conservatives did during the Covid pandemic. This could be paid for via changes such as increasing capital gains tax rates to match income tax, it argues.

The JRF analysis of changes in living standards over time differs from those of the Office for Budget Responsibility and other thinktanks such as the Resolution Foundation because of different ways of accounting for housing costs.

Despite Burnham’s promise to correct 40 years of economic missteps, Healey’s budget is expected to be relatively modest, with important decisions on tax and spending delayed until next year. These include when the UK will implement spending 3% of GDP on defence – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.

In his 28 October statement, the chancellor is expected to focus on filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer’s government in June; and laying out how the Treasury will devolve some income tax revenue to regional mayors.

A Treasury spokesperson said: “We know families are feeling the impact of higher prices, pushed up by conflicts overseas.

“The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That’s why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, capped bus fares in England at £2 in 2027, extended the 5p fuel duty cut, and frozen rail fares and prescription charges.”

Verstappen’s victory in Sepang should serve as a warning to Red Bull’s rivals

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:28:12 GMT

Improvements to the car are paying off as the team look to lay the groundwork for renewed success next season

The importance for Max Verstappen of emerging triumphant from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was writ large in the Dutchman’s pleasure at finally being able to drive a competitive car. In a ride with which he was comfortable and able to take to a dominant victory for Red Bull, Verstappen was in his element. With it came a sense of what might have been had he not been long out of the championship fight, but also what might be to come next year.

The transformation was so marked because for so long this season the car has been a handful – the reason Verstappen’s title hopes faded long ago. That the team have come back to deliver a win in such emphatic fashion was no little achievement.

In the opening period of the season, the RB22 was nowhere, deficient in almost every department. It lacked pace, balance, even consistency, and for all his skill Verstappen seemed powerless. He described it as feeling like a passenger in the car at times.

The four-time world champion wrestled it to a couple of podiums in the first half of the season but it was a sisyphean task. “At the start of the season, I really had weekends where I would turn the steering wheel and strange things would happen,” he said. Which, a rather understated critique, belies the fact that the last place a driver wants to be is in a car where he is unsure which way it is going to jump.

Red Bull, under Laurent Mekies, stuck at it and brought major upgrades to Miami and Austria. Yet the scale of what needed doing across so many facets of the car remained difficult to overcome. Only a month ago Verstappen could only qualify sixth at Monza, admittedly a power track where the relative paucity of their electrical energy deployment was a hindrance. It nonetheless suggested a win was as far away as ever.

Yet there were indications that each incremental development was bringing a greater understanding of the car and how to coax the best out of it. In Madrid, Verstappen qualified just over a tenth of a second off pole and had real pace in the race, which might have delivered more on a track where overtaking was possible. At the next round in Baku, Red Bull brought their final upgrade, including a development to the floor. In qualifying Verstappen was unlucky with yellow flags to start from eighth but in the race the car was rapid. He flew through the field, chasing the winner, Mercedes’ George Russell, to the flag right on his gearbox.

The car’s speed on the straights was noted by rivals, not least Mercedes, as Verstappen closed on Russell. Red Bull’s other driver, Isack Hadjar, who had spent three races out with a wrist injury, felt as if he had been given a new ride. “I definitely feel like I jumped in a car that’s way better than when I left it in Budapest,” he said.

What followed in Sepang was validation that Red Bull really had got it right. Verstappen took pole and won with a drive that exemplified his car’s improvements. The RB22 was quicker in a straight line than the Mercedes and fast in the medium and high-speed corners, its achilles heel previously.

On a track punishing to the tyres, the car was well-balanced, less damaging to the rubber, allowing better energy deployment. Having addressed problems which conflated with one another, the car coalesced into a more coherent whole. Verstappen described the process as having “pushed weaknesses out of the car”. It has taken them 16 meetings but on this form Red Bull are finally up with McLaren, Ferrari and Mercedes.

Their progress stands as testament to a team working collectively to tremendous effect. It is an achievement that must be acknowledged alongside building their own engine for the first time and delivering a win; a feat that is recognised across the paddock as perhaps beyond expectations and which was far from guaranteed to be successful as Honda, with more experience, have demonstrated all too clearly this season.

There may have been an element of the win in Sepang being track-specific. The fact the Mercedes upgrades deployed there did not deliver at all was a factor, and they must contend with Russell starting the Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid following an engine change after a late retirement in Malaysia. But the Red Bull is a different car now and how it performs on the streets of Singapore this weekend will be telling.

Verstappen will want more wins, but it is instructive how he and the team are viewing these final meetings. They want to end strongly and feed every possible piece of information into next year’s car. Hadjar said: “We have to try all the things, make all the mistakes now and do all the learning to arrive in 2027 ready to roll and start on high.” It is an ambition which will not be lost on their rivals, who know only too well how formidable Red Bull can be if they are quick out of the blocks.

Ties are back in fashion, thanks to gen Z – should we all be smartening up?

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:28:05 GMT

Sales at one UK retailer are up 200%, thanks in part to young people rejecting the informal look adopted by their middle-aged bosses

Name: Ties.

Age: Originated in the early 17th century.

Appearance: They’re back.

Where did they go? The fashion for wearing a suit with an open-collar shirt, combined with a Covid-inspired trend for working from home, had driven neckties to the edge of extinction.

And now they’ve been saved by some kind of selective breeding programme? They’ve been saved by a fashion-conscious younger generation returning to more formal codes of dress.

Do you have any evidence to support this claim? According to the menswear retailer TM Lewin, year-on-year sales of ties increased by 200% this summer.

I didn’t realise TM Lewin still existed. It’s also back from the brink: after closing all its physical stores during the pandemic, the company is beginning to reopen some sites.

So ties are in? Not everywhere – news of the resurgence comes just weeks after the House of Lords relaxed its rules to allow men to appear tieless in the chamber.

The Lords out of step with fashion trends? How did this deplorable state of affairs come about? It’s hard to imagine, especially when all they had to do was nothing.

How times have changed. Think of it as a generational backlash – the informal, open-collar look is now the preserve of well-off, middle-aged men. Young people don’t want to dress like the boss, so they dress up.

Where do ties come from anyway? They have their origins in the cravats worn by – and named after – Croatian mercenaries who served in France during the thirty years’ war (1618-48).

Nice story, but a cravat is not a tie. Fashionable neckwear evolved over the centuries, from the stock to the scarf to the neckerchief. The necktie we know today was patented in 1922 by a New York tailor called Jesse Langsdorf.

So neckwear stopped evolving more than a century ago? What changed over time was the fashion for certain lengths, widths, patterns and knots: the four-in-hand in the mid-Victorian era, the windsor between the world wars, the half-windsor in the 1950s.

Are any other endangered formal accessories being resurrected by impressionable young people, or is it just ties? Apparently, they’ve also forsaken trainers in favour of wearing leather loafers, oxfords and derbies to work.

That cannot be. It’s true – sneaker sales in the US have stagnated. And Cruz and Romeo Beckham have been spotted wearing suits with trouser braces.

What next? Top hats? Spats? Honestly, don’t give gen Z any ideas.

Do say: “The once-shunned necktie has returned, with the retail menswear sector riding on its coattails.”

Don’t say: “Can coattails be far behind?”

All hail the Death Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the Conservatives

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 16:26:06 GMT

The Tory leader is now too big for the party to allow her to fail, so everything she does is acclaimed a work of genius

Where’s AI slop when you need it? It could all have been so much simpler. Just ask ChatGPT to write me a leader’s speech in the style of Kemi Badenoch. Make it an hour and 10 minutes long, so plenty of room for padding. Go heavy on the slogans, cliches and the obligatory crap politician jokes. Ones we’ve all heard many times before. Not least at this conference.

Make the usual digs at Labour and put the boot in to Reform. The main aim of the speech is to try to reposition a party that is tanking in third place on 20% in the polls as the main opposition to the government.

And just to give everyone a reason to go home with a feeling of mild optimism, chuck in a retail offer at the end. An uncosted tax cut for people who are rich but don’t feel quite rich enough. The new multimillionaire common-or-garden lower middle classes.

Unfortunately, Kemi made the schoolgirl error of trying to write the speech for herself. And it was much the worse for it. What’s the point of having AI if you don’t use it? It was too long, too flabby. No real argument, just a collection of random thoughts. Andy Burnham in Liverpool it wasn’t.

Parts of it even seemed to bore Kemi herself. As if she was going through the motions. Lazy, even. That it was still by far and away the best speech of the entire conference is not really the point. More of a reflection of how dire the others have been. Four days of the Tories in Birmingham is a trial for anyone remotely sentient.

On the surface, the Tories have seemed a happy tribe this week. There has been a soporific tranquillity to the proceedings. Few members attending, nonexistent queues and above all no Robert Jenrick. Or even Liz Truss. How we miss her.

But the unity feels very fragile. The Tories are now Kemi and Kemi is the Tories. The party has bet the bank on her. Kemi even now calls herself the captain, coach and owner of the Tories. Everyone else is an also-ran.

This comes at a huge risk. Because Kemi has become almost too big for the Tories to allow her to fail. So they daren’t question her. Anything she does has to be acclaimed as a work of genius. Just walking on stage is enough to secure her a standing ovation. No one has ever quite walked like that before.

The party has been captured by the Kult of Kemi. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy that could lead them to oblivion. They have no idea if Kemi is messiah or lemming, but they are happy to go over the cliff regardless. They are out of other options.

Just don’t stop to ask why nothing the Tories seem to do is cutting through. Why the polls are stubbornly flatlining. Why it’s odds-on that beyond the few hundred people in the hall, no one will pay a blind bit of attention to her speech. It will be forgotten within a day.

Wednesday morning’s proceedings began with the Tory chair, Kevin Hollinrake. Kev’s dog got a bigger cheer than Kev. Next up was the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, a one-man cluster of antimatter. No man can suck the energy out of the room like Nick. The only thing that would cheer him up is a public execution.

Then the Philpster. The UK’s self-proclaimed superhero. The vigilante who took on the French. Endearingly, he still thinks the French navy knows who he is. Chris, most of the UK don’t know who you are. Nor do they care.

After this, things began to get surreal as each member of the shadow cabinet was announced and applauded as they took their seats. A bit like a third-rate talent show. The presenter still didn’t know who Nick Timothy was, despite having introduced him moments earlier. She also got Helen Whately’s name wrong. And there was one empty chair. Tom Tugendhat had invented an unmissable trip to India to get out of the embarrassment. Wise choice.

A spot of Elgar and then it was Kemi. There was a fight for the soul of the country. There’s always a fight for the soul of the country as far as the Tories are concerned. They don’t seem to realise that it was them that ripped the soul out of it.

after newsletter promotion

“What a great conference we’ve had,” she said. It was hard to know if she was being ironic. Other than the fact that everyone has been wandering round in brain-dead surprise that the Tories still exist, it’s been a disaster.

After that things went weird. As if we were entering a weird dystopia. Being asked to believe the unbelievable. Like when she said that her shadow cabinet was a united team that listened to one another. This after Kemi had literally said she was the party and that anyone who disagreed with her could go fuck themselves. The whole point of Kemi is that she listens to no one.

She also had a pop at Labour for putting all their faith in one man. Pots, kettles. As for Reform, she had nothing but contempt. You’d like to think that would rule out a possible coalition.

The one moment when Kemi became truly passionate – believable even – was when she talked about race. This was Kemi at her best, talking about something she really cared about. Even if she did imagine there was no racism in football in the 1970s and 80s. But this bit was all too short and the speech began to feel like it was dragging into eternity. We’d still be trying to stay awake well into the afternoon.

Finally the reveal – the inheritance tax reduction that would be funded by as-yet-unspecified welfare cuts. There would be no inheritance tax on anyone leaving their home to their children. With an extra million-quid freebie thrown in, in case you needed to do it up after your parents had let it get tatty. You could hear the cheers from the country’s stately homes echo around the hall.

Here was a party that really got it. Which was prepared to do something about the cost of living for the mega-rich. Even as Kemi was speaking, millions of ordinary citizens were phoning their brokers to liquidate their stock market assets so they could upgrade their £1m homes to something far more palatial. The property market in mega-homes had just gone wild. The people’s earl, Charles Spencer, could breathe easy. Althorp was safe. Let them drink champagne.

There was just time for Kemi to pay tribute to Jeffrey Archer – the Tories have a soft spot for a convicted conman who ruined several lives – and then came the extended standing ovations. An echo chamber is going to echo.

Abide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish it

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 15:57:46 GMT

One hundred years since the BBC first broadcast choral evensong, MP and former chorister Jonathan Davies hymns a beautiful and empowering collective experience that we should praise – and protect

Some sounds seem to belong to Britain. The peal of church bells. The brass band on a village green. The roar of a football crowd. And, heard from a cathedral at the end of the day, the extraordinary sound of a choir singing evensong.

This year marks the centenary of choral evensong on BBC radio. On 7 October 1926, when the BBC was in its infancy, listeners heard a live service broadcast from Westminster Abbey. A century later, evensong can still be heard on Radio 3 every week from cathedrals, churches, chapels and abbeys across the country. It is the BBC’s longest running outside broadcast and reaches hundreds of thousands of people every week.

For the listener at home, the radio can make a distant cathedral feel remarkably close. But we should not celebrate this simply as a remarkable broadcasting survival story. We should celebrate it because it represents something much bigger: a living part of our cultural heritage.

You do not have to be religious or particularly musical to understand the power of evensong. You do not even need to know what a Magnificat or an anthem is. There is something profoundly human about sitting quietly in a great building, hearing young and old voices combine in astonishingly beautiful music. Being given permission for 45 minutes of detachment from the frenetic pace of modern life. For some it is prayer, for others contemplation, inspiration or simply a moment of peace.

That is culture at its best: not something kept behind closed doors, but a collective experience. And that is why we should care about what happens when the ecosystems that sustain this tradition come under pressure.

Cathedral music is not simply about preserving an old repertoire. It is a living tradition, with newly written music sitting alongside pieces that have been passed down through generations. Around 3,000 children and young people currently sing as choristers in the UK’s cathedrals, churches and chapels, with thousands more taking part in youth and school choirs led by church musicians. Through these experiences they develop exceptional musical skills alongside confidence, discipline, teamwork and a sense of belonging to something much larger than themselves. Many take these skills into careers far beyond music.

There is also an important social mobility story here. A cathedral choir can give a child access to world-class musical training, extraordinary cultural experiences and educational opportunities that might otherwise be beyond their reach. But we also need to be honest about the barriers, too: affordability, access to music tuition and the unfamiliarity of cathedral culture can all restrict who gets through the door. Preserving this tradition cannot mean simply preserving the status quo. It must mean widening access to it.

Singing in a church choir as a child opened up worlds for me. Not just through the opportunity – as Thomas Cranmer put it – to “read, mark, learn and inwardly digest” the most sacred of texts, illuminated by a wealth of the most enriching music humankind has created. It instilled an appreciation of routines and hard work, and it taught me that you can achieve more through collaboration than you can alone. It also taught me that success is sometimes built on of the insights of failure. Something of which I occasionally have to remind myself as a member of parliament.

The charity Cathedral Music Trust is working hard to ensure the continuation of these sorts of opportunities and is leading a campaign to secure Unesco status for English sacred choral music. Their submission for Living Heritage status seeks recognition not for a historical artefact, but for a vibrant and thriving art form, one continually renewed by the children who sing it, the composers who add to its repertoire and the communities who participate in it. Unesco recognition would send an important message worldwide: that this is deemed worthy of recognition, investment and protection, and remains a vital part of the UK’s national cultural inheritance.

The UK rightly celebrates its great theatres, galleries and museums. We should be equally confident in celebrating a cultural and religious tradition that is performed every day, in buildings at the heart of communities, by musicians of extraordinary skill. A tradition that has reached so many people through the simple miracle of radio. We have a responsibility not simply to admire this wonderful tradition, but to protect it and to make sure that the next generation can claim it as their own.

Jonathan Davies is MP for Mid Derbyshire

From Bentley Pauncefoot to Yetts O’Muckhart, I’m obsessed with Britain’s weirdly named villages

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 15:49:25 GMT

I was stuck in traffic when a road sign set me dreaming. If the places on it were people, what would they be like? Could Leigh Delamere be anything but the glamorous heiress to a biscuit-making fortune?

Stuck in traffic in the Wiltshire town of Chippenham, I chanced upon a road sign to Christian Malford and Sutton Benger. Placenames that could be people are dotted across our green and pleasant land – it’s charmingly British, somehow. Waiting to escape Friday night rush hour, I found a persona for Christian Malford taking shape. I had him down as a child actor in one of the early Harry Potters. Sutton Benger was more of a stretch, but I settled on a precociously talented young footballer of Anglo-Norwegian heritage. He signed for Chelsea with great fanfare, but never really made the grade. Poor chap.

The traffic moved on, but my mind didn’t. Once on the M4, I was soon passing Leigh Delamere, the glamorous heiress of an American biscuit-making fortune, now fallen on hard times.

Back home, I dug out my late dad’s AA road atlas of Britain (2019 edition). How I loved scouring the index in search of more imaginary friends peopling our placenames. Fun for a feeble mind? Probably. Deeply satisfying? Certainly.

First, a mention for the mononymous. Patrick on the Isle of Man, Paul in Cornwall – and then there’s Barry in the Vale of Glamorgan, as we all know. A warm wave as well to Kelly in Devon and, in the Highlands, to Kirk and, sweetly, Arabella. There are two Lees, in Devon and London, and Leighs aplenty. Countless Prestons, too. And Bradleys. I make it three Martins and four Hopes. I’m assuming, by the way, that Hope Bagot in Shropshire and Preston Bagot in Warwickshire are somehow related.

Many of the first-second name combos are almost disappointingly mundane – no offence to George Green in Buckinghamshire, Roy Bridge in the Highlands or any of the three Rose Greens. By the way, these things can hide in plain sight – I lived next to a place called Hayley Green for most of my life without once realising it would make a perfectly charming girl’s name.

Moving on to slightly more engaging names, there’s Ash Thomas and George Nympton, both residing in Devon. Also Nevill Holt in Leicestershire, Rodney Stoke in Somerset and Kirk Deighton in North Yorkshire, while I’ve developed a bit of a fancy for Edith Weston in Rutland. In Kent, we find Dean Bottom, who must have endured terrible stick when he was a kid.

I must give an honourable mention to Sandy Balls. Sandy, sadly, doesn’t make the grade, as she/he is not a village, but an area of woodland in Hampshire. That said, there is a Sandy Balls holiday village. What exactly goes on there I haven’t dared to check.

It’s in the more intriguing (that is to say unlikely) names that I’ve found the greatest joy: Clifford Chambers in Warwickshire, for example. Surely by now someone called Chambers should have moved there, begat a son called Cliff, raised him to be a lawyer and then opened a practice. “Hi, I’m Clifford Chambers of Clifford Chambers in Clifford Chambers …” C’mon, someone, do it!

In neighbouring Worcestershire we find Chaddesley Corbett, surely a philanthropic 19th-century educationist, and Bentley Pauncefoot, the friendly but clueless youngest son of a local landowning noble, nicknamed Paunstar (obviously) by his chums at boarding school. Over the border in Shropshire we can go for an audience with Cleobury Mortimer, a big star in restoration comedy. Staying with arts and culture, North Yorkshire is in good shape with Burton Leonard, the handsome but troubled early 50s Hollywood heart-throb, and Ainderby Quernhow, a fantasy novelist, latterly doing good business with her well-received Olde English Book of Spelles.

Elsewhere, there are many foppish-sounding coves. To name but three, Hertfordshire’s Furneux Pelham, Danby Wiske in North Yorkshire and, my personal favourite, Worcestershire’s Flyford Flavell. In sport, Buckinghamshire is strong. There’s the widely feared West Indian fast bowler Aston Clinton and the footballer Lee Clump, the holder of several non-league scoring records.

I puzzled awhile over Quadring Eaudike in Lincolnshire, but concluded he had to be a pioneering mathematician. As for Huish Champflower in Somerset, Yetts O’Muckhart in Clackmannanshire and Zeal Monachorum in Devon, I’m afraid I’m stumped. I simply can’t find the characters to do these places justice.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Crush-worthy photography, camp sci-fi and a centenarian’s florals: five free exhibitions to see

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 15:16:35 GMT

A little exhibition of Daidō Moriyama at his artiest and strangest, like Warhol with added filth, is among the best on show in London’s free-entry commercial galleries this week

If it’s a crime to have a crush on an elderly avant garde Japanese street photographer then lock me up and throw away the key, because I have some seriously strong feelings for Daidō Moriyama. His ultra-confrontational, high contrast, aggressive take on photography just gets me blushing, what can I say.

This little exhibition is Moriyama at his artiest and strangest. In the 1960s he discovered Warhol and became obsessed. The works here find him playing with repetition and silk screening, printing up ghostly, painterly, effervescent monochrome images of stacks of soft drinks, neon lit crosswalks and peep show adverts. This is the grim, gritty side of Japanese urbanity, but you can see American capitalism creeping in and taking hold, slowly suffocating the streets.

He repeats an image of lips like Warhol’s Marilyn Monroe, duplicates a photo of people walking down a street, their bodies becoming indistinguishable from the adverts hanging from the high rises around them. Then he snaps a woman lifting her skirt, another stomping down the road in thigh-high boots. It’s like Warhol without the pretence, and with added filth. Hamiltons Gallery, London, until 30 October

Jenkin van Zyl is hellbent on cementing their place as English art’s ultimate hyper-camp weirdo, and their new show at Somerset House Studios is a pretty persuasive argument.

The exhibition is centred on a speculative sci-fi movie about some bleak company where tourists can inhabit other people’s bodies. But when the central character, a starlet called Mercy, comes to end the lease on her body, the line between reality and fiction starts getting anxiously blurry. Who is the real Mercy, and who is the clone? Who controls your identity? Who has access to what makes you you?

Its grubby atmosphere is reinforced by an immersive installation that replicates the film set as you walk in, with broken automatons, flickering lights and piles of rubbish, all bathed in a pink glow. It’s an unsettling, uncomfortable, dirty, dystopian bit of art cinema – like an overblown, fetishistic take on Terry Gilliam’s Brazil. Van Zyl has a singular aesthetic, and this is pretty much as watchable as this kind of art film gets. It stays with you long after you’ve escaped its unnerving clutches.

The gallery handout wants to make out like this is about technological advancement and ideas of authorship. But like all good sci-fi, this feels more obviously allegorical than that. It’s about identity, the versions of ourselves that we present and preserve online, or in public, and how easy it is to lose your grip on the true you. Like a lot of artists these days who grew up with the internet and reality TV turning their brain into gloop, Van Zyl is trying to make sense of a post-reality world, a place where identity can be constructed, but never fully controlled. Somerset House, London, until 29 November

There’s nothing all that pleasant, or even particularly green, about the England of George Shaw’s paintings. There are no rolling hills or quiet pub afternoons here in this excellent show of small works by the 60-year-old artist. Instead, there are endless potholes, crumbling masonry, darkened alleys and damp, muddy, miserable, mid-winter landscapes. This is the England of council estates left to rot.

His landscapes – always based on his native Coventry – are devoid of life. There are no humans here, only the places they’re desperate to escape. Every sky is overcast, every tree barren, every path sodden with puddles. A union jack has been left crumpled on the pavement near an empty bottle of booze in one, endless knobs have been crudely graffitied on garage doors in another. There’s a painting of a single cloud blighting a blue sky, another of a robin lying dead on its side. Suburbia has leached into the countryside like a toxic spill.

They are gorgeously painted, especially the smaller works: sticky with enamel, glossy and horrifyingly alluring, like staring at a car crash.

But the car crash here is England itself. Sure, Shaw has been painting the same views of the same bit of Coventry for 30 years, but in that time the country has continued to erode. His whole career is a living portrait of England’s slow collapse. This time it doesn’t just feel like perpetual decline – it’s terminal. Anthony Wilkinson Gallery, London, until 7 November

after newsletter promotion

The thing that’s so good about the main work in Tanoa Sasraku’s Turner prize installation – open now at Mima in Middlesbrough – is how perfectly it marries image with idea. Sasraku’s collection of corporate paperweights from oil companies acts as a horrifying symbol of the greed of that vile industry. Perfect.

Here at Vardaxoglou, Sasraku is showing works from another series, some of which are also on show at Mima, that don’t quite hit the same dopamine receptors. They’re all paper cut into the form of torsos, held together with clips. She places acetates of military camouflage on top of them and then pops them in a tanning bed, leaving behind the faintest impressions of the patterns.

They’re meant to evoke warfare, weapons crates and fruit boxes, all while alluding to Ken dolls, but they just look a bit like tea-stained gilets. The gap between image and idea, between the concept and its ability to communicate itself visually, is just a bit too wide. Vardaxoglou, London, until 31 October

You’ve got to hope you turn out like Ce Roser. The 101-year-old American artist has only got better with age. They call her an abstract painter, but all the flower paintings here feel pretty figurative. The earlier, flowerier works from the 1960s are nice, fuzzy, dreamy things. But the stuff from the 1970s, and then the watercolours from the 2010s … that’s where it gets good. Her work gets sparser and more minimal, but no less pretty. Landscapes and flora burst apart and writhe across expanses of white – they have all the aesthetic warmth and floral calm of the earlier stuff, but pared back and made lighter. I’m definitely worse at everything now than I was in my 20s. Let’s hope things pick up when I hit 90. VeneKlasen, London, until 3 December

Badenoch made the best of it – but the Tories still have a mountain to climb before any hope of No 10

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 15:08:39 GMT

Conference announcements on inheritance tax and childcare boosted the party’s mood, but the task is still holding off Reform, rather than any realistic bid for power

On paper, the traditional role of the journalist at a British party conference boils down to some simple questions: what was the mood of the assembled activists? Did the leader give a good speech? In practice, the changing nature of conferences and the media makes this superficially simple task more complicated than it may initially appear.

Any journalist covering the leader’s speech, for instance, will have watched it in full. But it will reach the vast majority of its intended audience in fragmentary form, through clips – and speeches are increasingly written with that reality in mind. The conference hall is not really the audience, or the full speech really the product. This adds a layer of complexity to the reviewer’s task.

Likewise, it is less meaningful than once it was to talk about the mood of the conference. Thirty years ago, when our political parties were much more robust social institutions than they are today, millions of Britons were party members through thick and thin, and thousands attended annual conference whether they liked the leadership or not.

It was this democratic culture that gave us the spectacular showdowns at Labour conferences in the 1980s, or Tory activists cheering Norman Tebbit’s excoriation of the European Union in the 1990s. But it is unthinkable now: most people disaffected with a party – especially the Conservatives – are simply not members of it; they certainly don’t take time off work and spend several hundred pounds to attend conference.

Even with that caveat, however, there is no doubt that the mood inside the Conservative party is considerably improved on last year’s. Manchester proved that Kemi Badenoch can make good use of a spotlight, even in otherwise extremely challenging conditions, and her position has improved markedly since then. Her personal ratings are up, her party’s polling has recovered (a little), her only real rival for the leadership has defected to Reform UK, and Reform has its own problems.

The policy side of things is helping, too. I was very critical of Badenoch’s decision to go as slowly as she did on policy, and do think that first year of near-radio silence did the Tories serious damage. But the eventual policy announcements have, so far, been generally well-considered; if they still tend to err too much on the side of caution, it is at least better than the alternative, the wild promises of an opposition which has abandoned all hope of office.

Birmingham has also confirmed that the Conservatives have recognised the need for a strategic pivot. Badenoch has come under fire from some quarters for returning to the party’s “comfort zone” on tax cuts and deregulation, rather than trying to reassemble Boris Johnson’s 2019 coalition and go blow-for-blow with Reform.

But that analysis fundamentally misunderstands the current state of play. As much as the gladiatorial spectacle of the “fight on the right” appeals to journalists, so long as the Tories and Reform are polling where they are, they are not really each other’s primary opponent. Reform’s immediate front lies through Labour; of the 98 seats where it placed second in 2024, 89 are held by a Labour MP.

The Conservatives’ front, in contrast, is much more southern, affluent and Liberal Democrat-facing. Many commentators, both inside the party and out, too quickly assume this means “liberal”, because they assume such voters should be Tory by default. This ignores the fact that, by 2024, the Conservatives did not actually have an attractive economic pitch to those voters. Badenoch’s bet is that a substantial number of these voters – both those who defected to the Lib Dems and a large share who party strategists identify as simply having stopped voting – can be wooed back with a strong economic offer on things such as childcare and inheritance tax.

It remains to be seen whether she gets the polling bounce that is the traditional marker of a successful party conference. But based on what I saw over the past few days, I would say this was broadly a positive event for the Tories.

I worry, however, that the party itself is over-reading it. Yes, its situation has improved – but that is clearing the extremely low bar set by two sets of catastrophic local elections in 2025 and 2026. Yes, Badenoch’s personal ratings have improved – but she remains in truth the second least unpopular leader, rather than a particularly popular one.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Tory loyalists can be perhaps forgiven, meanwhile, for playing up the “Kemi bounce”, which has lifted their party from about 17.5% to about 20% in the current polling average, while ignoring the “Kemi slump” that preceded it (she took the leadership when the party was at 26% on that same average). But you would not guess, reading the room in Birmingham, that the Conservatives are still several points shy of their disastrous vote share at the 2024 election.

Yet perhaps this is again a problem of the chimerical nature of conference. The party strategists I spoke to seemed quite realistic about their task at the next election: avoid extinction and remain the largest rightwing party. But the party leadership could hardly make that their top line: it would simply demotivate their remaining troops and be severely punished by the press.

It is therefore their difficult task to consistently strike an optimistic note without entirely falling for it themselves – and ours to try to work out if, or when, they have.

Henry Hill is political editor of the Critic
