British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 15:00:53 GMT

Sir James Goldsmith’s links to Hilton Head, South Carolina, add to mystery of Jane Doe 4, who claimed she was abused by Epstein in the 1980s

For Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire Goldsmith family was a gateway to elite society and he wanted to be in their circle.

The disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 facing sex-trafficking charges, longed for a billionaire’s lifestyle and cultivated the family’s friends, bankers, business associates and advisers.

But Sir James Goldsmith, who was knighted by the Queen in 1976 and became a prominent British politician, remained wary of the American financier and even “despised” him, his daughter Jemima recently told the Guardian.

Two decades before Epstein came under federal investigation, Goldsmith – who died in 1997 – told a confidant that Epstein was a “sexual deviant” who was recruiting children for illicit activities.

Goldsmith “told me not to have anything to do with him, that he was a pervert, and he didn’t want him near any of us. He had four daughters to protect,” recalled the famous French architect Robert Couturier, who designed opulent homes for Goldsmith in New York and Mexico.

Goldsmith’s alleged warning came around 1987, years before complaints about Epstein’s solicitation of young girls for sex began filtering into federal law enforcement. Epstein’s network of pretty “girls” evolved into what authorities describe as a global sex-trafficking ring that catered to the ultra-rich and powerful.

It would become a scandal that touched royals, politicians, businessmen, academics, foreign diplomats and celebrities around the world, and left more than 1,000 victims in its wake.

“That is the pity of it all. It was all preventable,” Couturier told the Guardian. Epstein, born on Coney Island, had been on the radar of New York’s elite since he first surfaced at society events, often on the arm of heiresses, Couturier said.

“He was a charmer and a talker. Lots of rich people are deeply gullible, as protected as they are from reality. No one did anything about it.”

In the mid-1980s, Sir James Goldsmith – known as “Jimmy” – announced he was making a shift in his US business operations. Goldsmith had hired a new chief executive who would open an office for him in Hilton Head, South Carolina, an emerging luxury resort.

Goldsmith’s Hilton Head office is rarely mentioned in writings about his reign as the “lucky gambler”, as Time Magazine called him, an adviser to US presidents who became one of the world’s richest men by betting on undervalued companies. His conglomerate, with command centers in Paris and London, had its US headquarters in New York, close to his elegant Manhattan townhouse where Goldsmith entertained and where the young Epstein trolled for wealthy clients.

Hilton Head at the time was undergoing a chaotic development boom that brought in a rush of speculators, shady operators and vacationers lured by star-studded golf tournaments and tennis matches. Its population, 11,000 in 1980, doubled in a decade. Its tiny airport was suddenly a busy landing strip for private jets, including a $10m Gulfstream owned by Goldsmith’s company that was parked there for quick hops.

Epstein developed a lifelong fascination with Goldsmith, his family and fortune, an investigation by the Guardian found.

Epstein’s connection to Goldsmith, and the presence of the billionaire’s company and his associates on a South Carolina sea island – which was attracting an infusion of investors – is potentially relevant because of an alleged sexual assault that is said to have occurred there in the 1980s. A woman known only as Jane Doe 4 claimed in four FBI interviews after Epstein’s 2019 arrest that he had assaulted her during his visits to the island in the 1980s, when she was still a teenager. She has also claimed the man she only knew as “Jeff” trafficked her to other men, including Donald Trump.

The White House has vehemently denied the allegation about the US president, calling it “completely baseless” and “backed by zero credible evidence”.

The Guardian has been examining records, digging into archives and conducting interviews to explore intersections of Goldsmith and Epstein and try to understand if Epstein, with decades of secretive movements and a web of global financial ties, might have had reason to be on Hilton Head in the 1980s when those alleged assaults by Epstein occurred. This remains a mystery, but Epstein’s relationship with Goldsmith provides some additional clues.

Those who dismiss the claim of Jane Doe 4 – including Epstein’s brother Mark – have cited the lack of a public record of his presence on the island as proof that her story is untrue. Mark Epstein told the Guardian he has “no knowledge of him being in Hilton Head”.

Understanding how Epstein won and retained access to power and privilege throughout his life is important as criminal investigations of his sexual abuse and financial crimes continue around the globe. Federal prosecutors in New York have opened an investigation into the two overseers – Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn – of Epstein’s $577m estate, according to the Wall Street Journal. Both have denied they knew of Epstein’s criminal behavior. The Department of Justice has said that Epstein “harmed” over 1,000 people, including minors who were sexually abused.

The justice department has released about 3.5m documents under the Epstein Disclosure Act, including reams of emails, letters and bank transactions. But the trove includes almost no records from the 1980s, leaving a large gap in the public’s understanding. Epstein’s alleged victims continue to accuse the justice department of a cover-up for holding back documents that might implicate Trump and other powerful men in Epstein’s exclusive circle. Trump has said he ended their friendship in 2004 after a real estate dispute and kicked Epstein out of his Mar-A-Lago club in 2007 for poaching employees.

It is unclear whether Goldsmith’s concerns about Epstein stemmed from specific encounters, and there is no indication that Goldsmith ever reported his concerns to local or federal law enforcement.

It took decades for the FBI to catch up with Epstein’s crimes. Federal investigators in Florida charged him in 2008 with soliciting sex from minors after a two-year investigation in which they interviewed young women, including some minors, who he paid for sexual encounters in his Palm Beach mansion. He served 13 months in jail under a lenient deal cut with federal prosecutors.

Until now, the earliest warning about Epstein’s criminal behavior is believed to have come in 1996, when one alleged victim – an artist named Maria Farmer – claims she alerted authorities that she was sexually assaulted by Epstein, according to a lawsuit she has brought against the FBI. Farmer has also claimed that Epstein stole nude images she had of her two minor siblings, which she kept for her personal use in her artwork. The FBI has said in response to the ongoing litigation, which now includes 34 alleged victims, that agents do not have a duty to investigate “every single tip that comes across their desk”.

Since Epstein’s death, Goldsmith has been portrayed as an important influence in his early career.

The New York Times last year described Sir James as a connection Epstein shrewdly calculated was “worth nurturing for the long haul”. It recounted a party scene at Goldsmith’s Upper East Side mansion where Epstein, trained in classical piano, serenaded guests with a piano solo from the grand entry hall.

Goldsmith’s warnings about Epstein came just as Epstein signed one of his biggest clients, the Ohio retail magnate Les Wexner, the founder of Victoria’s Secret, who was then ranked by Forbes as the 10th richest person in the US. Wexner says he severed the relationship with Epstein in 2007 after discovering he had stolen funds from Wexner.

Some questions about Epstein and Goldsmith may never be answered given the secrecy surrounding these events and the refusal of key sources to answer questions.

Meanwhile, the debate over the government’s release of the Epstein files rages on. Attorney general Todd Blanche has declined to release about 2.5m Epstein documents he deemed duplicative. An independent journalist, Katie Phang, is suing Blanche to try to force their release, and Blanche recently quietly turned over some of the documents related to Jane Doe 4 to a federal judge, who is reviewing the documents in his chambers.

Prominent figures caught up in the Epstein controversy include former US president Bill Clinton, former Prince Andrew, former Harvard president Larry Summers and billionaire investor Leon Black. Black was recently held in contempt of Congress for his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee in connection to its Epstein investigation.

Epstein’s emails about the Goldsmiths sometimes suggested bruised feelings and revealed he was watching the family from afar. He was not among the dozens of invited guests in 1997 to Jemima Goldsmith’s grand wedding party to the cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan, who served as Pakistani prime minister, according to the guest list.

Just before he finished his lenient 2008 sentence for sex crimes in Palm Beach, Epstein scolded a young Romanian admirer for turning down her exclusive invite to a swanky dinner at Jemima’s Oxfordshire estate.

“That was a BIG mistake,” he wrote in an angry 2010 email.

Epstein criticized daughter Jemima’s choice of husband, calling Khan – who is now divorced from Goldsmith and in jail on corruption charges – a “whacko”.

In a 2018 text, Epstein wrote of Imran Khan: “makes donald look like einstein. incapable of truth. , devout islamisist . many nuclear weapons. ( not erdogan or khomeni). he was married to two friends of mine. one daughter of jimmy goldsmith.”

After the family distanced itself from him, Epstein gathered gossip about James’s daughter Isabel’s haughty behavior and joked when a hurricane seemed destined to damage Las Alamandas, her posh Mexican resort.

“hurricane will hit isabel goldsmith resort and bye bye,” he wrote to a friend in 2015.

Epstein elevated his access to the British elite when, in 1990, he started dating Ghislaine Maxwell, the daughter of a British media baron, who hobnobbed with British royals and enhanced Epstein’s standing among upper-crust families like the Goldsmiths. Maxwell became Epstein’s closest partner in recruiting young women, according to her federal indictment. She is serving a 20-year sentence.

Three Goldsmith heirs told the Guardian in emails they never met Epstein and doubted their father had any business dealings with him. Isabel Goldsmith did not respond to messages.

“I’m not sure I had ever heard of Jeffrey Epstein before he hit the news for the first time. So I’m presuming my father did not know him,” said Ben Goldsmith, an environmentalist and investor who was 16 when his father died.

Zac Goldsmith, a conservative member of the House of Lords, said he never met Epstein and was not aware of his fascination with the family.

Jemima Goldsmith Khan, who owns a London-based film production company, said she never met Epstein. “I heard that my father despised him – he was certainly not a friend of his,” she said.

Sir James was a king of US corporate takeovers in a frenetic era of Wall Street deal-making, earning hundreds of millions by seizing control of vulnerable companies and cutting thousands of American jobs. Goldsmith sold his New York investments in 1987 and made a hasty exit back to London after correctly predicting the Black Monday stock market crash.

Epstein was a takeover amateur who concocted his own deals while working as a consultant to a shady Manhattan debt collection company, Towers Financial, whose chief executive, Steven Hoffenberg, was later convicted of running a $450m Ponzi scheme. Before his death, Hoffenberg accused Epstein of masterminding the scheme. Epstein was never charged.

Hoffenberg’s most ambitious effort was an attempted takeover of troubled Pan Am Airlines, the prestigious international carrier Epstein had fantasized as a boy about one day owning, according to an email from one of his friends.

Working from its Hilton Head office, Goldsmith’s takeover team had already analyzed Pan Am’s books and backed off from making an offer. Developer Donald Trump also flirted with a takeover bid but never made it, media reports show.

Couturier met Epstein through Isabel Goldsmith, the titan’s oldest daughter. Jet-setting Isabel became friendly – but not romantically involved – with Epstein, he said, and Isabel and Epstein both socialized in New York City’s nightlife scene. Epstein kept Isabel’s phone contacts at several addresses in his “little black book” later seized by the FBI as evidence.

Couturier had grown close to James Goldsmith and his long-term girlfriend, who hired him in 1981 to renovate a mansion on East 80th Street. Goldsmith cut famous takeover deals around the dining room table, and his catered parties attracted the cream of Manhattan society.

Isabel told Couturier that Epstein wanted to discuss hiring him for another renovation at a huge Upper East Side brownstone purchased by Wexner, he said. Epstein later moved into the restored mansion at 9 East 71st Street, about a half mile from Goldsmith’s, and decorated its dark wooded interior with his private art collection and gaudy fabrics. It became a center of his sexual misconduct, an address where the FBI in 2019 carried out boxes of photographs of alleged victims, massage tables and sex toys.

Wexner also owned a dilapidated historic townhome next door at 11 East 71st Street that needed total renovation. The house was eventually bought through a trust by Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, who has said he hardly knew Epstein, his nextdoor neighbor. Under questioning by House investigators, Lutnick acknowledged visiting Epstein for lunch at the predator’s Caribbean island, Little Saint James.

Couturier was approached and interviewed by the FBI in 2010, after Epstein’s first arrest. A record of the interview, which is included in the Epstein files, indicates that Epstein had approached Couturier for a high-paying project on Little Saint James Island, where he was asked to provide “decor and furniture appropriate for teenage girls, with pink furnishings and bunk beds”.

Couturier told the Guardian he remembered Sir Jimmy’s earlier warning. He withdrew from the contract, leading to a legal dispute.

Goldsmith was hardly a prude, Couturier said, but he had no tolerance for inappropriate behavior with children. Goldsmith’s own domestic life was what his daughter Alix once described as “unconventional”, with three wives, numerous girlfriends and eight children. Two children were born in New York to his longtime girlfriend, a French journalist who moved with him to the city.

Another link between Epstein and Goldsmith was Bear Stearns, where Epstein was a junior broker until he was targeted in an internal investigation of his trading practices. He quit in 1981 with an indignant resignation letter that was included in the Epstein files.

Goldsmith remained a major Bear Stearns client, and Epstein, who somehow remained on good terms with the brokerage top brass, invested his own and his clients’ money into the firm, which collapsed in 2008.

Epstein always kept an air of mystery around his business deals. In the 1980s, he described himself to friends as a “bounty hunter” who traveled the world to recover stolen money for rich clients.

He and Goldsmith knew many of the same influential people. The Saudi billionaire Adnan Khashoggi, an international arms dealer, hired Epstein in the 1980s for unspecified work, according to published reports. Khashoggi and Goldsmith were both trusted advisers to President Richard Nixon, who met with them after his 1974 resignation to discuss overseas income opportunities, according to a Nixon biographer.

Epstein became friendly with a wealthy international investor, Jean “Johnny” Pigozzi, who was in Goldsmith’s circle of advisers and is one of the trustees of Goldsmith’s estate, according to published reports. At one point, Epstein’s girlfriend Maxwell emailed Pigozzi to get price estimates for his French estate and nature preserve in Panama, saying she had an interested potential buyer, the emails show.

Pigozzi, an art collector and heir to an auto fortune, is best known in popular culture as the inventor of the “selfie” because of his candid photographs of the rich and famous, including Goldsmith. He did not respond to messages.

Goldsmith’s massive holding company, GOSL, had operations around the world and a corporate office in Manhattan run by his trusted team.

But in 1985, GOSL filed papers with the state of South Carolina seeking authorization to do business in the state, the Guardian found. It opened an office in Hilton Head, the home of Al Dunlap, a notorious corporate raider Goldsmith was hiring to run his US operations.

Dunlap had been living part-time on Hilton Head since the early 1980s when he was running a company that made paper cups. He was among the many corporate bigwigs who had discovered Hilton Head as a sanctuary for executives and government officials who needed privacy. Most exclusive neighborhoods were gated and developed on former rice plantations.

Dunlap – who died in 2019 – had the Wall Street clout to ask investors to come to him. A newspaper account describes one session in 1985 at a new Marriott waterfront resort in Hilton Head where Dunlap pitched a Lily-Tulip stock offering backed by Wall Street firms to 70 out-of-town investors before leaving on a global capital-raising tour.

Some locals say the atmosphere on the island was so frenetic, with investors and deal makers arriving for meetings, that anyone could slip in and out without notice.

Goldsmith’s office in Hilton Head was tasked with selling millions of acres of forest land the company had acquired in takeovers of US paper companies. Its vast new holdings stretched from the Pacific north-west to the Adirondacks, making Goldsmith’s company one of the largest owners of undeveloped US land.

The Guardian tracked down former GOSL executive Phil Lader, who was in charge of land sales, to ask if he recalled seeing Epstein in Hilton Head during the time GOSL had an office there. The short answer was “no”.

Lader was a Hilton Head resident and former chief executive at Sea Pines. In 1981, he founded the prestigious Renaissance Weekends, which drew luminaries to the island for private invitation-only retreats. He was especially close to Bill Clinton, who was governor of Arkansas when he and his wife, Hillary, began coming to Lader’s exclusive gatherings. Other featured guests included Wall Street executives, university and government officials and leaders in the arts and sciences.

Goldsmith hired Lader as a GOSL vice-president in 1986, just after he lost a Democratic party bid for the South Carolina governorship. Lader was appointed Clinton’s deputy White House chief of staff in 1993 and moved to London four years later when he was appointed ambassador to the court of Saint James’s.

Lader said he never met Epstein and “never heard the name Jeffrey Epstein in my years on Hilton Head”. Epstein reportedly made 17 visits to the Clinton White House and later flew Clinton on his private jet.

A partially redacted 2011 exchange in Epstein’s emails shows he was aware of Renaissance Weekends, which are promoted on social media as gathering places for “thought-leaders”. An unnamed friend asked if Epstein had heard of the gatherings.

“Of course,” Epstein wrote. Asked if it was “something i should do?”, Epstein wrote “yes”.

Renaissance Weekends were held in Hilton Head for 20 years, then moved to Charleston. Similar programs are also held in other cities.

The woman who would come to be known as Jane Doe 4 first called an FBI victim hotline to report her alleged abuse on 10 July 2019. It was four days after Epstein’s arrest at a New Jersey airport. The agent manning the phones recommended that she be interviewed in person, near her home in Vancouver, Washington. One of her close friends made a separate call to anonymously report Jane Doe 4’s abuse.

Jane Doe 4’s federal class-action lawsuit, filed later in New York against the Epstein estate, alleges she met Epstein around 1984, when she was a teenager, and had sex with him for several years when he visited the island. She said he rented properties, including a villa at Sea Pines, from her mother’s realty firm.

In four FBI interviews in 2019 she described her abuser’s specific sexual quirks – including his use of butt plugs. Several were seized when the FBI gathered evidence in Epstein’s home in 2019.

Some details squared with accounts given by other young victims who came forward during the previous Florida investigation. She described how he allegedly asked her to recruit friends and took nude photographs of her, also part of a pattern, and repeatedly plied her with drugs and alcohol. The FBI seized thousands of photographs and videos depicting victims when it searched his various properties.

The Marriott hotel on Hilton Head figures heavily in her allegations. She told the FBI about a pool party there with local teenage girls and older males. She claimed the older man she knew as “Jeff” made a brief appearance at the pool before taking her back to his rented villa. She also mentioned a neighbor she had talked with during the period of alleged abuse.

Her local attorney told the Guardian he sat in on the FBI interview and interrupted when she began describing telling other girls about “Jeff”. The lawyer said he feared the FBI might accuse her of aiding her abuser in soliciting other minors.

FBI notes in the case, which were first reported by the Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina, repeat the woman’s allegation that at one point, Epstein transported her to New York or New Jersey where she claims he introduced her to Trump, who forced her into a sex act. She estimated she was about 13-15 years old, which would place the dates between 1983 and 1985, but she acknowledged a fuzzy memory. Trump said in a 2002 interview with New York magazine that he had known Epstein for 15 years, which would date their relationship to 1987. The White House has denied Jane Doe 4’s allegations.

Jane Doe 4 also offered names of some of her high school friends who might have seen her with Epstein.

But there is no evidence the FBI ever followed up on the leads Jane Doe 4 gave investigators. Its interest in her case appears to have died abruptly when she asked agents what the point was of her continued cooperation and told them she intended to join a class-action lawsuit, filed by the Bloom Law Firm in December 2019.

A relative of Jane Doe 4 told the Guardian that she had been scarred by “layers of trauma” as a young girl from family tragedies and upheavals. She had spent time in foster care and had just finished elementary school when the family made its way south.

Jane Doe 4 declined to answer questions from the Guardian relayed through the relative, who considers her account “plausible” because she was often unsupervised in her early teens. Three friends contacted by the Guardian did not respond to messages.

Jane Doe 4’s attorney at the Bloom Law Firm told the Post and Courier she ultimately reached a settlement with Epstein’s estate but declined to give an amount.

Court records show a claim she filed with the Epstein victims’ compensation fund, a formal review panel funded by the estate, was denied. The dates of her alleged abuse are much earlier than most other victims who have come forward with claims.

In response to lawmakers’ questions about whether Jane Doe 4 had received a settlement from the estate, an attorney for Epstein’s accountant, Richard Kahn, said he could not recall details of all 60 women who settled with the estate outside of the compensation fund.

The record is far from definitive about whether Epstein ever visited Hilton Head during this time. He did not own a private plane in the 1980s, so no travel logs are available. Epstein did have other real estate development interests at that time, including a long friendship with a developer who was building an oceanfront golf course on nearby Kiawah Island.

Later records in the Epstein files show his plane landing at the nearby Savannah airport several times from 2013 to 2019, for unknown reasons. The emails show a redacted exchange in 2014 suggesting he was on Hilton Head for a March visit.

Kenneth Lannon, a retired FBI expert in child sexual victimization who has trained hundreds of law enforcement agents to investigate abusers, said it was “highly likely” Epstein had victims pre-dating his Florida arrest and that he probably “started out slowly and just got better and better at it as time went on.

The typical child sex abuser, he said, begins targeting and grooming potential victims soon after puberty, although they may come across as “nice guys” in regular social interactions. Money and the ability to travel freely make the crimes easier to pull off, he said.

Child victims are often so starved for attention they become compliant and have more than one encounter with the abuser.

Jane Doe 4 had a troubled life after leaving Hilton Head. She married several times and moved to the west coast. She returned to be with family in Georgia and was arrested in 2023 for stealing money from a dying man. She pleaded guilty and spent a year in jail. Her brothers were well educated; one worked for a few years as a Bear Stearns trader before the brokerage collapsed in 2008.

A family member told the Guardian in June that Jane Doe 4 was “staying off the grid” and lived in fear of retaliation from the Trump administration amid the ongoing controversy over the handling of the case.

The best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:

The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.

If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When you're ready to send a message, select ‘Investigations (Guardian US)’.

Finally, our guide at theguardian. com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.

‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 14:50:41 GMT

At Conservative conference, some worry about becoming a one-woman party, while others say party should thank their lucky stars they have her

UK politics live – latest updates

Kemi Badenoch has long said that the Conservatives were “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further.

“Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.”

These are bold words even for a politician known to possess an iron-clad self-confidence. But they are no exaggeration. Badenoch is not only outperforming her party in polling terms, she is busy remaking it in her own image.

The broad ideological direction was already set, with Badenoch saying explicitly at the start of this year that centrist ideas were no longer wanted. Some more moderate figures remain in her shadow cabinet, but they are signed up to a right-leaning agenda, including opposition to net zero and a bonfire of human rights protections.

Those around Badenoch say, however, that her control goes further, with policy decisions such as the move to grant free childcare to people with incomes above £100,000, announced on the eve of the conference, made simply because she believes they are the right thing to do.

“With policies it’s not about chasing certain groups of voters,” one shadow cabinet minister said. “She focuses on what she thinks needs to be fixed, what she feels is wrong.”

Talking her out of a policy decision, they said, was a tall order: “It’s not going to happen – it’s tablets of stone. She’s not going to change her mind. She knows what the policies have to be.”

Many political parties are, to a greater or less extent, a cult based around the leader, but this is particularly the case for the 2026-period Conservatives, where MPs say Badenoch is talked about on the doorsteps with an admiration and respect not accorded to their party more widely.

MPs recount how her name is raised unprompted. One said: “She’s brought up in a positive way. Crucially, in a world where most people couldn’t name more than a handful of politicians, they know who she is.”

This starring role was obvious throughout the Conservatives’ conference in Birmingham, not least Badenoch’s arrival, which saw her greeted by a flag-waving crowd of activists chanting: “Kemi, Kemi.”

Inside the venue, Badenoch was the heroic centrepiece of the party’s “Birmingham tapestry”, shown in mocked-up 12th-century form doing everything from chastising Wes Streeting to sitting in the turret of a tank.

Such veneration is not just wishful thinking by a party eager to move on from a revolving door of previous leaders. While last year’s conference was viewed as make-or-break for Badenoch, even with her party still bumping along at 20% or so in the polls her position is now seen as secure, with the Conservatives more unified than they have been for years.

This is in part the result of some serial malcontents leaving for Reform UK, especially Robert Jenrick, as well as the party’s diminished size in the Commons, which as one shadow cabinet minister notes, is too small for factions: “We could just about fill a corner table in Pizza Express.”

There are still private doubts, including Badenoch’s instinct to lean into culture wars rather than focus on the economy, which those around her believe is the party’s strongest electoral card.

Some party figures also wonder if Badenoch is thinking about election strategy at all with her very personal suite of policy choices, which in Birmingham mainly consisted of giving tax breaks to wealthier people.

This was capped in her end-of-conference speech with the announcement that a Badenoch-led government would exempt people’s homes from inheritance tax, an idea which, given that the levy only begins on property worth more than £500,000, is a largely theoretical idea outside London and the south-east of England.

While such policies could be appealing to prosperous home counties voters who defected to the Liberal Democrats in 2024, this does not seem to be the plan. During another TV interview, Badenoch chided her questioner for suggesting her tax cuts were aimed at bringing back such support.

“I’m very sad that you’re looking at this in crude electoral terms,” she said. “That’s how we’ve all got into this problem where we keep thinking about winning elections rather than thinking about what works.”

One former Tory strategist said there was a risk of incoherence: “I can’t understand what is being achieved with these announcements. Forget lots of the small ones, just use the money and do a big tax cut for middle earners.”

There was, they added, little chance things would change: “People are scared of her, to be honest. I think a lot of her team don’t know how to say no to her.”

However, much like football, politics is not a one-person game, and a star player or manager will only get you so far. And while Badenoch was at pains to praise colleagues in her speech, it is fair to say that the rest of the shadow cabinet is lagging.

Andrew Griffith, Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor, was feted by his boss for his private sector business expertise. But on Monday he gave a speech widely seen as one of the worst delivered to any conference in years.

It is a matter of profile as well as ability. While Badenoch is recognised by 90% of voters, according to YouGov polling, only 22% say they know who Griffith is. A number of his colleagues are on similar ratings, with pollsters saying even these are likely to be inflated by people who don’t want to admit ignorance.

The experienced Tom Tugendhat, now in the foreign affairs brief, does slightly better, on 46%. Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hits 50%, but this is because some people mistake her for the Olympic cyclist, now Laura Kenny, formerly of the same name.

There was some unease in Birmingham about Badenoch blotting out everyone else. “Isn’t there a danger we are becoming a one-woman party?” one activist asked a fringe of shadow cabinet members.

Others disagree. “It’s a normal dynamic for an opposition party that is unpopular,” said Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary. “It needs a strong popular leader that can pull it up and we should thank our lucky stars that we have her.”

Either way, most Conservatives now accept that, for now, it is up to Badenoch to chart the Conservatives’ course, whatever it involves. One ally said: “We win elections on the economy but there’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything.”

George Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UK

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 14:50:37 GMT

Veteran leftwinger has been ‘in exile in the east’ in Russia and not been to Holborn and St Pancras constituency since campaign began

George Galloway has been elected seven times to parliament, but his attempt to succeed for an eighth this week, in the London seat formerly held by Keir Starmer, is undoubtedly his most curious effort yet.

Since the byelection campaign began, the leader of the Workers party of Britain has yet to set foot in the UK, let alone the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, because he is in what he describes as “self-exile” after being questioned by counter-terrorism police at Gatwick airport a year ago.

Prolific social media feeds show that the veteran leftwinger has spent the past few weeks on a speaking tour in South Africa, with his most recent public appearance on Saturday at a pro-Palestine rally in Cape Town, though posts in the last 24 hours suggest he is in Shanghai, China.

Prior to that he was in Moscow, repeatedly making his hostility to Ukraine and Nato as explicit as his support for Palestine and opposition to apartheid.

“The biggest issue in the H&StP byelection is the path leading us to WW3 in Ukraine,” Galloway wrote on X in the middle of September, an argument that has not gained much traction with voters, though he has chosen to repeat it online – the only way he can reach voters personally before Thursday’s byelection.

Meanwhile, social media feeds show handfuls of Workers party activists campaigning in the constituency without their candidate, fighting a peripheral campaign in a byelection considered to be a battle between Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali and Zack Polanski, standing for the Greens.

“Sincere gratitude to my campaigners who are performing miracles on the ground in my enforced absence. Salute to the supporters they are encountering every day. We can win this. And me and my family can come home. Thank you,” Galloway posted at the end of September.

The campaign highlights an anomaly with Britain’s electoral law. Any British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizen over 18 may stand for parliament – as long as they are not bankrupt or members of the police, armed forces, civil servants or judges. There is no requirement to be a registered elector or other residency requirement, according to the Electoral Commission.

Last month, Galloway also revealed he had been “debanked” – his bank accounts suddenly closed – by the Lloyds-owned Bank of Scotland. “Thirty-nine years ago I opened a personal bank account with Bank of Scotland in Byres Rd Glasgow. Yesterday without explanation or notice they closed my accounts,” he posted on 4 September, threatening Lloyds with legal action.

The bank said it would not comment on individual cases, though account closures are rare. A Bank of Scotland spokesperson added: “Our policy is not to close a customer’s account based on political or personal beliefs and we make customers aware if we make the decision to close an account.”

Galloway chose to leave the UK after he and his wife, Putri Gayatri Pertiwi, were stopped for what he said was “a total of 11 hours” in September last year by “five armed police officers” after returning from the Russian city of Nizhny Novgorod and attending a World Youth Festival assembly.

Last month, the former MP said the first question police asked him was: “Why do you admire Mr Lavrov?” They were referring to Russia’s long-serving foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov. Posting on X, Galloway attached a photo of Lavrov smoking and added: “I could have just shown him this picture!”

Galloway told the broadcaster RT, the former Russia Today, in an interview in March this year that officers “took all our stuff and copied everything on our phones”, forcing them to miss a public meeting in London at which, his wife said in a post on Instagram, “the Chinese ambassador [was] waiting for us”.

Neither Galloway nor his wife were subject to any further legal action in a stop that took place under schedule 3 of the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019. This allows police to detain people to determine if they have been engaged in hostile activity, considered by investigators to be a low bar.

The former MP had appeared on a discussion panel with Lavrov in Moscow in June 2025, at the Forum of the Future, an event described as “far-right” by the Moscow Times, where Elon Musk’s father, Errol, and Alex Jones, the rightwing founder of Infowars, were also speaking.

In Galloway’s March interview with RT, where he had hosted a talkshow for nine years until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he said he was “now in exile in the east, and I must say that Moscow in the spring is quite the place to be”.

He was in Moscow in late April, speaking at the inaugural conference of Sovintern, an international pro-Soviet socialist network led by the opposition A Just Russia party, where a welcome address from the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, was read out.

In early September, Galloway released a video promoting his online talkshow, filmed from Moscow’s Red Square where he also said he would appear at a roundtable event on security at the city’s “prestigious university”.

On 13 September he participated in a public Sovintern discussion with Zakhar Prilepin, a leading pro-war author and propagandist who has fought in Ukraine and called for “the return of Kyiv to Russia”.

A day later, Galloway was selected as the Workers party candidate, and he shortly afterwards went to South Africa for a speaking and fundraising tour with the leftwing activist and former journalist Yvonne Ridley. He continued to post on social media from South Africa, frequently on international affairs.

He places a particular emphasis on Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this month Galloway posted an anti-Andy Burnham image, with the prime minister dressed in blue and yellow, the colours of Ukraine. “I want you to die for Ukraine. Conscription coming soon!” the caption read.

Particular criticism has also been reserved for Polanski, his most obvious rival for political support. On 25 September, Galloway posted: “I am with Russia Zack is with NATO. I am with an end to the war in Ukraine Zack is with Zelensky and risking WW3.” Galloway and the Workers party were approached for comment.

Cruel torment, depraved violence, evil turns: where did TV’s real baddies go?

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 14:11:15 GMT

From Carrie’s bullies to Cathy Ames, sympathetic backstories have made villains boring. It’s time to bring back truly awful villains – in all their deliciously sinful glory

The new Netflix adaptation of East of Eden largely sticks to the plot of the John Steinbeck novel. There are tweaks – the introduction of a wedding photograph, for example, which becomes a significant item – but otherwise, it is faithful to the book. That is, in terms of the plot. There has already been some discussion about what it has done to Cathy Ames, played with considerable ferocity by Florence Pugh. Cathy, who later changes her name to Kate, kills her parents by burning down the family house. She shoots her husband, Adam, and leaves her baby sons wailing and alone. She slowly poisons the brothel madam Faye, a woman who acts as a mentor to her and treats her as a daughter, while simultaneously tricking her into leaving her everything in her will. In the book, Steinbeck lets Kate reflect on killing Faye. She finds that she has “no feeling” about it at all.

She is a brilliant, brutal character, but on television, she becomes something else: complicated. Her cruelty remains intact, but Pugh and showrunner Zoe Kazan have fleshed her out and given reasons for her fury. They invent a scene that implies Cathy was abused as a child by two men in the woods, and when she takes her final bow, the series returns to this moment in flashback, suggesting that her campaign of destruction has been shaped by a life of trauma and pain. In Steinbeck’s hands, Cathy is cold and unfeeling. In the 2020s, Cathy is more sympathetic and less of a brute.

But Cathy isn’t the only character to be treated with softness. In the novel, Charles Trask, like Cathy, is violent and vicious. Early in the story, Charles beats his brother Adam almost to death, then returns with a hatchet with the intention of finishing the job. Adam survives only because he manages to roll his body into a ditch, where he hides until Charles gives up and goes away. On television, this scene, so chilling in the novel, is shortened to a beating, and a tearful Charles is shown to be full of remorse. He is lonely, lost and lovelorn. He is not really a brute either.

It is strange that, in an era where hostility and anger feel par for the course, whether online or in public discourse, there is a need to soften fictional characters who might otherwise be treated as pure villains. It also happens in Carrie, the latest take on Stephen King’s first horror novel, which has been turned into an eight-part series by The Haunting of Hill House’s Mike Flanagan. While heartfelt and gracious, its two main baddies have been entirely defanged. Famously, Carrie is driven to take bloody revenge on her school bullies and her fanatical mother.

In Carrie, the 2026 edition, there is bullying, though it takes root on social media, and there is fanaticism, though this becomes a fixed belief in anti-government conspiracy theories. Here, Carrie’s main tormentor, Chris Hargensen, has been given a terrible home life and neglectful parents. Carrie’s mother is a formidable force driven by misguided morals but with a fierce love for her daughter. Both of them do bad things, but they are no longer allowed to be bad people. It is empathetic all round, but it lacks the snarl and bite of a horror classic.

You can see it again in the recent glossy legal potboiler War. It probably depends on the podcasts you prefer, but there are few people who would still see billionaires as anything other than Dr Evils with a Mars-colonising complex. Not so in War, where Dominic West plays an investment banker turned social media mogul called Morgan Henderson. Henderson is divorcing his movie star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller), whom he has cheated on in the past. But Henderson, a billionaire, just doesn’t seem all that bad. He made his fortune by building a “nice” social media platform. He hides his assets and allows his legal team to play dirty, but only because they told him to. He writes sad, heartfelt letters to his ex. By the end of the series – spoilers ahead – he realises that they don’t need the courts, because they can just work it out, fairly and amicably, between themselves, because they’re just not awful people.

War is highly entertaining, but it could have been even more entertaining if it had let rip. Instead, like Carrie, it is too open-hearted to be vicious, preferring instead to give everyone a shot at redemption. This is not a bad thing, of course. It suggests that we are more receptive to empathy and redemption, and more open to kindness, if only in the realms of fiction. But if this softer touch is the direction of travel, television might be getting that bit less fun. Matthew Rhys won one of his Emmys for The Beast in Me, in which he plays an amoral, unrepentant sociopath. It might not have been one of the all-time greats, but it was deeply enjoyable, in part because Rhys’s character was so unapologetically evil. Sometimes, hate-watching is cathartic and necessary. Despising an antagonist who only behaves badly because they need more love in their life is less enjoyable. There’s no joy in rooting against a villain when you’re forced to feel bad about it.

Halloween is looming – this year, I’m ditching my cynicism and getting busy with the pumpkins

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 14:00:53 GMT

From Day of the Dead to Samhain, celebrating autumn is centuries old. Now, I want this to be a moment of magic and connection for my kids

Darker nights are drawing in, there’s a hint of a chill in the air and the supermarket’s seasonal aisles are groaning with spooky paraphernalia. Halloween is coming. Every year about now, I tell myself I’m going to get my hands on a pumpkin and bake a pie like the ones my mum would make with us when we were little.

Halloween wasn’t a huge deal in our house, and neither was baking, but I hold warm memories of helping my mum go through the steps that led us to one delicious latticed pumpkin pie and one ugly jack o’lantern that we would display in the window with pride.

As I got older, Halloween became an excuse to ride around on my bike looking for trouble or going to parties wearing risque outfits under the guise of them being “costumes”. Now, along with that proliferation of Halloween tat in the shops – mountains of plastic ghosts and witches, destined for landfill – cafe chains try to exploit my olfactory memory by lacing their products with artificial pumpkin spice flavouring. Simple magic has been lost, life has moved on and I realise I’ve never followed through on making that pie.

Now I’m a mum to twin toddlers, which means my hands are full – as strangers constantly remind me in the street – but I’m finding myself inclined to create some magic around this dark time of the year, especially at this dark time in the world. Never one to miss an educational moment, my mum would teach us that Halloween wasn’t always an American celebration of commercial excess. One of its predecessors was Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival still celebrated by some, which marked the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter, and during which the veil between the physical and spiritual worlds grew thin. A time for reflection and drawing your loved ones close.

Last year, my mother and I took the twins to a Dia de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) community event in Margate, led by local Mexicans. There was Mexican food and music, and even an altar where people could put pictures of lost family members and pets. It was a lovely cultural exchange that felt fun, meaningful and very much in the spirit of the season. Rather than just being about consumption, the event reminded me that Halloween, Dia de los Muertos or Samhain can also be wonderful opportunities for storytelling – something that should not be underestimated.

When I was five, my mother’s father died suddenly, and it concerned me to discover she didn’t hold all the answers about where he had gone. My questions multiplied and I’d sometimes stand in the playground watching other children running around and wonder why no one was talking about the fact that, one day, we were all going to die. The silence made it feel much more scary.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I have a lot of bones to pick with Disney, but our family loves the film Coco, which is set in Mexico during Dia de los Muertos. Miguel, the protagonist, crosses over to the Land of the Dead in search of his ancestors. Watching it as an adult makes me realise how much I needed stories like this as a child, that could have helped me make sense of terrifying unknowns such as death. We are living through scary times on so many levels and a celebration now feels like as good a time as any to build strength and resilience through imagination and the exchange of stories.

The twins are still small, but they have loved the books we got from the library with themes of witches and werewolves or yetis and fairies. I have paper Halloween decorations from last year stored with the Christmas ones and the twins have worn their bat costumes again to flap around the living room. These are moments that I treasure already.

They are remembering things now too, which means we are in a memory-building era. I am not going to kill myself with an unrealistic Halloween to-do list, and I don’t want to contribute to unnecessary waste, but this year I’m adamant that we will go to a pumpkin patch together, so they can connect this time of year to harvest and nature. And I’m going to make that pie, although I might have to invite my mum over to help us. I’m still getting started on all of this but I’m going to embrace the celebration in the spirit that my mother did, and try to add my own details to the story. Just don’t expect anything from me at Easter.

Iman Amrani is a freelance writer and producer

As You Like It review – there are no mere players in the RSC’s ravishing all-male escapade

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 14:00:52 GMT

Royal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-AvonWith a WWE-style wrestling match, playful eroticism and a fine cast including Hamilton’s Jonathan Groff, this is an exquisite production

‘To liberty, and not to banishment,” exclaims Celia to Rosalind, the exile who finds freedom in her disguise as a man. It is a key statement in Shakespeare’s transformative, gender-bending pastoral comedy, just before the usurping Duke Frederick’s court is replaced by the romance of the Forest of Arden. That big reveal brought a prolonged technical difficulty on the opening night of director Daniel Evans’ all-male production, which was paused for well over an hour so it could be fixed. The technical hitch aside, it is a ravishing staging, with stunning visual effects.

There is little comedy or light in the severe court, which contains an intimidating physicality to reflect Duke Frederick’s thuggery, with slaps, shoves and a magnificently constructed WWE-style wrestling match, complete with bunny girls keeping score. It is replaced by Arden’s verdant hills on Anisha Fields’ exquisite set, so beautiful they verge on the voluptuous. The black Elizabethan gowns of the court, Puritan-like but flecked with ornament, and designed by Colin Richmond, are stunning too, as is the chequered shadow-play of the early scenes, in Ryan Day’s lighting design. The breathtaking contrast of the switch between worlds is inevitably lost, following the long wait of the technical problem, but is nonetheless beautifully envisioned.

Jonathan Groff, the US screen star who is also Broadway theatre royalty thanks in part to his performance as the king in Hamilton, makes a fun Rosalind, perhaps too declamatory at the start, but more textured and subtle later on. He instantly establishes chemistry with Fisayo Akinade’s Celia who is a runaway highlight of this show, performing femininity without caricature, and bringing an added charge to their relationship – a playful, same-sex eroticism which sees Celia straddling Rosalind at one point.

The all-male casting brings depth and subtlety of meaning, proving ingenious rather than gimmicky, simultaneously nostalgic and of the moment: a nod to the Elizabethan age when boys and men played female parts, yet now more queer and transgressive. The love between Orlando (Elliot Barnes-Worrell) and Rosalind’s disguised male alter ego, Ganymede, stays rather superficial, but the homoeroticism is more effective in their quieter moments, when Groff almost prowls with desire. He is at his best when he is overtly performative – a male actor playing a woman (Rosalind) who is playing a man (Ganymede) – and makes it work without resorting to outright camp.

The comedy is light and frothy on the whole. Gary Wilmot, who is both Duke Frederick and the exiled Duke Senior, never overplays his lines. A fantastically prim Phoebe (Tim Preston) brings a kind of librarian comedy with her disdain for the shepherd, Silvius (Edward Judge), and her love-at-first-sight for Ganymede whose brute, masculine scolding seduces her. The ribald romance between Touchstone (Greg Haiste) and Audrey (Gareth Snook) is played for music-hall laughs, the latter is flamboyantly big-haired and archly bawdy, little short of a pantomime dame.

Arden itself is rural Wales. Could this be a personal vision of an idyll from Welsh-born Evans? There is a lung-opening splendour to the set as it rolls downstage, over the darkness of the court, and Shakespeare’s songs are replaced by Welsh folk hymns (music composed, arranged and supervised by Theo Jamieson). It is preceded by massive alarms made beautiful by sound designer Paul Groothuis, combining with lighting to conjure musical claps of thunder and lightning. The court could be Prospero’s colonised island, full of strange noises.

The only (other) glitch in the production is its pacing, which feels too slow in its latter stages, perhaps due to the big technical pause of the night. Yet the big reveal of Arden is still awesome, when it finally comes. Evans has created magic here.

At Royal Shakespeare theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, until 7 November

The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 13:00:04 GMT

Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump

Here is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by since The Social Network, written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast.

Sorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that he has borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint. It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged by courageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. (Having said that, this film does not say aloud the word “Trump” and rather cravenly declines to specify Maga activity.)

Mikey Madison sympathetically plays the unhappy, principled, supersmart Haugen, who is dismissed as a “disrupter” – and Sorkin leaves it to us to notice that this in other circumstances is what oligarchs smugly call themselves. Jeremy Allen White does a capable, unflashy, unrisky job as Horwitz, a stolid performance that perhaps, in sync with the film, tells us about the diligent professionalism of old-school print journalism. And Zuckerberg? Well, we were all hoping and expecting it would be Jesse Eisenberg again. (You’ve heard of Richard Linklater’s Boyhood; this would be Aaron Sorkin’s Techbrohood.) But no: it is Jeremy Strong, who does a very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet, modifying the torpid sadness of his Kendall Roy in TV’s Succession, making this the unhurried contempt of someone simultaneously burdened and energised by knowing he’s richer and therefore smarter than everyone else. (A famous line in The Social Network was “A million dollars isn’t cool. You know what’s cool? A billion dollars.” This film starts by telling us that Facebook is worth a trillion dollars.)

Zuckerberg, though, is almost a cameo, with no equals with whom he can exchange dialogue, only employees – although the film imagines one former investor-turned-critic called Charlie (Bill Burr) who heckles Zuckerberg’s practice performance before a confessional hearing, with Zuckerberg amusingly having to be told how to smile. Charlie is the angry, unheeded voice of conscience.

The resulting drama rattles along at an entertaining clip, although there are false notes. When Frances has secret meetings with Horwitz in a hotel, the film has her wearing a slinky evening dress, supposedly as a kind of disguise, so that if recognised it would seem like she was out on a date. Hmm, really? Or is it so that the movie’s female lead has scenes where she looks glamorous? Later, Horwitz affectionately tells her to be less “mean”. But she is not “mean”. She just speaks Sorkinspeak. So does Horwitz. The ubiquity of Sorkinspeak effaces the difference between all the characters.

The most disturbing scene comes at the very beginning, showing a drunk woman livestreaming her racist abuse of traffic cops; this is the woman whom Haugen recognises as an acquaintance of hers, radicalised by Facebook. Towards the end we glimpse her again, looking ambiguously appalled by what she has become. But would she be appalled in reality? Or is this just the film-makers’ wish fulfilment? The closing-credit titles – usually the platform for a film to promote and summarise its heroes’ achievements – concedes that Facebook still isn’t checking political ads. Plus, of course, the film is set at the start of the Trump interregnum of 2020-24, when it seemed as if the Capitol riots were the ultimate wake-up call and moderation had returned. Nowadays Trump and his tech bro courtiers are more vainglorious than ever, and the values of investigative journalism have been thrown out at the Washington Post by its owner Jeff Bezos. This is a film which doesn’t reckon with the future we’re living in.

The Social Reckoning is out on 8 October in Australia, and 9 October in the UK and US.

The Greens may yet win in Holborn and St Pancras – but what happened to the party set to ‘replace’ Labour?

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 12:30:39 GMT

On the eve of the byelection, Polanski’s pledge is to keep the government ‘in check’. It may not be enough to stop a drift back to the political margins

Only a few months ago, in the spring, there was a sense of giddy possibility about the Greens. Zack Polanski’s radical new leadership felt fresh and dynamic, especially compared with those of the other parties. Former Labour supporters, in particular, were switching to the Greens in huge numbers, Green candidates were winning across the country, and the party was second behind Reform UK in some national polls.

Like Reform, the Green party presented itself as a revolt against a failed status quo. Unlike Reform, the Greens’ urgent stance on the climate crisis gave them a potent moral authority: even many people who did not support them believed that the Greens were right about the most universal issue.

After an unprecedentedly hot summer, some of that authority and momentum remains. Last week, at the party’s bustling conference in Brighton, impressive-sounding statistics about the party’s growth this year – along with modern icons of Green success, such as Hannah Spencer, victor of February’s Gorton and Denton byelection – were presented to determinedly cheering delegates in crammed halls.

This week, in the high-profile London constituency of Holborn and St Pancras, where Polanski hopes to succeed Keir Starmer in Thursday’s byelection, the usual cheery squads of Green activists have been striding back and forth between wealthy streets and council estates, distributing thick bundles of a party newspaper with the front-page headline “Greens close in!”. Given the party’s recent election record, Polanski’s populist appeal and the possibility that some of the many local leftwing voters may see the contest as a low-risk way to warn Andy Burnham not to follow Starmer’s premiership rightwards, a Green win is not impossible.

But, even if it happens, the problems the party has accumulated since the spring will not have gone away. For some voters, the novelty of Polanski’s leadership has faded. For others his style, more radical and provocative than previous Green leaders, has allowed the party to shift to extreme positions, particularly on Israel, with the Brighton conference passing a motion (which the Jewish Polanski neither supported nor opposed) that “Zionism is racism”.

Meanwhile, Burnham’s confident, sometimes iconoclastic start as prime minister has removed Polanski’s unique selling point as a good communicator who does not accept the usually conservative terms of British political debate. In his conference speech, Polanski admitted: “Now I get asked, isn’t your job done?”

The idea that one of the Greens’ main purposes is to shift Labour leftwards and towards bolder climate policies, and that that approach is yielding results, was everywhere at Brighton, from mutually encouraging chats between activists in the queues to upbeat contributions from the main stage.

It’s not a role that should be dismissed as minor. The Greens’ influence over Labour – both undermining Starmer in record time by taking so many votes from his party and creating political space for Burnham’s coup and governmental refresh – has arguably been a sign of Britain belatedly catching up with other European democracies, such as Spain, where centre-left parties have long been forced to be bolder by more leftwing ones. After decades of Labour paying most attention to forces to its right, the Greens’ important place in Labour’s calculations makes a refreshing change.

And yet, being an influence rather than a definite national rival – the Greens are now about 20 points behind Labour in some polls – is undeniably a comedown. During Polanski’s first months as leader, he regularly said he wanted the Greens to “replace” Labour. Partly because of that apparent possibility, the Greens attracted respected leftwing strategists such as Michael Chessum and James Meadway, who had worked under Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership and became disillusioned by Labour under Starmer.

At some leftwing gatherings last spring, those who hadn’t switched to the Greens could feel a bit over-cautious and old-fashioned. It’s possible that the rightwing media even encouraged this shift, giving Polanski plenty of coverage, in order to divide the left and prevent Labour from ever holding sole power again.

With Labour’s electoral future now looking more promising, one of the Greens’ leaflets in Holborn and St Pancras modestly presents Polanski as “a strong voice … to keep Labour in check”. In his Brighton speech, Polanski said: “Vote Green and watch Labour move.” It’s a typically pithy and clever line: explaining the mechanics of politics to voters, and treating them like grownups, in ways that party leaders rarely do.

But it may not be an inspiring line for more tribal Greens who decided decades ago that Labour, and alliances with Labour, were not for them. Another Green conference theme was “Real hope. Real change.” It sounded defensive, and too similar to Labour’s conference theme the previous week: “Hope again”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The Greens do still hold the initiative on some issues: advocating rent controls, wealth taxes, an end to fiscal conservatism, and more radical climate policies, with Labour expected soon to allow a limited expansion of oil and gas drilling in the North Sea. There are also signs of the Greens positioning themselves as the party of the most disadvantaged, such as asylum seekers, benefits claimants and transgender people – groups that Burnham’s less judgmental government may treat better than Starmer’s did, yet probably within limits set by Labour’s considerable number of socially conservative supporters.

“We will always stand with … everyone who is under attack,” said Polanski in Brighton, a statement that could be seen as too vague, impractical and idealistic. Yet if this country is to become a more truly representative democracy – a possible upside of the current political fragmentation – why shouldn’t the most vulnerable effectively have their own party? The most privileged have had the Tories for centuries.

The astute political analyst Rob Ford suggests that the Greens’ poll decline “may not matter much” if the party still campaigns effectively and attracts strong support from the dozens of relatively youthful, highly educated and diverse urban constituencies. Thursday’s byelection will test that theory.

Yet either way, there is something disturbing about a party with such a crucial cause having to face a reduction in status. The Greens’ drift back towards the political margins reflects not just their own mistakes, but the reluctance of many Britons to face up to climate realities. As with Extinction Rebellion, it’s more comfortable to call them extremists and ignore what they say.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

The Jaguar Type 01: a £150k gargantuan getaway vehicle utterly useless in the city

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 12:29:24 GMT

Too costly for most, too large for UK car parks, and wheels bigger than a warlord’s pickup truck. But it does come in ‘London red’

Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV

The cutting-edge car du jour, even while very few will ever buy one, is a good index of what the world’s coming to. It’s a dress-for-the-job-you-want principle, on wheels: drive for the world you want to inhabit.

That’s why when Tesla launched the Model X with a bioweapon defence mode (2016!), we should have been much more worried than we were, and it’s why the Jaguar Type 01 Grand Tourer EV has a lot to say.

“A new era,” the heritage carmaker calls it, and it’s not wrong. But having test-driven the era (just with my eyes and imagination, rather than the car itself), I would like to return it to the showroom and choose pretty much any other era.

Its gigantic size alone makes it look as if it wants to wage war on the future. The whole point of the electrification revolution in motoring was that we could wean ourselves off energy profligacy and on to elegant sufficiency.

If you counteract all that with a car too wide (2 metres) and too long (5.2 metres) to fit into any UK car parking space, whatever advances you’ve made with aerodynamics cannot overcome the fact that you are hulking around something that looks more like a tank than a car, the atmospherics underscored by the glassless tailgate and 23-inch wheels.

To unpack that a bit, you can’t see into the back at all, the preference for all the other glass is blackout, and the wheels on a Toyota Hilux, the Chad warlord’s vehicle of choice, are between 16 and 18 inches.

All the aluminium in the world (73% of the car’s makeup) can’t put a dent in the 2.5-plus-tonne weight, and they’ve bust their own balls to reduce the drag coefficient only to arrive at one (0.23) easily bested by any average electric saloon (0.21).

The look it’s going for, according to the literature, is “monolithic”, but it’s a thin line, isn’t it, between an immutable colossus and a menace, so attempts have clearly been made in the design to introduce a note of friendliness.

It comes in peace, the Jaguar 01 GT; you can tell by the rounded nose, and the body design creating the visual illusion of a front-to-back taper. If it were in a cartoon, it would be driven by the heroes not the villains, but they’d be heroes with no domestic life who knew how to handle themselves. They wouldn’t be The Incredibles.

Traditionally, the Jaguar was driven by a guy in his 50s, wanting to signal to the world that he could afford a car that cost roughly half his salary. That’s what the company is now trying to steer away from, preferring buyers who are “rich, urban, very design literate, very technology literate”, according to Rawdon Glover, Jaguar’s MD.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Some texture on that 50-year-old of yesteryear, whose type I knew well: my uncle had a Jaguar. Its paintwork was maroon, its interior a buttery leather, which meant we all knew he was earning a tidy packet, and we weren’t allowed to bring our dog for Christmas in case he scratched it. That, in a nutshell, was the personality type, which – I posit – was bad enough.

Jag Persona #0.1 is different: he doesn’t want your social admiration, he wants you to jump out of your skin and get your children indoors at his approach, which you’ll see before you hear and only fleetingly, as he races from 62mph to 112mph in four seconds.

He wants you to know he has 150 grand in spare change (ticket price is £120,000 but the extras make that unlikely), and “urban” my aunt Fanny, there is no city situation in which this is a useful car. Regular city driving would be unbearable, given its width, and its standout features of power and agility (three engines, one at the front, one on each rear wheel) are best conceived for a getaway vehicle. Considering its gargantuan size, it doesn’t even have much space – only four seats and boot space that a Skoda Octavia would look at and laugh.

And yet, on the plus side, it comes in “London red”, inspired by our mansion blocks and doubledecker buses, our postboxes and room 32 of the National Gallery. These are all different reds, by the way, but then so are red trousers, yet their message is always the same: “I am the kind of person who would wear red trousers.” So if you see one, just think of that person and make them worse, times a thousand.

‘This is only the beginning,’ vows Mikel Arteta after signing £80m-plus Arsenal deal

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 11:13:33 GMT

Four-year-contract secures Spaniard’s future

Title winner is Premier League’s best-paid manager

Mikel Arteta has promised “this is only the beginning” of what he can achieve as Arsenal manager after signing a new long-term contract that would take his reign at the club beyond a decade if he sees it out.

The Spaniard is understood to have signed a four-year deal worth more than £20m a season, making him the best-paid Premier League manager. That is a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait to be crowned champions after three successive runners-up finishes.

Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City. After losing the Champions League final last season to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootout, the 44-year-old is targeting more success as he seeks to build a winning dynasty at Arsenal, where he previously served as captain under Arsène Wenger.

“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” Arteta said. “This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.

“This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.”

Arteta’s previous contract, which was due to expire at the end of this season, was believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal, to June 2030, cements his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world. His coaching staff have also signed extended deals.

“It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship,” said Arsenal’s co-chairs, Stan and Josh Kroenke. “Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal’s history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We’re determined to create many more in the years ahead.

“We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019. He has a deep understanding of Arsenal’s values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together.”
