‘I wanted to depart in the best way possible’: Kieran McKenna on Ipswich exit and future plans

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 11:00:08 GMT

In an exclusive interview, former Ipswich manager talks of his lasting affection for the club, savouring time out with family and friends and ideas for his next move

It was on the Portman Road pitch, bathed in bright early May light while immersed in the relief and joy of a third promotion in five years, that Kieran McKenna realised the moment was right. The thought had flickered earlier in the season that this might be his final campaign at Ipswich, only to be pushed into the subconscious by the Championship’s remorseless grind. “But standing out there, I felt this was probably time,” he says of those moments after QPR had been swept aside and a return to the Premier League assured. “Another big victory, a full stadium, in front of my family and the fans. It was an amazing way to go out on a high.”

Five months later McKenna has no regrets about electing to cut things short while the going was so good. The golf bag lying outside his garage speaks of a man enjoying the break and, more pertinently, of something bigger. His son has recently become interested in the sport and sharing those moments with loved ones, whether out on the greens or spending part of the summer travelling along the East Anglian coastline in a camper van, were among the biggest reasons to pause a soaring career. At 40, McKenna had spent two decades immersed in coaching; it was time to appreciate life’s essentials while continuing professional development at his own speed.

He had, as usual, been linked with moves away but the idea of a voluntary career break was hard for many to fathom when the decision was finalised in June. “For people on the outside it’s maybe a bit more difficult,” he says. “But those who know my path and my values, the ones closest to me who know me really well, I think they understood why I wanted to step out and what the benefits were of having a period like this.”

Not everyone in football saw it that way: the phone has rung with proposals for his next move but McKenna says those overtures arrived “too soon, especially given the way I left Ipswich”. Leaving through the front door, a luxury rarely afforded, made him proud and there is no desperation to leap back into the fray. “I’m certainly in no rush,” he says. “I’m enjoying the time I’m having and hopefully an opportunity will come along that’s right. I have an idea what that would feel like but football doesn’t always follow your plan.”

Since early September he has dipped his toe back in. That has involved tuning back into the process of watching and assessing games, while travelling to spend time with Bayern Munich, the Wigan Warriors rugby team and Colorado Rapids, who are managed by his friend Matt Wells. He has been working on foreign languages, topping up an already competent level of Spanish. This week he is visiting clubs in Spain and, next Wednesday, he will begin work as a technical observer for Uefa when Shakhtar Donetsk play AEK Athens at Stamford Bridge. “I wanted to give myself the best possibility to learn before taking on the next challenge,” he says.

More than once McKenna repeats an assertion he made after promotion in May: that 2025-26 was the hardest of his four-and-a-half seasons at Ipswich, during which he masterminded a dizzying rise from League One to the top flight that marked him among football’s hottest managerial properties. The pressure was heightened last season: Ipswich had gone down and were expected to bounce back, even though the remarkably close-knit core who had propelled them through the divisions were drifting away. In effect, he took two different teams to the top.

“You can see how it could really have gone in two distinct directions,” he says, making a comparison with the fall Luton experienced after a brief reacquaintance with the elite. “We had the feeling internally that if we didn’t work really hard to pull everyone together then it could have gone in a negative way.”

McKenna pulled them over the line and reached the end of his own journey. Along the way he had come close to departing more than once but jumping ship earlier would have jarred. “I had a lot of different opportunities to leave, could have left in many different circumstances really,” he says. “But I was always aware I wanted to depart in the best way possible, with the club on a high, back in the Premier League and with a great chance to build for what will hopefully be a really successful period.”

The hardest aspect of his final day, he explains, was looking down a camera and addressing the supporters with a five-minute speech in which he did not attempt to suppress his emotion. He reels off a list of coaching staff and other colleagues with whom the goodbyes were touching, meaningful, joyful. Many of the friendships, particularly with members of the “really, really special team” that he led to those successive promotions, will be lifelong. The night before this interview, he spent most of a journey back from London speaking to one of them.

He laughs off the idea he would have relished getting his hands on the £200m summer transfer spend – not to mention a new training ground whose design he influenced – that appears to have given his successor, Gary O’Neil, a better shot at survival. If anything, he suggests, it shows the club have begun their own new chapter. McKenna also emphasises the thought of potential reputational damage from a second relegation did not factor into his decision to quit. “It wasn’t about the thought of a worst-case scenario or what could go wrong,” he says.

It was about prioritising life where we meet, in the family’s home a brisk half-hour walk from Portman Road. He and his wife chose to stay in Ipswich, where their two children attend school, having become more than mere itinerants passing through. It so happens Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson kept homes nearby after moving upwards. McKenna has hero status here too, in these unassuming yet football-crazed surroundings. Although he keeps a low profile and locations for socialising are chosen judiciously, the overwhelming affection of a town and county often rear up.

“Everyone is respectful; all we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them, their family and their friends, and wishing me the best,” he says. “Moving down here together, going all in, making ourselves part of this community, it’s been another of the really positive things. It’s a little bit different living in the area where you were managing but it’s the right thing for us at this time.”

after newsletter promotion

Has muscle memory ever taken him on an early-morning drive to the training ground? “You’d think it might, but it’s just a different life. You’re not setting the alarm for 5.30am and driving there in the dark. You’re getting up with the kids and having breakfast with them, and you’re around when they go to bed. Although the geography is the same, the life is different.”

He does not think such a heady half-decade, in which a talent honed at Tottenham and Manchester United blossomed gloriously, has changed a grounded personality honed in rural County Fermanagh. “I probably feel about 20 years older,” he says. “But my friends at home were telling me in the summer that I haven’t changed since I was 10. I couldn’t have arrived at Ipswich with a better background as a coach but, on the other hand, if you’d given me a list of the things I’d have to deal with in the next five years I really wouldn’t have believed it. After going through so many things you’re wiser for the experience.”

Nonetheless the fact remains: taking a breather when the world is your oyster feels vanishingly rare in football management. Maybe everyone should do it. “But what’s right for me, after two decades coaching, might be different for a manager who only stopped playing three years ago,” he says. “It’s been a massive body of work. You leave United, pick your bags up, get in the car and five-and-a-half hours later you’re in Ipswich. At 35 you’re leaving your family behind, checking into a hotel 10 days before Christmas; you absolutely throw yourself into the job for the next four and a half years and the family do the same. I want to enjoy the time we have now, take this period to reflect and be in the best position I can for the next role.”

So what would that next iteration of McKenna’s career look like, in a perfect world? He has been linked with any potential vacancies at Celtic and his old employers Spurs; his name will be circling once the season’s sackings start, although Ipswich will be owed a sizeable fee for any role he takes this year.

“I’m always going to want to be somewhere where I can improve players, play attacking football and win games,” he says. “But beyond that I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community, trying to build something memorable. It was a really special opportunity at Ipswich and you want to do that again in your career. But you have to be ready to come in somewhere and get some short-term success as well.”

The chance will surely arise soon; it does not take a giant leap to imagine McKenna in a Champions League dugout in the next few years if the stars align. Until then the self-growth will continue and there will always be dispatches from Portman Road, where his brother and children are regulars. McKenna would rather look forward and will not beat that path for now. “I think that’ll be some way down the line,” he says. “They’re cracking on with the season. There’s nothing that can lessen my pride and love for everything we’ve been through. Hopefully I’ll be back in the stadium as an old hand, and some of the people will remember the times we had.”

They are unlikely to forget; McKenna’s aim is that, by then, at least one other set of supporters will have felt the magic too.

‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 10:53:33 GMT

From a breathless tango to a kiss that sent fans wild, the pair crafted a sensational seven-year TV crush. The real-life best friends talk first impressions, Casablanca moments – and having hot husbands

Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan on their heart-melting TV romance

“Dr Crane, your glockenspiel has sprung to life!”

It was a crush. An unexpected one. The psychiatrist Niles Crane (snooty, conflict-avoidant, married to a high-society wife with a fear of buffets) fell for his father’s physio, Daphne Moon (working class, Mancunian, reckons she’s a bit psychic) the moment he met her in his brother’s Seattle apartment.

Across seven seasons of the mega-sitcom Frasier, the crush took hold. Daphne remained seemingly oblivious, but the pair built a friendship and a will-they-won’t-they story that fans loved to be teased with. It made for some cracking episodes: from the pair being holed up in Niles’ candlelit mansion during a rainstorm (with that broken glockenspiel) in the side-splitting A Mid-Winter Night’s Dream, to a passionate leg-in-the-air tango after Niles’ divorce in Moon Dance (“Oh mama, I’ve got it all!”).

Daphne finally learned the truth the night before her wedding to Donny. The next morning, in her white gown, she knocked on the Winnebago in which Niles (four days into a bad new marriage himself) was hiding and told him to drive.

“Fasten your seatbelt, Daphne.”

“Fasten yours, Niles.”

It’s been 22 years since we last saw the pair on screen, but the stars Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce remain dear friends. Hyde Pierce attended – and had a near fatal car accident at – Leeves’ English wedding and he is godfather to her son. They are both in long-term marriages: Hyde Pierce and the writer-producer Brian Hargrove married in 2008 after 25 years together; Leeves and the TV executive Marshall Coben have been married for 30 years. In fact, John Mahoney, who played Marty Crane in Frasier, predicted Leeves’ relationship one day in the green room: “I always wanted kids and said to John: ‘I’m going to adopt,’” she remembers. “He said: ‘Do not do that now. Within a year, you will meet someone.’ And she did, at a Paramount party. “I don’t know how that happened.”

“I love you doing this,” Leeves laughs from her Malibu kitchen, as Hyde Pierce joins from a study (which features a bookcase Niles would be proud of) in his New York home. He claims to have just had his hair done – endearingly, he’s a bit frazzled – before asking for reassurance that no one will see this video. They’re more than happy, though, to tell the story of Daphne and Niles.

Jane Leeves: I was on the set on the first day of the pilot and I saw David walking in and crossing the bleachers. I went racing up to him like a mad fan because I’d been watching [the Washington-DC-based sitcom] The Powers That Be, which was cancelled for some bizarre reason – it was brilliant and he played the most odd and fabulous character. I don’t think you really had any dialogue, did you?

David Hyde Pierce: No, I played a suicidal congressman who only mumbled.

JL: I thought there was a calmness, a kindness and an intellect that was devastatingly sexy, I have to say.

DHP: Well, I thought: I can’t believe Paramount Studios doesn’t have security … No, I realised that I lucked out getting the best loon in the business.

JL: A couple of lunatics.

DHP: I knew her from Seinfeld and Murphy Brown – another show from the dark ages. And we just felt like kindred spirits. It’s safe to say that was true of the whole cast. They put a real family together.

JL: It was extraordinary, because I was the only person at that first table read who had read with Kelsey [Grammer]. So the chemistry was unknown.

DHP: Also, we did a photoshoot before the pilot and I remember Jane saying something about how there could be just a little something between us, and we ended up leaning on each other.

JL: I was pulling your tie.

DHP: Yes, and I liked it.

JL: The idea came into my head that they were polar opposites and it would be funny if he found her attractive – because she was also the opposite of Maris.

JL: Contentious.

DHP: A lot of sex.

JL: I love David. He’s a true gentleman in every sense of the word and the finest human being you’ll ever meet.

DHP: It was as it is now. We’re just best friends. Jane and her husband, Marshall, rented this wonderful shack near the ocean in Malibu. My husband and I, and our dog, would go over and stay. When they moved on, they talked to the landlord about us taking over the rental and we did that. We were very close.

JL: John Mahoney was asking me for my parents’ address [in East Grinstead, West Sussex] one time – he wanted to send them a card – and I read it out. And David went: “Muffin-on-Poot?” and the whole room just fell apart.

DHP: As a person from the US, everything is “something-upon-something” in the UK. That one just occurred to me and it seemed to stick. But it was with great affection.

DHP: For Niles, Daphne is far and above the most beautiful woman he’s ever seen in his life. Whatever aura she gives off just mesmerises him: her personality, the scent of her hair. He’s bewitched. He also thinks she’s completely beyond him, like a creature from another planet or from mythology or the woodlands or something. The fact that the relationship impossibly comes together is a beautiful surprise for him.

JL: For Daphne, it’s the kindness and gentleness. He’s so different from any man she’s ever experienced. She came from a family with seven brothers, these brutes, so to find that a man could be kind, an intellectual … it’s the same thing for her, it’s this magical man in front of her.

We kept the suspense of the Niles attraction to Daphne going for years and people often ask me: “Why did she not know?” Yes, part of her thought that [he liked her], but the other part of her would say: “Oh, what are you talking about? He’s married and look where you come from and look who he is. He’s a doctor, for goodness sake.” And that voice in the back of her head is what made sense of that seven years of longing.

DHP: The tango in Moon Dance was amazing.

JL: We rehearsed at lightning speed for that. [The episode was written for the pair last minute as Grammer was on “blue flu” strike to negotiate his contract. Unusually, eight of the show’s writers each wrote a part of the script. Grammer returned in time to direct and appear in short scenes.] We had to rehearse with a choreographer. I remember going to David’s house, because we were loving it so much, to rehearse at the weekend. [The director] Jimmy Burrows would have been appalled.

DHP: Our late, great director was famous for not wanting people to rehearse because he had such a keen sense of the rehearsal timeframe of a situation comedy, which is not like rehearsing for a play that’s going to run for months. Even the dog [Moose, who played Eddie] suffered if he learned the trick too soon – it would be ruined and he wouldn’t be able to recreate it in front of the live audience. Jimmy was very big on: “Don’t think it out too much beforehand, because it will blossom at the right moment.”

JL: I love the scene between us [in Mixed Doubles] when Daphne has been dating a Niles lookalike – he breaks up with her and runs off with Niles’ date – and Niles comes to tell Daphne. There’s a wonderful, sweet, gentle scene between them, like shades of Casablanca. [“If it’d been a different time in both our lives, we might actually have met. How do you suppose that would have gone?” Daphne asks him. “I would have said: ‘What are you doing for the rest of your life?’” he replies. They both, as friends, say they love each other.] It was such great writing – these writers were real romantics.

JL: Seven years is a long time and I think the audience was sort of begging to please bring this to a conclusion.

DHP: I think we all felt we had played that “these two people didn’t think they deserved each other and didn’t believe that they could ever end up with each other” and there comes a point where you just stop believing that.

One thing that the writers did very smartly: they got us together before people were tired of the suspense. I remember very well – speaking of moments that stick with me – when we kissed in front of the live audience. They lost their minds. That was the moment we finally came together. The creators also knew when to end the series; they ended it before any of us were ready. They didn’t want it to dribble off and have the network or the studio say: “Yeah, you’re done.” They wanted to be able to craft a final season. So I don’t know if there are things we wish they did, but I do think those two things were handled really well.

JL: The only thing I wish had been handled differently was the hiding of my first pregnancy. But those were different times. [When Leeves came back from hiatus, she was pregnant with her first child. Her bump was hidden in the series and in later episodes she was given a weight-gain storyline and sent to a “fat camp”.] Daphne and Niles had just got together. I came back and I was pregnant – and they probably thought it was too early for Daphne to be pregnant and they wanted to explore this relationship. But then again, it might have been interesting if she was!

DHP: I’ve never thought of that, Jane, that’s interesting, so off the rails: the idea that we see them run off together at the end of a season and when they come back they’re having a baby.

DHP: I don’t know if I ever did think of it as a love story for the ages … love story for the agents?

JL: There was an episode or two of Niles and Daphne every season. They were always such great fun. It wasn’t until season two that I realised this thing has legs. Niles’ reaction to Daphne in the room added another layer to Frasier’s apartment; there was this pushback between Niles, Frasier and their dad, and then Daphne comes in and there’s a whole other thing going on. But yeah, by season two, I realised that they were mining this.

DHP: One of the cool things about it, too, was that it’s such sophisticated writing: knowing not to say anything when you have set up a dynamic between two characters. The whole audience knows, when Daphne walks into a room, exactly what Niles is thinking. And, eventually, vice versa. There could be comedy there, it could be poignant, it could be a million things – but it was not a show where it was a joke a minute, getting three jokes on the page. It was a different style. That’s between all the characters, in some ways. You got to know us so well.

JL: Oh my goodness. It’s friendship, it’s respect, it’s love. And admiration. I admire my husband, I admire his character. He’s my best friend. And he’s hot. That helps.

DHP: Are you talking about my husband or your husband?

JL: Oh, both of them, darling.

DHP: All of those things. I was thinking about both Niles and Daphne on the show, and me and Brian, or Jane and Marshall – what is romance? It’s a poetic thing. I think it’s possibility. Even having been together for ever, there’s just this air of possibility that the whole world has, because you are together.

JL: I think I know what you’re saying: being with the right person seems to make everything possible.

DHP: Yeah.

JL: You’ve got a good one, too.

DHP: I agree.

JL: We’ve always had such respectful fans. I don’t know if there’s been a wild one!

DHP: One of my favourite was in the States when the show first started to air. It was at a set time on a Thursday night or a Tuesday night: therefore, the people who wanted to watch Frasier watched it because they knew when it was on. But then there was a point where it went into syndication, which meant suddenly it was on reruns. I remember walking down the street in New York City. A garbage truck drove by and one of the guys hanging off the truck shouted: “Yo, Niles!” And I thought: oh, there’s a whole new audience getting to see the show.

JL: I get the same thing in New York – New Yorkers are more open. But I always just get: “Hey, it’s the virgin from Seinfeld.” It’s so bizarre. I’m like: “Not any more …”

JL: I kept Daphne’s wedding ring and engagement ring.

DHP: The green room over the years became covered wall to wall with stills from every episode that our production photographer, Gail, took. At the end, we walked through and took pictures that were meaningful to us. [He turns his camera to a photo in his office.] It’s the three of us [him, Leeves and Grammer] at the piano. I’ve got a million more and they’re all around.

JL: We have millions. There’s a little gym upstairs and they cover the walls up there. That was the saddest thing for me, before the show was even over. We hadn’t even started rehearsing that week and people were taking those off the walls. I was like: “No, leave everything this way, I don’t need everything to change.”

DHP: I think Marshall took a load of those [the photos in Leeves’ book]. Those are great.

JL: To persevere. Don’t ever give up on the dream. It would have been so easy for Niles or Daphne to say: “Well, that’s just ridiculous.” But Niles never gave up that longing. And so many people were in his ear saying: “Niles, you fool, you’re sticking your knife in the toaster!”

DHP: Love comes when you least expect it and it takes seven years.

JL: But it’s worth it in the end.

Why do billionaires have so many children if they’re not prepared to parent them?

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 10:00:41 GMT

Kim Kardashian’s revelation that she has five nannies for four children caused a ruckus. But the world of the ultra-wealthy throws up far more extreme approaches to childcare

“I have the best advice for women in business,” Kim Kardashian told Variety in 2022. “Get your fucking ass up and work. It seems like nobody wants to work these days.”

The billionaire got a lot of flak for this comment but no one can accuse her of being a hypocrite. It takes serious graft to spin a sex tape into lasting fame and a business empire. That said, like many high-flyers who preach the importance of hard work, the Skims co-founder isn’t above outsourcing the less glamorous domestic labour. She has primary custody of the four kids she shares with her ex-husband, Kanye West, and, according to an interview with the Sunday Times, employs five nannies to take care of them: “One nanny on duty, four on rotation,” she said. Despite having more nannies than kids, she apparently still does the school run. And I bet she doesn’t turn up at the school gate with yoghurt on her shirt like I do.

The revelation about Kardashian’s numerous nannies has caused a bit of a ruckus. Largely because there’s nothing people love more than judging how a woman mothers while ignoring the dad. And I’ll admit I was a bit judgy at first. But, look, if I could afford to contract out all the boring bits of parenthood I would too. You’re not a better mother because you’re running yourself ragged doing absolutely everything.

Back to being judgy though: while there’s nothing wrong with getting help, I don’t really understand the point of having four kids if you don’t have time to parent them all. Particularly as Kardashian’s kids weren’t oopsies: numbers three and four were born via a surrogate because of complications in her earlier pregnancies.

But of course, four kids is rookie numbers compared with some other breeding-obsessed billionaires, many of whom seem keen on procreating but not parenting. The Russian-born tech mogul Pavel Durov has more than 100 biological children in 12 countries via sperm donation. The Chinese billionaire Xu Bo is reported to have more than 100 children via surrogates. And obviously there’s Elon Musk, who has 14 known children.

Meanwhile, for the rest of us it’s getting tougher to afford kids at all. A 2024 Pew Research Center study found that, among adults under 50 who say they’re unlikely to have kids, 36% cited costs as a key factor. Having big families used to be associated with lower economic status. But research shows that’s gradually being flipped on its head. Having multiple kids, and a team of nannies to take care of them, has become the ultimate status symbol. Albeit the only status symbol that’s going to grow up demanding therapy.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Arsenal and Chelsea set to miss a month of next WSL season due to Club World Cup

The Guardian Wed, 07 Oct 2026 09:20:10 GMT

Back end of 2027-28 season likely to be ‘challenging’

Fixture contestion a growing area of concern

The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to the Club World Cup, with Arsenal and Chelsea likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month.

The Guardian revealed last week that the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup is set to be awarded to the US, with transatlantic travel to cause additional problems for European sides, while the proposed dates of 5-30 January will clash directly with the WSL.

Fifa has yet to confirm the qualification criteria for the Club World Cup but the Guardian has learned Arsenal are guaranteed to be involved as 2025 Champions League winners and Chelsea are likely to join them, although they would lose their place if Manchester City win this season’s Champions League. Based on this season’s schedule, an extended run in the Club World Cup would mean the two English clubs missing up to four WSL match weeks plus the fourth round of the FA Cup, playing havoc with the fixture list and causing major congestion at the end of the season.

Uefa will be granted places for six clubs: five to qualify automatically and one to take part in a six-team qualifier before the tournament, with the three highest-ranked clubs joining 13 automatic qualifiers to form a 16-team competition. While the process has still to be ratified by the Fifa council, it is understood Uefa’s spots will be given to the Champions League winners between 2024 and 2027 – currently Barcelona as the two-time champions and Arsenal, with this season’s title still up for grabs – topped up by the highest-ranked clubs in Uefa’s Champions League coefficient table.

Chelsea are third in that table for the current four-year cycle, behind Barcelona and Lyon with a 17-point lead over fourth-placed Bayern Munich, and cannot be caught. Based on the current rankings, Bayern and Wolfsburg are next in line to qualify, although the latter have not qualified for this season’s Champions League and will not accumulate additional points, so are likely to be overhauled by Real Madrid or Paris Saint-Germain. Fifa plans to cap the number of participants from each country at two, so City winning the Champions League would cost Chelsea their place.

The WSL declined to comment as it has yet to be told of Fifa’s plans for the tournament, but sources conceded its impact is likely to prove challenging. The WSL has a winter break, which is scheduled for 21 December to 10 January this season, and although that could be pushed back slightly, aligning it with the Club World Cup is not viewed as practical due to the congested calendar.

As well as creating a lopsided ­season, moving the winter break would result in a backlog of WSL fixtures during the period when the Champions League knockout stage begins at the beginning of February. The issue of fixture congestion is a growing area of concern in the women’s game and 2028 will be particularly problematic due to the Olympic football tournament taking place in Los Angeles in August, just before the start of the European domestic season.

The International Olympic Committee has expanded women’s football to 16 nations at the 2028 Games, and unlike the men’s version which is restricted to players under 23 with three overage exceptions, senior internationals are permitted to take part.

Fifa’s imposition of the Club World Cup in the middle of the European season has exacerbated the problem, and last month European Leagues, a lobby group, extended its legal complaint to the European Commission about the world governing body’s alleged “abuse of power and dominant position” to include the women’s game.

‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 20:00:23 GMT

Israeli communities shattered by Hamas massacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives

Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.

He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.

“I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.”

Siegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.

Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians, including 36 children, according to records kept by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.

The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.

Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.

“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.

The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.

A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.

Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.

In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.

Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.

The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed.

Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality.

In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack.

The cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance.

But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss.

“There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?”

He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.”

One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped.

When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza.

“I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.”

The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64.

“What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva.

“I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.”

The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign.

For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive.

Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.”

“When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.”

She has written a book, Survived to Tell, about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond.

After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has.

He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.”

Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings.

In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms.

Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications.

The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation.

Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence.

“You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away.

Both US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection.

Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu.

A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister.

Netanyahu, who is battling a corruption trial and could be more vulnerable legally if he loses power, is pushing to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and his coalition partners are calling for ethnic cleansing and annexation of Palestine.

The war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children.

Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens.

Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit.

Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security.

“I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.”

Forced to Retire Over Epstein, Ex-College Leader Keeps Campus Ties

The New York Times October 07, 2026

The Epstein Files

Advertisement

Supported by

Leon Botstein is no longer president of Bard College, but he continues to teach and play a prominent role in the school’s signature music programs.

By Adam Nagourney

As dusk settled over Bryant Park, the conductor Leon Botstein walked slowly across the stage, settling into a stool in front of the American Symphony Orchestra. The crowd sprawled across the lawn on this late-summer evening did not seem to notice that he had taken his position. Mr. Botstein raised his baton and started a performance of Copland’s “Fanfare for the Common Man,” competing with police sirens and the whine of passing buses.

Nearly 80 minutes later, Mr. Botstein, with a wave and a suggestion of a smile, walked off the stage to respectful applause.

For Mr. Botstein, this warm reception may prove little more than a brief moment of respite. After a half-century as a prominent figure in academia and music, Mr. Botstein, 79, was forced to retire in June as the president of Bard College, a post he had held since 1975. That came in the face of detailed revelations in Justice Department documents about his longstanding friendship with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, including a visit by Mr. Botstein to Mr. Epstein’s island retreat and exchanges of friendly notes, even after Mr. Epstein’s conviction on solicitation of a minor for prostitution. Mr. Botstein has said his dealings with Mr. Epstein came as part of his efforts to raise money for Bard.

The college’s independent review of the case, conducted by the law firm WilmerHale, found that Mr. Botstein had done nothing illegal but said that his relationship with Mr. Epstein raised concerns about his leadership. “In his public statements and his statements to the Bard community, President Botstein minimized and was not fully accurate in describing his relationship with Epstein,” the report found.

But Mr. Botstein, embattled and polarizing, has held on. He has continued to teach at Bard, the liberal arts college 100 miles north of New York City. (He is on sabbatical now to complete a book on Mahler.) He remains the artistic co-director of the Bard Music Festival and runs The Orchestra Now, the graduate-level program for musicians at Bard. He leads the American Symphony Orchestra, the resident orchestra for the Bard festival. And he continues to live at the official college home for the president, while the college finishes renovating an off-campus home for its former president. College officials said he was being provided housing in part as recognition of his long service to Bard.

Mr. Botstein’s decision to hang on in such prominent positions, with the support of the college, has caused distress in many quarters of the campus community.

Current and former staff members of the Fisher Center for the Performing Arts, founded by Mr. Botstein in 1990, signed an open letter to the Bard board of trustees saying that Mr. Epstein had “instilled a broad sense of distrust in Botstein’s ability to be an effective, transparent leader in any capacity at the College.”

The letter noted that Mr. Botstein had agreed to step down, but — in a plea that was by all appearances not heeded — asked that the board “not further engage Leon Botstein in any contract related to music and performing arts activity at Bard College.”

Moira Donegan, a columnist for The Guardian who was an undergraduate at Bard, said in an interview that “Botstein’s ongoing connection to Bard reflects the institutional values of the college, which has shown throughout this saga that it prizes Botstein’s cult of personality over the safety and dignity of women students.” (Ms. Donegan was the creator of an online spreadsheet from October 2017 that allowed women to list men in the media industry who they accused of sexual misconduct.)

Mr. Botstein declined a request for an interview on the advice of lawyers, who are representing him in a House Judiciary Committee inquiry, led by its ranking Democratic member, Jamie Raskin of Maryland, into Mr. Epstein’s dealings with Bard and Mr. Botstein. But in a lengthy written statement to The New York Times, Mr. Botstein made clear he has no intention of moving to the sidelines, asserting he had much to offer the college and the world of classical music.

“Bard has been my professional and intellectual home for six decades, and its success will never stop mattering to me,” Mr. Botstein said. “My continuing involvement is about completing and keeping alive musical and artistic projects that are unique and contribute to Bard, and to the economy and life of the Hudson Valley as well as to the broader world of the arts.”

“I wish I’d never met Epstein,” the statement continued. “I did not know then what a monster he was.” He said he was driven to befriend Mr. Epstein by “my urgent responsibilities to raise resources for an institution committed to the arts that was struggling to find donors who claimed to be interested in supporting the arts.”

Asher Edelman, an American financier who is a member of the school’s board of trustees and a longtime friend of Mr. Botstein, said the criticism minimized what he described as Mr. Botstein’s career of building Bard as a cultural force in central New York.

“They are lucky he’s around,” Mr. Edelman said of Mr. Botstein’s critics. “They wouldn’t have that school around if he hadn’t been around. They should kiss his feet. They are in a place that is extraordinary and it’s only because of him.”

Bard is now in a difficult position as it searches for a new president and close what has been a divisive and embarrassing chapter for a distinguished college, even as Mr. Botstein remains active on campus. For now, the school is in limbo; Bard officials said a new president was not expected to be in place until the beginning of 2028.

“The last six months of the academic year were a challenging time on campus,” said Jonathan Becker, the acting president. “Many people have different views on what happened and might have happened. I think what’s most important right now is everyone is forward looking. We are just moving on. I am trying to restore normalcy.”

“He has a very minor footprint on campus,” Mr. Becker said of Mr. Botstein. “I’ve seen him once since I became acting president. He’s not been a visible presence on campus.”

Before the revelations about his entanglement with Mr. Epstein, Mr. Botstein was renowned for how he had elevated Bard College and for being a promoter of off-the-beaten-track classical music, with the summer music festival and the American Symphony Orchestra. At the Bryant Park concert, a performance honoring the anniversary of Sept. 11, he conducted George Walker’s “Lyric for Strings” and Charles Ives’s “The Gong on the Hook Ladder.”

His inventive programming of the summer festival is one reason it gained so much attention; in much of the classical music world, Mr. Botstein is better regarded as a curator than as a conductor.

“The Bard Music Festival is our football team,” said Christopher Gibbs, who is the festival’s artistic co-director with Botstein. “That is something that has brought a great deal of attention to the college.”

“A lot of people are sophisticated enough to know that fund-raising can be a nasty business, and you take risks,” he said. “But when it comes down to what we are doing with music here, people understand that it was through Leon’s fund-raising that they are sitting where they are sitting and seeing what they are seeing.”

Mr. Botstein, in his statement, said that at this stage of his life, and with the arts “under assault both politically and financially,” his work was as important as ever.

“I am particularly conscious that I do not have an unlimited amount of time in which to do this work,” he said. “I am not oblivious to the actuarial tables or to the real-life reminders, including the recent death of my older brother, that time is not on anyone’s side. There is a humility that comes with recognizing that the runway is getting shorter.”

Yet his view of his future at the college is not shared with many of his colleagues these days.

Karen Painter, a professor of musicology at the University of Minnesota who has worked at the Bard festival, said the school needed to sever all its ties with Botstein, given his history of dealings with Epstein. “It’s time to move on,” she said.

Leon Botstein was forced to retire as president of Bard College because of his ties to Jeffrey Epstein. But he is still a presence on campus — teaching, running the summer music festival. Botstein and some top campus officials say he is why Bard is what it is today, a cultural force in New York, after 50 years as president. Many critics want him to disappear. Here’s the story.

Because of an editing error, an earlier version of the headline with this article misstated the circumstances in which Leon Botstein left his post as president at Bard. As the article correctly noted, he retired he did not resign.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Adam Nagourney is the classical music and dance reporter for The Times.

Mamdani Draws Anger With Oct. 7 Statement Focused on Palestinians

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

After calling the anniversary of the attacks on Israel “profoundly painful,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani denounced Israel’s military action in Gaza, prompting criticism from some Jewish leaders.

By Liam Stack

Mayor Zohran Mamdani ignited intense anger from Jewish groups on Wednesday when he issued a statement marking the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 attacks on Israel that focused largely on the suffering of Palestinians in Gaza.

The mayor posted a 211-word statement on social media that made reference to “the horrific war crimes” committed by Hamas and called the anniversary “profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers.”

However, the bulk of the statement provided a detailed denunciation of Israel’s military actions in Gaza since the attacks, which Mr. Mamdani described as a “devastating, ongoing genocide.” He did not provide a similarly detailed account of the killings of Israelis and abductions of hostages.

“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he said, referring to Oct. 7, adding: “That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing.”

The remarks by Mr. Mamdani, who has a turbulent relationship with much of New York City’s Jewish leadership, were highly anticipated and closely scrutinized because this is the first anniversary of the attacks on Israel since he took office in January.

And Wednesday’s statement was notably different from those released by other elected officials, including Gov. Kathy Hochul, who described Oct. 7 as “the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust.” In its own statement, the City Council highlighted the story of an Israeli Jew who was hidden from Hamas by a Bedouin Muslim farmer on the day of the attacks.

Some pro-Israel Jewish leaders, and the Israeli government, accused the mayor of minimizing Jewish and Israeli pain on a day of profound grief.

Rabbi Ammiel Hirsch, the president of the New York Board of Rabbis, said Mr. Mamdani’s statement was “morally perverse” and “like sticking a knife into the pain of the Jewish community in New York and in America.”

“It is so offensive to so many Jews that it is hard to describe how offensive it is,” he said. “And it exacerbated the feeling that American Jews and New York Jews have had since he first came to prominence, which is that he has a problem with collective Jewish empowerment and he hates the state of Israel.”

The UJA-Federation of New York, a major Jewish philanthropy, took issue with Mr. Mamdani’s description of the war in Gaza, saying he had chosen “to respond to the grief of Jewish New Yorkers by advancing false and inflammatory attacks against Israel — not only inappropriately shifting the focus away from the victims of Hamas’s cruelty, but also placing Jewish New Yorkers at risk.”

Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, called the mayor’s statement “an attempt to hijack the anniversary of Oct. 7 and turn it into yet another propaganda attack against Israel.”

But some progressive Jews defended the mayor. Sophie Ellman-Golan, a spokeswoman for Jews for Racial and Economic Justice, a group supportive of Mr. Mamdani, said his statement on Wednesday had “struck exactly the right tone.”

“I think this is a really painful day for so many reasons,” she said. “It has been three years since that day, and three years of genocide. To act like there was a horrific attack and then nothing happened afterward — we cannot fail to acknowledge that.”

The uproar was a reminder of the degree to which the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has infused the mayoralty of Mr. Mamdani. The mayor’s comments echoed a statement he made on last year’s anniversary, reflecting his consistent stance on a fraught issue even as his platform has grown significantly.

Mr. Mamdani has clashed with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, most recently last month when Mr. Netanyahu denounced the mayor in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly, calling him an antisemite and saying that Jewish New Yorkers were less safe under his leadership. Mr. Mamdani, who has repeatedly called Mr. Netanyahu a war criminal, accused the prime minister of using the speech to spread “baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”

The terrorist attack on Israel resulted in the killings of roughly 1,200 people, including civilians and military members, and the abduction of 251 hostages. Israel’s subsequent campaign in Gaza has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, according to a count from Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants but which includes thousands of children.

Israel’s conduct of the war has drawn broad international condemnation and caused a significant drop in public support for the country in the United States, its most important ally. That shift in public opinion has been especially pronounced among Democrats and young people, with a majority of both groups expressing a negative view of the Jewish state, according to the Pew Research Center.

Those reactions have occurred against a backdrop of rising antisemitism, including some high-profile hate crimes in New York City.

Last month, the mayor released a plan to fight antisemitism, which highlighted tens of millions of dollars that had already been allocated for hate crime prevention. Some pro-Israel Jewish groups criticized the plan for not mentioning Israel.

On Wednesday, pro-Israel and pro-Palestinian groups planned separate events to express their grief and outrage over the Oct. 7 attacks and the ensuing war, which has devastated Gaza and spread to Lebanon, Iran and elsewhere in the Middle East.

Many Jewish organizations planned to hold ceremonies to remember those who died in the 2023 attacks, including an event at the Museum of Jewish Heritage and a candlelit vigil in Union Square organized by Israelis for Peace New York, where organizers said they would also mourn those killed in Gaza.

For their part, pro-Palestinian groups said they would protest Israel’s military action in Gaza — which a U. N. commission and some international and Israeli human rights groups have described as a genocide, a claim the Israeli government has denied — as well as the wars in Lebanon and Iran.

The mayor’s outreach to pro-Israel Jewish groups has outraged some pro-Palestinian activists who accuse Mr. Mamdani of betraying their movement.

To underline that point, the organizers of a pro-Palestinian rally planned outside City Hall on Wednesday said the demonstration would express opposition both to the war in Gaza and to Mr. Mamdani.

“The mayor’s claim of solidarity with the Palestinian people is meaningless when it is followed by no action and capitulation to Zionist pressure,” the organizers said in a statement.

Tamar Glezerman, an organizer of the Israelis for Peace vigil in Union Square, said it was important to treat Wednesday as a day of mourning “while also not ignoring the aftermath of this massacre,” which she described as a genocide in Gaza.

“There is this fallacy out there that if you mourn or feel the pain of one side, that somehow cancels the other side or legitimizes violence against the other side,” added Ms. Glezerman, whose aunt was killed in the Oct. 7 attacks.

The mayor is expected to attend the vigil, which he did last year alongside other elected officials.

Liam Stack is a Times reporter who covers the culture and politics of the New York City region.

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

María del Carmen Abascal, aged and ailing, became a symbol of the country’s housing crisis when she was evicted two weeks ago, prompting mass protests and triggering national elections.

By Carlos Barragán

Reporting from Madrid

María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home last month prompted widespread protests in Spain and prompted the prime minister to call national elections, died on Tuesday.

“We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today,” her representatives said in a statement shared on Tuesday evening, using the shortened form of her given names, by which Ms. Abascal had become widely known across Spain.

Ms. Abascal was evicted from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years on Sept. 23, after police broke down her door. She was carried out on a stretcher and admitted to a hospital suffering from exhaustion.

Days later, as her condition failed to improve, her lawyer reached an agreement with the company that owned the apartment that would have allowed her to return once she was discharged.

“This solution came too late,” said the statement, signed by the tenants’ union, her lawyer and her family. “An absolutely avoidable situation following an agonizing process.”

The eviction touched a nerve among Spaniards fed up with the housing crisis. Tens of thousands of people, many of them young, took to the streets for days across the country, protesting skyrocketing rents and evictions. Hundreds have also camped in Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s most famous square, and have no plans to clear out.

The eviction also brought about the end of the minority government of the left-wing prime minister, Pedro Sánchez. After a housing bill he presented last week, aimed at restricting evictions and freezing rents, was rejected in Parliament by a majority of conservative legislators, he called snap elections for Nov. 29.

“My deepest sympathies to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Mr. Sánchez said on social media. “A warm embrace as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today.”

Ms. Abascal’s eviction marked a “turning point” in the history of Spain, putting housing at the center of the national debate, her representatives said. Her representatives, who asked that the family’s privacy be respected, said her death would strengthen their determination to “defend the right to housing and fight against speculators.”

“And above all, we will honor what she always asked of us,” the statement said: “Fight, keep fighting for what is yours.”

Scientists have sequenced his genome for the first time, hoping the world’s oldest land animal can offer clues into the genetics of longevity.

Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise living 1,200 miles off Africa’s west coast on the remote island of St. Helena, spending his days on the sun-dappled grounds of the official home of the governor. Credit...

Supported by

By Monique Brouillette

Dr. Joe Hollins slides a thick welding glove onto his left hand and grips a cotton swab tightly in his right. He squats down to eye level with a 400-pound giant tortoise, cradles its head with his gloved hand and carefully wedges a finger into its mouth to prop open its razor-sharp beak. With his other hand, he tries to swab its cheek.

Dr. Hollins, a veterinarian, has only about five seconds to get the DNA he’s after before he risks getting punched with a thick, scaly leg.

The first swab comes back covered in half-chewed carrot — a favorite snack. He tosses it aside and tries again. The tortoise, named Jonathan, looks mildly annoyed.

At about 194 years old, Jonathan is the world’s oldest known land animal. He’s an Aldabra giant tortoise living 1,200 miles off Africa’s west coast on the remote island of St. Helena, spending his days on the sun-dappled grounds of the official home of the governor. (At the time of his arrival on St. Helena, he was at least 50 years old, a determination his keepers made based on size.)

Although he shows some signs of aging, like cataracts that have left him mostly blind, he still has excellent hearing and a strong libido. He enjoys greeting visitors, having his neck petted and delivering loud belches for the crowd that gathers around his paddock during mealtimes.

In June, after Jonathan was erroneously declared dead by some media organizations, the Guinness World Records added him to its list of global icons, honoring his superlative status. And on Wednesday, he reached another milestone when a study announced that his genome had been sequenced for the first time.

“We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive,” said Steve Horvath, a biologist who studies aging at the University of California, Los Angeles, and an author of the study, which was published in the journal Science Advances.

Jonathan gave scientists the rare opportunity to study what happens to an animal’s genome over the course of nearly 200 years. But obtaining the DNA wasn’t easy: The researchers were not permitted to take a blood sample, the gold standard in DNA sequencing, because of the risk of infection. And because the island is served by only one often delayed commercial flight per week, the swabbed saliva had to travel by boat.

The researchers were committed to the idea, though, because they were curious if Jonathan’s DNA held secrets about aging or longevity. Just think: When this tortoise was presumably born in 1832, Charles Darwin was only 22 years old and hadn’t yet visited the Galápagos Islands, where he would dream up his theory of natural selection.

After sequencing the sample, the scientists compared Jonathan’s genome with those of tortoises 100 years his junior and found some molecular differences, especially in genes involved with DNA repair and the maintenance of the protective caps on chromosomes, called telomeres. As organisms age, DNA accumulates damage and the telomeres shorten, a process thought to drive aging. The results hint that this species may have evolved to be more resilient to age-related decline, but further testing is needed.

The team also discovered that Jonathan shared some genes with other long-living species like naked mole rats, which can live to 40 and rarely get cancer.

Perhaps most interesting is what they found when they looked at the tortoise’s epigenome, which is a map of the chemical tags that regulate the genome. These tags change with age and can lead to erratic gene activity. As expected, Jonathan had age-related changes in his epigenome similar to older humans, but there was an exception. Notably, the control switches linked to mitochondria were well preserved, similar to those of a young tortoise. Mitochondria, the molecular power plants inside cells, have long been linked to healthy aging.

The potential for learning from the biology of animals that live extraordinarily long lives is exciting for scientists who study aging. “Each of these long-lived species has some kind of special trick,” said Steve Austad, a biologist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. “And some of those may turn out to be relevant to human aging.”

“The results integrate very well in the wider puzzle of what longevity is,” said Björn Schumacher, who studies aging at the University of Cologne in Germany. He urged caution, though, in concluding that Jonathan would help us understand why humans age and what we can do about it.

Jeanne Calment, for example, was the world’s oldest person at the age of 122. She attributed her long life to a diet rich in olive oil and port wine. She also smoked cigarettes. Does that mean we should all smoke and drink red wine? Probably not, Dr. Schumacher said, and we should use similar caution when drawing conclusions from Jonathan.

Jonathan’s advanced age could be an outlier because of his round-the-clock veterinary care, diet of fresh vegetables and protected lawn at the governor’s house.

The molecular results offer tantalizing clues, however — ones that scientists are keen to explore further. “If we had 1,000 animals like Jonathan, it would be easier to understand his longevity,” said Dr. Stephen Clark, lead author of the study and the founder of Kallel, a nonprofit dedicated to studying the genetics of aging. In the future, Dr. Clark hopes to analyze more Aldabra tortoises and other long-lived species by gathering data that offers some hints for us spry chickens, too.

America Feels Trapped in the Twilight Zone. This Man Can Help.

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Alan Sepinwall

Mr. Sepinwall is a TV critic and the author of the forthcoming “Serling: A Journey Into the Twilight Zone With TV’s First Visionary.”

Before he created “The Twilight Zone,” Rod Serling was stuck. He’d established a reputation in the TV industry as, basically, Aaron Sorkin before Aaron Sorkin: a celebrated writer of weighty adult dramas that grappled with big contemporary issues like political corruption or the dehumanizing nature of corporate life.

He also frequently battled sponsors over what he was allowed to write and how far his scripts could go. When he worked to create a fictionalized version of the 1955 lynching of the Black teenager Emmett Till, for example, the final product was so watered down by sponsor and network pressure that it resulted in what he’d later describe in an interview with Mike Wallace as “a lukewarm, vitiated, emasculated kind of show.”

Serling didn’t want to make that kind of show. So after he was instructed to remove virtually all references to contemporary politics from a teleplay about a United States senator titled “The Arena,” he had a realization: “I probably would have had a much more adult play had I made it science fiction, put it in the year 2057, and peopled the Senate with robots,” he wrote of that experience.

Serling apparently applied the lesson of “The Arena” to a broader canvas, as he started writing speculative stories that were at sharp right angles to our own reality, in an anthology series that premiered in 1959 with the title “The Twilight Zone.” Because the series, which often featured fantastical scenarios, always with a surprising final twist, was so stylized, Serling found he could finally tell the unvarnished truth.

Almost 70 years later, at a moment when our own situation can seem increasingly ominous and surreal — when it’s hard to look anywhere, from political corruption to corporate malfeasance to the barrage of everyday headlines, without feeling as if you’ve traveled into a fifth dimension, beyond that which is known to man — Serling’s shrewd tactic for addressing political subjects offers an instructive response.

Contemporary television has often struggled to respond to the current political darkness; while shows like “The Good Fight” directly confronted the first Trump administration, few shows have done that during the second term. Some satires like “South Park” have taken direct aim, while others like “Saturday Night Live” have often seemed at sea when it comes to dealing with political turmoil.

With “The Twilight Zone,” Serling realized he could use allegory to make his political points. After all, how could a network censor or a viewer angrily insist that a story was saying something controversial about the world when it centered on a three-armed Martian?

This might help explain why “The Twilight Zone” still seems so incredibly — and at times, depressingly — relevant. Serling and his collaborators repeatedly and stealthily tackled such subjects as prejudice, creeping authoritarianism, the dangers of humans being replaced by technology and the peril of conformity as a societal ideal in ways that still resonate. Many episodes, when rewatched now, feel like they could have been written five minutes ago.

The show hit on social questions we have yet to adequately answer. Serling, a Jewish American who enlisted in the Army to fight Nazis during World War II, wrote often with his collaborators about the dangers of fascism and how easily people can succumb to its allure, including in such episodes as “The Obsolete Man” (a librarian is sentenced to death in a dystopia where books are outlawed) and “He’s Alive” (a hatemonger rises to power through coaching from Hitler’s ghost). In “The Brain Center at Whipple’s,” an aloof owner of a manufacturing plant gleefully replaces his flesh-and-blood workers with machines, unmoved by pleas from his former factory manager about the value of human thought and emotion; eventually, he himself is replaced by a robot.

“Number 12 Looks Just Like You” is set in a future where everyone upon turning 19 is forcibly transplanted into one of a handful of conventionally attractive bodies. It’s like today scrolling an Instagram feed where everyone is using the same filters or going down a rabbit hole about looksmaxxing. And the impulsive, destructive behavior of President Trump has often been likened to aspects of the plot of “It’s a Good Life,” an episode about an omnipotent child named Anthony Fremont who holds an entire town under his thumb.

Serling’s influence is evident all over modern culture. A legion of current storytellers, in television, film and literature, owe him a debt, from Steven Spielberg to Guillermo del Toro, from Curry Barker (as seen in his 2026 horror hit “Obsession”) to Ryan Coogler (“Sinners”). Charlie Brooker, creator of the anthology series “Black Mirror,” has talked about what he learned from Serling’s use of genre devices and the freedom they gave Serling to say what he wanted to say. “If he hadn’t had that rock for the river to flow around,” Mr. Brooker told me, “would the stories feel so resonant now? Or would we only read about them in academic books about the history of television?” Mr. Brooker went on to note: “Because he was forced to enter the world of metaphor, it’s the thing that gives him a superpower.”

Serling’s storytelling superpower grew from a desire to regain a lost affection for humanity — another effort that might prove instructive to us today. During his service as a paratrooper in the Pacific theater of World War II, a teenage Serling witnessed people dying under gruesome, often pointless circumstances. At 20, he watched as a close friend was decapitated in front of him by, of all things, a supply crate dropped from an airplane, and soon came perilously close to death himself.

These experiences left him traumatized and despairing about the depths to which his fellow man was capable of sinking. They also forced Serling to examine why people so often make terrible choices and whether there’s hope for them to do better in the future, a theme that would animate his TV writing. In “The Twilight Zone,” characters are often offered a magical second chance — and the ones who can’t change frequently earn karmic justice of a supernatural variety.

Despite his celebrity and acclaim — and his unnerving prescience — Serling struggled with self-doubt for much of his career. In the years leading up to his 1975 death of a heart attack at the age of 50, he gave an interview suggesting his accomplishments would soon be forgotten.

“I’ve written articulate stuff, reasonably bright stuff over the years, but nothing that will stand the test of time,” he said in 1972. “The good writing, really good writing — like wine — has to age well with the years, and my stuff is momentarily adequate.”

Not only did Serling underestimate his influence, but he also failed to see how the tactic he adapted would prove to be the most successful way to process perilous times. If the Serling who gave that interview could, like some of his characters, travel forward through time, he might be dismayed that so many of the problems he wrote about still aren’t resolved decades later. But he would also see that the best way to describe the legacy of his work isn’t “momentarily adequate,” but a different phrase he repeatedly recited as the host of “The Twilight Zone”: “as timeless as infinity.”

Alan Sepinwall is a TV critic, most recently for Rolling Stone, and the author of the forthcoming “Serling: A Journey Into the Twilight Zone With TV’s First Visionary.”
