If the Kennedy Center Is ‘Dangerous,’ Why Is the Symphony Rehearsing There?

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

The National Symphony Orchestra is practicing inside a building that President Trump and his allies say could fall on their heads.

Musicians with the National Symphony Orchestra still arrive at the Kennedy Center almost every weekday morning for rehearsals, entering through a parking lot door. Credit... Elizabeth Frantz for The New York Times

Supported by

By Elizabeth Williamson

Elizabeth Williamson reported from a designated safe area in the underground garage of the Kennedy Center.

The shuttered John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts is a deadly place. Just ask President Trump.

This week he said it was “a great danger to anyone who walks inside.” Last month he said that a security guard had narrowly avoided “certain death” after a storm brought down a five-foot piece of ceiling plaster, injuring no one. The center, he said, is in a “virtual state of collapse.”

And yet on most weekday mornings, 100-odd members of the National Symphony Orchestra arrive for rehearsals in the shell of their former home. This week they are rehearsing in the center’s main concert hall for upcoming performances in the Maryland and Virginia suburbs of Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5, Haydn’s Symphony No. 85 (“La Reine”) and Stravinsky’s Scènes de Ballet.

The theme, as advertised on their website, is “music that finds hope and vitality in the face of adversity.”

So far, none of the musicians have encountered collapsing concrete garage decks, falling 2,500-pound roof sections or “electrical explosions”— risks the center’s management says lurk everywhere.

“We’re just happy to work,” a violinist said last week, while hustling into the building through a parking lot entrance. The violinist, and all other musicians interviewed as they entered the building, asked not be named for fear of retaliation against the orchestra, which still has financial ties to the Kennedy Center.

One musician expressed the hope that her colleagues would “shut up” and focus on music, not politics.

Another said that the orchestra’s presence in the building reinforced the view by some former employees that the administration’s portrayal of the building’s problems have been exaggerated.

“The absurdity of this is mind-blowing,” a longtime symphony patron said.

A Kennedy Center spokesman, P. J. Elliott, said this week that the concert hall was perfectly safe for the musicians but not for the public. The hall “is not a restricted area to essential staff and N. S. O. musicians,’’ he said in a statement. “Musicians can rehearse in it safely during the closure.” He did not explain why.

The development is the latest in the saga of Mr. Trump’s takeover of the center. Briefly: Less than a month into his second term, the president purged the Kennedy Center board of Biden-era appointees, installed allies who made him chairman, then announced that the place would close for two years of renovations. Democratic lawmakers on the board said it was an excuse to avoid the humiliation of plummeting ticket sales and fleeing artists.

In December, Mr. Trump put his name on the center, a living memorial to a slain president, but a judge ordered it off. When he was again denied last month, the president decreed that the renovation would not begin until courts allowed his name on the building front. He followed with a threat to tear the entire place down.

While the drama plays out, one of the nation’s premier orchestras still needs a place to practice for its 2026-27 season, with concerts now in six different places across the region. They and the center’s Opera House Orchestra, which now performs in an annex called The Reach, are the only paid performances that have survived Mr. Trump’s takeover. Local music lovers call it a tribute to the orchestras’ resilience.

One morning last week, the musicians drove up to a center underground parking garage, Lot A, their instrument cases riding shotgun. They parked their cars and headed through a door with a paper sign taped on it that said “NSO This Way.’’ At one point the orchestra’s conductor, Gianandrea Noseda, glided up carrying a garment bag and paused to hug staff members holding the door.

Matt Floca, the center’s Trump-appointed director, said in reports to the board and the media this year that “moisture infiltration has caused corrosion and weakening of the concrete deck throughout the garages. Hundreds of compromised areas have been identified.”

But Mr. Elliott, the center’s spokesman, said the musicians follow “routes assessed as safe by facilities and management” to the main concert hall. The unsafe areas, he added, are “off limits.” The center continues to rent out its parking garage by the day and month.

David Z. Seide, a lawyer representing the former employees, said in an interview that the orchestra’s rehearsals “confirm what we’ve been saying all along. The building is not a threat to public health and safety.”

“This is part of a pattern of the government routinely saying one thing and doing another,” said Norm Eisen and Kyle Freeny, lawyers representing Representative Joyce Beatty, Democrat of Ohio and an ex officio Kennedy Center board member, who sued Mr. Trump to keep the building open and his name off its front.

Mr. Floca has said that the closure is temporary and is reassessed weekly. Critics, including congressional Democrats, question how things got to this point when Congress appropriated $257 million for a full renovation more than a year ago, and pays annually for maintenance. They speculate that the week-by-week closure is a tactic to circumvent a judge’s order that the center remain open.

In the meantime, the main building’s cafeteria and restaurants have long been closed. A couple of the musicians said they bring bag lunches to eat backstage during their hourlong break. Others dip out to Tazza, a nearby cafe that has struggled since the closure. They have agreed to wear hard hats on the rare occasions they venture outside the concert hall.

“There is a loneliness about it,” an orchestra employee said. “I remember seeing so many different faces from so many different departments, and that just doesn’t happen. You’re often the only one.”

After Mr. Trump put his name on the building, the orchestra’s audiences fell by as much as half. The composer Philip Glass withdrew his new symphony from a scheduled debut with the orchestra, and Béla Fleck, the Grammy-winning banjo player, pulled out of three performances. Its executive director, Jean Davidson, left in March, saying, “It’s no secret that this has been a really hard year.”

Amid an exodus of performers, audiences and donors, the Washington National Opera, also housed in the center since its opening, moved out. But the fates of the National Symphony Orchestra and the Kennedy Center are more deeply intertwined. The center oversees the orchestra’s budget, topping it up when ticket sales and donations fall short, which amounted to about $17 million this year.

In February Mr. Trump began demanding the center close by early July, which would leave the orchestra homeless. The orchestra’s budget request for 2026-27 languished for months without approval from the Kennedy Center board, preventing it from booking alternate venues and retaining guest performers.

Kennedy Center patrons formed Save Our Symphonies, a group supporting the orchestra and other center musicians in financial limbo. World-class performers volunteered to play in private homes, condominium lobbies and other local spots, pausing to explain their situation to Washingtonians while taking care not to talk politics, grant media interviews or otherwise anger the president. The performances have netted them new fans and donors.

The orchestra still lacks an approved budget, but in August received a green light from the Kennedy Center board to book the current season. It announced the dates only weeks before the first performance.

The musicians last month signed a new, four-year contract. An enthusiastic crowd attended the season-opening celebration at the Music Center at Strathmore in North Bethesda, Md., cheering as the concert opened with the national anthem.

“It will be an interesting season,” Mr. Noseda told the audience. “A bit tiring here and there, but also more exciting.”

Elizabeth Williamson is a feature writer for The Times, based in Washington. She has been a journalist for three decades, on three continents.

Rubio Urges Europe to Awaken From ‘Slumber’ and Uphold Western Dominance

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

In Greece, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Western nations must embrace an earlier ethos of exploration and conquest as part of their civilization, to remain ‘at the head of the world.’

By Edward Wong

Edward Wong is traveling with Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Europe. He has reported on international news for more than two decades as a foreign and diplomatic correspondent.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Wednesday for Western nations to rejuvenate their civilization so they can maintain their dominance in a world of wars, economic uncertainty and technological change.

“Today, we find ourselves at a crossroads,” Mr. Rubio said in a speech in Athens, with the Acropolis and Parthenon bathed in the golden light of a Mediterranean sunset behind him.

“The next decade will write the story of the next century,” he said. “The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline. We’ll either choose to act now, or lose the choice to act at all.”

Mr. Rubio’s speech sought to highlight the ideological tenets of an American conservative movement whose adherents see President Trump as their leader.

Some of its intellectual architects argue that citizens of the United States and Europe should not apologize for the choices made by their ancestors, including exploration and conquest of other peoples and lands. Instead, they say, citizens should embrace that earlier ethos, as their countries seek an edge in the military and economic competition with China and other non-Western powers.

Men of ancient Greece, Mr. Rubio said, “knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor in fighting to defend its interests above all else.”

“They believed — fiercely — in the ideal of the ‘great man’: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds,” he added.

Mr. Rubio’s visit to Greece was the centerpiece of a three-nation European tour, and it was the second time he has used the continent as a backdrop for an ideological speech.

His remarks in Athens echoed lines he delivered to European leaders in a February speech at the Munich Security Conference, where he spoke of the possible “civilizational erasure” of Europe. However, in the new speech, Mr. Rubio did not use that contentious phrase — one embraced by far-right American and European nationalists pushing for strict limits on immigration.

As he did in Munich, Mr. Rubio praised the builders of empires — Alexander the Great, who conquered the “entire known world” (an exaggeration of the size of the territory he controlled), as well as Julius Caesar, Charlemagne and Hernán Cortés — the Spanish conquistador whose troops violently toppled the Aztec rulers of Mexico.

Mr. Rubio also talked about crimes committed against ancient Greece by a Persian army that ransacked Athens 2,500 years ago. He invoked “the legendary last stand of 300 Spartans” at Thermopylae against the Persians.

With those references, Mr. Rubio was adopting the rhetoric of some conservative commentators, who, during the American wars in the predominantly Muslim countries of Iraq and Afghanistan, emphasized the heroism of the 300 Spartans faced with what they called rapacious warriors from another civilization.

Later in the speech, Mr. Rubio denounced the “radical mullahs of Iran” — the country located on the land of ancient Persia.

He went on to link the philosophical and political pursuits of ancient Greece to “the architects of European Christendom,” who designed soaring cathedrals, and to colonial settlers, who embodied “the American frontier spirit.”

“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago,” he said.

Nations, he said, must have “the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail.”

Mr. Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, criticized Western governments that had “opened our borders” in recent decades, a theme he also addressed at a news conference on Wednesday morning.

There, he called for greater cooperation between the United States and Greece to restrict migration and immigration.

“Greece is also a very close strategic partner on border security and the fight against mass migration,” Mr. Rubio said while standing beside Giorgios Gerapetritis, the Greek foreign minister.

“What we do not wish to see under any circumstances is that the birthplace of the West is threatened by bad decisions, by actions, by failure to address challenges,” Mr. Rubio added.

Mr. Gerapetritis told reporters that Greece was trying to address “challenges” from “mass migration.”

Mr. Rubio also praised Greece for being on track to spend at least 5 percent of its annual gross domestic product on defense, a benchmark that Mr. Trump insists NATO allies must meet.

Mr. Rubio is scheduled to fly to Portugal on Thursday, his third stop on a tour that started in Iceland.

After the news conference, he visited the U. S. Embassy, where he was introduced to a crowd by Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former romantic partner of Donald Trump Jr., the eldest son of the American president.

An investigative article in The Wall Street Journal has raised questions about potential conflicts of interest in Ms. Guilfoyle’s involvement in energy deals in Greece. Democratic Congressional leaders are calling for an inquiry.

When asked at the news conference about the allegations, Mr. Rubio said he would not discuss them in public.

“Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here,” he said, as Ms. Guilfoyle sat in front of him.

Edward Wong reports on global affairs, U. S. foreign policy and the State Department for The Times.

What to Know About the Fears of a Plague Outbreak in Russia

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Russian authorities aren’t saying much about the death of a woman who worked in a lab studying plague. But experts say any risk of contagion would be limited.

By The New York Times

Is there an outbreak of plague in Russia?

The short answer: We don’t know. The slightly longer answer: A woman who works in a remote Siberian lab that studies plague has died of pneumonia. The lab has been locked down and the Russian authorities aren’t saying much, which has fueled speculation and rumors.

There’s a lot we still don’t know. The Times has gathered all the available information and talked to experts to try to make as much sense of it as possible. (Spoiler alert: Don’t panic.)

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of Irkutsk’s Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, seems to have died of a mysterious pneumonia earlier this month. Her death prompted Russian health authorities to quarantine the hospital where she died, along with the institute’s staff and other people who were in contact with her. So far, so unsettling.

Yes. The plague has been with us a very long time. There are still a few hundred cases every year, mostly in Madagascar and Democratic Republic of the Congo, but also in the United States, Russia and other countries.

Many people know the plague as the “Black Death,” a pandemic that is thought to have killed at least a third of Europe’s population in the 14th century.

Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes plague, has infected humans for thousands of years, also circulating among rodents and other small mammals, which serve as long-term reservoirs, and fleas, which spread it.

There are three main ways that plague can infect humans: Bubonic plague occurs when the plague-causing bacteria multiplies in the lymph nodes, usually after a bite from an infected flea. Septicemic plague occurs when the infection spreads to the bloodstream. The most virulent type is pneumonic plague, which causes a severe rapid-onset lung infection and can be spread through a cough or sneeze.

Left untreated, pneumonic plague can kill a victim within days. But all three types of plague respond well to antibiotics if they are taken quickly. Based on the information we have so far, most experts aren’t too worried.

The fact that Shipilova worked in a lab studying plague, which is supposed to have robust protections against the microbe escaping, is concerning.

The lack of details from the Russian authorities has unnerved many around the world who remain scarred by the Covid-19 pandemic. At that time, it was an authoritarian government in China, where the virus originated, that covered up information.

In the immediate aftermath of Shipilova’s death, Russian authorities were very terse. They failed to clarify her whereabouts before her death or to address questions about whether an accident had taken place at the institute.

When health officials and the United States government began asking questions, the Russian authorities gave additional information. (On Wednesday, U. S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was “incumbent” upon Russia to share more with the world. “We’re watching it very ​closely, hour by hour,” he said.)

Russia said yesterday that Shipilova had been vaccinated against the disease and no “emergency situations” had been identified at the lab. (One caveat: It’s not clear how effective the available vaccines are.)

Russia’s health regulator also said there are “no epidemiological risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region.”

Maybe — but it’s been a while. In the 14th century, according to one account, a Mongol army catapulted plague-infested bodies into the Crimean city of Caffa.

In the modern era, a defector from the Soviet Union’s bioweapons program once claimed his government stockpiled “dozens of tons of smallpox and plague” that could be loaded onto bombs and missiles.

The existence of an active biological weapons program in Russia, which has historically sourced strains from anti-plague institutes, has added to global concerns.

In an annual threat assessment this year, U. S. intelligence agencies said Russian scientists were continuing to develop new chemical and biological weapons capabilities. The State Department, in its arms control compliance report last year, said Russia maintained an offensive biological warfare program in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention.

Based on what we know so far, no. For all the unknowns, experts say that even if plague were confirmed in Shipilova’s death, the risk of widespread contagion would be limited.

Reporting by Paul Sonne, Edward Wong, Chris Buckley, Oleg Matsnev Milana Mazaeva and Alina Lobzina

August Lamm wants you to put down your smartphone and reclaim your life.

Four years ago, August Lamm had 200,000 social media followers and posted regularly on Instagram. In her new book, she is urging people to ditch their smartphones. Credit... Casey Steffens for The New York Times

Supported by

By Amanda Hess

One hot summer day, August Lamm stood cheerily behind a booth in Tompkins Square Park, offering a stack of pamphlets titled “You Don’t Need a Smartphone.” The cover featured a retro photograph of a woman lying on the floor and talking on a landline. She looked ecstatic.

Lamm had come to the park, in part, to invite participants to a “downgrading” event that evening, in which she would lead phone addicts toward less-connected devices. The crowd floated silently past. Their ears were stuffed with AirPods. Their eyes were watching their phones. The people who most need Lamm’s help, she has found, are the least likely to look up and notice her.

Lamm, who is 31, was like them once. Four years ago, she was an art influencer with 200,000 social media followers. Then she traded in her smartphone for a 2002-era Nokia cellphone. Later, she pawned her laptop. Now she’s working to divest herself from email. And she’s become an advocate for disengaging from technology and, as she puts it, “reclaiming your life.”

At the park, Lamm wore a thrifted black top with a paper clip in place of a missing button. She appears somewhat out of time, her face cleansed of TikTok makeup trends and her silhouette freed from the long jorts that have seemingly drop-shipped onto everyone in her age bracket. Unled by Google, unfed by DoorDash, unmatched on Hinge, she navigates a version of New York where seemingly everyone else is locked in a tragic embrace with a personal device. When she walks outside, she is now the rare human who is alert and open for engagement.

Soon Louis Toledo, 73, sidled up to the booth, the white cords of his headphones swinging from his chest pocket. “Phones, huh?” he said. “No one calls me.”

He told Lamm about his divorce, his relationship with his siblings, his difficulty in grade school, his service in the Air Force and his condominium in Puerto Rico, before returning finally to the topic of the smartphone, and his suspicion that “the G5, G4, 5G, whatever” can “kill your sperms.”

“Well,” Lamm said, empathizing: “At least you don’t need them now.”

He saw things differently. “Listen, I got more to offer you today than you could imagine,” he said. “We can have two kids and live beautifully in Puerto Rico.”

She asked if he would be willing to get rid of his smartphone, and when he said no, she smiled sadly. “That’s a dealbreaker for me,” she said.

A young couple approached, brandishing a flip phone. They had been experimenting, they said, with leaving the house with one smartphone between them.

Passerby asked if Lamm was affiliated with dumbphone companies, or the Luddites, or the Summer of Ludd. Over the past few years, the smartphone resistance has grown: there is the phoneless weekly Brooklyn gathering Phone Free Adelphi; the 30-day group challenge Month Offline; the biweekly techno-critical event bulletin NYC Off Tech; and the Luddite Club, with chapters from Santa Monica High School to Stockholm, Sweden.

Lamm has emerged as a kind of bard of this scene, writing about her own experience divesting from technology and encouraging her peers to replace mindless scrolling with actual books. Now she’s selling one: After moving 20,000 copies of her self-published $10 zine “You Don’t Need a Smartphone,” Vintage published an updated and expanded paperback under the same title this week.

It’s a practical guide to a post-smartphone life: Lamm draws her own maps and checks her email once a week at the public library. She advises carrying a compact mirror and deck of cards, as if passing down the ancient texts. The book is also a deeply observed account of what everyone else is missing. “Ironically, looking at screens is how we tune out the sad state of our public spaces,” she writes. “We can’t bear to face a crowd of indifferent souls. It’s mass rejection.”

After an hour and a half at the booth, Lamm packed up her materials and dragged them under the sidewalk umbrella of a nearby poke spot. She was underslept. The previous evening, she had attended a birthday party for the publisher of an offline low-tech zine, and “as happens when you don’t have a smartphone, I did not take the optimal train trip back home,” she said.

Downgrading is the inverse of optimizing. It’s a wandered path, logistically and socially. “I feel very out of touch,” Lamm said without concern. “People don’t feel the need to communicate any cultural trends in real life anymore, because they’re assuming that you’re getting it online,” she said. “I didn’t know who Chappell Roan was for like a year.”

As we finished our rice bowls, it began to rain, which caught Lamm by surprise. Soon it was pummeling the Lower East Side. A stream formed down Avenue A, rushing toward her “downgrading” event. She worried the storm would suppress turnout.

“I really need to start looking at the weather,” she said. “I need to get a newspaper delivered to my house.”

Lamm got her first iPhone shortly after she got her first period. It was, she writes in the book, “a treasure chest,” a “dozen gifts in one.” Later it would bring a bigger prize — she would leverage it to become a working artist, one who made a living not through connections in the art world but through followers on social media.

After college, where Lamm studied South Asian art history, she took up crosshatching, a drawing style forged in the Middle Ages that she savvily repositioned for the Instagram age. As she worked by day in a Berlin ice cream shop, she gained an online following for drawings of tiny ink animals that she photographed posed with a pen in a kind of digital illusion — a koala seems to hug the barrel; a pigeon perches on the uncapped tip. Lamm posed herself for Instagram too, where she had morphed into a recognizable type — an indie artist of the 2010s, with bangs and slim high-waisted jeans. She sold drawings and consultation sessions to her followers, as well as an online guide to how they, too, could make a living as an artist on social media.

Art Instagram is assumed to be one of the cozier parts of the internet, but for Lamm it was high-stress. When the fire alarm went off in her apartment building one morning, and she missed posting her daily drawing at the optimal time, she had a panic attack on the lawn.“I was going to lose my credibility, my algorithmic rank, my income if I took that day off,” she said.

But she also found that the more emotional she got on the app, the more attention she got for her work. “When I posted about being anxious, having a breakdown, going through a breakup, I would sell more,” she said.

She took a break from Instagram in 2022, but not on purpose. After entering the wrong password too many times, she was locked out of her account for three months. The timing felt catastrophic: She had a book on crosshatching coming out that she hoped would be a bridge to a writing career. She had been diagnosed with a degenerative spinal disorder, and when it flared, she said it was difficult to draw, and to use her phone. “I couldn’t tap with my thumb,” she said. Now, on the eve of her book’s publication, her platform collapsed.

When Lamm’s account was finally restored, she felt as if she had returned to a different Instagram, one ruled not by static photographs but by looping short-form videos. Meta paid her a few hundred dollars to make her first reel, and she was overwhelmed by how much time it required — time she could be drawing or writing. Her monthslong banishment had shown her just how reliant she was on tech companies.

This knowledge was at first horrifying, and then liberating. By the end of the year, she had traded in her smartphone for a less advanced model and deactivated her social media accounts.

With the phone gone, “my thoughts grew back,” she writes. Her memory was so sharp that she wondered fleetingly if she could be a “late-blooming genius,” she jokes. She read “Anna Karenina” and “Moby Dick,” recorded diaristic folk songs in her bedroom, and wrote a novel, “Lambing Season,” based on her experience moving into a ramshackle home with a student pilot she met on the internet. She supported herself by busking, freelance writing and selling that pamphlet, which answered all the questions she kept fielding about surviving without a smartphone.

Sometimes strangers examine Lamm’s life (she is from Connecticut) and assume she must be secretly rich. Her real secret is living “very cheaply,” she said. “It’s not a comfortable existence.”

Lamm said she left home when she was 16, shortly before her stepmother was incarcerated for running a pyramid scheme out of the living room. When her father died in 2024, Lamm was left to pay the funeral costs. The privilege of the low-tech lifestyle is not necessarily one enjoyed by the leisure class, which, she writes, “devotes much of its leisure time to screens.”

In 2025, Hilary Redmon, the head of nonfiction at Knopf, was working from home one day when her college-age daughter wandered into her office, looking at her phone. “Have you heard of August Lamm?” she asked. “I have to get rid of my phone.”

Redmon downloaded a PDF of Lamm’s zine, and was struck by her voice. “It made an impact on my daughter, who is pretty quick to dismiss people trying to influence her to do anything,” Redmon said. Soon Lamm had been offered a two-book deal, for the anti-smartphone book, and her novel.

Lamm arrived for her downgrading event at Nightclub 101 looking as if she had run through a sprinkler, which did not trouble her. Without the practice of constant self-surveillance, she had lost “the reflex of self-consciousness,” she said.

She dried off as she zipped around the moody basement space, preparing her various offerings. She set out a group of bound short stories published by Loose Tooth Press, which she co-founded with her friend Magdalene Kennedy.

Kennedy is one of the people Lamm calls on her flip-phone when she needs a human being to access the internet on her behalf. “She was at the bookstore and she was like, ‘I’m looking for a book on how to make decisions, can you look it up for me?’” Kennedy said. “And I tried, but there were so many books on how to make decisions.”

Next to the Loose Tooth stories were copies of Lamm’s new zine, “Archaic,” which you can’t read or buy online. The first issue includes a letter from Dave Eggers and poems by Tao Lin.

It’s an outgrowth of Lamm’s Center for Archaic Networks, a group she founded that’s “dedicated to the study and revival of human networks pre-dating social media.” She recently spent $100,000 of her book advance to put a down payment on a $320,000 house in upstate New York, where she will live and host a residency where applicants can stay for a week or two and lock their devices in a safe for the duration.

“I’m so excited to have this privilege that everybody else in human history had,” she said, “which is just to live in a house where everyone is present.”

In the end, the rain did not deter dozens of young New Yorkers from Lamm’s event. Gabriel Hurlbert, 26, met Lamm at a downtown literary reading in 2024, and started exchanging letters with her. He arrived at Nightclub 101 that evening with two smartphones, one provided by his employer, Deloitte.

“My relationship to my phone, for long stretches of time, has been like that between a heroin addict and heroin,” he said, though he believes the phone itself is symptomatic of a deeper problem. “I haven’t really located the source of the malaise,” he said.

On a bench, Lamm handled a small collection of minimalist phones that she had been gifted by Keyphone, which sponsored the event; by night’s end, she’d have given them all away. She has become a kind of Luddite influencer. Dumbphone companies have offered to pay for a mention in her book, and her publisher’s marketing team has floated the idea of a brand partnership. (She’s not interested).

I asked Lamm if she’d considered reactivating her dormant 180,000-follower Instagram account for the book launch. She had never fully deleted it, in case of emergency. “This does not qualify as an emergency to me,” she said.

When Lamm stepped onstage, the stakes of her project became clear. In battling the smartphone, she was fighting for her time, and for her mind, but also for some company. She could not bear to do this alone.

Lamm read an excerpt from the book, in which she lamented that her fans often told her that her zine changed their lives. But they still have smartphones. “They were theoretically in favor of the movement, and yet personally unable to partake,” she said. “They wished me the best with my activism. They had no doubt it would make a difference.”

As she spoke, a woman in the audience lifted her phone and zoomed in.

Amanda Hess is a writer at large for The Times.

Texas Plans Execution After Botched Lethal Injection in Tennessee

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Jamaal Howard’s lawyers are seeking information about the lethal injection drug, the same medication used in Tennessee’s failed attempt last week.

By Jesus Jiménez

A Texas man scheduled to be put to death Wednesday for fatally shooting a convenience store clerk in 2000 will be the first person executed in the United States since a botched attempt last week on a death row inmate in Tennessee.

The man, Jamaal Howard, 46, was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in 2001 in the killing of Vickie Swartout, 42. Mr. Howard was 20 when he shot Ms. Swartout, who was working at a convenience store in southeast Texas, and stole $114 from the cash register and a carton of cigarettes.

Mr. Howard is scheduled to be executed on Wednesday at about 6 p. m. Central time, but his lawyers have asked Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas to delay the execution by 30 days while they wait for more information on the drug that will be used in the execution. Texas uses pentobarbital for lethal injections, the same drug used in the failed execution last week of Christa Pike in Tennessee.

Lawyers for Mr. Howard had filed a motion with the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals on Tuesday night asking the court to stay Mr. Howard’s execution out of concern that the injection could be botched, as it was for Ms. Pike. The appeals court on Wednesday denied the motion to stay the execution.

Lawyers for Mr. Howard also filed petitions that are pending with the U. S. Supreme Court that argue Mr. Howard’s execution should be stayed because he has an intellectual disability.

The Texas court’s ruling leaves it to Mr. Abbott or the U. S. Supreme Court to halt the execution.

Mr. Abbott’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Lawyers for Mr. Howard said they had asked the Texas Department of Criminal Justice what drug they planned to use on Mr. Howard and for details on where it had been stored. The department has not shared those details with Mr. Howard’s lawyers, instead asking the Texas attorney general whether that information must be disclosed.

“We do not ask you to decide anything about Mr. Howard’s case other than this: that he should not be executed with a drug whose history the state has refused to let his lawyers see, within days of the same drug failing in another state,” Mr. Howard’s lawyers wrote in a letter to Mr. Abbott.

As of Tuesday, Ms. Pike, who survived two doses of a lethal injection drug last week, was conscious and speaking, her lawyers said. Ms. Pike was receiving medical care at a Nashville hospital, and her prognosis was unclear.

An earlier version of this article misstated the amount of money Mr. Howard stole. It was $114, not $114,000.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Jesus Jiménez is a Times reporter covering North Texas. He is based in Dallas.

Russia Says It Found No ‘Emergency’ in Plague Lab

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

New information around the death of a lab worker, including a statement that she had been vaccinated against the plague, came as U. S. officials demanded more data.

By Paul Sonne

Reporting from Berlin

The Russian authorities said on Wednesday that a researcher at a Siberian anti-plague institute who died from a mysterious pneumonia had been vaccinated against the pathogens she worked with and that no “emergency situations” had occurred at the lab.

Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian health regulator, issued the statement after the United States urged Moscow to be more forthcoming about the possible public health incident and the World Health Organization asked for more information to make an accurate assessment of any threat.

The paucity of details in Russian official statements and the absence of international health officials on the scene have led to questions about the Russian government’s insistence that it has the situation under control. The world has remained on high alert about public health threats in the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic.

On Oct. 2, Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old researcher at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, died from pneumonia of an unknown origin at a hospital in Shelekhov, the town where she lived, prompting fears of a pneumonic plague outbreak.

Ms. Shipilova had been vaccinated and therefore “had immunity to the dangerous infections she worked with,” the Russian health regulator said on Wednesday. The statement implied that Ms. Shipilova had a lower risk of contracting the plague, though vaccination would not definitively rule out becoming ill with the disease.

Rospotrebnadzor also said that two commissions monitoring biological safety had inspected the institute. “No emergency situations were identified during work with pathogenic microorganisms,” the health regulator said.

Tests on Ms. Shipilova’s remains, the regulator previously said, had not found evidence of any of the microorganisms she worked with at the institute.

Medical observation has been completed for more than 90 percent of the people Ms. Shipilova had been in contact with, and “no health impairments related to infectious pathology were detected,” the Russian regulator added. Nearly 5,000 laboratory tests revealed no hazardous pathogenic microorganisms, its statement said.

“Preventive and anti-epidemic measures have been organized to an exhaustive extent,” it said in the statement. “There are no epidemiological risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region.”

The Russian authorities released the additional information after the State Department sent a formal diplomatic note, known as a démarche, asking for more detail about what happened.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also voiced the request publicly on Tuesday during a trip to Iceland, noting that the United States was monitoring the situation.

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very ​closely, hour by hour.”

Ms. Shipilova’s unexplained death prompted the Russian authorities to quarantine part of the hospital where she was taken, as well as the institute’s staff and other people whom she had come into contact with in her final days. Other facilities in and around Irkutsk also implemented restrictive measures, in some cases as a precaution.

In the immediate aftermath of Ms. Shipilova’s death, the Russian authorities gave only sparing public statements, failing to clarify the researcher’s whereabouts before her death or to address questions about whether an accident had taken place at the institute.

Aleksei Tsydenov, the governor of the Buryatia region, which borders Irkutsk, initially said that Ms. Shipilova had died of the plague, without naming her, and then edited his statement to say that she had “possibly” died from the illness.

The Russian health regulator also waited five days after Ms. Shipilova’s death to reveal her vaccination status. An independent Russian publication, People of Baikal, cited a former intern at the institute who said all employees were vaccinated against the plague as a precaution.

The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, has regularly referred questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which has not held any news conference on the matter. President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia has not publicly commented.

The existence of an active biological weapons program in Russia, which has historically sourced strains from anti-plague institutes, has added to global concerns.

In an annual threat assessment this year, U. S. intelligence agencies said Russian scientists were continuing to develop new chemical and biological weapons capabilities. The State Department, in its arms control compliance report last year, said Russia maintained an offensive biological warfare program in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention.

The relatively thin details from the Russian authorities have unnerved U. S. officials and others around the world who remain scarred by the coronavirus pandemic and efforts by the authoritarian government in China, where the virus originated, to cover up information.

The Chinese government has so far offered a muted response to the reports from Russia.

“China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation in the field of infectious disease prevention and control, including the plague,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said on Tuesday in a brief response to a question about whether Moscow had notified Beijing about the possible plague case.

Pneumonic plague causes a severe, rapid-onset lung infection and is considered the most virulent form of the plague. It results from the same bacteria that cause the bubonic and septicemic plagues.

Unlike Covid-19, the disease can be treated effectively with antibiotics, but it must be caught very quickly.

Plague is endemic to Siberia and Russia’s Far East, where the bacteria that causes the disease circulates in wild rodents and their fleas. One of the tasks of institutes like the one in Irkutsk is epidemiological surveillance of such threats.

Experts have said that even if plague were confirmed in the Russian case, the risk of widespread contagion could be limited.

In a statement on Monday, the W. H. O. said that based on available information, “the public health risk to the general population appears to be low.” But on Wednesday, the organization said it had not received sufficient information from Russia to complete a full risk assessment.

The organization’s leader, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said in a statement that the Russian health authorities had informed the W. H. O. that the Irkutsk region had not registered any confirmed cases of the plague. Russia told the agency that an epidemiological investigation had been conducted, with contacts of the deceased observed and tested, and “no high-threat pathogens had been detected.”

Mr. Ghebreyesus said the W. H. O. had requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.

The New York Times was not immediately able to identify any credible media reports of a second employee from the Siberian institute coming down with pneumonia. In a news conference on Wednesday, Mr. Ghebreyesus said the W. H. O. did not assess whether such reports were credible and could ask for information even based on unverified social media posts.

“We have asked Russia to respond to this,” he said. “Any reporting that comes, we cannot ignore it. And credibility of the media is not our mandate.”

W. H. O. officials said they wanted to establish what caused the pneumonia in Ms. Shipilova and could offer Russia help with additional testing.

Her mother, Svetlana Shipilova, said in an interview with a local Russian news outlet, Glubina, that she was upset about friends believing “nasty stuff” about her child, including an unverified report that suggested her daughter had become ill after breaking a test tube.

“Not all doctors even realize that a test tube is impossible to break. Even if you throw it against a wall,” she said from quarantine. “Only an amateur could say that. Even hypothetically, it’s simply impossible to spill or break. They’re so protected.”

Three people who knew Darya Shipilova echoed that sentiment in comments to The Times, describing her as a diligent and responsible person who was being tarnished with unverified reporting that she had made some sort of mistake at work.

President Trump has offered help to Russia in dealing with the situation, but Russian officials have responded by saying that they have it under control.

“It is always very good when offers of mutual assistance are made,” said Mr. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump told reporters that he would hold a call “very soon” with Mr. Putin to discuss the matter.

Elena Sofina, the deputy mayor in Shelekhov responsible for social affairs, said in a statement on Tuesday that Russian officials could handle the situation themselves. She called the matter “completely under control.”

“A dangerous diagnosis has not been confirmed, but we are still following all protocol measures,” she said, adding, “We continue to work.”

Edward Wong, Chris Buckley, Oleg Matsnev Milana Mazaeva and Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.

Whistle-Blower Says I. R. S. Leaked His Tax Records in Retaliation

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Brian J. Visalli, a veteran investigator of tax fraud, said in a lawsuit that the agency had sent his personal and tax information to federal prosecutors.

By Jesse Drucker

An Internal Revenue Service investigator sued the agency this month, claiming officials illegally leaked his confidential personnel records to federal prosecutors to punish him for years of whistle-blowing on the agency’s failure to tackle tax dodging.

Brian J. Visalli, a 24-year I. R. S. veteran, specializes in investigating complex offshore tax shelters. He has publicly criticized the agency, writing articles about its unwillingness to aggressively target schemes that multinational companies use to skirt their taxes. He contributed to two reports published by the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration: one on conflicts of interest within the I. R. S. and the other on the agency’s refusal to investigate advisers who design and sell aggressive tax strategies.

He says the I. R. S. is using relatively small mistakes in his personal tax return to retaliate against him. The suit claims the I. R. S. illegally disclosed his employee and tax information to Justice Department prosecutors to discredit and fire him. The lawsuit was filed in the U. S. District Court in the Northern District of Illinois. The Internal Revenue Service did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Visalli’s investigations included a probe into Malta pension plans, a tax-dodging strategy used by wealthy Americans. To fight the crackdown, promoters of the scheme hired lobbyist Ken Kies, who last year became the top tax official in the Treasury Department under President Trump.

In the past year, Mr. Visalli has written articles in Tax Notes, a trade publication, criticizing the I. R. S.’s record on pursuing multinational tax dodgers. He attacked his employer for failing to use a 2010 law requiring transactions that generate tax benefits to have “economic substance.” He said the agency suffered from “institutional cowardice.”

The refusal to invoke that law “represents a fundamental abdication of the IRS’s responsibility to protect the fiscal foundation of American government from sophisticated tax fraud masquerading as legitimate business planning,” he wrote.

The agency has turned tax enforcement “into a negotiation in which the government starts from a position of weakness and retreats from there.”

Jeffery Kadet, one of Mr. Visalli’s co-authors and an adjunct professor on tax law at the University of Washington, called him “exemplary in his focus on understanding” complicated corporate tax strategies. “He has an energy and a commitment to the rule of law that is exactly what we, as a society, need,” Mr. Kadet said.

Mr. Visalli’s criticism of the I. R. S. and the “abusive tax industry” has drawn attacks from right-wing groups. Chuck Flint, president of the Alliance for I. R. S. Accountability, a group that opposes the agency, with headquarters at a Houston mailbox, told The Washington Examiner in May: “This guy is just the latest in a long line of people at the I. R. S. that seem to take matters into their own hands.”

The lawsuit claims that the I. R. S. sent Mr. Visalli a letter in August 2023 stating he failed to fully pay his tax liability on time for 2021. The agency found the failure was an “oversight” and “not willful” and proposed a one-day suspension, then reduced it to a counseling letter, which managers often use to document minor misconduct. But he claims his supervisors escalated the episode as an excuse to push him out of his job. In late summer 2024, Mr. Visalli filed a whistle-blower retaliation complaint with the U. S. Office of Special Counsel, an independent federal agency that protects employees from reprisal for whistle-blowing.

Mr. Visalli said that an assistant U. S. attorney told him a few weeks later that Justice Department Tax Division personnel were describing him as “impaired” based on a Supreme Court case, Giglio v. the United States, which requires prosecutors to disclose to defense lawyers any past evidence of dishonesty by a law enforcement official involved in a case.

“For a federal criminal investigator, a Giglio label is a scarlet letter,” according to the lawsuit. The characterization “that Visalli was a witness whose credibility was so compromised that it had to be disclosed to criminal defendants, could only have originated with unauthorized disclosures by I. R. S. officials concerning an investigation into a financial disclosure previously made by Visalli.”

In March, Mr. Visalli met with a special agent for the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration to report his supervisors’ actions.

Despite internal findings in March that his tax failures were an oversight, the agency moved a month later to remove him from his job. He is still employed by the I. R. S.

Mr. Visalli is seeking damages for a withheld annual performance reward along with medical costs — including anti-depression medication and expenses from a stress-induced fall and hospitalization — following the news of his pending removal.

Jesse Drucker is an investigative reporter for the Business section and has written extensively on the world of high end tax avoidance.

Trump’s Retreat: From the Gulf to Britain, American Forces Pull Back

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Threats to U. K. Air Base

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

A war that was intended to demonstrate the reach of American power has now done the opposite. It is a lesson in unintended consequences.

By David E. Sanger and Eric Schmitt

David E. Sanger and Eric Schmitt have reported on American conflicts and geopolitical strategy for the Times for more than forty years. Mr. Sanger is a White House correspondent and Mr. Schmitt covers the Pentagon.

To hear President Trump and his aides describe it, the rush to withdraw 12 B-1 bombers from an air base in Britain over the weekend was a prudent precaution, in response to a threat they refused to describe.

It was no big deal, Mr. Trump insisted, and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, tried to wave it away by noting that the Pentagon is “constantly reallocating resources where ​they need to be.”

But to anyone watching the deployment of American power around the globe in the seven months since Mr. Trump decided to attack Iran, it was another glaring example of how, time after time, Mr. Trump and his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, have been forced into retreat, pulling back military forces that had been deployed to the Middle East and Britain as a deterrent.

Over the past several months, as the conflict has dragged on, the Iran war has come to reveal enormous new American vulnerabilities, forcing changes that the Pentagon was not contemplating a year ago. But it has also proved a bitter lesson in the unintended consequences that have flowed from Mr. Trump’s war of choice.

Mr. Trump intended the attack on Iran as another demonstration of the American military’s extraordinary power, following the successful bombing raid on three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 and the seizure of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela from his bed in Caracas in January.

But rather than enhance American power, the war has constrained it. The closing of bases in the Middle East and limiting the use of one in Britain have, at a minimum, vastly complicated the logistics of projecting power. American bombers can still reach their targets, of course, but only by flying from the United States, requiring more time and refueling. American carrier groups can still patrol in the Arabian Sea, outside the Persian Gulf, but now they must be resupplied from Diego Garcia, an island in the Indian Ocean 2,200 miles away, requiring additional weeks and huge costs.

But most importantly, the rapid withdrawals have taught a lesson to the Iranians — and potentially to other adversaries — that they hold the power to chase out a superpower. In Europe, Mr. Trump and Mr. Hegseth are thinking of reducing American forces on their terms and their schedule. In the Middle East and Britain, their hand was forced.

American and British officials said on Monday that the bombers were rushed out of the British base after commanders received specific, credible information that Iran-backed operatives were planning to launch drone strikes against the aircraft and U. S. troops from right outside the fence.

The suspected plotters may have been inspired in part by an audacious attack that Ukraine launched against Russia last year when it smuggled drones deep into the Russian heartland and launched them from semi trucks. The strikes damaged or destroyed at least a dozen aircraft.

That and other attacks have recalibrated the Pentagon’s understanding of military vulnerabilities. Suddenly, keeping forces out of missile range is not enough. Drones and cyberweapons have reshaped the battlefield.

The president rightly says that Iran’s entire navy was sunk in the initial military action, and its decrepit air force is out of business. And the country is teetering on the economic edge, crippled by the naval blockade that has brought its oil exports to a trickle.

But that has not stopped the Iranians from forcing American aircraft and personnel to flee their once-secure bases — farther and farther from Iran. American personnel were evacuated from bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, all of which were within Iranian missile and drone range. Some of those bases were so badly damaged that inside the Pentagon there is little interest in rebuilding them; they will be moved farther away, if Congress grants the funding.

The waterways are a more complex story. But the United States has been unable to guarantee “freedom of navigation” through the Strait of Hormuz or parts of the Red Sea. And for the past half-century, that was one central American justification for a continued presence in the Middle East.

Dana Stroul, the Pentagon’s top Mideast policy official during the Biden administration, said the abrupt transfer of the dozen bombers back to the United States could have internal and external ramifications.

“Such a hasty decision is intensely disruptive to operational planning and force morale,” said Ms. Stroul, now at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

“The more concerning issue is at the strategic level, the Iranians are likely to internalize a dangerous lesson — that by demonstrating the ability to get close to U. S. military bases far beyond the Middle East, Trump can be pushed around,” she said.

Mr. Trump and his defenders have a very different narrative of events. On the campaign trail for the midterm elections, he has portrayed Iran as on the brink of collapse, its currency plummeting. The naval blockade on all shipments in and out of Iran, he insists, is choking the country, and will force it to make a deal. Any description of Iranian progress, he insists, is “fake news,” promulgated by news organizations that are writing about munitions shortages and other setbacks because they are disloyal to the country.

For the first time, Iranian officials have acknowledged the economic pain. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted this week that Iran has a new oil minister, and then asked on social media, “Considering Iran has not loaded a single barrel of crude onto a vessel since August 25th, what is the oil minister managing?”

Moreover, administration officials describe the evacuations as prudent, short-term measures. And it is possible that the rushed-away B-1 bombers may return to the R. A. F. Fairford air base, which has been a mainstay of U. S.-British military cooperation since it was built in preparation for the D-Day invasion in 1944. Even if the threat precludes return, Air Force officials insist they can carry out their long-range missions from bases in the United States.

The Pentagon wants to think about new bases in Israel and Jordan, but those would require congressional approval and take years to upgrade or build anew. When Mr. Hegseth spoke to troops last Wednesday, he did not mention the destruction at the Mideast bases. Instead, he talked about putting states in competition for a new, vast base inside the United States.

This was not the plan when Mr. Trump announced the attack on Iran on Feb. 28. Mr. Trump was looking for a victory in a few days, then five or six weeks. Mr. Trump demanded “unconditional surrender,” and three weeks into the conflict declared Iran’s total defeat. Last Thursday, he said Iran would fold “right after the election.”

Instead, Iran bombed U. S. bases across the Middle East in retaliation, forcing many American troops to relocate to hotels and office spaces throughout the region, raising questions about the Trump administration’s preparations for the war.

Iran figured out where many of the troops were staying, some in unprotected hotels, and began to target them as well. It wasn’t only military targets: the C. I. A. station in Saudi Arabia was also hit, though it is still unclear whether the Iranians targeted it, or got lucky striking a diplomatic compound.

Many of the 13 main military bases in the region used by American troops were quickly rendered uninhabitable, with the ones in Kuwait, which is next door to Iran, suffering perhaps the most damage.

Six U. S. service members were killed in a strike on Port Shuaiba that destroyed an Army tactical operations center. Iranian drones and missiles also targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base, damaging aircraft structures and injuring personnel, and Camp Buehring, damaging maintenance and fuel facilities.

In Qatar, Iran struck Al Udeid Air Base, the regional air headquarters of U. S. Central Command, damaging an early-warning radar system. In Bahrain, a one-way Iranian attack drone struck communications equipment at the headquarters of the U. S. Fifth Fleet. At Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, Iranian missiles and drones damaged communications equipment and several refueling tankers.

Now Iran “is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense,” Mohammad Ayatollahi Tabaar, an associate professor of international affairs at Texas A&M’s Bush School of Government and Public Service, wrote in Foreign Affairs earlier this month.

“That means it will neither stay the course nor compromise with Washington,” he added. “Instead, it will start doing even more to hurt the economies of the United States’ regional partners and to decimate global energy markets, as well as expand its attacks on U. S. military infrastructure.” He predicted it could attempt to seize some of the largely abandoned U. S. bases in Gulf Arab countries, though so far it has avoided any such ground actions.

Senator Christopher S. Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut and a member of the Foreign Relations Committee, visited the Persian Gulf region this week to see the damage and said on social media that he had been denied entry to the Al Udeid base. A Pentagon spokesperson said Mr. Murphy had been warned before his trip that he would not have access to the base, under restrictions Mr. Hegseth had imposed at the start of the war.

The subject of the bases is such a sore one for the Pentagon that it has refused to provide Congress with cost estimates to repair or rebuild the facilities, which lawmakers said could run tens of billions of dollars. It is unclear what is motivating the refusal to discuss the topic, though a price tag that big could become political fodder for candidates opposing the war.

Instead, there is now serious planning at Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, to reposition and reshape its facilities in the region.

“The financial costs have continued to climb by billions each month, even as the administration refuses to acknowledge the munitions crisis we face or admit the costs to rebuild bases heavily damaged by Iran,” Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the ranking Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said last month.

An earlier version of this article misidentified the day that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth mentioned a plan for a new military base in the United States. It was last Wednesday, not last Thursday.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U. S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

Bondage Photos Weren’t Part of the Campaign Plan

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

But Chris Gallant, a Black Hawk pilot and Democrat who is running to represent Long Island in Congress, is making the most of life post-tabloid reveal.

By Jacob Bernstein

Reporting from Suffolk County

Chris Gallant dressed for an afternoon of shooting at a Long Island gun range in a tight Adidas T-shirt and purplish jeans.

In his right hand, he held a Sig Sauer case containing two of his own handguns. A third was tucked into his jeans.

It was a Tuesday a little more than a month from Election Day, when Gallant, a 37-year-old Black Hawk helicopter pilot, will face Nick LaLota, the Republican incumbent who is vying for a third term representing New York’s First Congressional District, which stretches from Huntington past the Hamptons to the tip of Long Island.

Gallant, who was taking a break from canvassing and phone banking, headed down a flight of stairs, handed the attendant his firearm license and ordered up his rounds.

“It’s just practice,” he said, with the rehearsed modesty of a fledgling politician. “Trying to get good at something.”

Gallant then proceeded to fire dozens of shots at or close to the bull’s-eye at the end of his lane.

“Pretty good, right?” he said.

Beyond practice, of course, Gallant allowed that shooting is also a way to relieve stress, which has been in ample supply recently.

Last month, The New York Post revealed that Gallant had appeared in varying degrees of undress in promotional photos for Mr. S Leather, a San Francisco fetish brand.

The images were taken for the company’s website in early 2010 when Gallant wasn’t yet 21. One shows him in a cage, wearing a harness and a muzzle, with another man behind him performing a sex act on him.

A second image had him above the same man, again in leather, this time receiving oral sex.

At Gallant’s request, the people at Mr. S deleted the shots sometime before he announced his candidacy for Congress in August 2025. But thanks to publicly available web archives, finding them was perhaps inevitable. (Despite calling it part of a political hit job, he said he has “no idea” who was responsible for alerting The Post.)

The Post presented the story with typical tabloid panache, with a headline that read, “NY Dem House candidate modeled for XXX-rated BDSM ads while serving in National Guard.”

A photo of a much younger Gallant in a harness at the Folsom Street Fair in San Francisco also became the subject of a Suffolk County Conservative Committee Facebook post that said “Is this who you want to represent us in Washington D. C.?”

The LaLota campaign did not directly address the images. And Gallant seemed to decide that the photos were a chance to show that a person in public life can contain multitudes.

Specifically, Chris Gallant can be a Long Island-raised Black Hawk pilot in the Army National Guard who flew choppers during one of his two tours in Kuwait, worked for five years as an air traffic controller at John F. Kennedy International Airport, serves as a volunteer firefighter and is an unabashed gun owner as well as a union man who posed for those photos almost 17 years ago, not because he was manipulated but because he was into it.

“I mean, all my friends know I’m kinky” as hell, he said, using a saltier word. “I make Christian Grey look like amateur hour.”

It was his first in-depth interview since the images were widely shared. He wanted to make clear that he — like his outfits in those pics — had little to hide.

We were seated on a red leather sofa in the living room of his cozy clapboard house in Amity Harbor, which happens to be just outside the limits of the district he hopes to represent. (LaLota lives in Amityville, also outside the district, he pointed out.) Recent issues of The Advocate and Army Aviation Magazine were stacked on the coffee table.

In front of the house was a small yard and a white picket fence.

“I just thought, ‘If my family can accept me, the world can,’ and that’s how I lived my entire life,” said Gallant, who was wearing jeans and a fitted gray Rag & Bone sweater.

His mother, Barbara Solony-Cohen, was in the kitchen, having driven up from her home in North Carolina, along with his friend Jason Hewitt, a TD Bank branch manager, whom he met at a gay ski week in 2014. They were scheduled to go canvassing later that evening. Absent was his fiancé, Mike Ingram, a National Guard infantryman who Gallant said is stationed in the Middle East.

Gallant said he hadn’t anticipated that this long-ago campaign for a fetish-wear brand would become public as it did. “I mean, you had to go hunt for this,” he said.

After The Post published its article, his team had conversations about the viability of his candidacy. But there are limited options available seven weeks out from an election.

So Gallant, who has the air of many a good-looking guy who has seldom if ever been told there’s anything he can’t do, started to see about working the situation to his advantage.

Maybe it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” he said, only half jokingly.

Less than 48 hours after the Post story, he uploaded a video of himself to Facebook, speaking into the camera and calling the photo release a “coordinated political hit meant to drive me out of this race.”

Then, his social media team posted a new ad of him in a tight black T-shirt that showed off his Marvel-worthy biceps. The slogan running across it read, “Make Politics Sexy Again.”

Sexiness, the ad went on to say, includes his plans for improving the lives of the voters in his district, including support for veterans and lowering the cost of living on Long Island.

If Gallant somehow prevails, several Democratic consultants said, it will most likely be in a squeaker.

Jon Reinish, a Democratic strategist and former aide to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, said New York’s First Congressional District had not been won by a Democrat since 2012. “But in a wave election, it’s definitely in play.”

One option for Gallant? Lean further into his image as a fit guy enjoying his sexuality, Reinish argued. “The Democrats have been librarians for too long.”

In the interview at his home, Gallant seemed to be contemplating just that kind of playbook. At least, he was not wringing his hands over photos from 2010.

“My most difficult thing was always getting my name out there or trying to improve that,” he said. “And there’s definitely been a name-recognition increase on the world stage.” He noted that “The Daily Show” had covered his modeling: The first joke told was that Gallant was getting his butt beaten, “but not in the polls.”

Gallant knows that the punchline is a little generous; it is an uphill climb in a district that has been represented by a Republican since 2015. His newfound attention might not help him “in the district” with the voters who matter.

And there remains the question of whether the photographs for Mr. S will be the biggest bomb to drop.

Messenger Papers, a conservative news site, published a piece about Gallant that insinuated that he had worked as an escort as recently as 2024 under the name Joe Flint, and that Flint was discussed on a site where patrons of escorts go to compare notes.

Gallant denies any such thing happened. He said that there may have been stolen pictures floating around online, and that perhaps, they could have wound up on escort sites.

Emails to the men who had discussed hiring Flint on the site went unanswered.

But at a recent town hall, held at a sports bar in Middle Island, more than a hundred people showed up, and no one seemed interested in his sex life.

“Whatever, everyone has a social media history,” said Renee McKeon, 50, an independent voter who works as an administrator at the Suffolk County Sheriff’s Office and who said she planned on voting for Gallant, despite having cast a ballot for President Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. “During Trump’s first presidency, there were guardrails,” she said. “The corruption is much more rampant now.”

For more than an hour, Gallant was hazy about policy, but he was perfectly capable of running through his opposition to everything he believes President Trump has helped bring about, from the war in Iran to the fast-tracking of ICE agents.

During a question-and-answer session, one person asked Gallant about a recent comment made by LaLota, in which his opponent called him “weak and woke.”

“I’ve carried people out of burning buildings; I’ve flown helicopters in the Middle East,” Gallant said. “If that’s weak and woke — well, I just think that’s inaccurate.”

Another asked him what should be done regarding misinformation online.

As a supporter of free speech, Gallant said he wasn’t sure exactly.

Still, he had some advice. “Don’t get your news from social media. Unless you’re going to look at mine.”

Jacob Bernstein reports on power and privilege for the Style section of The Times.

H. I. V. Research Networks Face Uncertain Future Amid Funding Delays

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The networks also develop treatments and preventions for other infectious diseases and were instrumental in testing the Covid vaccine.

By Apoorva Mandavilli and Benjamin Mueller

The future of four large research networks that test vaccines and treatments for H. I. V., tuberculosis and emerging infectious diseases is in limbo after weeks of delays from the Trump administration in launching the process to renew their funding.

Scientists are worried that the delays could foreshadow the end of the networks, at least in their current form.

H. I. V. researchers grew more concerned on Friday when they received word from the National Institutes of Health that they should temporarily hold off on launching new studies that had not yet enrolled participants and that would not be complete by Nov. 30, 2027, when their current funding is set to expire.

Delays to medical research spending have become a chronic issue during the second Trump administration, and funding for the networks may yet be renewed. But some scientists warned that any delays could jeopardize the safety of participants in clinical trials, derail time-sensitive studies and disrupt staffing and resources.

“Just the loss of momentum that will happen when you don’t have funding is enormous,” said Dr. Emily Erbelding, who led an infectious disease division at the N. I. H. before she was ousted from the agency in 2025. “I don’t know whether the powers that be are understanding that these days,” she added.

The Department of Health and Human Services did not answer questions about whether or when the N. I. H. would kick off the process to renew the networks’ funding beyond next year.

A department spokeswoman, Grace Davis Jamison, instead sent an emailed statement that said the administration was planning continued investment in H. I. V. research that delivers “meaningful results.”

The networks’ leaders said their worries stemmed from the Trump administration’s cuts to H. I. V. work generally. The administration has made sharp reductions to foreign aid dedicated to fighting H. I. V. It has overhauled the work of a landmark global H. I. V. program and has fired roughly a third of staff from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s division for H. I. V. prevention. It has proposed steep budget cuts to H. I. V. surveillance and prevention nationwide.

Last year, the N. I. H. ended a $258 million multisite program whose work was instrumental to the search for an H. I. V. vaccine. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been heavily critical of the hunt for a vaccine, writing in a 2021 book about Dr. Anthony S. Fauci’s “vain obsession to develop an H. I. V. vaccine” and testifying before a House panel last year that federal spending on the goal “accomplishes nothing.”

The current funding delay affects Advancing Clinical Therapeutics Globally, a network that formed 40 years ago, as well as the H. I. V. Prevention Trials Network, the H. I. V. Vaccine Trials Network and the International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials Network, which were formed years later. Together, the four networks work in dozens of countries and have conducted hundreds of clinical trials. They total more than $300 million each year, most of which comes from the federal government, although the exact amounts vary as studies begin and end at various times.

The programs’ large footprint has enabled them to develop tools to prevent and treat H. I. V., including in marginalized or rare populations such as pregnant women, adolescents and people who are resistant to multiple available drugs.

Having a ready base of researchers, data systems and communities of participants has also helped in other health crises. The networks were used during the coronavirus pandemic to quickly enroll tens of thousands of participants to test vaccines and treatments — including a monoclonal antibody treatment used on President Trump.

Funding for the networks and their research sites is renewed every seven years. But questions over their future have grown since the Trump administration delayed publishing so-called notices of funding opportunities, a formal signal to scientists that the renewal process would begin. The federal government had said it expected to post the notices by Aug. 25. As of Wednesday, they still had not gone out.

A federal official said that the notices were under review by H. H. S., which is led by Mr. Kennedy, who has overseen vast cuts to many federal health programs. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the review process.

The second Trump administration has significantly pared back the release of funding opportunities across medical research topics and left many such notices in limbo. It has also subjected the notices to new layers of political review, slowing their release.

Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the N. I. H. director, has alarmed some scientists by pushing to steer federal spending away from basic research on new H. I. V. vaccines and treatments and toward studies of how to deploy existing tools for fighting the disease.

“We have the tools we need — the technological tools,” Dr. Bhattacharya told a Senate panel in May. “We just need to understand how to use them to end the H. I. V. epidemic.”

Dr. Bhattacharya has been a staunch supporter of lenacapavir, a treatment that includes injections taken twice a year that prevents H. I. V. infection. But many H. I. V. experts note that only a vaccine or cure can stop the epidemic, which still affects more than 40 million people worldwide and kills more than 500,000 people each year.

Sudden disruptions to clinical trials will halt progress toward ending the epidemic, they warn, and undermine carefully cultivated trust with communities, particularly those that tend to avoid engaging with the health care system.

“It’s hard work and it’s very fragile,” said Dr. Wafaa El-Sadr, who helped lead the H. I. V. Prevention Trials Network until last year and leads studies in Harlem and the Bronx. “What took 40 years to build on here could just collapse in a minute without continued investment and commitment.”

November 2027 may seem a long way away, but the large, complicated projects require at least that much planning time, said Dr. Chris Beyrer, the director of the Duke Global Health Institute and the leader of a study funded by one of the networks.

“You have to lay out the laboratory plans, the statistical and data management plans, the organizational structures and most importantly the scientific agenda for the next seven years,” he said. Without continuity in grants, “you start to see implications early, much earlier than the actual day that funding expires.”

Until now, the granting cycles had rolled along predictably since the networks began. N. I. H. program officers would in fact solicit feedback from researchers involved in the networks even before creating the funding notices. None of that happened this time, according to the leaders of the networks, and even many of their contacts at the N. I. H. were unsure whether and when the documents would be released.

Some experts said they worried the N. I. H. might dismantle the networks and fund individual grants instead.

Trials for the Covid vaccines relied heavily on the infrastructure and highly trained work force of the H. I. V. networks. That sort of effort “would be very difficult to do if you were just funding protocol by protocol,” said Dr. Erbelding, who was one of the leaders of the effort.

Some scientists said they were concerned the administration might limit research to sites within the United States, ending international collaborations. H. I. V. and other infectious diseases are far more prevalent elsewhere in the world, they noted.

In the early 1990s, Dr. Myron Cohen set out to study the influence of sexually transmitted diseases like syphilis on H. I. V. transmission. “If I tried to do that in the United States, it would have taken me 1,000 years,” said Dr. Cohen, a former leader of one of the networks and a professor at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

Instead, “by working in Africa, we were able in maybe six months to answer some really very fundamental questions,” he said.

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.

Benjamin Mueller reports on health and medicine. He was previously a U. K. correspondent in London and a police reporter in New York.
