Pete Hegseth’s ‘Vast Overcorrection’

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Opinions

A Special Forces veteran joins the columnist David French to assess Pete Hegseth’s leadership.

By David French and Mike Nelson

Produced by Jillian Weinberger

What impact has the Iran war had on the U. S. military? As the conflict drags on, the Times Opinion columnist and Iraq war veteran David French speaks with the former Special Forces officer Mike Nelson about the way Pete Hegseth, the secretary of defense, has tried to remake the military in the midst of the war, and what the Democrats should do if they win control of Congress in January.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.

The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

David French: As some listeners might know, before I went into journalism, I served in the U. S. Army. I was a judge advocate general officer, an Army lawyer. I deployed to Iraq in 2007 and served for almost a year. So I can say from some degree of experience that I’m worried about the way Pete Hegseth, the secretary of defense, is managing the war in Iran.

News clip: There are new, concerning reports of deteriorating morale among troops. News clip: Months of strikes on Iran have severely depleted the U. S. military’s supply of missiles, especially advanced interceptors. News clip: Some family members expressed concerns — prolonged deployment is affecting sailors’ mental health.

My friend Mike Nelson spent more than two decades in the Army, retiring as a Special Forces officer. He is a fellow at the National Security Institute, and he joins me today. Welcome, Mike.

Mike Nelson: Morning, David. Thanks for having me.

French: Mike, before we dive into details, how would you rate how Hegseth is faring so far, sort of top line? How much is he changing the military under his leadership? And just putting aside the rhetoric, substantively, how much is he changing the military? How long-lasting could these changes be?

Nelson: Well, I’m going to surprise a lot of the people who have read anything I’ve written, primarily at The Dispatch, about Secretary Hegseth, and I’m going to say the truth is that not every one of Secretary Hegseth’s ideas are bad or wrong, but many of them are. And more important, many of his correct ideas are not necessarily where a secretary of defense should be focusing. He was correct to say that there had been myriad distractions that had been placed on the Department of Defense that took away from some of the war-fighting focus, or deterrence focus, being ready for future operations. We saw it in his speech last week. He’s primarily a showman, so he has his canned catchphrases that he likes to say.

Archival clips of Pete Hegseth: No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals. Just warriors. […]

We do bad things to bad people. […]

Maximum lethality, not tepid legality. Violent effect, not politically correct.

And for months, we have been hearing “No dudes in dresses,” specifically saying that he has changed the policy so that there cannot be transgender service members anymore. OK. That decision was made months ago, and he just continues to hit the greatest hits. All right, what next? The next part, the “no beardos” thing, right? He was correct that shave waivers were probably overused and oversought in a disciplined military, and too many people were getting them, and it took away from the overall military bearing. OK. That’s what we expect battalion sergeants major to focus on.

French: Yeah, I was going to say that this is not a secretary of defense-level issue, but ——

Nelson: So he is focusing largely on these tactical-level, really — he commands, or leads, the single largest organization in the United States, and he is focused on these very small-ball issues that we actually empower and pay really professional noncommissioned officers — these sergeants and sergeants major — to do on his behalf. All he has to say is: “This is the new policy. Go forth and do great things.” Instead, he’s bringing people to D. C. to make sure they hear it straight from him. I think a lot of his ideas, which might be correct, are distractions, or at least for what he should be focusing on, where he’s supposed to be at the strategic level, merging those tactical effects with the strategic goals of the United States — and that’s not happening, and we see that playing out with the war in Iran.

Additionally, before I move on, like I said, he has some good ideas. Recently, in his speech, he had Fortress America, I believe is what he called it, which was basically hardening U. S. installations to make sure they were on independent power grids and not susceptible to cyberattacks. That’s a good move.

Besides that, he is also making some really bad moves. So we’ve seen his focus on warrior culture and physical training, and things like that coming at the cost of some of the innovations that we should be focusing on as an American military. I think he is damaging not only our progress in getting ready for the next conflict, but he’s also potentially causing negative effects in military leadership by purging those innovators who currently exist and replacing them with sycophants who are primarily motivated by personal loyalty.

French: I’d love for you to tell listeners a little bit more about your service. I think it’s safe to say it was a bit different from mine. I served as a JAG officer in Iraq. You were a Special Forces officer, tip of the spear. And it seems to me that it’s as if Hegseth is kind of trying to reshape the military into that entire archetype: the Special Forces warrior. Do you think he’s trying to remake the military in that image of almost, like, the Spartan Special Forces warrior? What’s happening here?

Nelson: I think you’re right that there is this archetype that filtered out. And it’s kind of a disservice to what the military was doing as a whole.

The war, if you think about the way the war started and culminated, there are two examples that I think a lot of people have in their minds. There’s the beginning of the war with Task Force Dagger, my old unit, 5th Special Forces Group, riding horses with the Northern Alliance, which is one side of S. O. F., working by, with and through local resistance.

French: And just to interrupt you for a second — S. O. F., Special Operations Forces?

Nelson: Right. And then the other side of that, you have kind of — in Kathryn Bigelow’s movie “Zero Dark Thirty,” the raid on Osama bin Laden SEAL Team 6 conducting a direct-action raid — our most elite direct-action Tier 1 forces conducting these kinds of incredibly hard to pull off raids and doing them with great skill. That does not portray at all what the everyday experience of a lot of soldiers were, which was largely conducting patrols, conducting local governance, all sorts of things that went into the war that aren’t as easily translatable onto film or in really cool-looking Instagram pictures.

I do think that the secretary, his whole concept is predicated on the idea that the Joe Biden years particularly focused far too much on creating social experiments within the military, and that distracted from the core function of fighting wars. And there are certain examples where there were distractions. There were things that took away from just the time available to conduct training. But it’s a vast overcorrection that he’s engaged in.

And as we look at the transformation of war, we are going to need people who have that warrior ethos, but that’s only one part of the combined arms fight. We are also going to need a lot of innovators, a lot of analysts, a lot of people who can integrate the new technologies. So the secretary’s focus tends to be a little bit myopic just on one part, and one part that was applicable several years ago, but not necessarily looking at all the new layers that are required.

French: We’re going to get into this a little bit more, but I’m struck by the different image that he has of a soldier compared to what the Ukrainian Army looks like, which I think might be very indicative of your point, because the Ukrainian Army is not an army of extraordinarily heavily muscled, high-T special operators. The average age is shockingly high. I’ve seen some measures say the median age of a Ukrainian soldier might be in the late 30s or early 40s, which is more like the age I was when I dragged myself through officer basic at Fort Lee. And also, it’s got a — frankly, Mike — a bunch of nerds doing drone warfare. And so it strikes me that he’s articulating a kind of physical image of a warrior that, as you were saying, doesn’t match the diversity of the needs that we have.

Nelson: Right. We do need infantrymen to be able to move long distances, carrying large amounts of weight on their back, with very little sleep and very little food. But yes, Ukraine is right now what I refer to as the lethal laboratory. They are leading the way in demonstrating what is the future of warfare, and it is a mixture of both new technologies and old truths of war that will endure forever. We are missing the opportunity to learn from our Ukrainian allies, but the generals who were trying to do that are no longer part of the D. O. D. They’ve been purged out.

French: I’m so glad you raised the generals, because I had a conversation with one of the fired generals not long ago, and this person pointed out that, in essence, they were fired for following orders. In other words, the Biden administration handed down some edicts and some orders regarding D. E. I. — diversity, equity, inclusion and other things — and as loyal soldiers, whether they agreed or not, they saluted and they carried out those orders. And Hegseth comes in and essentially says: Well, if you were carrying out the orders that were the priority of the previous administration, you’re woke, you’re weak, whatever, and you’re gone.

And one of the fears that was expressed to me by this former general was that, well, does that then set a precedent that if you are a general officer and you follow the orders of an administration, that the next administration will come in and purge you, replace you with general officers who have to then follow their orders, who will then only be purged by the next administration?

It strikes me that the Trump administration is setting a precedent here that if actually carried out by other presidents would be catastrophic for the integrity of the military. And it’s setting a precedent that, given enough time under the current administration, could be catastrophic for the idea that merit matters as much as political fidelity. But it was very chilling to me to hear the general essentially say, “I was fired for following a lawful order.”

Nelson: Right. So a lot of the criticism that Hegseth has steered toward these generals — who implemented, as you said, the lawful orders of the previous duly elected president and the civilian leadership through the secretary of defense — focus on two things, largely. Well, three things, I guess: D. E. I. in general — kind of a big umbrella — the Covid-19 vaccine mandate and the withdrawal from Afghanistan. Everything that was just listed, we can disagree with or think were bad ideas or conducted poorly, and all of them were lawful orders from the duly elected president through the civilian leadership. Right now, there’s a great deal of discussion about generals rejecting Secretary Hegseth’s guidance. There are two places that I have concern about legality: One being the overall legality of the war with Iran, and the second being the Sept. 2, 2025, boat strike, at the beginning of Operation Southern Spear.

But outside of that, I think it’s fair to say that I disagree and think that most of Secretary Hegseth’s stuff or ideas are bad ideas — counterproductive and potentially damaging in the long term — but they are legal. And would he want these same generals that he’s propping up to be fired immediately in 2029, in January, because they implemented his orders? The secretary needs to remember that his predecessors gave legal orders, whether he agreed with them or not, and he is in a position now to implement new policy, and that’s fine. We may disagree with it, but they are legal orders.

French: Before we move on to the Iran war, there’s another element, and this is kind of the entree into it. So moving from what is the culture of the military, what’s happening with generals — the secrecy that we have seen around the Iran war. And I want to be really careful about this question, because there are ways in which secrecy is absolutely imperative. So, for example, there was a famous moment during earlier iterations of the Iraq war where Geraldo Rivera is embedded with American troops. And Mike, I don’t know if you remember this ——

Nelson: I do.

French: He essentially maps out an upcoming attack. In other words, he talks about what’s about to happen, what we’re about to do, and if Iraqi forces were watching these feeds, they would have had foreknowledge of an American attack. It’s an example where secrecy’s really important. You don’t broadcast what you’re about to do. And when we had embedded media, they would get briefings on upcoming attacks, but they were under an agreement that they were not going to discuss that until the appropriate time, when everything unfolded.

But I think a lot of listeners would be really surprised at how closely connected the media was, at least to my work, when I was in Iraq. We had embedded media throughout the entire period: L. A. Times, Reuters, Times of London, Stars and Stripes — and they were able to report from the front, what we were doing. And in my experience with the guys, the cav troopers I served with, 99 percent of them wanted to talk to the media. They wanted people to know what we were doing. But you were in a very different part of the world. You were in the Special Operations world, the ultimate level of secrecy applied to you.

Talk me through your own experience with the media, and how you see the connection between the media, the military and the American public.

Nelson: Well, I’ll talk about that specifically, the role that the media plays in understanding what the American military does, but then, also the steps that led us to the secrecy, as you point out, about the war in Iran with this Department of Defense.

I had a general officer that I worked for who I have near cultlike devotion to — one of the finest officers I’ve ever known, one of the finest human beings I’ve ever known. And I saw this person. I’ve worked for him twice: once in a Special Operations task force in Afghanistan and once at a much higher strategic level. And he used to always bring media with him on his in-theater engagements. And I heard a pretty prominent member of the media ask him once why he did so, because so many other members of the military were at least shy around the media, or maybe cautious around the media. And he said, “The American people deserve to know what their military does on their behalf, and you’re how they find out.”

And I thought that was just a distilled-down, virtuous statement about the role of military operations in a healthy republic. Right now, we are engaged in a conflict that started out unpopular and is growing more unpopular as it goes. There’s never been a less popular war since World War II, since modern polling.

And part of the problem is, because the American people do not trust what the government is telling them about the war, about the causes for it, about the conduct of it, about how it’s going, about how it’s going to be resolved at the end. And part of this, we know that the president has his own unique relationship with the media and unique relationship with how he presents the truth of what he’s doing or what his administration is doing. But the secretary and the Department of Defense as a whole owe a part of this, too, or are complicit in this, too. From the beginning, we saw that Secretary Hegseth had what seemed to be a primary motivation of controlling the narrative of what he was doing — not so much what the Department of Defense was doing, but what he personally was doing. Controlling his own image and those who had the ability to shape it.

He implemented attempts to control what the media would report from the Pentagon, famously purging out or at least having most of the legacy media leave physical spaces in the Pentagon when they wouldn’t agree to preapproval of their stories. They’ve been replaced largely with alternate media that are, in some cases, sycophants; in some cases blend the boundaries between what is media and what is public relations, because we’ve had people who are both wearing the hat of new media, credentialed by the Pentagon, and special government employees working for the Department of Defense without disclosure. We’ve had other people who haven’t been officially brought on as special government employees, but have publicly said that they’re advising the secretary on what to do. So he wants to tell his story through supportive media only. Additionally ——

French: Can I interrupt you on that real fast? I want to drill down on that, because that has not gotten the attention it deserves. Now, listeners, the conflict of interest should be very obvious.

And that’s something that, in my view, is utterly symbolic of the corruption around this administration. But that is a perversion of the role of the military. It’s a perversion of the role of the media, and I just wanted to put an exclamation point behind that. So, anyway, please continue.

Nelson: And we should be clear: In previous administrations, Republican and Democrat, we’ve seen the crossing over between media and government officials back and forth. People who were in the administration then became hosts on cable news. But there’s a clear delineation of which role they’re filling at which time. They’re never wearing both hats at the same time, and if they are, they’re never hiding the ball from the public that they’re attempting to influence. We’ve seen the secretary and Sean Parnell, his primary spokesman, respond to any critical stories by flatly claiming that everything is fake news.

Now we see, whether it’s stories about the damage done to Naval Support Activity Bahrain, the Port of Shuaiba, critical shortages on some of our interceptors — all of this is immediately reported as fake news: It’s not true; the war is going gloriously.

And there’s never a revisiting of the actual facts. Now, this is a problem because I don’t think, and I may be overstating things, whenever we go to war, there are going to be costs. The fact that the administration is trying to paint it as though there are no negative effects makes them seem even more disingenuous.

French: Well, you’re getting to something, and we’re sort of rolling into the war itself right now. And it strikes me — and this is something that I’ve been banging the drum on from the beginning — that, let’s suppose you’re a supporter of the war in Iran and, like I’ve said, I’ve long been an Iran hawk. There are circumstances where you could convince me, if you went to the public and you presented evidence, that striking Iran would be in the national interest, in compliance with the laws of war, that it would be the right thing to do. But it was never tried. They never went to us.

And one of the points that I’ve tried to make to people is that this isn’t just a matter of dotting the I’s and crossing the T’s on some sort of archaic constitutional requirement when everybody knows it’s just the president anyway. No. Democracies are supposed to go to war with the support of the people, because a democracy with the support of the people can be one of the most potent war-fighting enterprises in world history. But a democracy that goes to war without the support of the people can underperform, can fail at accomplishable tasks, because it lacks that support.

How have you seen this decision? We can set aside the legality, the constitutionality, just for a moment. Practically, how have you seen that decision to not go to the American people work itself out in the actual conduct of the conflict?

Nelson: Well, as you point out, they teach this in the woke war colleges that Secretary Hegseth has a problem with. There is this thing called Clausewitz’s trinity, right? And one of them is the will of the people, and you need popular support, particularly when we talk about a republic.

One of the, arguably, advantages that Iran has in this conflict is that they don’t have to have popular support. They are already repressing their people. You know, I don’t think they have too much concern for the suffering of the people as they endure the effects of the conflict. But in hindsight, a lot of people look at the war in Iraq and judge it as this horrible decision, and George W. Bush is ultimately responsible, and he needs to answer for what decisions he made, as any president does.

But people forget the Bush administration spent about a year making the case for a war with Iraq. The American people overwhelmingly agreed with it, and the Senate overwhelmingly agreed with it. We’ve either, as you said, sought congressional approval, as is required by the Constitution, or it’s been for limited national security means. But usually those have also come along with the “My fellow Americans” from the Oval Office statement, not a middle-of-the-night video released via Truth Social, where there are myriad reasons revealed.

In that statement on Feb. 28, the president said, “To the great, proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” which sounds a lot like regime change, and that’s ——

French: That is the natural meaning of those words.

Nelson: Correct. Yeah. Why now was not entirely clear, and what we are trying to accomplish is not entirely clear. And that all leads into the fact that, as I said, starting on Feb. 28, this war was already underwater. The administration never felt like they needed to make the case for it, I think in part because they modeled this after Venezuela. It would be over before we ever had to make a justification, and it would be seen as gloriously victorious. That has not been the case. And I think part of that — I don’t know this for a fact — is if Secretary Hegseth is presenting all rosy information to the American people, he may also be doing that to the president himself, underplaying the risks and saying that the military can accomplish everything that he wants.

French: So let’s talk through the course of the war itself. And so there were a number of goals articulated. At first it seemed to be regime change — “The hour of your liberation is at hand.” And then, mainly through Secretary Marco Rubio, you began to see a bullet-point checklist that this is what we want to accomplish. They changed their tune on regime change pretty quickly. After a few days, it was: Regime change? What regime change? What we really want to do is sink the Navy, cripple the Air Force, degrade — to the point, at least, of potential destruction — their missile and drone arsenal, end any capacity for future nuclear development, and doing so while keeping the Strait of Hormuz open to minimize damage to the American and global economy.

And it seems like they’ve accomplished essentially one of those bullet points, which was destroying a big chunk of Iran’s conventional military. But, as you and I both know, the Iranian Navy and the Iranian Air Force were not keeping us up at night. That was not the source of the danger from the Iranian regime. And so it looks like none of the other objectives have been truly accomplished. And it seems like the definition of victory now, Mike, is changing to: But if we can pry the Strait of Hormuz back open, then we’ve won the conflict.

How are you seeing the actual course of the conflict, and if any of these other goals are going to be accomplished?

Nelson: So going back through, I’m going to go through the negatives and then maybe the causes for hope. So, as you said, regime change, we shouldn’t forget that really what started this whole interest in striking Iran again were the popular protests in January. We talked about the — a lot of talk right now — if there is a justification. As a matter of fact, the administration will counter those who express concerns about the war by basically accusing them of wanting to help Iran get a nuclear weapon, and we will never let Iran have a nuke. I agree with that premise. We did a ——

French: I don’t want that, either.

Nelson: Right. And we did a great deal to set back the Iranian nuclear program in the summer of 2025 with Operation Midnight Hammer. We haven’t done anything, really, since then to affect the nuclear program. We have probably incentivized the Iranians to have even more of a desire for a nuclear weapon as a deterrent, as a trump card to prevent any kind of future attacks. The way they see the president talk about North Korea — you pointed out that we have basically put the Iranian, or specifically the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps Navy, at the bottom of the sea — and that’s a good thing.

But that’s an operational effect. The fact that they are still able to threaten traffic in the Strait of Hormuz means they have found alternate means to affect the maritime domain. We have destroyed a fair amount of their missile capability, and they’ve used a lot of it. But as we’ve seen in reporting, Iran may have retained more of their missile capability than we originally thought, and also, as has been reported, we have used a fair amount of our interceptors defending the region against these.

Opening the strait, as you point out, it’s not a goal of the war because it was the condition that existed before. It’s just a condition that we need to correct because of the war. We have now, I believe, settled into the best of all bad options.

French: I was going to ask that. Have we learned here? Just from a military perspective, are we doing better? And if so, how?

Nelson: So there was a lot of focus last week, when Time released the transcript of their interview with President Trump, and they asked him why he had rejected an Iranian cease-fire negotiation, and he said: Because I wouldn’t agree to something now that I wouldn’t have agreed to a year ago, and it has to be more than the strait.

That was an excellent answer from the president. The resolution of the war has to be more about relieving those conditions I just listed, where we are, in almost every aspect, worse off than we were a year ago.

And the smart play is now the long-term blockade and economic pressure against Iran. The downside of that is that it’s going to exacerbate, or at least keep in the fore, some of the economic pressures that have affected American consumers. But again, the war’s unpopular. Gas prices are not going to go down before the midterms, which is, I’m sure, front of mind for the president, and it’s going to require — kind of like George W. Bush did after the 2006 midterm “thumping,” as he referred to it — he still, despite the unpopularity of the Iraq war, made the correct decision to pursue what was known in the United States as “the surge,” but which enabled the Sahwa, the Sunni Awakening in Iraq, and helped stabilize the region.

The president is going to need to resist the urge for dramatic means, and to keep the course of economic pressure, I think. That’s the best option he has.

French: I’m glad you brought up the surge because one of the things — as I wrote this some time ago — the only thing worse than starting an unconstitutional war is losing an unconstitutional war. And that seemed to be what we were on the verge of. Are you seeing this administration essentially reaching a point where, if it achieves reopening the strait, they’ll then just declare victory and then say, “It’s essentially over. We won”? How do you think this thing actually ends here in the real world?

Nelson: I think, and I don’t mean to overuse an expression, but the devil’s in the details. I do think that, No. 1, there’s going to be some agreement about reopening the strait, but there will probably, for the president to accept it, be some kind of language about an agreement on the nuclear program. I think the most likely place that we will fail to achieve our objectives is we are going to sell out the Iranian people. The Iranian people are going to continue to be oppressed, and probably even more so. In the memorandum of understanding, there was language about us not interfering with the domestic affairs of the Iranian regime, which meant, I think, de facto turning a blind eye to future repression, executions, human rights abuses, etc. So I do think there’s going to be a range of options.

We have the strait and nuclear program at the top, with the strait being the most easily discernible — whether it’s legitimate or not — and then support to the Iranian people at the bottom. Somewhere in there, we’re going to find a range of what we’re going to agree to.

French: I could talk to you forever, but let’s kind of wind down here. Let’s put on a different hat for you. We’re recording this less than a month before the midterms. All indications seem to be that the Democrats will improve their position — at the very least, maybe take one, maybe two chambers. If they do take control of Congress, what should they do to constrain Trump and Hegseth? What should they not do? Put on your “I’m advising Democrats for the good of the service and for the good of national security” hat.

Nelson: Well, I think one of the immediate questions is that the Massie-Hegseth impeachment motion will have to be voted on. So that’s going to, at a minimum, cause embarrassment for the administration and for Secretary Hegseth himself, because I don’t think it’s likely he’s going to be removed from office, but I do think it’s likely he’s going to get more votes against him than he probably realizes. And that will probably cause embarrassment for all involved.

I do think there’s a chance, if the president is unaware of how unpopular the Iran war is, that after the midterms he may seek to find someone, just as Secretary Donald Rumsfeld resigned after the 2006 midterms, that Secretary Hegseth may be not long for this world in the administration if the president looks for someone to point the finger to.

The other thing we’ve seen right now with the lame-duck Republicans who the president did not support in their primaries and now have basically nothing to lose — many of them went along with some of the War Powers votes to restrain the war in Iran. And I do think there’s a danger in those kinds of votes becoming more popular as, No. 1, after the elections, when there are more Republicans potentially who have nothing to lose during the lame-duck session; or in the new Congress, when there’s even less of a red representation in the legislature. I think that highlights the importance of the president making the case that he has not made yet, neither to the American people nor to Congress, why it is important. He defaults to these very short bumper-sticker answers: We should pay more for high gas prices than Iran getting a nuclear weapon.

There needs to be more of an explanation for what the long-term strategy is. Again, I think he has settled on the best option available, which is long-term imposition of economic pain and blockade of Iran. That is the one most likely to achieve any kind of success, but that’s going to require more support that he currently does not have.

French: All right. That’s a great way to end it, Mike. Thank you so much for joining me. I really appreciate it.

Nelson: Thanks for having me.

In the episode, Mike and I talk about the increasing divide between America's civilians and the warrior class that Pete Hegseth is trying to build. I think this divide is bad for democracy. How do you propose closing it?

Thoughts? Email us at theopinions@nytimes. com.

David French is an Opinion columnist, writing about law, culture, religion and armed conflict. He is a veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom and a former constitutional litigator. His most recent book is “Divided We Fall: America’s Secession Threat and How to Restore Our Nation.” You can follow him on Threads (@davidfrenchjag).

The School Near Paris That Shows Why French Students Are Protesting

The New York Times October 07, 2026

Student Protests in France

Advertisement

Supported by

Angered by poor classroom conditions, students at Paul Éluard High School in a suburb of the capital were among the first to blockade their campus during an ongoing round of unrest.

By Ségolène Le Stradic

Ségolène Le Stradic reported from Seine-St.-Denis, France, speaking with teachers and students at a school at the heart of France’s protests.

When students at Paul Éluard, a high school in a working-class suburb north of Paris, arrived for the first day of school, they found classrooms lacking chairs, tables and reliable electricity, students and teachers said. With the school under renovation, students were being taught instead in prefabricated buildings with bad insulation, filthy toilets and regular power outages, they said.

Then came the staffing shortage. Two mathematics professors were moved to another school, leaving no one to cover their classes for over a week. There were no replacements for the school’s absent psychologist or careers adviser, they said, and there was only a single part-time nurse to provide on-site medical care to roughly 2,000 students.

“It was a completely chaotic way to welcome students,” said Irène Cailleteau, a mathematics teacher at Paul Éluard since 2020. “It was an extremely difficult way to start the year.”

Those are among the frustrations that have fueled a surge of student protests since late September, both at Paul Éluard — one of the wellsprings of the unrest — and at hundreds of high schools across France.

Thousands of students, sometimes backed by teachers like Ms. Cailleteau, have blockaded their schools to protest widespread teacher shortages, creaking school infrastructure and grueling schedules — and to demand an overhaul of the national system that allocates places in higher education programs.

The movement, which was bolstered on Tuesday by union-led rallies in more than 40 French cities, has divided the country and inflamed political tensions, particularly after many demonstrations descended into violence. Some protesters have shot off mortar-style fireworks, burned public buildings and looted shops, while rights groups and jurists have accused the police of disproportionate force. In just over two weeks, more than 6,500 people have been arrested, and more than 750 police officers, as well as roughly 300 students and staff members, have been injured, according to French officials.

At the demonstrations at Paul Éluard, footage showed largely peaceful protesters, disrupted by some participants who pulled down part of the school fence and set fires in the street outside. That led the authorities in late September to order the school’s closure, ban protests in front of it and arrest several students.

The school’s principal and the local branch of the Education Ministry declined to comment on the accounts in this article. The office of the regional president, Valérie Pécresse, said that her administration had recently invested about $50 million to improve the school, which is among more than 50 in the area, a suburb called Seine-St.-Denis, that has been newly renovated.

To students and teachers at Paul Éluard, that investment doesn’t do enough to reverse decades of neglect, both at the school and in the wider district.

In Seine-St.-Denis, a sprawling area with a large immigrant community, the unemployment and poverty rates far exceed the national average. That inequity is mirrored in the district’s education system: 61 percent of middle and high schools in Seine-St.-Denis and its neighboring areas had a missing teacher at the start of the year, according to a survey by a major labor union of more than 1,000 French schools. That was eight points higher than the national average.

“The problem is national, but it’s three times as bad in the suburbs,” said Bilel Narjissi, a senior at Paul Éluard and a member of the school’s student council.

Recent students and teachers at Paul Éluard said classes had spent an entire school year without a professor in some subjects, including philosophy, which heavily affected students’ preparation for their senior exams.

France’s education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Tuesday that the number of teaching vacancies had fallen by more than half over the past year.

But students said they had yet to feel meaningful change.

Zakarya Boukhadda, a 16-year-old at Paul Éluard, said at a rally this week that there weren’t enough special educators at the school, especially “for students with neurodivergent conditions or autism like myself.”

Paul Éluard, founded in 1965, was named for a French writer whose poem “Liberté” became a widely read ode to freedom during World War II.

Over time, the school bearing his name became synonymous with decline.

In May 2023, staff members created a social media account comparing the high school to the Titanic. Pictures and videos showed cracked and crumbling walls, leaking or collapsed ceilings, and flooded floors. Those conditions were also described in interviews with former and current students, who recalled rats scouring the hallways.

In late 2024, regional officials reported finding parts of the school in a state of disrepair, warning of fire doors that had been wedged shut, a blocked emergency exit and signs of vandalism.

Ms. Pécresse’s office said that the regional government had tried to resolve the structural problems at the school, including by waterproofing its buildings, adding fire doors and providing more security, as well as investing the $50 million, about 45 million euros, which would go toward “a comprehensive transformation of the entire site.”

But to the students and their supporters, those additions are too little too late and have left students cooped up in substandard temporary buildings while the renovation goes on.

Bally Bagayoko, a far-left local mayor, told journalists at a rally on Sunday that the regional council’s response was “contemptuous.”

“They say, ‘We’re giving you 45 million,’” said Mr. Bagayoko, who has often joined demonstrations in solidarity with the students. “That means, ‘Be satisfied with what we’re giving you, be happy that we’re giving you anything at all,’” he added

Mr. Bagayoko, 53, grew up in the area and recalled studying in badly insulated buildings when he was a student himself.

“How many times did I sit in a classroom where there was so much construction going on?” he asked. “We were sitting there in our coats because we were freezing our butts off,” he added. “That’s why it’s unbearable to see those who have the power to act pretending that they’re just now discovering this.”

Ms. Pécresse has dismissed Mr. Bagayoko as a rabble-rouser, pledging on social media to send him “the bill for the 100,000-euro replacement of the gate at Paul Éluard High School.”

“Let the mayor take responsibility for his actions,” she added. “I’ve taken responsibility for mine: a complete renovation of the high school.”

For some at Paul Éluard, the conditions at the schools compound the perception that the national leaders care little for the area or its alienated and underprivileged residents, many of whose families come from France’s former colonies in Africa.

“They simply don’t care about us,” said Zorah Adrachi, 19, who graduated from Paul Éluard in the summer hoping to study psychology or train as a teacher. Despite passing her senior exams, an achievement that generally guarantees entry to university, Ms. Adrachi is among thousands of young high school graduates who have not been offered a place on a higher education program, leaving her in limbo.

Mr. Narjissi, the student council member, who wore the French tricolor on the collar of his woolen coat, said he would not give up the fight for better learning conditions.

“Maybe our parents didn’t dare pursue executive careers or positions of responsibility,” he said. “But tomorrow we’ll be the members of Parliament, we’ll be the mayors, and we’ll keep going and we won’t give up.”

Ségolène Le Stradic a reporter and researcher for The Times, based in Paris.

The Big Questions About Jeffrey Epstein: What The Times Has Learned

The New York Times October 05, 2026

The Epstein Files

Advertisement

Supported by

By The New York Times

More than 60 Times journalists have delved into the life of the sexual predator whose secrets spurred an international reckoning over money, power and complicity. Leer en español

Few, if any, figures in recent history have caused as much legal, political, financial and reputational upheaval as Jeffrey Epstein. A convicted sex offender, Mr. Epstein was connected to many of the world’s richest and most influential people and institutions. He died in prison in 2019.

The public fascination with Mr. Epstein intensified after President Trump initially refused to release federal investigative records after pledging to do so. In late 2025 and early 2026, Congress and the Justice Department did release millions of pages of documents related to Mr. Epstein that have helped answer questions, though many mysteries remain.

The New York Times has been investigating Mr. Epstein’s finances, enablers and possible co-conspirators since his arrest on federal sex-trafficking charges in 2019. Based on our continuing reporting, here is what we know.

The most recent revelations about Mr. Epstein include:

Karyna Shuliak, 37, stands to inherit as much as $100 million from his estate, according to files released by federal authorities. A native of Belarus who met Mr. Epstein when she was 21, Ms. Shuliak has not been identified as one of his victims nor was she seen by federal authorities as a co-conspirator in his sex trafficking. He helped her in many ways, including her attaining U. S. citizenship and getting her into dental school.

He grew up in an insular world, in Sea Gate, in Coney Island, which was then a mostly working- and middle-class Jewish refuge. The picture of his boyhood we found contains the fuzzy outlines of his future self: From a young age, Epstein preferred the protective company of a tight group of brainy boys and fixated on girls. Was a monster hiding in plain sight?

The brother and sister-in-law of Virginia Giuffre, one of Mr. Epstein’s most prominent victims, are featured in an ad targeting Representative Jeff Crank, a House Republican who is facing a tough re-election race in Colorado. The ad, released by his Democratic challenger Jessica Killin on Oct. 5, criticizes him for blocking the release of federal files related to Mr. Epstein and accuses him of refusing to meet with the relatives of Ms. Giuffre, who died by suicide last year. A Times analysis identified at least 35 congressional races with TV or digital ads that mentioned “Epstein” since January 2026. Many featured candidates running against what they called the “Epstein class.”

The House in September unanimously agreed to hold the billionaire investor Leon Black in criminal contempt of Congress after he refused to appear for a deposition and turn over documents to a key panel investigating Mr. Epstein, a longtime friend of his. It amounts to an official recommendation that the Justice Department bring federal charges against Mr. Black.

Links to all of our coverage can be found here.

Mr. Epstein has been accused by prosecutors and victims of raping, abusing and trafficking girls and young women. It was a vast, yearslong operation that involved:

In the mid-2000s, federal and state authorities identified more than a dozen such teenage girls in Florida. In many cases, Mr. Epstein’s longtime companion Ghislaine Maxwell recruited them under the pretense that they would be masseuses for a wealthy man at his mansion in Palm Beach.

Federal prosecutors later accused Mr. Epstein of abusing and trafficking dozens of girls at his townhouse in Manhattan, as well as in Palm Beach, from at least 2002 to 2005. He lured some by posing as a talent scout for Victoria’s Secret.

After he served time in a Florida jail for soliciting prostitution from a minor, Mr. Epstein appears to have shifted focus from underage victims to young women. He was often surrounded by aspiring models from Russia and Eastern Europe, some of whom later said they felt trapped under his control.

Some have accused several of those friends and associates of rape, though the men deny it.

They have accused him of raping or abusing them, including when they were girls — allegations that in some cases date to the early 1990s. At least one of those women, Virginia Giuffre, has died by suicide.

The federal government repeatedly missed opportunities to fully investigate or charge Mr. Epstein, until 2019. The missteps and lost opportunities included:

In 1996, Maria Farmer called the F. B. I. to tell the agency that Mr. Epstein had stolen nude photos of her underage sister. It ignored the tip for roughly a decade.

In 2005, the parents of a 14-year-old girl told the Palm Beach police that she had been paid to give a sexual massage to Mr. Epstein. That set off a state and federal investigation. While the authorities identified dozens of underage victims, the Justice Department — including the U. S. attorney for southern Florida at the time, Alexander Acosta — negotiated a deal: Mr. Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to soliciting prostitution from just one minor.

The agreement also shielded any “potential co-conspirators,” including his female assistants, from prosecution. Though Mr. Epstein served his sentence in the county stockade, he was allowed to spend much of his jail time working from his office.

After being released early from his 18-month sentence, Mr. Epstein was welcomed back into elite society, attending parties, hosting dinners and continuing to do business with major financial institutions.

In the 2010s, a number of federal agencies, including the Drug Enforcement Administration, investigated Mr. Epstein, but he wasn’t charged.

In 2016, lawyers for some of Mr. Epstein’s victims urged federal prosecutors in New York to investigate him for sex trafficking. The prosecutors chose not to.

It wasn’t until 2018, after the newspaper wrote a series about the 2008 deal in Florida, that federal prosecutors in New York opened a criminal investigation. It culminated in Mr. Epstein’s being charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

Mr. Epstein amassed a nine-figure fortune through scams, fraud and the careful cultivation of billionaires and banks. His financial success involved:

Mr. Epstein’s first big break was landing a job at Bear Stearns in 1976. He eventually resigned after being caught improperly lending money to a client and violating rules around stock offerings, but he used the connections he forged there to jump-start his career as a financial trickster.

In the 1980s, Mr. Epstein, claiming to be a financial savant, engaged in a series of escalating scams.

In the late 1980s, a mutual acquaintance introduced him to Leslie Wexner, who ran the two retail companies. Mr. Wexner entrusted Mr. Epstein with full control over his finances before cutting ties with him around 2007. Mr. Wexner later said Mr. Epstein stole more than $100 million from him.

In 2012, Mr. Epstein began working for his longtime friend Leon Black, the co-founder of the private equity firm Apollo Global Management who said the money was for tax and estate planning work. Mr. Epstein also introduced Mr. Black to young women.

From the late 1990s through 2013, JPMorgan Chase, arguably the world’s most prestigious bank, serviced Mr. Epstein, despite employees’ concerns about his potential money laundering. In 2013, he switched to Deutsche Bank, which also ignored repeated red flags.

The combination of great wealth and a reputation for seeming to know everyone enabled Mr. Epstein to insinuate himself into the lives of important people in politics, business, the arts and academia. His strategy entailed:

As his fortune grew, Mr. Epstein made big donations to prestigious universities like Harvard and to individual scientists. The money led Nobel laureates and other leading intellectual figures to regularly socialize with and seek favor from him, and their presence helped grow his circle of influence.

Some of the doctors and others bent or broke the ethical rules of their profession, which allowed Mr. Epstein to offer perks to other acquaintances, like access to premier medical care, investment opportunities with hedge funds or a potential edge in school admissions.

Mr. Epstein’s vast Manhattan townhouse became the venue for regular dinner salons for an eclectic mix of artists, scientists, intellectuals, lawyers and businessmen. Visitors were greeted with photo arrays exhibiting Mr. Epstein’s ties to the ruling class.

One of his most valuable connections was to the former president. The relationship helped catapult Mr. Epstein into the public spotlight and secure his image as a whisperer to the rich and powerful.

Mr. Epstein also boasted extensive Wall Street connections to C. E. O. s (like James Cayne and Jes Staley); investment tycoons (like Glenn Dubin and Mr. Black); and powerful lawyers, like Brad Karp and Kathy Ruemmler. A secretive law firm would later try, and fail, to fix Ms. Ruemmler’s image. Ms Ruemmler told a House committee in July that Mr. Epstein “was a masterful liar.”

He had a long friendship with Stephen Hanson, a New York City restaurant mogul who performed an array of tasks for Mr. Epstein, including arranging jobs, visas and entertainment for women. And he collected high-profile friends and associates overseas, including Prince Andrew, the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak and top Norwegian politicians.

Bill Gates, the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist, told a congressional committee in June that Mr. Epstein exploited information about his extramarital affairs “to pressure me to re-engage with him” after Mr. Gates had begun to sever ties with him.

Mr. Epstein was friends with Mr. Trump long before he became president, and he developed a relationship with Mr. Clinton during his time in the White House. Those relationships involved:

The two men became good friends in the late 1980s, hanging out together at casinos, Mr. Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate and other venues. A note and sexually suggestive drawing containing what appeared to be Mr. Trump’s signature was included in a 2003 book for Mr. Epstein’s birthday. Mr. Trump has denied writing the note.

Some of Mr. Epstein’s victims, including Ms. Giuffre, were recruited by Ms. Maxwell from Mr. Trump’s Florida club and residence, where Ms. Giuffre worked as a spa attendant. Mr. Trump said last year that he cut ties with Mr. Epstein in the early 2000s because he “stole” his female employees, although the relationship also deteriorated when the men fought over a piece of Florida real estate.

Shortly after Mr. Clinton was sworn in as president, Mr. Epstein made his first visit. Visitor logs show that he came back numerous times during Mr. Clinton’s first term, though it is unclear how often he met the president. In 1995, Mr. Clinton wrote a get-well-soon note to Mr. Epstein’s mother on a Post-it.

In 2002, after Mr. Clinton left the White House, Mr. Epstein flew him and others to several African countries. The trip was one of the first times that Mr. Epstein attracted significant media attention.

Mr. Epstein’s New York mansion showcased photos of him with each of them. When Mr. Trump became president, Mr. Epstein at times presented himself as someone who had inside knowledge about the administration, though it was most likely an act. Both Mr. Trump and Mr. Clinton have said they knew nothing about Mr. Epstein’s criminal activity.

Behind the scenes, the Epstein crisis was paralyzing the Trump administration to a far greater extent than the public knew. In their public statements, Trump’s advisers were full of bravado, dismissing the crisis. In reality, it was consuming the highest ranks of the administration.

Mr. Epstein’s inner circle and the financiers and banks that enabled him faced allegations of wrongdoing. But U. S. prosecutors charged only one person other than Mr. Epstein. The legal trail included:

She is the only person other than Mr. Epstein to face criminal charges in the United States. In 2021, she was sentenced to 20 years in prison. Some Republicans have expressed support for the idea that President Trump would pardon her.

In the months after Mr. Epstein’s death, federal authorities investigated a number of Mr. Epstein’s former personal assistants, who were accused by some victims of participating in his sex-trafficking operation. Prosecutors considered charging at least one, but they ultimately opted not to, perhaps because she said she was also one of Mr. Epstein’s victims.

Federal prosecutors apparently didn’t interview or subpoena Mr. Wexner, Mr. Black and Mr. Epstein’s longtime accountant Richard Kahn and lawyer Darren Indyke. A federal document described Mr. Wexner as a co-conspirator, though his spokesman denied that the government ever considered him one.

But the House Oversight Committee issued subpoenas to Mr. Black in June, and in September, held him in criminal contempt of Congress over not responding — a move that amounts to an official recommendation that the Justice Department bring federal charges against Mr. Black.

Federal authorities interviewed women who accused Mr. Black and Mr. Staley, a former top JPMorgan executive, of sexual misconduct — allegations that both men deny. Prosecutors relayed those accusations to officials in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which did not bring charges.

As part of their investigations into Mr. Epstein, federal prosecutors subpoenaed the two banks that provided him with the greatest financial support, JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank. The prosecutors appeared to have quickly decided against charging either institution with wrongdoing.

Police departments and prosecutors in some other countries recently have taken a more aggressive approach. In Britain, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former prince, and Peter Mandelson, a former top government official, have been arrested in connection with Epstein investigations. Neither has been charged.

We are tracking that fallout here.

Mr. Epstein spent 36 days at the now-shuttered Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City before he was found dead in his cell on Aug. 10, 2019. The medical examiner ruled his death a suicide.

For the most in-depth investigation yet into his death, we consulted tens of thousands of pages of newly released documents, obtained Mr. Epstein’s own notes handwritten in jail — never before made public — and interviewed dozens of people related to the case. We found abundant evidence that for weeks before his death, Mr. Epstein had written about and discussed the idea of suicide and attempted it at least once, and possibly three times.

The circumstances around his death include:

Mr. Epstein was found unresponsive with a cloth tied around his neck in his cell two and a half weeks before his death. He denied trying to take his own life, but he was psychologically evaluated and placed on suicide watch for barely a day.

The cellmate, Nicholas Tartaglione, said the note was written by Mr. Epstein. It was sealed by a federal court for years. The Times successfully petitioned the court to unseal the note in May 2026. It has not been authenticated but bears similarities to known writings by Mr. Epstein.

As one of the highest-profile federal inmates, Mr. Epstein was supposed to be under close supervision and to have a cellmate. But he was left alone in a cell on the evening of Aug. 9, 2019. Other inmates reported to jail authorities that he was despondent.

Guards were supposed to make regular rounds to check on prisoners. But on Mr. Epstein’s last night, the two guards on duty in his area stayed by their desks. The guards were criminally charged, but the charges were withdrawn as part of a deferred prosecution agreement.

Mr. Epstein was found unconscious early on the morning of Aug. 10 with a strip of orange bedding cinched around his neck. He was soon pronounced dead, in what was later ruled a suicide.

From virtually the moment his death was announced, there have been doubts and unfounded speculation about the circumstances. His brother, Mark Epstein, is among those who don’t believe he killed himself. The Department of Justice re-examined the death in 2023 and found no evidence of a conspiracy or criminality.

The phrase usually refers to the millions of Epstein investigation documents that Congress directed the Justice Department to release. But there have been more. Over the years, all three branches of the U. S. government have released records, and media outlets, including The Times, have obtained documents through leaks or public records requests. The materials include:

In August 2019, a federal appeals court unsealed one of the first main caches of Epstein-related files, part of a defamation lawsuit brought against Ms. Maxwell by Ms. Giuffre, one of Mr. Epstein’s most outspoken victims. The files included depositions, photos, flight logs and other materials that gave the public a powerful glimpse into Mr. Epstein’s crimes and network. The morning after the files were unsealed, he was found dead in his jail cell.

The trove of documents dribbled into public view in 2023 during a court fight between the U. S. Virgin Islands and the bank. Those files showed the chummy relationships between Mr. Epstein and senior bank executives.

In 2025, The Times obtained thousands of Mr. Epstein’s photos and documents, which showed the inside of his Upper East Side mansion — including surveillance cameras in his bedroom area — and some of his correspondence with men like Woody Allen and Mr. Black.

Bloomberg News published several articles based on thousands of emails from Mr. Epstein’s Yahoo account. Those emails and others were later posted for public perusal on a site called Jmail.

After taking office in 2025, Mr. Trump backtracked on his earlier pledges to release the government’s files on Mr. Epstein. That led to a political uproar. Congress then passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which required the administration to release its files. In December and January, the Justice Department released millions of pages of records.

The Justice Department said it decided not to release many other records, because they would identify victims or could jeopardize ongoing federal investigations. Other documents appeared to simply be missing. That has stoked speculation about a possible coverup.

The Justice Department blacked out the names of some government lawyers or potential co-conspirators. It failed to protect victims’ names and included nude photos of potential victims. The Justice Department’s internal watchdog is now investigating whether the department’s disclosures followed the law.

Elon Musk’s America PAC Is Quietly Funding November’s Most Consequential Elections

Wired October 07, 2026

Elon Musk’s America PAC is focusing its war chest on the most consequential Senate races this midterm cycle—and doing so by financing attack ads on Democrats, as voters nationwide sour on the Trump administration’s agenda.

The trend of political parties and outside groups focusing on trashing their opponents is not a new phenomenon. But America PAC's approach has been unusual: for every dollar it has spent supporting GOP Senate candidates, it has spent almost three dollars attacking Democrats.

To monitor America PAC's spending ​on digital ads and mailers this cycle, our ace team at WIRED has created a live tracker that updates daily and highlights where Musk's political contributions are heading as we enter the waning years of Trump’s second term.

The political stakes are especially high for Republicans this midterms cycle because of the possibility of Democrats taking the majority in the US Senate, should the party flip four battleground races and retain three of the Senate seats it currently holds.

For Musk, the implications of a Democratic-controlled Senate would also be far-reaching, as he personally could become the target of congressional investigations, while his companies might be affected by bills related to tech and AI regulation.

For the critical Texas Senate race, America PAC has poured more than $9.4 million into ads opposing Democratic candidate James Talarico and roughly $1.8 million into ads backing Republican candidate and ​state ​attorney ​general Ken Paxton​.

The lopsided spending here is perhaps the least surprising of all of the close Senate contests. ​Paxton comes with so much personal baggage—from facing impeachment charges that were eventually dropped to having his wife (who has since endorsed him with an ad that doesn’t mention him by name) file for divorce on “biblical grounds”—that trying to boost him with ads highlighting his background is tough.

Republicans in Texas also cannot realistically do positive ads of President Donald Trump and Paxton together, since both men have terrible approval ratings.

The largest single expenditures by America PAC have been two $1.3 million digital media buys opposing Talarico. America PAC has not put any money into television ads, which is being handled by other groups, like MAGA Inc., the Trump-affiliated super PAC.

Meanwhile, the Senate Republican Conference–affiliated Texas PAC has so far booked the lion's share of television ads. Punchbowl News reported last month that Texas PAC has booked around $120 million and was looking to buy $100 million in ad slots before November 3.

In Ohio’s Senate race, America PAC has spent $3.3 million against Democrat Sherrod Brown compared to $1.6 million supporting Republican candidate Jon Husted.

Husted has been struggling to distance himself from supporting data centers at a time when voters in the state have become fed up with rising costs associated with the projects. Husted has been tagged as "the face of data centers" because of a planned Nvidia data center project in Ohio that will be leased by OpenAI, and for his past support for data centers when he served in the state government.

The effort by Brown to cast Husted as the champion of data centers has in fact been so effective that a memo by the Senate Republicans' campaign arm in August said it was tying an anchor around the neck of Husted's public polling.

At a rally this week in Ohio, despite the cratering public support for data centers, Trump could not help himself and declared to the crowd: “We want them.” Husted’s campaign quickly replied that it should be a “local decision.”

In Iowa, America PAC has spent $1.5 million hitting Democratic candidate Josh Turek, while only spending roughly $100,000 supporting the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson—the biggest disparity, according to the WIRED tracker.

To put that another way: To date, Musk's political operation has spent a staggering 14 times more attacking Turek than supporting Hinson.

This could be because Hinson has taken great pains to distance herself from Trump's agenda. She recently called on Trump to ban diesel exports and end the Iran war (after previously voting six times against the House resolution to end the conflict), after Turek called for both of those measures.

To illustrate the upside-down nature of this race, Hinson recently launched attack ads against Turek, accusing him without evidence of having “received tens of millions in support from men in the Epstein files,” a remarkable situation given that Trump has sought to tamp down any mention of the files because of the negative blowback on him personally.

Once again, pro-Republican ads are likely not helpful when the candidate is trying to run a race apart from Trump and is barely ahead in the polls in what should be a safe Republican seat. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, Hinson was just one single, solitary point ahead of Turek.

The Science Behind the Nobel-Winning Technology That Controls Neurons With Light

Wired October 07, 2026

The Karolinska Institute awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine to researchers Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin, and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg. Their discoveries led to the development of optogenetics, a technique where scientists can turn individual nerve cells on or off using beams of light.

According to Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Medicine, “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of.” No other technique allows for such precise study of a living brain, helping researchers better understand the functions of our nervous systems as well as various neurological diseases and disorders.

But this prize is not just a celebration of neuroscience. It also serves as a triumphant example of what can happen when different disciplines of biology converge, as the findings that served as the basis for the development of optogenetics emerged from research in microbiology.

At the end of the last century, Peter Hegemann began a series of studies to understand how the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas is able to detect and react to light. Previous research documented that Chlamydomonas has an “eye spot,” a small orange dot on its surface that contains a light-sensing molecule called retinal.

Hegemann used tiny electrodes to measure the electrical signals generated by the alga and to expand our understanding of this structure’s rapid response. The scientist discovered that the organism was capable of producing an electrical impulse about 0.5 milliseconds after receiving light. This response time is 20 times faster than that of the human eye, whose light detection process takes at least 10 milliseconds.

Hegemann suggested that light detection in the alga must be the result of a much simpler process than that identified in the human eye. In the early 1990s, he proposed that the eye spots contained a protein that both detected the light and responded to it, likely opening as a channel to let ions through. At the time, this hypothesis sparked controversy. Many ion channels had been documented up to that point, but none could respond to light on their own.

To test his theory, the scientist attempted to isolate the light-sensitive proteins from the eye spot. However, when removed from their natural environment, these proteins became unstable. Later, a group of Japanese researchers sequenced the complete DNA of Chlamydomonas, which allowed Hegemann’s team to identify two genes that would create proteins with the expected characteristics of a possible light-sensing channel.

Georg Nagel took the next step of verifying the function of the genes. He introduced copies of each of the identified genes separately into different groups of frog eggs. The eggs began to produce the corresponding proteins, which eventually localized to the cell membranes. Nagel then turned on the lights.

Both proteins functioned as ion channels that opened when exposed to light. He named the genes channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2. Further experiments showed the protein produced by this second gene—called ChR2 for short—opened especially quickly, the flow of ions occurring in just 0.2 milliseconds. It explained the extraordinary speed of the light reaction originally observed in Chlamydomonas.

When the researchers introduced the gene into mammalian cells—which do not normally respond to light—the cells generated an electrical signal when illuminated. This is what got the neuroscientists particularly excited.

Ion channels are important across many types of cells, but they do some especially heavy lifting in our nervous systems. The electrical impulses that neurons use to communicate with one another, as well as other tissues in our body, are mediated by the flow of ions in and out of the cell. If you can control the ion channels, you can control the neuron.

This is where Karl Deisseroth comes in. Deisseroth was searching for a method that would allow him to toggle the activity of specific nerve cells in a living brain. In his view, this tool could expand our understanding of brain functions and open new avenues for treating conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.

Following the discovery of ChR2, he asked Nagel for the DNA sequence so he could introduce it into rat nerve cells. The neurons, growing in dishes, produced ChR2 and, when illuminated with blue light, reacted immediately—sending an electrical impulse that propagated to other neurons. This result, obtained in 2005, was decisive in establishing ChR2 as a tool for neuroscience.

In the following years, Deisseroth, Hegemann, and Nagel collaborated to identify other proteins capable of activating or deactivating neurons using different wavelengths of light. With this toolkit, researchers can now design experiments where one group of neurons is turned on by one wavelength of light and another set of neurons is controlled by a different wavelength.

The term optogenetics was coined in 2006 and has since been implemented in a variety of studies. “Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment,” the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute stated in a press release.

The Best Prime Day Pet Deals to Shop Before the Sale Ends Tonight

Wired October 07, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Amazon Prime Day now happens several times a year, including Prime Big Deal Days, which end tonight. This sales event is the best time for pet parents to snag an otherwise expensive automatic litter box or pet camera for much less money before prices dip again before Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales.

As the Reviews team’s pet tech reviewer, I’ve tested many great pet gadgets, as well as many that don’t live up to their promises. I’ve scoured Amazon to find the best discounts on WIRED-tested pet tech that I think is actually worth buying during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days. Want more Amazon Prime Day deals? Read our Absolute Best Prime Big Deal Days deals roundup and live blog.

Be sure to check out our related Amazon Prime Day shopping guides to ensure you’re making the most of the sales, including how to avoid scams and sketchy wares on Amazon, Amazon Prime perks you might not know about, and Amazon Prime Day tips.

The Best October Prime Day Deals to Grab Before They’re Gone

Wired October 07, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Amazon’s fall Prime Day sale—also known as Big Deal Days 2026—is live. The sale started yesterday, October 6, and runs through midnight tonight. As with all Prime Day sales, you'll need to be an Amazon Prime member to take advantage of the discounts.

It may only be October, but it's never too early to jump on that holiday gift shopping. We've combed through all the deals and found the best ones, based on our years of testing and reviewing. WIRED's picks for the best Prime Day deals only include products someone from our team has personally tested and reviewed. We track prices using several tools to avoid falling for fake discounts. There are no shoddy knockoffs or overpriced products among our recommendations, just good deals on great gear.
