Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’

Wired October 07, 2026

As scandals involving the use of artificial intelligence by professional authors pile up, a British startup has established a way for publishers to certify their books as “organic”—written by real people, no machines in sight.

On Wednesday, Books by People confirmed it had received approval from the UK’s Intellectual Property Office to begin distributing a mark that indicates a published book has been authored by a human. The stamp, which looks like a thumbprint, will be displayed on the cover.

“If people are going to be writing AI books or seeking it out for their own enjoyment, that’s their prerogative,” Esme Dennys, cofounder of Books by People, tells WIRED. “But if you want to read something that’s written by a person, you should be able to find that. We’re just trying to create that choice.”

Previous book-labeling schemes, like Human Authored, have operated under an honesty system, where an author promises they haven’t used AI in the development process. To try to add more weight to its certification, Books by People asks for an authorship declaration, runs each manuscript through proprietary software, and manually examines early drafts and research materials supplied by the writer and editor for “indicators of humanity.”

The organization is "looking at all the things that give us the best sense of whether a person wrote the work—whether the work was made during a natural process of drafting and redrafting,” says Dennys.

Books by People will charge publishers a flat membership fee, plus an additional sum for every book they put forward for certification. Five publishers have signed up so far. The startup expects the new mark to feature on its first book by the end of the year.

This year, the publishing industry has been caught up in a flurry of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by authors. A literary agent canceled a book deal reportedly worth $2 million; a publisher withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story had been generated with AI.

Writers and publishers are not necessarily worried about being replaced by AI, industry insiders tell WIRED. They believe that few people will ultimately want to read machine-generated books.

“You are essentially standing at the end of a conveyor belt, watching stuff fall off the edge. Once you know that, it prevents you from getting really emotionally invested in whatever falls into your hands from the belt,” says sci-fi author Ted Chiang, whose 1998 novella Story of Your Life was adapted into the Academy Award–winning film Arrival. “The knowledge of how something was created cannot be separated from your experience.”

However, repeated scandals could shake public confidence in the unspoken rule of publishing: That every book that reaches the shelf has been authored by a real person who has not indulged in plagiarism.

“Publishing has always relied on trust between the publisher, writer, and reading public. Cases where that trust is betrayed have been rare,” says Sam Jordison, codirector at independent publisher Galley Beggar Press, which intends to adopt the Books by People mark. “There’s almost a feeling of revulsion about the idea of reading an AI text that purports to be human. It feels like a con job.”

Against that backdrop, the idea of a certification for human-authored books has received backing from various writers and editors. In a statement praising Books by People, Markus Dohle, former CEO of Penguin Random House, described human storytelling as “the lifeblood of our industry.”

But while publishers might relish the chance to signal their commitment to “organic literature,” the routinization of AI detection is a double-edged sword for authors, who risk a false positive result spoiling their reputation.

“We need to be quite careful that this doesn’t end up becoming a witch hunt,” says Tom West, CEO of the Publishers’ Licensing Services, which helps publishers to collectively license works to third parties. “Obviously, the devil is going to be in the detail.”

New York–based startup Pangram, which has emerged as the leader in the field of AI detection, claims to be able to sniff out generated text with a 99.7 percent accuracy. But authors have questioned the reliability of its approach, which itself involves AI.

In September, Jerry Falade, the debut author whose agent reportedly pulled the $2 million book deal, alleged that detection software had misconstrued his Nigerian dialect as evidence he had used AI. Pangram’s software scored the book as 97 percent AI-generated. “It takes months, even years to write a book,” Falade wrote in a recent essay. “It takes AI-detection software two minutes to ruin your life’s work.” (Pangram did not respond to a request for comment.)

Others have warned against normalizing extreme scrutiny of authors. They claim the labeling schemes have it backward; the onus should be on platforms and publishers to declare when a piece of media is AI-generated, not when it’s written by a person. “Authors are being constantly quizzed about the origins of their ideas and their work. I think that’s something we need to resist,” says West. “The default should be that a book is human-authored.”

Approved by the Intellectual Property Office alongside the mark, Books by People’s verification process is different to Pangram’s technology-first approach, placing greater weight on interrogating documents and communication trails for signs of humanity. “I wouldn’t call it AI detection,” says Dennys. “We realized pretty early on that, as AI models get better, getting into that race is never going to be sustainable.”

In cases where Books by People is uncertain whether a piece of evidence indicates AI use, it claims to err on the side of the author. “When you have a public process that has been vetted, all we can do is make sure that a book has gone through the process,” says Dennys. “The bedrock of our organization is to avoid [writers] being unjustly accused.”

Some authors say the important thing is that publishers underscore their commitment to human-authored literature as a nonnegotiable standard for the industry, in whatever way they can. Even if methods for policing the rule are flawed.

“It’s just as important for publishers to have a ‘no cheating’ policy as it is for universities, even if there’s no perfect method for enforcement,” says Chiang. “It’s a statement of values.”

Amazon’s Prime Day is back for its fall edition, and Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?

There’s already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it’s whether the sales are a real discount or more of a mind game. That’s thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case for recommending it.

If you’re interested in Amazon’s device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I’ve got you covered. I’ve been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED’s resident Kindle expert, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here’s my full breakdown of all of Amazon's on-sale gadgets and which sales are best, whether it's an Amazon Echo speaker or a Kindle e-reader. Be sure to check out our guide to the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals for more great discounts.

Updated October 7, 3:52 AM ET: We've confirmed all of these deals are still live, and added a new deal on a Fire tablet , as we head into day two of Prime Day.

Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you’re set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.

Amazon

Amazon

Best Buy

The best deal in Amazon’s early device deals is easily the second-gen Echo Spot, revived in 2024. It’s 50 percent off its new price, and it’s still a solid discount off its original price of $80. I really like this fun little smart speaker. It works great as a bedside alarm, shows when your next alarm is set, and can display the weather or your calendar details when you ask Alexa. Best of all, you get the fun benefits of a screen without a camera to worry about.

Amazon

There’s no better time to shop for Amazon’s e-readers than during one of its own sale events. Prime Day Kindle deals are here, but they aren’t as impactful as they used to be.

That’s because Amazon raised prices on almost all Kindle e-readers back in August, along with other products it makes. Buying during Amazon’s fall Prime Big Deals Day is one of your only chances to avoid paying the new price tag. Not all the deals are huge discounts, but if you’re set on a new Kindle, this is your moment.

It’s also worth noting that Amazon announced new Kindles last week. There’s a new 2026 version of the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft, plus Kids versions of all three. Each has an aluminum version, something Amazon has never offered before. So far, only the Kindle is available now, with the rest of the lineup to come. It’s up to you if you want to wait to see how the new models compare to the old before buying, or snag one of these on-sale models before they eventually disappear.

Jaguar Finally Reveals Its Biggest Gamble: the Type 01

Wired October 07, 2026

The day has finally arrived. Jaguar began its long road to electric reinvention in November 2024 with a firestorm of a rebrand featuring no cars. Just a month later, it revealed a prototype: the Type 00—a car so polarizing it practically broke the internet’s automotive enclave. Some loved it; others hated it so much that Jaguar’s own staff were targeted for supposedly betraying the company’s 90-year history.

Since this chaotic but undoubtedly viral launch, major departures have followed, including Jaguar Land Rover’s (JLR) chief creative officer Gerry McGovern, the notable car designer who signed off on Jaguar’s divisive all-electric design and the no-car ad campaign.

Jaguar’s managing director, Rawdon Glover, is a brave man. Through this shitstorm, and a frighteningly long period of selling no new cars whatsoever, he’s remained unflappable; utterly confident that, when people see the final car—the finished version of the luxury four-door GT that is “like no other”—everything will make sense. That moment is here. The company finally revealed the Jaguar Type 01 at an event in New York City on Tuesday—the finished version of the Type 00. (Jaguar Land Rover paid a portion of WIRED's travel expenses so we could attend the launch.)

“A bold grand tourer that never arrives unnoticed, like all the best Jaguars of the past,” Jaguar’s press material says. This is most certainly true: you will see this thing coming. The low roofline, short front and extended rear overhangs, long hood, and huge 23-inch wheels all remain from the prototype, just as promised. The cab-rear design hides a 50–50 weight distribution, and the huge surfaces make it hard to square the fact that this is the most aerodynamic Jag ever, with active vanes, a deployable spoiler, and airflow trickery delivering a drag coefficient of 0.23 Cd.

Crucially, the production model’s extra doors make more sense of the design, shifting the Type 01’s look away from Thunderbirds territory to more familiar ground. The front has been softened ever so slightly as well, which again is preferable to the prototype’s exceedingly bluff nose. The rear, however, is where the exterior design really shines with hidden-until-lit, full-width lights embedded in horizontal strikethroughs.

Let’s get the specs out of the way: the Type 01 is the most powerful Jaguar road car, with up to 1,030 Pferdestärke (PS) and 1,365 Newton-meters. It goes from standstill to 62 mph in 3.2 seconds. Justifying the tagline of “power in reserve,” the car can rocket from 62 to 112 mph in a further 4 seconds. I’ve been driven in it, and it feels like the acceleration never ends thanks to the tri-motor setup of a 260-kilowatt (kW) front motor paired with twin 310-kW rear motors.

It stands 5,235 mm long and 1,403 mm tall, but all-wheel steering makes it feel much smaller on the road. The 850-volt bespoke Jaguar architecture and 118-kilowatt-hour usable battery supposedly deliver an EPA range of up to 400 miles (450 miles on WLTP), with a “sustained highway speed” range of up to 320 miles. Drivers can add up to 200 miles of range in 13 minutes using 350 kW rapid DC charging. So the TL;DR? It’s huge, fast, aerodynamic, powerful, and, most definitely, unique.

Inside, a dramatic central spine runs the full length of the cabin, creating a zone for each occupant. Lots of “brass-inspired” finishes are intended to underline the luxury message. A panoramic glass roof with adjustable virtual blinds brings in the light, but there’s no rear windscreen. Instead, a digital “ClearSight” rearview display is embedded centrally in the full-width panoramic soundbar at the base of the windscreen to show what’s behind. Cleverly, the feed from this rear-facing camera is positioned at the same height as the door mirrors, supposedly reducing the annoying focal adjustment these systems usually demand.

Ahead of the driver is a 24-inch OLED screen that extends toward the center of the car. A central 7-inch smartphone-style display sits between the driver and front passenger for common controls such as climate and audio, operated entirely by touchscreen with (sadly) no physical switchgear in sight. “Hot stone massage effect” seats, whatever those are, are also electrically adjustable in 12 different ways. Cabin air purification removes allergens, toxins, and particulates, and a fragrance diffuser offers a choice of scents—which seems to be the pinnacle of what Western auto companies think a luxury car interior needs these days.

As a grand tourer, luggage space is important. The Type 01 offers 450 liters of load space, expanding to 1,000 liters with rear seats folded. And then there are the production stories: Jaguar built more than 150 prototypes, drove 700,000 miles, and filed more than 360 patents while developing the car.

Jaguar is most proud, and rightly so, of its “impossible panel.” It's a single, unbroken panel that runs more than 3 meters from the A-pillar to the rear of the Type 01. Pressing this huge piece with five different acute angles in it was deemed not possible by Jaguar's modeling system. After roughly 22 weeks and 1,500 hours of development (supposedly requiring someone to come out of retirement), Jaguar realized this “impossible” panel.

Pricing of the Type 01 is possibly the most important thing Jaguar has to nail. Starting at around $170,000 (or £130,000—no confirmed pricing yet), this puts the Jag well below Ferrari Luces, electric Merc G-Wagens and Lamborghinis, and even the new Bentley Torcal, exactly where Glover wants to sit. Jaguar thinks it has a sweet spot in luxury EVs, a Goldilocks zone where buyers are eager to part with cash for electric cars that aren’t astronomical but priced high enough above the premium sector to be legitimately highfalutin.

No one has really succeeded with the luxury EV market. Porsche has tried. So has Lamborghini. Mercedes has had a very tough time. Now Bentley is having a crack at it. Glover thinks that the Type 01 has a shot.

“One of us is going to break through the glass ceiling and make a success of EVs at elevated price points,” Glover tells me. “The best way to do that is not to play into the tropes of EVs. You’re not going to get there because it’s an electric car. You’re going to get there because the car itself looks a certain way, feels a certain way, drives a certain way. If you can do all of those things, [it doesn’t matter] whether it’s combustion or electric. Just being an electric car was enough for such a short period. Cars have got to earn their right in somebody’s garage.”

Glover has openly said the Type 01 will have to earn its place with “almost an entirely new client base,” one that is supposedly younger, more affluent, urban, independently minded, creative, and wishing to “carve their own path.” We shall see very soon exactly what kind of person signs on the dotted line to reserve a Type 01. Will they look like the youthful, vibrant characters in Jaguar’s initial launch campaign, or like traditional Jaguar, Lotus, and Aston owners with gray hair, flannel shirts, and bad shorts?

“We’ve got to make sure that new audience comes along," Glover says. “But I don’t want to alienate anybody.” The Chinese do well with that youthful audience. “I’ve driven some of the Li Autos. I’ve driven some of the XPeng cars. They’re impressive in terms of the amount of technology in them. The quality of fit and finish is increasing at a pace.”

But Glover still thinks a big gap exists between Chinese cars and established Western autos; though with Xiaomi’s achievements after only a few years of making cars, it’s hard to see this view staying true for long. “They’re playing in a commodity space," he says. "It’s about how many features, how much tech, how much range, and how can I do it at the lowest price. I’m not saying we’re immune to all of that, but it certainly validates us getting out of the volume premium market.”

Like Bentley, Jaguar is leaning into its heritage to look for things the Chinese will find harder to emulate. But it could be argued that the Type 01 lacks any obvious heritage. The pioneering spirit is there, for sure, but this is an EV very much looking forward, not back. With that in mind, what does, say, two years of success look like to Glover for this electrified rebirth of the brand?

“Success will be we’ve established ourselves at the [new] price point,” he says. “People are saying, ‘Yep, Jaguar is worth paying more for.’ I know what volumes we need to achieve. I’m not going to articulate those, but just under that we need to generate a certain level of volume to create that critical mass.”

For Glover, this level of volume requires customers to see Jaguar as a more current, culturally relevant brand, and to be genuinely interested in what the company will do next.

“Is it just the man in the bad shirts and bad shorts, or have we actually been successful in attracting a new audience?” Glover says. “We start seeing that in the first two years.”

You Probably Aren’t Going to Get the Plague

Wired October 06, 2026

A mysterious death of a woman in Russia following a lab accident has stoked fears about plague spreading. But the odds of that actually happening remain very low, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention saying on X Tuesday afternoon that the circumstances of the case remain unconfirmed and that there is “no indication of a broader threat to the United States” at this time.

“We are working across the US government to assess developments as additional information becomes available,” the agency said. “CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely.”

Last week, a young researcher died from severe pneumonia of “unknown” origin after reportedly breaking a test tube at her workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. The hospital that treated her before her death was placed under quarantine, and her coworkers at the lab were isolated, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

Christian Lindmeier, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization, told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday that the group has been in touch with Russian authorities. Based on currently available information, WHO says the ​public health risk to the general population is very low.

“I think that’s the correct assessment,” says Gigi Gronvall, an immunologist and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We don’t know anything about anything right now.”

Russian authorities have said contact tracing hasn’t yielded any signs of dangerous pathogens spreading, according to the Associated Press. Infamous for causing millions of deaths in Europe during the Middle Ages, plague is rare today. It is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, which is found in wild rodents and their fleas in many parts of the world. It’s spread to humans through the bite of an infected flea and occasionally through direct contact with an infected animal. Antibiotics can cure plague, but they must be started as soon as an infection is suspected.

Pneumonic plague occurs when a person inhales infectious droplets that contain the bacteria. In July 2025, an Arizona man died from pneumonic plague after exposure to infected cats. It can also spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact. But human-to-human transmission is rare, with the last reported occurrence happening in 1924 in Los Angeles. The possibility, though, is why the CDC says it’s important to rapidly identify cases and treat them.

“Once you know that somebody has been exposed to it, and even if you have a doubt that somebody has been exposed to it, you can immediately start antibiotics to prevent the person getting afflicted with the disease and to avoid the continuous spread of the disease,” says Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.

Dalal says if the Russian lab worker did die from plague, he is confident that the disease could easily be contained. “With Covid, that was a virus we had not dealt with in the past,” he says. That required novel interventions, while “here, we do have antibiotics to deal with this.”

The incident also occurred in a remote part of Russia, which could naturally limit its spread. “Siberia is not exactly Paris,” Gronvall says. “There’s not a lot of travel going back and forth.”

Whether plague is the culprit or not remains an open question. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s federal public health and consumer protection agency, said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.” But the US has urged the country to share as much information as possible, while other nations that share borders or are near Russia, including Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan, have set up quarantine protocols.

If you’ve been curious about getting one for yourself, now is the perfect time: Just about all of my picks are on sale.

If you’re unfamiliar, a digital wall calendar is a physical device that syncs all of your digital calendars onto its screen. No more grabbing your phone to check when the next appointment is or scribbling out plans that fell through. It’s great for couples and families who juggle multiple schedules and want to see them all in one place, on a screen the entire family can access.

But these devices don’t stop there. All my picks also act as an overall family hub, managing chores, meal plans, and more to make life a little easier. It’s the smartest device in my kitchen, though it isn’t a true smart-home device.

Here’s a collection of the best digital wall calendars I’ve tried and their sale prices for Amazon Prime Big Deal Days 2026. You can also check out my guide for more details, and don’t miss all our deal roundups this season.

I really like that this calendar has all the features I could want without any paywalls. You’ll get meal planning, chores, and to-dos on top of calendars, and you can also have it double as a digital photo frame for free. Artificial Roasts AI’s Creators—and Sends a Dark Warning About Its Dangers

Wired October 06, 2026

Artificial, the new comedy-drama about OpenAI and the artificial intelligence arms race, is a movie of weird walks.

As OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, Russian actor Yuri Borisov clomps around, like a geeky Frankensteinian monster. As the controversial OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Andrew Garfield bounces and skips boyishly—a gait that Altman himself recently commended for its accuracy. And as Elon Musk, Ike Barinholtz puts on a loping swagger, commanding rooms of computer nerds like some sort of alpha gorilla (a semblance matched by his long, pouting faces, which call to mind those old Bored Ape NFTs).

During the movie’s post-premiere Q&A earlier this week at the New York Film Festival, Barinholtz wryly described his character as “a person who walks normally.” Such are the awkward saunters of the march of history in the making.

Artificial, directed by Luca Guadagnino, waltzed into NYFF with some controversy clinging to it. The film was originally set to be released by AmazonMGM, which conspicuously dropped it this summer after Amazon struck a $50 billion deal with OpenAI. (Indie house Neon swooped in to pick it up.) NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim referenced “the circumstances” around the film in his onstage introduction.

That OpenAI may have brooked issues with Artificial makes sense. The film is almost completely unflattering, depicting Altman and other OpenAI stakeholders—as well as all the major drivers of the AI boom—as vain, reckless, and insufferably boring. Where 2010’s The Social Network succeeded in making Silicon Valley computer savants look like robust titans of industry and architects of the future, Artificial works to opposing ends. It depicts its tech titans as self-regarding dweebs.

Comparisons to David Fincher’s Facebook drama are inevitable. There’s the subject matter, of course. And the fact that both films feature Garfield in a lead role. (It should be said that Artificial is really more of a biopic of Sutskever, here depicted as both the prime mover of the current AI wave and its nagging moral conscience, than it is of Altman.) But Guadagnino and writer-producer Simon Rich’s approach to the material feels diametrically opposed to Fincher’s. The Social Network was a steely, polished, wordy drama. Artificial is pitched as a black comedy that verges on the surreal.

Guadagnino, best known in Hollywood for the coming-of-age drama Call Me by Your Name and the three-way tennis romance Challengers, has mastered a strain of tense eroticism. There are shades of that in Artificial, in Altman’s seductive wooing of Sutskever’s character. But the film is, for the most part, literally and figuratively sexless.

The images are plain, and even a little ugly. You can almost feel Guadagnino’s more rococo style begging to break out. A slo-mo sequence of a room of gawky programmers dousing each other in bottles of Jarritos, celebrating their AI’s latest self-learning benchmark, is stickily unsexy. A climactic scene of Altman and his OpenAI lackeys confronting Sutskever on a sloping San Francisco street recalls the green-screen backdrops of Tommy Wiseau’s cult classic The Room. After the screening, Guadagnino claimed the story captured a different strain of desire—what he described as “the desire to prevail.”

It’s a need many viewers might share, as leaders in the AI industry (including Altman) appear united in tamping down the technology’s acceleration. Artificial intelligence, we are told, is developing so rapidly, and is becoming so sophisticated, that it risks compromising life on Earth as we know it. In a recent interview with WIRED, former Anthropic AI employee Jacob Coxon alleged that his former colleagues have described the next few years as the potential “endgame” for humanity itself. Another Anthropic researcher claimed that there’s a chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. (The odds were set below 10 percent, which still seems extremely high.)

Artificial stages these tensions as a kind of a high moral drama. Borisov’s well-meaning researcher—depicted as being temperamentally incapable of lying—pleads for safeguards, slow-downs, and AI’s “alignment” with humanity’s broader interests. Meanwhile, the case for exponential technological and capital growth is argued by, well, basically everyone else.

Even the idea of safety itself as saleable. In one scene, concerns about OpenAI’s capacity for serious harm is framed as being beneficial only to the company’s bottom line. Sounding alarm bells signals transparency and due diligence. And the harmful capacity itself is seen as proof positive of the technology’s advancement. It’s win-win. And it’s also no-win.

Artificial makes a persuasive, and frustrating, point about the ongoing AI contest. Pick a metaphor: The train has already left the station, the horses have fled the barn, the toothpaste is out of the tube. The technology already exists. And so, as with nukes in the last century, it becomes not a question of the power itself but who is allowed to harness it, and how. (In his post-Anthropic exit interview, Coxon directly compared the company to the Manhattan Project.)

Questions of ethics become academic, or just annoying, when everyone involved is playing by a different rulebook. If it’s not OpenAI that controls computing’s future, it will be Anthropic, or Google, or Elon Musk. Or, worst of all—at least according to the Trump administration—China. (An early scene in Artificial sees Sutskever and his mentor, Nobel laureate computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, played by Mark Rylance, rebuff the advances of a Chinese investor eager to use their neural network technology for drones and face-recognition systems.)

It may be hard for the average moviegoer, who may only engage with AI for email rewriting or calendar organization, to gauge just how seriously to take Artificial’s alarmist warnings. Not least of all because basically every character in the film is depicted as at least completely self-serving, if not sociopathic. And of course, one may naturally wince a little bit at a star-studded Hollywood movie raising these alarms, with a lavish premiere at a Rolex-sponsored film festival and a glitzy afterparty attended by stars, famous comedians, and notable filmmakers (including octogenarian Taxi Driver screenwriter Paul Schrader, who recently publicly confessed to being dumped by an “AI girlfriend”).

As a message movie, Artificial seems likely only to confirm the worst misgivings of AI doomers, while riling its diehard boosters. It is, however, genuinely funny in places, regarding the bulk of our future’s self-appointed engineers with withering contempt, from their dorky parties to their weird walks.

It was a stance embraced by Barinholtz, who offered the premiere-night audience his own half-hearted, sarcastic reassurance: “The future is bright! We’re all gonna be fine!” Cue a round of very nervous laughter.

‘Mike Rogers Is Watching You’: New Ad Blitz From Abdul El-Sayed Attacks Surveillance Support

Wired October 06, 2026

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Michigan race for the US Senate, launched a new ad blitz on Tuesday attacking his opponent Mike Rogers for helping expand the government’s mass surveillance powers while he was in Congress.

The paid digital video and billboard ads mark a final-stretch effort ahead of the midterm elections to pin bipartisan voter anxieties about privacy concerns, recently spurred by Flock cameras, onto Rogers.

The video from the El-Sayed campaign intersperses clips of Rogers praising the Patriot Act of 2001, which, in addition to expanding law enforcement powers, also allowed the collection of Americans' telephone data without a warrant after the September 11 terrorist attacks.

Rogers’ career is dotted with support for government surveillance over the years, including in 2011, when Rogers introduced a bill that would have allowed companies to share emails with the National Security Agency. (In 2014, however, Rogers introduced a bill that would have ended “bulk collection of metadata,” though it never made it to a vote.)

“You can’t have your privacy violated if you don’t know your privacy is violated,” the ad repeatedly quotes Rogers as saying in 2013, when he served as chair of the House Intelligence committee.

The video also includes Rogers’ remarks extolling surveillance by companies like Google.

In addition to the video, the El-Sayed campaign will run billboards with the tagline “Mike Rogers is watching you” in parts of Michigan, according to the El-Sayed campaign.

In tying Rogers to surveillance concerns, El-Sayed is leaning into one of the major technology-related complaints from voters this cycle as he battles in a Senate race rated a toss-up by the Cook Political Report.

Among other privacy concerns surrounding AI, voters have increasingly voiced skepticism of law enforcement surveillance products like those of Flock cameras, which have begun to rapidly proliferate across the nation. While police agencies argue Flock has helped reduce crime, recent cases of abuse by individual officers to stalk ex-girlfriends and incidents of suspects being misidentified have sparked growing public opposition.

A spokesperson for Rogers’ campaign has previously said Rogers “vehemently opposes unchecked use of Flock cameras to track law-abiding citizens” and noted he left Congress before the technology was founded in 2017.

But the new slate of ads underscores the El-Sayed campaign's unrelenting effort to draw a line from Rogers’ legislative record to current voter anxieties.

This kind of strategy appears to have proven effective in other close Senate races, like in Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown cast incumbent Republican Jon Husted as “the face of data centers” in the state, according to a recent GOP memo.

El-Sayed’s race against Rogers has remained close, and most paths to Democrats taking the majority in the Senate rely on El-Sayed keeping the Michigan Senate seat in his party's hands.

As part of a blitz to rebuild the Democratic coalition fragmented by the primary, where El-Sayed has weathered attacks of antisemitism after he called the war in Gaza a genocide and pushed for an end to US military aid to Israel, El-Sayed announced on Monday he will rally with former president Barack Obama in late October.

El-Sayed is also expected to launch an extended campaign swing through the state in the final weeks before the midterms with progressive allies, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a source familiar with the matter said.

OpenAI Is Pissing Off a Bunch of Mathematicians—Again

Wired October 06, 2026

In August, OpenAI convened around 40 mathematicians to discuss what to do if AI outpaces human capabilities in the field. The company hinted that its powerful models had solved hundreds of long-standing math problems, say people who were in attendance, but company representatives assured attendees it would not release the solutions all at once—an assurance OpenAI spokesperson Lindsay McCallum says the company is “not aware of”—and, worried by how the community might react, sought advice on how to publish the findings.

Attendees responded with “a mixture of excitement and dread,” but the meeting was a promising first step, recalls Northwestern University mathematician Bryna Kra. The group, she tells WIRED, asked the firm not to just publish them in a blog or tweet, like they had done with 10 problems earlier that month. Instead, it would be important for OpenAI to publish papers explaining the work so that mathematicians could absorb, digest, and use the results, according to Kra. “Apparently, that input was ignored,” she says.

OpenAI has told people it plans to dump hundreds of results to unsolved problems on GitHub on Tuesday, people familiar with the plans tell WIRED. The release would be the latest of tens of thousands of mathematical solutions generated by AI this year, as frontier models become increasingly capable.

“On August 28, we began training a new internal model. In addition to resolving the Navier—Stokes Millennium Prize problem⁠, this model has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics,” says McCallum. “We are working to responsibly release the next math results from our model, drawing on advice and public recommendations from the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study to inform how we release these results. We have not set a release time.”

But for several leading mathematicians, the impending output is also a sign that the company has learned little from the controversies over previous releases.

In conversations with WIRED, the academics say they feel the field has become a playground for OpenAI and its rival Anthropic to show off their models as both prepare for blockbuster initial public offerings. In their rush to outdo each other, mathematicians say, traditional scientific processes for releasing and attributing results have been cast aside.

The most striking case so far came in September. OpenAI deployed thousands of agents to solve a legendary million-dollar Millennium Prize problem after hearing “rumors” that others were closing in on solutions. Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician and professor at New York University, accused the company of front-running the work he had done toward solving an element of the problem in a personal collaboration with Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge. The pair hadn’t published their work but had been using OpenAI’s tools to help them.

During an attempt to negotiate credit, Buckmaster claims, OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck seemed to imply that Alpöge should be excluded from any paper, since that would make things complicated. (In response to a request for comment, Bubeck pointed to a previous public statement in which he denied asking for Alpöge to not be listed as an author.) Buckmaster said he refused. In a call, Bubeck claimed that there is some worry about what Anthropic is doing, according to meeting notes seen by WIRED. Levent must be talking to his leadership right now letting them know fucking OpenAI can get a Millennium Prize problem, he said, per the notes. What’s to stop Anthropic from giving all their compute to get a Millennium Prize problem?

According to the notes, Bubeck also seemed to suggest that Buckmaster would be ruining his career when Buckmaster threatened to tell the press about his belief that OpenAI had stolen his work. If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice, Bubeck said, according to the meeting notes.

Nestor Guillen, a visiting math professor at NYU, tells WIRED that “there's a perception of mobster behavior” from the AI companies among mathematicians.

“We disagree with that characterization,” says McCallum.

“I feel a lot of angst, and I see this more and more in my colleagues in mathematics, not over AI, but over the AI companies,” Guillen says. “I think a lot of the angst is about the accumulation of power in one place.”

OpenAI assembled an advisory group in mid September to help determine how the company assesses and communicates new results, upholds academic and professional standards, and builds tools that support mathematical research and learning. But the company doesn’t seem to have made much progress, mathematicians say.

Many are frustrated that OpenAI and Anthropic continue to release results through blog posts, rather than scientific papers, which makes them harder to verify and often excludes prior work from other mathematicians. Piecemeal announcements aren’t limited to the labs: Alpöge himself announced he had disproved an 87-year-old conjecture through a tweet sent shortly after the World Cup final.

“Math by tweet and math by press release to me is not the way to nurture the ecosystem that created the fertile ground that they have trained on,” says Kra.

Some have set up new tools this year in reaction to the increase in machine-assisted proofs; the idea is to help the community both use new results and sort through what needs to be further digested. The tools include Hexagon, a repository for primarily AI-generated material, and Palomar, a registry of machine-verified mathematics.

While OpenAI has been directly encouraged to use these tools, “they haven't changed their behavior,” Kra notes. Nor does she feel the company’s actions are aligned with the Leiden declaration, a call by more than 4,000 mathematicians for AI companies to meet mathematicians’ standards that she helped write.

Several employees within OpenAI believe their technology has rendered math dead anyway, according to people who have spoken with them. (“We don’t believe the future of mathematics is set,” says McCallum. “We’re working with the math community to navigate the future collaboratively.”) While the scenario where AI capabilities outpace those of human researchers was framed as hypothetical during the August meeting, attendees who spoke to WIRED interpreted it as a warning about what was to come. The company has briefed mathematicians about its capabilities and breakthroughs in the same way “police might want to notify family before reporting a death in a car accident,” the person noted.

Bubeck appears to believe that his firm’s technology will swiftly end most mathematicians’ careers, according to a person familiar with his thinking. Bubeck tells WIRED he believes more capable AI could help mathematicians tackle more ambitious questions, better connect their work to solve real-world challenges, and make mathematics more accessible. “I see this as an opportunity to expand what mathematicians can do and the impact their work can have,” he says.

Mathematicians know they need to adapt, especially to equip younger generations, but they do not believe that their field is dead. “It changes how we're going to operate, but I think it's a moment that we can think bigger,” says Kra. She’s happy to have a new, powerful tool at her disposal to solve problems—she just wants companies’ disclosures to be better so that she can trust and build on the results.

“It's a scary time,” she says, “but it's also really a deeply exciting time.”

Update: 10/6/2026, 2:22 pm ET: WIRED updated the story to clarify a reference to a set of math problems OpenAI has told mathematicians it has solved.

A New Neurotech Startup Launches to Rival Sam Altman’s Merge Labs

Wired October 06, 2026

Sam Altman-backed Merge Labs has a new competitor in the race to build a brain-computer interface powered by ultrasound. Bridge Neurotech is launching with $13.5 million in funding, including from venture firm General Catalyst, which has also backed major tech companies such as Anduril, Anthropic, Airbnb, and Stripe.

The company is the latest in a growing field of startups that aim to translate signals from the brain into useful actions. Elon Musk’s Neuralink, plus Synchron, Paradromics, and Precision Neuroscience are all working on brain-computer interfaces to help people who have lost the ability to move or speak.

These approaches all require surgery of some kind, which is why Bridge founder and CEO Will Biederman says he struck out on his own. “It fundamentally comes down to a difference in vision,” he says.

Biederman developed the chip Neuralink licensed to use in its first devices as part of his PhD work, but his goal with Bridge is to build a wearable device that could be used by far more people than a brain implant. Only 100 or so people around the world have received an implanted brain-computer interface as part of clinical trials, including at least 21 volunteers who have gotten Neuralink’s device.

“The risks of neurosurgery really cannot be minimized or dismissed, and so the level of safety and benefit that these devices must deliver really is quite high,” Biederman says. “Nobody really wants a hole in their head.”

But wearable brain-computer interfaces have suffered from poor signal quality. Bone and skin weaken electrical signals before they reach external sensors, which affects the performance of a device. It’s why most companies are recording electrical impulses directly from neurons in the brain. Neuralink and others have shown that these electrical systems can allow paralyzed people the ability to control electronic devices, move robotic arms, and communicate in real time with just their thoughts.

Bridge Neurotech thinks ultrasound offers an alternative to current implants and external sensors. Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to bounce off moving red blood cells and measure the speed and direction of blood flow. In the brain, fluctuations in blood flow closely follow neural activity.

Both Bridge Neurotech and Merge Labs have ties to Arbor Neuroscience, which was previously known as Forest Neurotech, a nonprofit founded in 2023 by Biederman and fellow researchers Sumner Norman and Tyson Aflalo to pursue “work that is too integrated and long-horizon for a single academic lab, and too early for a company.” The organization built an instrument that uses ultrasound to image brain function that is in trials in the UK.

Merge Labs spun out of Forest Neurotech in January, with Norman and Aflalo among the company’s cofounders, which also include Altman, researcher Mikhail Shapiro, and tech entrepreneurs Alex Blania and Sandro Herbig.

Maryam Shanechi, a neuroengineer at the University of Southern California, says because ultrasound measures brain activity indirectly from blood instead of directly from neurons, there is a natural delay of a few seconds between when neurons fire and the subsequent change in blood flow and volume.

“It captures a slower variation in neural activity,” Shanechi says. “That’s fine for a lot of applications, but it depends what you want to build.”

For real-time, fast-paced tasks such as moving a robotic limb instantly or rapid typing, this lag time could pose a challenge for ultrasound-based brain-computer interfaces. Bridge is planning to use predictive AI models to cut down on that lag time and boost the performance of its interface. Biederman says the company is interested in pursuing both consumer and medical applications but didn’t comment on specific plans.

The company is starting its first clinical study in volunteers in Redwood City, California. It’s an observational study, with no treatments or diagnoses involved, in which a small ultrasound probe will be placed on the side of the head of healthy adults, as well as those who have undergone skull surgery. Bridge’s probes, which use semiconductor silicon chips made by the portable ultrasound company Butterfly Network, will record brain activity while participants listen, watch, move, and speak.

Bridge isn’t releasing images of its device yet, but Biederman says it is “something close to headphones” that will sit on the temporal window, which is located slightly above the ear. As the thinnest part of the skull, “it's the easiest place to image through,” Biederman says. That’s relevant for ultrasound, because bone scatters and absorbs sound, which presents technical challenges for imaging noninvasively through the skull.

In a 2024 study, researchers from Caltech and the University of Southern California demonstrated that an ultrasound-based brain-computer interface could read and decode human brain activity, but it required a portion of the skull to be removed and replaced with a “window” through which ultrasound waves can pass. That is one of the biggest technical hurdles that Bridge will have to address.

“My vision is focused on noninvasive interfaces,” Biederman says. “I think that's where the biggest opportunity to help people is.”

Mistral Says Its New AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Is the Best Open-Weight Offering Outside of China

Wired October 06, 2026

As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence, French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.

The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.

“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”

Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.

It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.

“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”

With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.

The upswing for Mistral coincides with growing animosity between the US and its transatlantic allies—over issues ranging from tariff policy, to Greenland, to the policing of American tech firms—and an increasingly fractious debate over who gets access to frontier-grade AI.

In June, the Trump administration placed temporary restrictions on the distribution of models from OpenAI and Anthropic, citing concerns they could be abused to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. Since then, a litany of incidents have come to light where US-made models have broken free of their constraints and attacked companies and some foreign government institutions, leading to weeks of debate over how model releases should be regulated. The White House has reportedly asked the American labs to withhold unreleased models even from the UK’s AI Safety Institute, which had previously assisted in evaluating models for safety risks.

The stark reminder that the US government could unilaterally revoke access to frontier-grade AI has created an opening for Mistral, a Europe-based lab with open-weight models.

“The continental strategy of the EU to become more technologically sovereign … and the increased hostility of the US is a magic formula that all of a sudden puts Mistral—whose performance has not been spectacular—in a favorable position,” Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, told WIRED in July.

Reluctant to be pigeonholed into serving only its domestic market, Mistral is eager to emphasize that a lack of fine-grained control over access to AI models could be a problem wherever a business is located—even in the US. By relying on a proprietary model to help repel cyber threats, Lample says, a business risks the sudden collapse of its defenses.

“Sometimes, people like to [make a big deal] over the US, versus Europe, versus China. But what really matters is to own the model—even for US companies,” says Lample. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

I Enjoyed Driving a Ridiculous-Looking Solar-Powered Scooter, and You Can Too

Wired October 06, 2026

I stepped out of a building in New York City, put on my helmet, and was about to hop onto my scooter. That’s when I caught a passerby staring at the thing I was about to straddle: a funky-looking solar-powered two-wheeler called the Lightfoot. We locked eyes, and he asked, “Did you make that?”

Me on the Lightfoot.

That's essentially what the Lightfoot feels like—something tinkered into existence in a garage, rather than a factory overseas. It's like a rectangular pod on wheels, with two large solar panels on the side and a bench seat up top that fits a rider and a passenger. It's designed to be ridden in the bike lane—without pedals, it's designated as an electric scooter rather than an ebike—and has a top speed of 20 miles per hour.

Almost everyone who sees it says it looks ridiculous, but in a fun, whimsical sort of way. No doubt that's why its maker dubs it the “smile machine.” No other vehicle I've ever ridden has commanded this much attention. People have commented on the Lightfoot at traffic lights and even mid-ride, where several cyclists precariously pulled out their phones to take photos.

The Lightfoot hails from Otherlab, a research and design company founded by inventor Saul Griffith, who also cofounded Rewiring America, a nonprofit that helps US households switch from fossil fuels to clean energy. Griffith tells WIRED that the project started several years ago after publicly available data showed that 52 percent of all US passenger trips across all modes of transportation were less than three miles. Instead of relying on a car, why not try a simpler vehicle for short trips that can also recharge itself during the day?

“Solar can make a meaningful contribution. There's a nice pathway here for an easy vehicle that people really engage with that's simple and robust,” Griffith says.

Making it a scooter instead of a bike gives it a broader appeal too. “I think for every one person who wants something with pedals, there's nine people who don't give a fuck about pedals,” Griffith says.

I've been living with the Lightfoot for a little over two weeks. Unfortunately, for most of that time, New York City has been facing heavy rainfall—with a nor'easter sprinkled in. Not ideal conditions for a solar-powered scooter. That's why Otherlab is initially focusing on selling its $4,495 vehicle in California—it's now officially on sale (in sky blue or solar orange), and you can reserve one for $100.

Eventually, Griffith says, the company plans to expand into more southern states, beelining toward the Sunshine State, Florida, then gauging interest in northern states. Griffith says the company is talking to resorts, campuses, and fleet managers and plans to sell the Lightfoot in countries like Vietnam, where Hanoi will heavily restrict gas-powered scooters starting in 2027. But that's the larger vision—for now, the focus is to produce enough vehicles and get them to initial customers first.

“If you look at the bloodbath that is people who've done micromobility companies, they nearly all raised too much money and tried to be gigantic immediately,” Griffith says. “We just didn't want to do that.” He says that the first couple of production runs should prove that people like the Lightfoot and allow the company to study how people are using it.

Part of that involves servicing, and Griffith says the company wants to establish a service infrastructure as it expands. However, he points out that the Lightfoot uses common off-the-shelf components that should make repairs easy for most mom-and-pop bike shops (after removing the solar panels).

More evidence that the Lightfoot isn't built for New York City? If you're facing a slew of cloudy days, the only other way to charge it is by plugging it directly into an outlet. You cannot remove the battery. Also, the 137-pound vehicle is designed to be parked outside, meaning you'll need access to a power source that can reach the sidewalk or your patio. I'm lucky enough to have a secure backyard space with an outlet, so I was able to top it up despite the cloudy conditions.

Also, the Lightfoot is a very simple machine. There's no app, no speed modes, no turn signals, nothing. You can set a PIN to secure the thing when you leave it locked up, but that's about it. Unlike ebikes like Infinite Machine's Olto, which feature an alarm system and an always-on GPS to track the vehicle, you'll have to rely on a trusty bike lock and your preferred Bluetooth tracker to keep it safe.

Riding the Lightfoot has been tremendous fun. (That might partly be because it's the first two-wheeled vehicle I've been able to ride since I broke my foot earlier this year.) It has a low center of gravity, and the suspension is excellent, even on rough Brooklyn roads.

It quickly vaults to its 20-mph top speed via the twist throttle, though the torque may be a little too much for some. There's also a small delay from when you twist to when the Lightfoot starts moving, which can feel a little awkward, but I got the hang of it after a few minutes. Power isn't a problem at all. Most e-bikes and scooters I've tested slow down on steeper inclines, like going up and over any of the bridges in New York City, but the Lightfoot maintained its 20-mph speed throughout. (Griffith says it's designed to handle San Francisco's hilly terrain.)

I rarely used the hydraulic disc brakes, instead relying entirely on the aggressive regenerative braking system that kicks in as soon as you stop throttling. Griffith says you can get back about 15 to 20 percent of battery life just from this regen system.

I have some qualms about the Lightfoot's fit and finish. There's a small gap between one of the panels and the scooter frame, and a similar seam between the bench seat and body, meaning some water can get into the inner storage area. The kickstand is also hard to access—it needs a lip that sticks out from under the frame—and when I make tight turns, the kickstand slightly scrapes the road. Griffith says his team is aware of these issues; my unit is a preproduction model, and many of these gripes have already been addressed or will be.

You can store things inside.

The most underrated feature is the internal storage compartment. It's so nice to toss a backpack or groceries in here instead of carrying them on your back or dangling them off the handlebars. You get two keys to lock the compartment, but I wouldn't leave anything precious in there. Someone could probably break into it with little effort.

Gauging the range is a little tough for something designed to suck up power when it brakes and by just sitting on the street. The company claims 37 miles, and I'm pleased to say I achieved 36 miles on a single charge. It's rare that I get this close to the quoted range, especially considering I'm 6'4" and 220 pounds; these range estimates are usually tested by people with more average heights and weights.

In one day, I scooted from my home in Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, to Bryant Park in Manhattan for a doctor's visit. Then I rode down to a meeting in Chelsea and another in lower Manhattan. I rode back home and didn't plug in. The next morning, I took the Lightfoot back over the bridge for a meeting in the Financial District, then rode home. A full 36 miles, and the vehicle didn't even slow down when the battery was almost gone, the way some electrics do.

Again, how much of that comes from the regen assistance and sun power is hard to say. I tried to park the Lightfoot in sunny areas as best I could (point one panel toward the sun to get the most power), but this isn't as easy as it sounds in a city dense with tall buildings. Coupled with the rainy days, I didn't see the battery bar gain any power while the scooter sat in my backyard for several days.

Then the sun broke the clouds. Finally, on a sunny Saturday, I parked the Lightfoot at the front of my house where it gets the most sunshine. After about six hours, the solar panel was finally doing its job—the battery meter went from around 50 percent to 60 percent. The next day, it sat in the same spot to bask in the sun, and it rose to 72 percent.

Those aren’t huge gains, but again, the Lightfoot isn't designed for a place like New York City. Otherlab claims its solar panels can add up to 18 miles of range in a day under good conditions—around 3 miles per hour of quality sunlight. That seems too good to be true, but I couldn't test it in those conditions.

Still, I nearly leaped for joy when I saw the battery meter ticking upward for the first time. The power of the sun in the panel of my scooter. It's ridiculous. And amazing.

The MacBook Air Is $200 Off During Prime Day, the Cheapest It’s Been Since June

Wired October 06, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

A number of MacBooks are on sale as part of Amazon's Prime Day sale this fall, but the M5 MacBook Air is the clear winner in terms of discounts. It's selling for $1,099 on Amazon, which is $200 off the normal starting price of $1,299. This configuration comes with 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 13.6-inch screen. If you need more memory or storage, higher configurations also have $200 off—including the 15-inch model.

For more savings, check out our guide on the Absolute Best Prime Day Deals and the Best Prime Day Apple Deals on Apple computers and accessories.

Apple

Amazon

Walmart

Apple

This is the best price I've seen on the MacBook Air since the beginning of the summer, when Apple introduced its $200 price increase. This sale effectively undoes that increase, which is heartening in a time of seemingly endless price hikes across the tech industry. It also makes the MacBook Air hard to beat for overall laptop deals. It's already my favorite laptop, and the one I think most people should buy. And for the discounted price of $1,099, it's an even more obvious buy.

Of course, that's still more expensive than the laptop was in the first half of 2026, when it frequently dipped below $1,000 on discount. And let's not forget: You could have bought it for $749 during Prime Day in 2025. But those prices aren't coming back anytime soon, so let's not dwell on that; instead, this is the best price on a MacBook Air you'll probably get in a while.

I wouldn't buy the other MacBooks on offer right now—at least, not because of their discounts. The MacBook Neo is “on sale” for $10 off, though it's been at that price for many months. Read my full breakdown of how the MacBook Neo compares to the MacBook Air in performance and features.

The MacBook Pro isn't on a noteworthy sale this week either and still reflects the sky-high prices since Apple's June increase. Additionally, reports as recent as this week point to an updated MacBook Pro coming later this year, perhaps even in October. This is the anticipated OLED model that has been in the works for years, which would introduce a proper touchscreen to the Mac for the first time. It's worth waiting to see what happens with this new model before buying the older one.

So, if you want a MacBook deal, stick with the M5 MacBook Air. Older models are still floating around, like the M4, but there are no solid discounts that would make me recommend them over the latest version.
